en: In the Preface to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Direct Pointing*, it is stated that ten days after attaining enlightenment, the Great Awakened One, Śākyamuni, immediately preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. He did so because he regarded the afflictions inherent in the stages of sentient beings as the immovable wisdom of all Buddhas;
it was as if he were directly bestowing the throne of jewels upon the common masses. Therefore, this is not something for those of the three vehicles.
One who is able to believe with true discernment will realize that at that time, the śrāvakas present in the assembly neither saw nor heard [the transmission].
Nevertheless, when the flower was finally held up, the golden-colored dhūta alone received the entrustment of the separate transmission.

Although Ānanda succeeded him and became the Second Patriarch of India at the moment the flagpole was overturned, his awakening occurred during the occasion of the bell being struck to test for permanence. Thus, it is said:
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is also the Dharma-seal of the Chan school. Throughout past and present, those who have commented upon it have each excelled in their own strengths.
My teacher, the Venerable Tianran, while in meditative seclusion at Danxia, completed his *Direct Pointing* commentary in three months, just as the anniversary of his birth approached.

Recently, sweet dew descended upon the grove of bamboos. Now, as I receive and humbly read this, the auspicious sign of the blue lotus blossoms from the tip of the brush, and the light of the red pearl reflects from the ground of the mind.
No subtle traces remain; all vestiges have been erased. Every word is its own true color, borrowing no flowery rhetoric.
This inconceivable subtlety truly sets it far apart from the works of other masters. They all...

Each who has attained the gate of enlightenment likewise finds this so; yet, because their capacity for discernment (*jñāna*) has not been forgotten, they often allow words to obstruct the intent and cling to the medicine until it becomes a disease.
To examine the origin of this, it does not go beyond the ability to infer that the mind is non-existent and that there is a nature apart from sensory objects.

Now, that which can be inferred is delusive and lacks substance when separated from objects; this is the teaching of the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata did not say that one should seek [the nature] within the true permanence of the nature.
Is it that coming and going, delusion and awakening, birth and death are ultimately unattainable? True awakening is effortless; what fault lies with the sense faculties and their objects?
To the utmost extent, one may speak of the transformation of names while the substance remains untransformed, yet one has not yet been able to dissolve both delusion and awakening simultaneously.

If delusion and awakening are not dissolved, the constant radiance is immediately obstructed. If the false does not exist, where then is the true? To claim "awakening" in the present moment already falls into circuitous deviation.
Therefore, it is directly shown: there is not some separate "True Reality" existing prior to the objects of thought or outside of mental images.
If one claims that the discriminating mind perishes along with its objects, then there would be no non-discrimination;

yet, if consciousness were not born together with its objects, each would become a distinct entity—where then could the realms be established? Therefore, it is directly shown: this is based solely on what is [commonly] called...

Those who possess the totality of nature abandon conceptualization and yet something further remains; they do not realize that what is called "conceptualization" is necessarily non-existent once the totality of nature is abandoned.
If one is not clear about this, how can one be called a "perfectly enlightened" one? Therefore, to destroy the mind and destroy the eyes is a crime for which execution is added;

to distinguish between the correct and the inverted, to take names as realities, and to divide essence and function into superior and inferior—all these are but the analysis of views manifest before one's eyes.

Humanity and the Dharma follow one another in sequence; the realization of emptiness within emptiness is lost in sudden awakening. Through severance, that which was hidden becomes manifest, yet the proliferation of conceptual play regarding causes, conditions, and spontaneity grows ever deeper.
Only through cultivation can perfection be achieved, and thus the boundary between the Buddhas and sentient beings becomes increasingly remote.

If one could sweep away [all distinctions] simultaneously, only then would one believe that both cause and effect are illusory. Therefore, within the ocean of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), thought and deliberation are fundamentally absent. (Forty)

For nine years, he did not utter a single word. If one were to say, "This refers to the provisional," "This refers to the real," "This refers to seeing," "This refers to cultivation," "This refers to perfect interfusion," or "This refers to sequential unfolding," then as soon as it becomes a substantialized dharma, it is no longer of definitive meaning.

Even down to the passage, "The intrinsic awareness is necessarily luminous; delusion renders it a 'luminous awareness,'" how could establishing an interpretation based on the sutra not be perfectly clear? Yet, within that intrinsic awareness, one gives rise to grasping.

If the mind clarifies the capacity to produce objects, yet fails to realize that these objects come together with delusion, and thus gives rise to a mind of indifference toward enlightened awareness, then those objects will inevitably obstruct clarity.

If one fails to realize that both the true and the false must be abandoned together, it will result in both awareness and the objects of clarity being subject to error, as stated in the second part of the Tathāgata’s teaching.
How can one know that both clarity and ignorance do not exist as even a single entity within the Tathāgatagarbha? Therefore...
Furthermore, I have shown it directly for them, saying: "The clarity of awareness does not obstruct the constancy of the fundamental awakening of nature;
how could the fundamental awakening of nature harm the inherent distinctness of the clarity of awareness? For those who awaken to this principle, [delusion] can dissolve like ice on the spot.

Yet, whenever one reaches a precipice, a sense of hesitation immediately arises; this is because the sacred realm has not been relinquished and ordinary sentiments compete to arise. One must simply recognize this.

First is "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). To transmigrate through the four modes of birth is called "confused thought. To successively ascend to Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is called the "Ultimate Fruit. Both of these are external to the [true] state;
they do not accord with the primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Therefore, it is further directly shown: "If one abandons confused thought, there will necessarily be no Dry Wisdom;
likewise, if one abandons Dry Wisdom, there will necessarily be no Ultimate Fruit. Thus, taking confused thought as Dry Wisdom is like [having something that] appears to exist...
From awakening to delusion, one reaches the stage of "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-vijñāna). Yet, looking back upon one's own chaotic thoughts, one regrets not having remained in stability;
it is as if one were conceding what one lacks. Only then does one realize that delusion cannot be found. Since delusion cannot be found, what need is there for awakening?
After the Sage attained the Way, he returned to the original state of those sentient beings, wherein the dimensions of the dharma-realm were extinguished.

He manifested the body of the dharma-realm, expounded the affairs of the dharma-realm, and revealed the principles of the dharma-realm. Had they formed a holy understanding of this, they would have immediately succumbed to various delusions.

Even if one were to directly bestow the precious throne upon an ordinary person, I fear that such an ordinary person would not be fit to receive it again. Those śrāvakas sitting in the assembly did not see [this].

I have not heard of it. It is of the same profound appreciation as the breaking of the smile. How could my current explanation possibly add further thought to that which is already inconceivable within our Master’s own inconceivability?
Having finished reading the Commentary, I have thus jotted down these observations as they occurred to me.

Because the finger exists due to the moon, it is not what is grasped by the moon. If one considers the overall purport of this entire scripture, it constitutes a comprehensive treatise already transformed into a seamless celestial robe (*devadūṣya*).
All sentient beings, within this single original title, fully manifest the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*).
Upon opening this scroll, all becomes clear; there is no dust that is not cleansed. This is precisely seeking the root within the branches and tracing the source upward from the details.
It is perfectly acceptable to extend what is drawn forth as an aid for those of dull faculties. Written by the Dharma-heir Jinshi, prostrating with humble reverence.
Preface.
The Elder [Ming]yu carved his commentary on the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* with the aim of providing a direct pointer to its essential meaning; it was completed in three months.

His discourse penetrates deeply into the principle and frequently upholds the ultimate direction, truly sufficient to serve as an aid for those of superior faculties. Monastics and laypeople from near and far have thirstily yearned for the flavor of this Dharma.
The Grand Governor, Duke Fu Zhujun, subsequently donated his own funds to complete the carving of the blocks for its circulation; how easy this was!
Formerly, when the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai heard that this sutra was held in secret esteem in India, he gazed toward the west morning and night, prostrating himself with earnest devotion.
"I vow to arrive in this land soon. After more than a hundred years had passed, the śramaṇa Prajñāmitra finally brought it with him.

Because the prohibitions of his own country were strict and rigorous, he was unable to succeed several times; he therefore inscribed it on a fine white cotton cloth and hid it within the flesh of his own arm.
He traveled by sea and arrived at Suizhou (Canton). At that time, the Chancellor Fang Rong was serving as the Governor of Nanquan;

he invited [the master] to the Wind-Banner Hall of Heli Monastery to perform the translation, personally acting as the scribe. Consequently, the phrases and sentences within the sutra are all clear, fluent, and meticulously analyzed.

Master Fu had not yet met the Elder, nor had he read the commentaries on the sutras, yet he urgently desired to circulate [this work], finding joy in ensuring that the rain of the Dharma might be evenly distributed.
Is this not because he possessed a profound karmic affinity with the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s exposition of the supreme truth?

Indeed, when Bodhisattvas take the benefit of sentient beings as their primary concern, whether they approach matters from the perspective of phenomena or principles, though there may be degrees of depth, upon ultimate investigation...
The ultimate destination is originally of one essence. Formerly you governed Qingyang; now you pacify Western Guangdong.
Your discernment is transcendent and your command is swift. In every gesture, you never fall into ordinary paths.

In this assembly, as Mañjuśrī, you destroy the heterodox and assist the orthodox, selecting the perfect penetration, yet ultimately you transcend the duality of "is" and "is not. This is your spiritual capacity.
The resonance of these signs is analogous; through phenomena, the principle is revealed.

May you, Sir, together with all sentient beings of the great earth, enter the gate of perfect penetration and non-obstruction, and personally realize the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown of the head. Through the principle, phenomena are revealed:
may all who read this, together with you, give rise to the bodhicitta and manifestly perceive the thirty-two transformation bodies of Avalokiteśvara, thereby uplifting this age and its people.

If one were to ascend to the governance of the ages of Fuxi and Huangdi, then both the Dharma-methods of the Elder [Bodhidharma] and the circulation of Master Fu [Taoxuan] would be left without fault.
Residing at Danxia, I, Bianpan Tan, respectfully compose this General Treatise on the Direct Pointing to the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Danxia, Shi Tianran, Hantsi.
Before the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, there were no names for Buddhas and no names for sentient beings. This very moment is precisely the Way; it is simply that no one awakens to it.
How magnificent these words! They may truly be called "revealing the light in the midst of broad daylight"—an exclamation upon the vast and boundless.

Throughout the entire tide of existence, awakening is the very cream of clarified butter (*sarpis*), while delusion remains a lethal poison. This is why the room was closed in Mahāgama and speech was silenced at Vaiśālī.

It is not merely that the true mechanism is beyond all dependence; it is truly because the ultimate Way is difficult to express. When the seat for *bodhi* was spread, he was already about to manifest *parinirvāṇa*;
yet when his chest was opened beneath the twin trees, he further declared that not a single word had been spoken. Such is the purport of these preceding and subsequent events.

From beginning to end, the entirety is fully presented. Within the twelve divisions of the scriptures, all that is real serves as a skillful means. Throughout the three periods and five teachings, the provisional and the lesser are entirely subsumed within the wondrous and perfect.
How could the dharma-realm have any knowledge? It shares the same awakening throughout beginning and end; the light of wisdom reflects itself.
Embracing both the true and the delusory within its perfect permanence, this has been so from the time of the ancient patriarchs down to the present day.

It stirs the coming and going of the myriad spirits, yet does not share the anxieties of the sages; it exhaustively investigates the ultimate aim of the Tripitaka, yet finds that the affairs of the common people are fundamentally difficult to clarify.
Since one is inherently never deluded, when could there ever be further awakening? To point to your flickering flames as Bodhi is merely to give rise to solitary [delusion].
The Venerable One’s vision returns nirvāṇa to saṃsāra. Who can recognize the mind of Great Enlightenment? One must know that deluded circling is non-awakening;

only then will one believe that the wondrous is none other than ignorance. To unify the three periods of time within a single kṣaṇa, and to dissolve the ten directions within a single thought-moment—this is the most difficult to merge.
A single movement of thought immediately involves as many afflictions as the sands of the Ganges. Before one has even gained self-confidence, time has already shifted.
Spontaneous activity is as indistinct as the *wangxiang* (the "imageless" state). This daily life of the common person is precisely where the supreme sages direct their minds.

Whether regarding existence or non-existence, the ignorant remain outside; these are matters that leave the realized ones speechless. Movement is likewise not false, for the nature of wisdom is fundamentally clear and still from the beginning.

Where, then, does the ultimate reality reside? It is as tranquil and luminous as empty space; it is not even beyond the kalpas—how could it be said to belong to the present time? True Suchness is without...
Nature is luminous or obscure according to conditions; arising and ceasing depend upon the mind. Subject and object manifest in mutual dependence.

From the realm of the one true reality, deluded views give rise to self and other. Within the gate of illusion, mind and matter are separately established. The six sense objects press in and block; the two conditions of motion and stillness prevail.
The five aggregates solidify, and the wise and the ignorant each cling to their own views. Entering through the gateway of the eye, it is called "form."
Entering through the gateway of the ear is called "sound. The nose, tongue, body, and mind each have their own distinct functions;

yet fragrance, flavor, touch, and phenomena likewise manifest in mutual correspondence. What difference is there between the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*)? Even their differentiation is constant. This is merely the delusory realm of the self and the mind of the self;
it is, in fact, the true wisdom and true principle of the sacred spirit. Such distinctions must necessarily be realized all at once.
Sitting in the Tathāgata’s place of enlightenment, one remains forever unaware throughout one's entire life.

Who can point out the realm of worldly toil to open the eyes of the deluded masses and lead them to the same ultimate return? The continuous succession of birth and death begins with the mind of lust.

To discriminate based on false conditions arises fundamentally from the nature of seeing. This nature is originally not "seeing"; it relies upon the sense organs to manifest. The mind itself is not lust; it is obscured by form, and thus one perceives form.
The mind is darkened; when conditions arise, the mind is stirred. Within this same mind and consciousness, distinctions between superior and inferior emerge.

Because the mind harbors conceptualization, one must realize that conceptualization is itself the mind. How could there be anything temporary or permanent? Once awakening and delusion are distinguished, one knows the source from which the cycle of birth and death flows.

Are the mind and its objects not fundamentally identical? Realize that the eternally abiding nature is constant; what is seen and heard does not change. Even if one exhaustively investigates the seven locations [of the self], what is the use of mere erudition?

Furthermore, the radiance of the face shines forth, revealing that the faculties and natures are each perfectly luminous. The worlds merge and open, signifying the mutual inclusion of the body and the land in successive layers.

Body and mind are fundamentally without expansion or contraction; it is only because their essence and function seem to have obstructions to their perfection that the two kinds of roots remain unclarified.
Consequently, the perceiving subject lacks substance when separated from its objects. Therefore, before one's very eyes—
The characteristics of these perceptions can be distinguished. While the mind of darkness remains deluded, the lamp can reveal colors;
yet, that which perceives in this way is the eye, not the lamp. The eye can reveal colors; yet, this nature of seeing is the mind, not the eye.

One may then begin to believe that the fundamental mind is eternally abiding while the eyes have their periods of impairment and clarity. That which abides is called the host; that which does not abide is called a guest. It is also like space.
Fundamentally, it is tranquil and still; it is only the dust of phenomena that moves and wavers. The nature of the mind is true emptiness, yet birth and extinction follow from thought.

How can you not know that thought is the object of perception? Yet you have not yet clarified that the mind itself is necessarily indestructible. This is because you have long remained in delusion, such that the mind has become identified with conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).

By using conceptualization as the condition for the mind, the mind perishes along with the conceptualization. When one departs from conceptualization to seek the vision [of the mind], that vision reveals the conceptualization and brings it to its end. Therefore, they are distinguished.

Apart from these, the fundamental nature remains as a latent potential, awaiting its manifestation. Although it appears for a brief moment when confronted with an object, even after passing through many years, it remains as if in the present.
Observing the body’s transition and decay, one sees that every thought-moment is incessant; yet observing the river, it remains vividly as it was, no different in childhood or old age.
When facing an object, one understands it clearly without falling into discursive thought; when recollecting, it is distinct without the need for repeated study. Therefore...
Know that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings resides only before one’s eyes. To endure seeing the Tathāgata enter nirvāṇa is for it to flash into a thought-moment;

yet, because it is not reached by the power of discrimination, it points directly to immediate perception (*pratyakṣa*) at that very moment. If one turns back for even a brief instant, kalpas as vast as the universe will seem like yesterday.
Furthermore, by investigating the locus of inversion and examining the cause of its loss, one finally realizes the nature of seeing and hearing.
Deluded by form and emptiness, one cannot be said to have attained awakening; yet the mind that neither arises nor perishes still resides within the body—how can this not be delusion?
One arm is no different from another, yet each is labeled as "upside-down" or "right-side-up. When the entire tide is already mistaken, who can discuss the floating bubbles?
To fail to realize this and instead falsely presume to take charge, treating the ever-abiding ground of the mind merely as an object of awakening, is what constitutes present experience.

The sound of the Dharma is merely that which is capable of being perceived. Since the discrimination of that which perceives has no inherent nature, the mind-nature that realizes this must have something to which it returns.
How could you know that these eight kinds of distinctions all belong to the mundane world, while the essence of the eight kinds of seeing is ultimately not external to you?
The objects before you are material things; your seeing is not something else. Your awareness is not intermingled with them.

Sentient and insentient beings remain distinct and separated by their respective substrates; each is individually all-pervasive. Within this vision, how could there be a distinction between internal and external?

Nor is there any interruption or continuity. The substance of emptiness is not fixed as square or round. While the explanation of the principle is extremely detailed and clear, the words used for proof still maintain a sense of limitation.
If one points to what is realized as being correct, one must necessarily regard the cognizing faculty as incorrect. Thus, right and wrong are clearly distinguished.
Things and the self are difficult to transform. When seeking manifestation within things, one must first sever the mind that seeks awakening; this is the exhaustion of all that is not.

Furthermore, when one exhausts the consciousness that is capable of awakening, the Great Way is impartial. This is not something the Two Vehicles can deliberate upon; it is the Samādhi of abiding in itself.

One must possess great wisdom to be able to speak: the characteristics of flowers are fundamentally empty, and Bodhi is all-pervasive. Both "is" and "is not" are discarded; there is only the single Manjusri.

When both "one" and "two" have perished, wondrous awakening stands solitary and suspended. Were it not for one who has profoundly penetrated the source of the Dharma, few would not be deluded by taking this to be a divine self (*ātman*).
Furthermore, if one lingers among the four types of views, one will again mistakenly take them to be causes and conditions. This is the primary meaning.
Contemplate this: among all the various phenomena of the world, if one single illumination is brought forth, there shall be no other thing;
thus the four meanings are fulfilled. It stands far beyond light and darkness, penetration and obstruction. If you can see the seeing itself, you will suddenly realize Bodhi.

If you wish to know the source from which seeing arises through awakening, you must recognize the source from which seeing is produced. When you see the true nature of the fundamental substance, you will realize that objects are obtained through delusion.

Due to false views regarding objects, clarity and subtlety were consequently confined within the sense organs. Once the mind is known to be without delusion, the essence of vision immediately transcends the sensory dust.

"Individual karma" is a metaphor for the sense organs; "shared karma" refers to the vessel-world. Since the delusion of the organs has been cleared away, it is like the sudden disappearance of a red cataract.
Since the capacity of the vessel was originally empty, it is like a circular reflection that was never there to begin with. True wisdom is without seeing; true—

In principle, there are no defilements. From this moment forth, what the eyes see follows from the present; what is perceived depends upon the past. The lands of the ten directions are entirely wondrous and luminous;
whatever is seen and heard in their very place has never been false. Within the Tathāgata-garbha, the aggregates and sense bases are all true;

within the nature of True Suchness, the sense fields and elements are fundamentally real. Essential form is empty of self-nature, and so on, up to the awakened clarity and the true consciousness, which are inherently pervasive throughout.
Furthermore, according to what sentient beings know, from this point it is revealed that they have attained what they never had before. With confidence in the mind-essence, there is nothing external;
it does not reside within the body. Looking back, the ten realms depend upon emptiness and are contained within the mind.

There is a poignant sense of returning to the source and a profound compassion for those who share the same substance. Having already attained the Dharma-body, one hopes to eliminate subtle delusions regarding persons and dharmas.

Discriminative [afflictions] are easy to abandon, yet the latent tendencies of co-nascent [ignorance] are difficult to perceive; one must still rely on the exhortation of others to resolve shared doubts.

When purity suddenly arises, one realizes that the manifest clarity of awareness is established as delusion. As similarities and differences are perceived alternately, the conditioned existence of sentient beings is initiated.
Once the world has been formed, sentient beings undergo flux and transformation; causes and conditions encounter one another, and karmic fruits follow in succession. This occurs within awakening.

Within the arising and ceasing of clarity, it is like a mirage tossing with waves; yet within the wondrous luminosity of the fundamental nature of awareness, it is like the great void, eternally still.
To awaken to this source requires no external aid; one must simply believe that the awakened nature of sentient beings is ever thus.
How could delusion have a cause? Who would say that the world of wondrous emptiness still exists? Whether the sun shines or clouds darken, whether the wind moves or the sky clears—emptiness remains.

Emptiness is unmoving; all phenomena flow into one another. Contemplate that their nature is fundamentally real, while their appearances are fundamentally delusory. When appearances are combined with delusion, they form distinct characteristics;

when appearances are combined with nature, they are entirely real. Reality is simply wondrous, enlightened clarity—wherein everything is "not. Reality follows conditions to be omnipresent—wherein everything is "just this.
From this, it responds to the conventional and the ultimate, manifesting as ordinary beings and as sages; such is the response of Great Enlightenment.

Moved by the eternal pervasiveness of the Buddha’s compassion, [the author] reflects that all sentient beings, when they bring their thoughts to fulfillment, rely entirely upon the wondrous guidance to manifest the sound of original truth.

This breaks open the sutra scrolls within a single speck of dust, universally reflecting like the light of the ocean. Only then does one believe that wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally perfect and that delusion arises without cause;
it must cause this frantic nature to suddenly cease, so that the supreme purity is primordially pervasive. Having realized that nature is empty, one dwells no longer in birth.
Death. Awakening to dependent origination, one does not abide in nirvana. These three types of continuity remain as if within a dream;

through a single moment of cultivation, one briefly emerges from the entanglements. None of these can be attained through deliberate effort, so how much less could they be accomplished through frivolous conceptualization?
Therefore, when awakening the initial resolve, one first contemplates the ground of practice, and subsequently must carefully eliminate [delusions]. This is the arousal [of the mind].
The seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing of clarity are themselves the ultimate permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

If one can simply discern birth and death with precision, one may immediately accord with Nirvana from afar; no longer following delusion, one spontaneously becomes still and profound, like clear water appearing before one.
There is no need to wait for the removal of mud; one reaches the source directly. How could this surpass pure clarity?

It is only that within delusion, the fundamental nature is ignorant, and consciousness arises conditioned by sensory objects. After awakening, the knots must be discerned: one must track down the thief and seek out the matchmaker.

To obstruct discrimination at the initial mind and to dissolve habitual seeds through subsequent wisdom is still called "expedient means"; it does not yet constitute perfect cultivation. This is the explanation.
Sixth, the identity of the same: both adhesion and detachment revolve together. When the vessel is removed and emptiness is contemplated, the same and the different are suddenly withdrawn.

If one knows that within the wondrous perfection, the adhesion of the stillness has suddenly vanished, then the purity of the *vijñāna-indriya* (the faculty of ultimate meaning) is originally present. Darkness and light arise from seeing; through delusion and ignorance, it becomes obscured.
The faculty’s cognition is not the object; by not following after them, it is naturally liberated. How could the essence-nature of the seven types [of faculties] not be firm and solid?
It is only upon hearing the sound of the pestle that its efficacy is verified; the cognitions of the six gates are eternally wondrous—how could they be differentiated by waking or sleeping?

The wondrous nature is fundamentally pure; one should understand that delusion is merely a manifestation of this clarity. When awakening is attained, the knots of the mind should be untied; then the sense organs and their objects will be free from fault. This nature relies upon the power of purity.

Principle and practice mutually complete one another. By discerning the clarity or stagnation of the faculties and their objects, one borrows a mirror to reflect the myriad capacities of sentient beings.

Thus, one awakens to the direct and swift path within cultivation, suddenly transcending provisional teachings. All phenomena of form are gathered within the eye; those who were formerly deluded by what they saw now awaken through that very seeing.
The sounds of the ten directions are all reached by the faculty of hearing; those who are no longer obstructed by the ear return to the ear itself.

Turning back, hearing returns to awakening; the mechanism of non-abiding is suddenly transformed. When emptiness and awareness are perfectly complete, who can understand the silence manifest before them?
This is the original realization of Avalokiteśvara, through which he has attained perfect penetration. When Mañjuśrī selected the faculties, this was praised first as the most skillful means.
Selecting twenty-four sages, he points to the single gate of the three periods of time. Based on awakening and perfect cultivation, there are definitively only two [paths].

Cultivation follows awakening, while the untainted [path] has three aspects. Practice is devoid of falsehood; one cuts off the demons of craving and views. The mind is as straight as a string, becoming the ground of true causes.
Present karma is easy to control, yet one's own current conduct may be contrary; habitual tendencies from the past are difficult to eliminate. It is like...
Relying on supernatural power, the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is thus established; such empowerment depends upon another.

However, while the wondrous and subtle phrases are realized through one's own self, all Buddhas of the ten directions are born from them. For those practicing in future generations, they need not rise from their seats.
If one wishes to give rise to the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-jñāna-bhūmi), it must ultimately first proceed through gradual advancement and increase, further awaiting fulfillment.
After these fifty-five minds, one then fully realizes the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition. This serves as a broad model for practice;
to depart from this is to enter a deviant path. If one attains direct and swift awakening and clarity, it will naturally accord with right contemplation in silence.

There shall be no case where the three karmas are not purified or the six sense faculties are not cleansed, such that one may serve as a paradigm for humans and devas. Thus, these ten causes—*not*... [text ends]... [implied: ...are sufficient].

As for the six retributions, they do not intersect; how then can one avoid errors in *dhyāna*? Thus, when those of pure emotion enter the earth realms, it arises solely from a single moment’s deviation.
Likewise, even if those of pure thought ascend to heaven, one must know that when their retribution is exhausted, they will still fall.

To investigate the mind and consciousness to the furthest reaches of the Four Emptinesses (*catur-ākāśa*), yet remain dissolute and deluded, leads to rebirth in Avīci. The Buddha-nature transmigrates according to one's thoughts.
Rising and sinking are nothing other than deluded sentiments, like the turning over of one's own hands.

If you can simply recognize that they are your own original mind and do not follow after intellectual views, you will be able to accord with the nature of awakening and suddenly realize the state of the sages. Within *samādhi*, both gain and loss are utterly extinguished.

At the point where the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are exhausted, no objective realm remains. From beginning to end, proceeding from the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) into the state of a sage (*ārya*), one surveys what has been realized and finds it does not exceed the original resolve.
This is something the Dharma-eye cannot fathom; how could the celestial Māras find an opportunity?

If one merely relies on the teachings to progress in cultivation—entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through ethical discipline (*śīla*)—yet fails to achieve self-awakening in accordance with the times, one cannot avoid being reborn due to that very excellence.
When the mind clings to objects, it falls into perverse thoughts; when a single thought stirs, one is immediately seized by demons.

When birth and cessation have already ceased and the nature of consciousness manifests before you, you mistakenly take this for Bodhi and lose your true insight and vision. You then compose various treatises, failing to investigate the wondrous perfection.
Even for a Śrāvaka fixed in their nature, it is not permitted that they have seen their nature; those who attain the limited realization of a Pratyekabuddha remain far removed from Nirvāṇa.

Therefore, it does not proceed by gradual accumulation; rather, the mind opens directly. This is equivalent to passing through deep meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) one after another until consciousness is shattered, which is termed "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-jñāna*).
[In this case], one suddenly enters the Diamond [Samādhi]. That [process] proceeds from awakening to cultivation, whereas this proceeds from cultivation to awakening.

For those who cultivate toward awakening, they first practice the distributive method and subsequently achieve perfect integration (*yuanrong*); for those who awaken through cultivation, they first achieve perfect integration and subsequently practice the distributive method. Awakening—

Thus, they awaken together, yet differ in their mutual perspectives; they practice together, yet distinguish between what is difficult and what is easy. For those who achieve sudden awakening, there is the danger of conceptualizing distinctions within the Principle (*li*);
for those who engage in gradual cultivation, there is the constant fear that phenomena (*shi*) will become muddled across many divergent paths.

Therefore, the distinction in principle arises from losing the true essence of awakening, while the confusion of phenomena stems from the constant dread of following numerous byways. Thus, one realizes the nature of reality (*xing*), leaves behind worldly dust, and transcends all divisions.
Distinguishing them, one follows conditions with sovereign ease; the true mind is without delusion. Transcending right and wrong through wondrous wisdom, awakening is both precise and detailed;
cultivation should lead to perfect liberation. Practice is sealed by principle, so that the meaning of distinctions remains unimpaired;

principle is adorned by practice, so that the fundamental gate is never overstepped. As the aggregates dissolve in succession, how could they obstruct perfect interfusion? Thus, the realms are differentiated according to their causes.
It is clear that one does not sink into partial realization. The originally awakened pure mind is fundamentally free from dust and defilement;

it is only through the conceptualization of false thoughts that form and mind first appear. Form exists because of emptiness; contact is known through separation. Memory is not forgetting, and how could arising be total extinction?

Even when arising and ceasing have already revolved within the profound stillness, they enter into union and become even more manifest at the limits of consciousness. Therefore, although the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)...

Exhausted! It is difficult for the awakening mind to become perfect. Since those of the Two Vehicles have already mistakenly entered the realm of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), those with the initial resolve still erroneously equate it with the nature of form (*rūpa*).
Their realization of principle is not yet perfected; as soon as they approach the gate of liberation, they immediately turn it into an object of aversion.
With deluded attachments not yet exhausted, they boast of practices that deviate from the Way, which ultimately lead to nihilism. Although all phenomena are empty, [the delusion persists].
In the single truth, where can one dwell? The mind of the triple world has already been severed; how could current activity be confused with the innate?
Since the eyes of the thousand sages have transcended, there is no body to fear as an obstacle to phenomena. Therefore, the simultaneous pecking and hatching must return to the master craftsman.
The True Sect of Non-attachment has not yet been called noble or honored. This scripture reveals that one must first purify the consciousness-mind before reaching ultimate, perfect cultivation;
this also means discarding even "sacred understanding" (ārya-dṛṣṭi). Only when practicing among the diverse classes of beings is one permitted to share the same marketplace.
Who is not a seer? Who is not a hearer? What the eyes see is not form; what the ears hear is not sound. The entire body is the Great Function, encompassing all.
In both antiquity and the present, at this pivotal juncture, wisdom is obliterated and folly severed; objects and self are equalized beyond the kalpas.

Yet even this still belongs to the realm of following traces, and does not yet reach the true destination. To accomplish it through silence, one must not seek its outward signs; to illuminate it through the spirit, it resides in the person themselves.

Direct Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Samādhi (Concluded) The Direct Commentary on the *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa-tathāgataguhyahetu-bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā-nītārtha-sarvabodhisattva-sarvacaryā-śūraṅgama-sūtra*, Scroll One.
Compiled by the monk Tianran Hanyi of the thirty-fourth generation of the Dong lineage,
and collated by his dharma heir, the present-day monk Danguī,
who has read the current *Bianleshuo*.
*Śūraṅgama*, here translated as "Ultimate Solidity," is the name of the Great Samādhi. It is the true samādhi of intrinsic nature;
when mindfulness is tranquil, it is indestructible, devoid of temporal limits, and without entering or exiting.

In terms of its essence, it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm: vast yet without exterior, subtle enough to enter the infinitesimal gaps, transcending all marks and free from views. Therefore, it is—
The Buddha’s crown is used as a metaphor; the mark of the Buddha’s crown cannot be seen.
Speaking in terms of causes, the subtle, secret, and tranquil illumination of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions cannot be known by intellect nor recognized by consciousness.

Speaking in terms of cultivation and realization, it is the true cultivation of one's own nature, which does not fall into stages and does not rely on merit. This is what is called the definitive meaning (nītārtha), not the non-definitive.

Regarding its meaning: from the perspective of the greatness of essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*), it is called the Tathāgata; from the perspective of the greatness of function (*vṛtti-mahattva*), it is called the Bodhisattva.
When combined with the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, there is nothing that is not fully perfected in the ultimate state where cause and effect are simultaneous.

Now, although the self-nature of all sentient beings is pure, each fails to perceive it for themselves; this is precisely the non-awakening of the ordinary person. To attain [this awakening] is to obtain the Great... [text ends].
The profound fullness of the Sage: when vision is present, it is not vast—like the entire Bohai Sea confined within a floating bubble.
Because it is vast, it is not seen—like a single drop cast into a great abyss. This is the Great Uṣṇīṣa of sentient beings.

When vision is present, it is not subtle—the sounds and lights leak into the objects of cognition. When it is subtle, it is not seen; for empty space has no place from which it can be observed. This is the [Uṣṇīṣa] of all...
This is the secret cause of the Tathāgata’s birth. To see and cultivate while not yet realizing is for the dharmas before one's eyes to still persist;
to forget seeing and take that as realization is for the measure of the single truth to be withdrawn. This is the definitive meaning of the cultivation and realization of sentient beings.

When seeing and practice are not subtle, who can know that "sufficiency" is itself an obstacle to the eye? Only when subtle practice is no longer seen does one begin to believe that liberation transcends action and practice is perfected. This...
This is the Samantabhadra of myriad practices for all sentient beings. When there is seeing, it is not fixed; objects proliferate within the space between the eyes and the mind.
When there is concentration, nothing is seen; consciousness vanishes within the midst of manifold arising. This is the ultimate solidity of sentient beings.

The title of the sutra is established at the outset, reaching the ultimate point of the Tathāgata’s principles and practices regarding cause and effect, which do not transcend the self-nature purity of each sentient being.

Because there is no self-view within it, awakening is realized as perfect awakening, and cultivation is practiced as perfect cultivation. From beginning to end, one does not fall into heterodoxy or external paths.
As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "All sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment. To know that they all realize it is itself not being a sentient being;
if one is not a sentient being, then there is also no realization. What the Tathāgata does is to directly take what is present before us.

Regarding the capacity of the faculties (*indriya-gotra*): since it accords with that which is neither right nor wrong, how could it be something that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are capable of conceiving?
The first section: The Introduction. This is divided into two parts. First, the general pattern of various sūtras. This is further divided into two parts. First, the time and place of the teaching.
Thus have I heard at one time.
When the Blessed One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda asked what words should be placed at the beginning of the collection of the sūtras.
The Blessed One said: "One should place: 'Thus have I heard at one time. Therefore, this serves as the general rule for all sūtras. The word "thus" (iti) refers to...
Regarding the sutra that is spoken: "I heard" means that Ānanda personally heard it from the Buddha. "At one time," refers to the time when the sutra was being correctly preached.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in the city of Śrāvastī.
Śrāvastī is fully called Śrāvastī; this means "Abundant Virtue.

Because within this city, wealth, the five objects of desire, extensive learning, and liberation—all four—are fully sufficient, it is so named. Jetavana is called Jetavana, also known as Śītavana; this means "Victory in Battle.
When the Crown Prince of King Prasenajit was born, it coincided with a victory in battle; therefore, [it was named after that].

It was named after its two founders, Prince Jeta and Anāthapiṇḍada. When Anāthapiṇḍada, the Elder, covered the ground of Prince Jeta’s garden with gold to purchase it as a vihāra and invited the Buddha to preach the Dharma there, the Prince was moved and donated the groves of trees as well; thus, they were both honored together at that time.
△ Second, listing those in the assembly who were listening:
He was together with a great community of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus; all were great arhats free from outflows (anāsrava).

The term *mahāsattva* (Great Being) has three meanings: first, a great number; second, a significant name; and third, superior virtue. The term *bhikṣu* (monk) likewise has three meanings in this translation:
first, a mendicant (*yācanaka*); second, one who terrifies Māra (*mārabhīṣaṇa*); and third, one who destroys evil (*pāpavināśaka*).

There were one thousand two hundred and fifty people, including the five disciples such as Kauṇḍinya, one hundred followers each from the schools of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and the teachers of the three Kāśyapas.
There were one thousand followers. Regarding the fifty people from the householder Yaśas, the mention of "five" is merely a rough approximation.
There are three outflows (*āsrava*): first, ignorance; second, desire; and third, existence. An Arhat likewise has three designations: first, the Worthy One (*arhat*);

second, the One Who Has No Further Birth (*anuppāda*); and third, the Slayer of the Foe (*vadhaka*). The Worthy Ones of the Two Vehicles remain within the realms of humans and devas, whereas the Worthy Ones of the Mahāyāna [transcend them].

The "non-arising" of both the mundane and supramundane two vehicles merely brings an end to and liberation from *pariccheda-vidagdha* (segmented existence). The "non-arising" of the Mahāyāna, however, also involves the departure from *pariṇāmi-vidagdha* (transformative existence).

In the two vehicles, the "slaying of the thief" merely exhausts the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*). In the Mahāyāna, the "slaying of the thief" means that the five abodes (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) are forever extinguished.
Thus, this group being praised must belong to the Mahāyāna. As stated in the fourth chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the "Four Reliances," those who are called *arhats* [belong to this category].
Having severed all afflictions and cast off the heavy burden, they have attained their own benefit and accomplished what was to be done; abiding in the tenth stage,
these sons of the Buddha maintain the teachings and skillfully transcend all realms of existence.
Born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma, and having attained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma, they are called "sons of the Buddha.
The *Avataṃsaka* praises the assembly as dwelling in the realm where all Bodhisattvas abide, protecting and upholding the wheel of the True Dharma of all Buddhas.
Whether in the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm—dwelling amidst these various realms of existence—they are not bound by those elements; therefore, they are called "virtuous."
He transcends [the mundane].

He is able to perfect dignified deportment within the lands and follow the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma. He is wonderfully worthy of being entrusted with the teachings, purifying the *vinaya* and establishing a grand model for the three realms.
His response-bodies are infinite, delivering and liberating sentient beings; he rescues those of the future and transcends all worldly burdens.
Regarding the first two lines: Guishan said, "Manifesting bodies according to lands and using a proper countenance to awaken beings" refers to the meaning of *lun-yuan* (wheel-perfection).
Master Weiqu said, "Having received the teachings from the Buddha and personally realized them as already perfected, one is able to expound the Buddha's words to transform the multitudes."

The *Yizhu mengchao* (Annotated Testament) states: "Entrust the Dharma so that it may be transmitted; entrust [beings] so that they may be delivered. *Vinaya* is translated here as "law" (*lü*). Law refers to the Dharma;

the Dharma comprises gravity and lightness, permissions and prohibitions, observances and transgressions. It is by means of this that one tames both self and others. The three realms—desire, form, and formlessness—are thereby purified and made solemn.
This may serve as a model for the three realms. As for the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*), there are briefly two types.

The first is the response as a Great Being, intended for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages. The second is the response according to species, intended for the twelve classes of sentient beings, their number being immeasurable.
Although this sutra was initiated by Ānanda’s request for instruction to deliver those of that time, it truly also extends its salvation to future generations.
He caused them all to transcend the burdens of worldly defilements.
Their names were Mahāmati Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila,
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Upānanda, and others, who served as the leaders.
Śāriputra is here translated as "Son of the Śāri Bird. Because his mother’s eyes were like those of a śāri bird, he was named accordingly.
*Mahā* is here translated as "Great. Maudgalyāyana is here translated as "Of the Mung Bean Clan" (*Cai-shu-shi*). An ancient seer of antiquity constantly ate mung beans;
his mother belonged to that lineage, and the name was established based on her ancestry. He was foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Mahākauṣṭhila is here translated as "Great Thighs."

He was the brahmacārin Dīrghanakha, who took "non-acceptance of all things" as his tenet. He challenged the Buddha with a question intended to force him into defeat, but subsequently renounced the world and entered the monastic order.
Pūrṇa means "Full"; Maitrāyaṇī was his father's name and Maitrāyaṇī was his mother's name.
Because he bears the names of both his parents, he is called "Son of Maitrāyaṇī. Subhūti means "Good Fortune," and is also called "Born of Emptiness."
He was foremost in the realization of emptiness. Upānanda (here translated as "Dust-nature") received this name because he attained the Way through contemplating the emptiness of sensory objects.
He was called a "foremost" because he served as a leader and guide for the assembly.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable Pratyekabuddhas who had attained the stage of no-more-learning, together with those at the beginning of their practice, all of whom came to where the Buddha was.

It coincided with the time when the bhikṣus concluded their summer retreat and held the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; bodhisattvas from the ten directions sought to resolve their doubts and, out of reverence for his compassionate yet majestic dignity, came seeking the profound meaning of the Dharma.

Immediately, the Tathāgata spread his seat and sat in tranquil ease. For the sake of those in the assembly, he proclaimed the profound and abstruse Dharma. The pure multitude at the Dharma feast attained what they had never experienced before.
With the *kalaviṅka* voice of a seer, his sound pervaded the worlds of the ten directions, and Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gathered at the site of enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī is the foremost among them.
*Pratyekabuddhas*—translated as "solitary awakeners"—appear in worlds where no Buddha exists; they attain enlightenment through quiet dwelling and contemplation of the transformations of phenomena.

*Pratyayabuddhas*—translated as "conditioned awakeners"—appear in worlds where a Buddha exists; they follow the instructions of the Buddha and attain the Way by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination.

Those who have attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and realized its fulfillment do not advance further. Śrāvakas who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) and have not yet reached the stage of no-more-learning are all called "beginners" (*ādikarmika*).
Newly resolved Bodhisattvas who have entered the stage of perfected faith (*śraddhāparipūrṇa*) are likewise called "beginners. This is the appropriate designation.
From the sixteenth day of the fourth month, the summer retreat (*varṣā*) begins; when it concludes on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, it is said:
The Summer Retreat (*varṣā*). During the ninety-day period, whatever doubts may arise that one cannot resolve oneself are left entirely to the monks to raise;
this is called *pravāraṇā* (Self-Indulgence). A Bodhisattva is fully termed *bodhisattva*. This translates as "Awakened Being" (*jue youqing*).
Furthermore, *bodhi* is translated as "Unsurpassed Wisdom," and *sattva* is translated as "Great-Minded Sentient Being. *Kalinga* is fully termed *kalaviṅka*, a celestial bird.
The name [Mañjuśrī] has a harmonious and elegant sound, which is a metaphor for the Buddha’s voice. Mañjuśrī is also called Mañjuśrī;

this is translated as "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (Miaojixiang) or "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode). Mañju represents fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and possesses the eye of discerning phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-cakṣus*).
These appear repeatedly throughout the sūtras.
The preceding section on the general principles of the various sūtras is concluded. △ Second, the origins of these two sūtras, divided into four parts. First, King Bimbisāra invites the Buddha.
At that time, King Prasenajit was observing a fast on the anniversary of his father’s death. He invited the Buddha to the inner palace and went out himself to welcome the Tathāgata.
He prepared an extensive array of rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors, and also personally extended invitations to the great Bodhisattvas.

Within the city, there were also elders and lay devotees who were simultaneously feeding the Sangha, waiting for the Buddha to come and respond to their offerings. The Buddha then commanded Mañjuśrī to lead and distribute the Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha and the Arhats were invited by various patrons of the fast-day (upāsaka).
Prasenajit—here translated as "Victorious Army"—was the King of Śrāvastī; he was superstitious.

On the very day his late father, the former king, passed away, it happened to be the day of the Saṃgha’s Pravāraṇā ceremony. [This took place] within the inner palace quarters. The elder was one who possessed both virtue and wealth.
This is the designation [of the Buddha]. "Householder" (居士) is a title for one who guards the Way and possesses few desires.
II. Ānanda’s Alms-round and His Detention. Only Ānanda had previously accepted a separate invitation; having traveled far and not yet returned, he was unable to join the sequence of the Sangha.
Since there were neither an Elder (上座) nor a Preceptor (阿闍黎), he returned alone on the road. On that day, no offerings were available. Immediately, Ānanda took up his alms-bowl (應器).
As he wandered through the city begging for alms in succession, he first sought out his final donor to serve as the host for his meal.

Without distinguishing between the pure and the impure, or between those of noble Kṣatriya lineage and the Caṇḍālas, he practiced universal compassion, making no selection among the lowly or the humble.
He resolved to bring to full completion the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings.
Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for being Arhats whose minds were not impartial;

he admired how the Tathāgata had expounded the unobstructed Dharma to deliver them from doubt and slander. As they passed through the city moat, they walked slowly toward the city gate, their majestic deportment solemn and composed.
Regarding the Ritual for Solemn Reverence and Purification: At that time, Ānanda, while on his almsround, passed by a brothel and encountered the woman Mātangī, who possessed great illusory powers.
Using the *Sāvikāra* mantra of the ancient Brahmā, she drew him into her bedchamber;
as he was touched and caressed by her body, his precept-body was on the verge of being destroyed.
Ānanda means "Joyous Celebration. When the Buddha attained enlightenment, it was reported that King Droṇodana had suddenly given birth to a son;
King Śuddhodana bestowed this name upon him accordingly. He was not included in the regular monastic order, meaning he was not in the ranks of those attending the midday meal.

Nevertheless, he served as the *sthavira* (Elder) at the commencement of the summer retreat (*varṣa*). *Ācārya* means "Model" or "Preceptor. According to the Vinaya regulations, when monks go out [on formal business], they must follow [the instructions of] the *ācārya*.
The two masters: this explains the cause for falling into error. *Pātra* means "a vessel of proper measure";
it may be made only of clay or iron, and its size must accord with the Dharma. *Dānapati* means "donor"; one who practices giving without a virtuous mind is called the "last" [type].
*Kṣatriya* means "lord of the fields. At the beginning of the kalpa, humans ate non-glutinous rice, and each established their own boundaries.
He cultivated [the land] and promoted those of virtue to hold positions of authority; this was the beginning of kingship.

Caṇḍāla means "killer" in this language, referring to butchers and slaughterers—so-called because they act regardless of whether one is pure or defiled. Kāśyapa means "Drinker of Light" (or "Radiant One") in this language.
Subhūti abandoned the poor to beg from the wealthy, while Mahākāśyapa abandoned the wealthy to beg from the poor;

both were rebuked by the Tathāgata, who said that those who exclusively seek the poor harbor much doubt, while those who exclusively seek the wealthy harbor much slander. The moat surrounding a city is called a *huáng*.

As for a bhikṣu, he should accept offerings during the hours of *chén* and *sì*; this is what is termed "fasting" (*zhāi*), for when interacting with sentient beings, one cannot help but observe the fast. [This concerns] Mātanga.
This is called "original nature" (*prakṛti*). Later, after she left the household life, she was called Bhikṣuṇī Caṅgśī (Chengxing), following her ancient title.
Sāṃkhyā (Sobika-la) means "Golden Head"; he was a non-Buddhist practitioner of asceticism who received this mantra by serving Brahmā as his teacher.

Regarding the śrāvaka’s unconditioned precept-body (*asaṃskṛta-śīla-svabhāva*), it arises at the time of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of one motion and three proclamations). It belongs to the mind; if the mind changes, the precept is immediately destroyed. As for "will bring... [it refers to the consequences of such destruction].
A prophecy of what was yet to come. △ Third, the decree for Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go forth to protect [the king].
The Tathāgata knew that the arts of seduction were being employed against him; when the fast was concluded, he returned. The king, along with his great ministers, elders, and lay devotees...

They all came together to follow the Buddha, wishing to hear the essential points of the Dharma. At that time, from the crown of the World-Honored One’s head, there issued forth a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness.
From within the light, thousand-petaled jeweled lotuses were produced, upon which emanated Buddhas sat in the full-lotus posture and proclaimed divine mantras.
The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go to protect them; thus the evil spells were extinguished. He then guided Ānanda and Mātaṅgī back to the place where the Buddha was.
That the Tathāgata did not speak it himself, but rather had a manifested Buddha from the light atop his head speak it, was to demonstrate all supernatural powers.
All these are matters governed by wisdom; yet within the essence of formlessness (*animitta*), there is neither movement nor fluctuation.

It silently accommodates the deluded affairs of sentient beings, who undergo needless toil and exertion, while in their own nature (*svabhāva*) there is neither gain nor loss. Upon a single moment of awakening, one returns once more to what is originally possessed.
Mañjuśrī represents fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); because this fundamental wisdom can subdue heterodox and external views, he is thus designated.
The Emperor issued an edict for him to go and protect [the Dharma]. △ Fourth, Ānanda’s lamentation and request for cultivation.

Seeing the Buddha, Ānanda prostrated himself and wept bitterly, grieving that since beginningless time he had been devoted solely to extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) without fully perfecting the power of the Path (*mārgabala*).
With earnest devotion, they entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the initial expedient means of the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* by which they attained Bodhi.
At that time, there were also Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with the great Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions, all of whom likewise desired to hear this;
they withdrew from their seats and remained silent, awaiting the holy instruction.
The World-Honored One once said: "I and Ānanda, at the abode of the Buddha Śūnyarāja, gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Ānanda always delighted in extensive learning, whereas I always applied myself with diligent vigor. Thus we know that mere hearing is not equal to actual realization."
*Śamatha* is here translated as "quiescence. *Samādhi* is here translated as "contemplative observation. *Dhyāna* is here translated as "the non-duality of quiescence and observation.
Taken collectively, these are called *Śūraṅgama*; taken individually, they are *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*. This is because...

The eternally abiding true mind is both eternally quiescent and eternally illuminating; this non-duality of quiescence and illumination is precisely what is meant in Nirvāṇa by the equality of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because Śrāvakas possess an abundance of concentration and a deficiency of wisdom, they do not perceive the Buddha-nature.

Because Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes possess an abundance of wisdom and a deficiency of concentration, they perceive the Buddha-nature only partially. From this, one knows that the Buddha-nature consists in the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom.
...and so forth. The eternally abiding true mind is characterized by the non-duality of stillness and illumination; one should understand it through this principle of non-duality.
Guishan once correlated this with the Three Contemplations of Tiantai, while Juefan offered a slightly different interpretation, yet they share the same underlying intent.

This does not accord with the "eternally abiding true mind" mentioned in the following passage, for that sutra refers to the delusion of the faculty-nature and its restoration to the original nature-awakening.
There is "tranquil illumination" (jizhao), which cannot be compared to those who rely solely on the cultivation of meritorious effort;
Tianru’s supplementary commentary follows the former explanation, which should be regarded as the definitive interpretation.
The first part, the introductory section, is concluded. △ Second, the main body of the teaching (*śarīra*). This is divided into four parts. First, directly revealing perfect enlightenment.

This is divided into twelve sections. First, investigating the mind. This is divided into eight sections. First, indicating the cause of the constant abiding and the flow-and-turning [of birth and death]. This is divided into four sections. First, examining the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

The Buddha said to Ānanda, “You and I share the same life-force; our feelings are equal to those of siblings. When you first resolved to seek enlightenment within my Dharma, what superior signs did you perceive that caused you to suddenly renounce the deep and heavy affection for the world?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha, “I saw that the Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks, which are supremely wondrous and extraordinary.
His physical form is translucent and radiant, like lapis lazuli. I have constantly reflected upon this.”
This mark is not produced by sensual desire. Why is this? The breath of desire is coarse and turbid; it is characterized by the mingling of stench and the chaotic mixture of pus and blood.

It cannot give rise to the supreme, pure, wondrously luminous mass of purple-gold light. For this reason, out of thirsty longing, he followed the Buddha to shave his head and don the robes of a renunciant.

The Buddha emerged from King Śuddhodana; Ānanda emerged from King Droṇodana. Since Śuddhodana and Droṇodana were born of the same lineage, they are also called "of one breath" (*tóngqì*), as brothers share the natural order of heaven.
To interrogate their minds and interrogate their views serves as the textual inquiry for what follows.

"I have seen the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks" is the answer regarding what was seen. "I constantly reflect upon them myself" is the answer regarding the mind. [The passage continues with] the marks of the Tathāgata.
Excellent. From the well-placed feet up to the crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*), there are thirty-two [marks]. △ Second, distinguishing between the Real and the False.

The Buddha said: "Excellent, Ānanda! You all should know that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have had their births and deaths continue in succession because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. They employ various false thoughts; these thoughts..."
Because it is not true, there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

The awakening to this nature is called the mind (*citta*); the profound stillness and perfection of the mind is called nature (*prakṛti*). Those who do not understand [this] hold that the mind and nature have no essence.
This compliance with non-awakening is fundamentally due to being deluded regarding the Truth. Because of this delusion, one discriminates according to objects without self-awareness;

thus, there is cyclic existence, which is termed "delusion. Regarding the origin of truth and delusion, it is intended to indicate that the manifestation of the True Mind is solely the sense-faculties (*indriya*), while the continuity of the deluded mind is solely consciousness (*vijñāna*). Therefore, in the following text, the inquiry into the mind begins by—
The delusions of conceptual discrimination are exhausted, and subsequently, the truth of the seeing-nature is revealed.

If one awakens to the non-discriminative nature of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) by means of this seeing-nature, one will finally realize that all discrimination is entirely true and that the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) is not false.

One is deluded regarding the eternally abiding true mind and treats it as false conceptualization; thus, throughout the day one dwells in false conceptualization without knowing it to be the eternally abiding true mind.
This is what the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* refers to as the Buddha-nature transmigrating through the five paths.
While currently transmigrating, those who mistakenly take false conceptualization for the true mind should observe where this continuity of birth and death resides.

Regarding this point, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "If one attempts to discern perfect enlightenment while still remaining within saṃsāra, that nature of perfect enlightenment will itself become subject to the cycle of transmigration.
The Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi said: "The non-arising of the preceding thought is the mind; the non-extinction of the succeeding thought is the Buddha.

Thus, we know that the arising and ceasing of every thought-moment is not the Buddha-mind, and that which remains within saṃsāra is not perfect enlightenment. Even if delusive thoughts possess an inherent nature...
Furthermore, you must know that true wisdom has no substantial body; once this is decisively understood, you should not yet recklessly assume it to be a mere vague permanence.
△ Third, the instruction on the direct mind:
"If you now wish to investigate the true nature of the luminous manifestation of unsurpassed Bodhi, you should respond to my questions with a direct mind."
Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same path, they all transcend birth and death by means of a straightforward mind.
Since their minds and words are straightforward, from the beginning through the end of the stages of attainment, there is never any trace of crookedness in between.
Unsurpassed Bodhi is the Unsurpassed, Perfectly Equal, and Perfect Enlightenment of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Yet all of them achieve it by manifesting and clarifying true nature; therefore, this is indicated first. Master Zhao said:
"A direct mind means that the inner mind is truly upright and there is no falsehood externally. Master Xianxiu said: "The mind directed toward principle has no divergent paths. To manifest...
The mind is the beginning; ultimate realization is the end. In the interval between these two, one must sever all divergent paths.
In the daily activities of sentient beings, their entire being is delusion; therefore, the Tathāgata specifically brings forth the direct mind right before them.
The essential point is to reveal it clearly within the course of dialogue. Thus, in the following text, one attains its source through direct observation;
the mind gives rise to joy and delight, and consequently, one subjects it to sevenfold scrutiny until the emotions are exhausted and wisdom depleted.
Only then can one turn back and be capable of inference. Although it is not yet finalized before one's eyes, one may nevertheless use what has been clarified to penetrate what remains obscure.
Nowadays, when people observe this, they all claim that the capacity for discernment is not my mind, and that the complete nature exists apart from sensory objects;

yet they do not realize that even this "darkening of the mind" and solitary illumination is still a state of internal dwelling in seclusion. When the timing shifts and the opportunity is lost, it remains a state of being separated from objects and lacking substance.
Clinging to their own limited views, they attempt to harmonize them with the words of the Sage; how can such mental discourse be considered straightforward? How could it be?
It is beyond words. Therefore, one should know that the Tathāgata’s initial earnest exhortation was not without purpose. △ Fourth, investigating the mind and the eyes:
"Ānanda, I now ask you: when you first resolved your mind upon the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, what did you use as the object?"
"What is it that you see? Who is it that feels this love and delight? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, such love and delight arise from my mind and eyes.
Through the eyes, I behold the supreme marks of the Tathāgata, and in my heart, love and delight are born. Therefore, I have resolved to cast off birth and death.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you have said, this true love and delight is caused by the mind and the eyes. If one does not recognize..."
If you do not know where the mind and eyes reside, you will be unable to subdue worldly afflictions.
It is like a king who, having been invaded by bandits, dispatches troops to eliminate them; those troops must first know the location of the bandits.
That which causes you to wander in saṃsāra is the fault of the mind and eyes. I now ask you: where, precisely, are the mind and the eyes located?
"What is it that sees? refers to seeing clearly. "Who is it that feels love and delight? refers to the mind clearly discerning.

Thus, the phrase "this love and delight employs my eyes and mind" is a comprehensive answer regarding the eyes and the mind. The statement "seeing through the eyes gives rise to love and delight in the mind" is a detailed answer regarding the eyes and the mind.
"Dust" refers to the six sense objects; "weariness" refers to being agitated by these six sense objects, such that the mind is beset by the toil of sensory dust.
The basis [of delusion] is like the master of a thieves' den; that which is directed by the dust-like afflictions is like the thieves' guide. This is the source of ultimate delusion.
Various schools all divide the mind as belonging to consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the eyes as belonging to the sense organs (*indriya*);

thus, there are differing views regarding whether to refute the mind or the eyes. I, the ignorant one, say that one refutes their delusion, not the mind or the eyes. As the subsequent scripture says: "This is the mind, not the eye. Thus...
Furthermore, what need is there to select and refute [opposing views]?

One is about to reveal the true mind and manifest the nature through the sense organs; yet you say that one must first know where the thief is located, claiming that it is the eyes and mind that cause you to wander in saṃsāra.
Why is this? You must understand that the thief is originally the citizen; the citizen has no fault.
Consciousness has erroneously fallen into the unwholesome; the mind and eyes are likewise so. True awakening is without inherent nature, yet it is deluded by that which it illuminates.

As the faculties and objects become partitioned, one wanders through successive cycles of rebirth. When the cause of this fault is identified, the labor of these visual afflictions is suddenly extinguished;

these very four sense-objects are then called the "clear and bright eyes. What difference is there between the mind’s discriminative nature and wondrous contemplation? To transform their faces and follow one another is to realize that the thief was originally my own son.
This is also like the case where governing does not alter the people.

The first part, concerning the initial exposition of the causes for the permanence and the flow-and-turning [of the mind], is concluded. II. Grasping that the Mind Resides Within. This section is divided into four parts. First:
Directly Grasping that it Resides Within the Body.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all ten types of ordinary beings in the world alike maintain that the consciousness-mind resides within the body.
Even when one gazes at the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, they appear to be on the Buddha’s face;
yet when I now observe these four sensory objects of the floating roots, they are seen only upon my own face. Thus, this consciousness-mind must truly reside within the body."

Regarding the twelve classes of living beings: those that are empty and dispersed are excluded because they lack the characteristic of a body; those of earth and wood are excluded because they lack the characteristic of a mind.

"Floating" and "coarse" are distinct categories and not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The five sense organs are all endowed with eight factors: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—earth, water, fire, and wind—which act as the creators;
and the four derivative objects (*upādāya-rūpa*)—form, odor, taste, and touch—which are the created. Here, "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the sense of being defiled or stained. 2. [The second section]
To illustrate this present convention, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You are currently sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall; look at the Jeta Grove—where is it now?"
“World-Honored One, this great multi-storied pavilion, the Pure Lecture Hall, is located in the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden, now known as the Jeta Grove; yet it actually stands outside the grove.
“Ānanda, what do you see first when you are inside this hall? “World-Honored One, while I am inside the hall, I first see the Tathāgata, and next I observe the great assembly.
Only after looking out in this manner do my eyes fall upon the grove and the garden. “Ānanda, as for your gazing at the grove and the garden...”
"For what reason is there seeing? World-Honored One, because the doors and windows of this great lecture hall are wide open, I am able to see far from within the hall.

The hall is inside the garden, and the grove is outside the hall; this is based on the interior and exterior of the objective realm, which establishes the sequence of what is covered and what is seen."
First, one sees what is before, and then observes what follows. Furthermore, regarding the sequence of seeing, one should first see within in order to subdue the mind dwelling inside.
When you gaze at the groves and gardens, by what means does the seeing occur? This also serves as an answer to the question concerning the lecture hall, doors, and windows;
here, the lecture hall is used as a metaphor for the body, and the doors and windows for the sense faculties. A direct explanation states: Ānanda clings to the view that seeing arises from...
Because the eye exists, there arises the question: "How can there be seeing? The subsequent scripture asks: "While you are inside a room, can the door see?
This implies the point that it is not the eye [that sees]. △ Third, consolation and extensive demonstration.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden-hued arm from amidst the great assembly and stroked Ānanda’s head. He then announced to Ānanda and the entire multitude:
"There is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices."
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have all transcended through the single gate of the Path of Sublime Adornment. Listen attentively now!
Ānanda prostrated himself and humbly received the compassionate instruction.
