Having previously established the agreement to await future inquiry, this initial consolation broadly indicates the gateway of cultivation. Samādhi.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* Sūtra states: "The World-Honored One entered the King of Samādhis, the Wondrous Samādhi;
all samādhis are subsumed within this samādhi. This is precisely that samādhi; therefore it is named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King.
It is fully endowed with the myriad practices, arising in accordance with the nature [of reality], and the two adornments of merit and wisdom are used to adorn the source."
Because its nature is thus, it is called "Sublime Adornment. It is a single gate through which one transcends; there are no bypaths and no waiting.
What is termed *samādhi* and *dhāraṇī* is this very *samādhi-dhāraṇī*, which possesses such fundamental distinctions:
its essence is great and its function is great. All Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained sublime adornment by following this path.
Juefan regards *samādhi* as merely a resource for transformation, whereas Miaozhuangyan identifies it as a skillful means (*upāya*).
The *Lotus Sūtra* passage concerning King Miaozhuangyan that he cites also takes the body to be a different path in order to clarify the principle of skillful means.
While this reasoning is indeed profound and mysterious, it seems not to be the essential point of the original sūtra. △ Fourth, exhausting the argument that [the body] is not internal.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "It is as you have said. While your body is in the lecture hall, with its doors and windows wide open so that one can gaze far out at the groves and gardens, there are also sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata, yet see those outside the hall. Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One, it is impossible that one who is inside a hall should not see the Tathāgata, yet be able to see the groves and springs outside; such a thing cannot exist.

“Ānanda, you are just like this. Your mental faculty is all-encompassing and clearly aware. If the mind that is clearly aware before you were actually within your body, then you should first perceive the interior of your own body.
Is there any sentient being who first sees what is inside their body and only afterwards observes what is outside?”

Regarding external objects: even if one cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, one certainly ought to have clear understanding of the growth of nails and hair, the shifting of tendons, and the throbbing of pulses.
How can you not know these? If you do not know what is within, how can you know what is without?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind which perceives and knows resides within the body—is untenable.
This thorough investigation shows that the mind is not within the body. Therefore, using the body in the hall as an analogy for the mind within the body:
the body in the hall first sees the Tathāgata, yet the mind within the body does not see what is inside the body. By this, one knows that the mind is not within the body.
Furthermore, "that which exists" refers to that which is necessarily non-existent; "that which somewhat exists" likewise depends upon it.
The expression "first seeing and later looking back" implies that something should exist which ultimately does not.
Even if one cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, the growth of nails and hair, and the movement of tendons and pulses are clearly evident;
this should certainly suffice for understanding. Furthermore, he raises further difficulties, essentially clarifying that one simply cannot see the internal organs.

The first two sections on the attachment of the mind to being within are concluded. △ Third, the attachment of the mind to being outside. This is divided into two parts. First, the actual attachment to what is outside the body.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata, and I have realized and understood my own mind."
It truly resides outside the body. Why is this? It is like the light of a lamp burning within a room;
that lamp must first illuminate the interior of the room, and then, through its doorway, reach the courtyard beyond. Yet all sentient beings do not see [the light] within their own bodies.
To perceive only that which is outside the body is like a lamp placed outside a room; it cannot illuminate the interior. This principle must be clear so that there may be no confusion;
it accords with the Buddha’s definitive meaning (nītārtha). Could it be that I have fallen into error?

Having exhausted the investigation of what is within the body, one consequently doubts what is outside the body, as it seems non-existent according to reason. Nevertheless, sentient beings are deluded regarding external objects;

drifting along with conditions, they cannot master themselves. Comparing this to the attachment to the internal, there is no difference in their degree of inferiority or superiority. △ Second, exhausting the notion that [the self] is not external.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "These bhikṣus have just now come from the city of Śrāvastī, begging for alms-food, and have returned to the Jeta Grove.
I have already finished my midday meal. Observe these bhikṣus: when one person eats, are all the others satiated?"
Ānanda replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Although these bhikṣus are all arhats, their physical bodies and lives are distinct.

How could one person cause the multitude to be satiated? The Buddha told Ānanda, “If the mind that perceives, knows, and sees were actually outside the body, such that the body and mind were external to one another and did not interact, then what the mind knows would not reach the body.”
"It cannot perceive it. Perception occurs at the boundary of the body; the mind cannot know it. "I shall now show you my hand, as soft as *tūla* cotton.

When your eyes see it, does your mind not discern it? Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda, "If perception and knowing were mutually aware of one another, how could they be said to be 'outside'?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind which perceives and knows dwells [within]—is incorrect."
It is impossible for [consciousness] to exist outside the body.
The food of one person cannot satisfy a multitude; this is a metaphor for how the mind and body would not be mutually aware if they were external to one another.

Since they are now known to be mutually aware, it is evident that [the mind] is not external to the body. "Bolus-food" (piṇḍāhāra) refers to substantial food (kavaḍīkārāhāra), meaning food that exists in physical segments capable of being grasped.
"Susukā" means "having already fasted. Wēnlíng says: Having returned from begging for alms to the forest, he then raised up the assembly currently present before him who were eating food;
therefore, he said, "I have already completed my fast. "Tūlā" is fully called "Tūṣāra," which here means "frost. The Buddha’s hands are soft and supple.
It is like *tūla* cotton.

The above concludes the three attachments regarding the mind being external. △ Fourth, the attachment to its hiding within the sense organs. This is divided into two parts. First, the primary attachment to its hiding within the sense organs.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has stated, because it does not see internally, it does not reside within the body."
The mind knows itself; because they are not separate, it does not exist outside the body. As I now contemplate, I know it resides in one place.
The Buddha asked, "Where, then, is that place? Ānanda replied, "This cognizant mind neither knows the interior, yet it is able to see the exterior."
As I reflect upon it, the faculty is hidden within the root, just as if someone were to take a crystal bowl and place it over both eyes;
although there is something covering them, it does not obstruct vision. That faculty perceives forms and immediately discriminates them.
Yet, as for this mind of mine that is conscious and capable of knowing, I do not see it internally because it resides within the faculty; yet it clearly gazes outward without obstruction.

Because the faculties are hidden within, Ānanda used a crystal cage over his eyes as a metaphor for the faculties enshrouding the mind. He did not realize that while the eyes could see through the crystal, the mind could not see the eyes themselves, because the eye is not an object of perception.
This will be further investigated in the following text. △ Second, exhausting the notion that [the faculties] are not hidden within.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said, that which is hidden within the root is like lapis lazuli. That person should take a cage of lapis lazuli and place it over their eyes;

they would then see the mountains and rivers. Would they see the lapis lazuli? "Indeed, World-Honored One. That person, having placed a cage of lapis lazuli over their eyes, would truly see the lapis lazuli.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If your mind were to merge with [the object] as the lapis lazuli does, [you would likewise see it]."

If you can see mountains and rivers, why do you not see your own eyes? If you could see your eyes, the eye would be identical to its object, and thus it could not function as a faculty that follows [the object].
If you cannot see them, how can you say that this cognizing consciousness is latent within the faculties like crystal joined with them?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of conscious cognition lies latent within the sense organs like glass—is impossible.

Those organs follow what is seen, and immediately thereafter, they engage in discrimination; this is the characteristic of the eye and mind following one another. If the eye were able to see itself, then the eye would [be both subject and object].
The objects are identical; therefore, it does not constitute "following" [the object]. If one cannot see, then the mind is not hidden within the faculties as if behind crystal.

Thus ends the fourth calculation regarding the mind being hidden within the faculties. △ Fifth, the analysis of the opening and closing of light and darkness. This is divided into two parts. First, the primary attachment to the opening and closing of light and darkness.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have now further reflected thus:

within the body of these sentient beings, the internal organs reside in the center, while the orifices are situated on the outside. Where there are internal organs, there is darkness; where there are orifices, there is light.

Now, when I am facing the Buddha, I open my eyes and see light, which I call 'seeing the external. When I close my eyes and see darkness, I call this 'seeing the internal. What is the meaning of this?"

Because where there is a covering, there is darkness; where there is an aperture, there is light. Thus, to claim that one can see the external without seeing the internal merely persists in the doctrine that the mind resides within the body.
2. Thoroughly investigating the non-opening and closing of light and darkness.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "When you close your eyes and see darkness, as for this realm of darkness, does it face the eye or not face the eye?
If it faces the eye, the darkness is in front of the eyes; how can it be considered internal? If it were internal,"
Dwelling within a dark chamber where there is no sun, moon, or lamp, this darkness within the room is entirely your own scorched bowels.
If you do not confront it, how can it become an object of seeing?
Ānanda, you claim that seeing darkness constitutes seeing the interior; however, since this darkness is directly before the eyes, it cannot be established as being "inside.
Furthermore, there is the difficulty that within this room, in the midst of darkness, one sees nothing but your own scorched entrails; yet, when not facing [an object], there is no seeing.
In sum, this serves to prove that the perception of darkness is not internal.

If one were separated from external vision, then what is internally established would be as follows: when the eyes are closed and one perceives darkness, it is called being "within the body"; when the eyes are open and one perceives light, [it is called being outside].
Why do you not see the face? If you do not see the face, internal reflection cannot be established.
Previously, by taking that which faces the eye as "external," it could not be established as "internal.

Now, even if you grant that seeing apart from the external is incorrect, yet you claim that seeing darkness establishes its internal reflection, then seeing light should likewise be established as an internal gaze. Therefore, it is asked: "Why?"
If one does not see the face, internal gazing cannot be established; thus, "internal facing" is not logically tenable.
This is because, since darkness is right before the eyes, it cannot constitute seeing the interior. It is just as when light is right before the eyes, it should not be called "internal gazing."
If, upon meeting, this cognizing mind and the visual faculty were actually in empty space, how could they be said to be within?
If they were in empty space, they would not be your own body; in that case, when the Tathāgata now sees your face, it would likewise be your body.
Your eye has already perceived this; the body’s contact is not what perceives it. If you insist that both the body and the eye perceive it, there would have to be two cognitions.
Consequently, your single body would become two Buddhas. Therefore, you should understand that your claim that seeing darkness is called "seeing the internal" is incorrect.
Such a thing is impossible.
Furthermore, if you admit that seeing the face also constitutes being internally facing, then both the mind and the eyes would exist solely within empty space.
Since they would not constitute an internal state and would not be your own substance, it would follow that when a Tathāgata sees you, he too would be your body.
This is difficult to resolve. If the eye perceives while situated in empty space, then the body ought not to be aware [of it].
If one claims that both the body and the eye perceive, then there is the further difficulty of having two Buddhas in a single body. All such arguments are merely empty sophistry.
To prove that seeing is luminous and must certainly not be directed inwardly, it follows that seeing darkness cannot constitute an internal confrontation.

The above concludes the section on the opening and closing of light and darkness. △ Sixth, according to the place of conjunction, divided into two parts. First, the actual adherence to the conjunction.
Ānanda said: "I have often heard the Buddha instruct the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise. Because...
"Because dharmas arise, various kinds of mind arise. This is the Buddha’s original intent.
It means that due to the non-awakening and deluded movement of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, the sense organs and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*) manifest through transformation.
Furthermore, stirred by the winds of the sense organs and their objects, the waves of consciousness arise in turn. Here, we cite only the principle that "because dharmas arise, mind arises."
Illuminating the words below, I now reflect:
I contemplate the very substance of my own mind-nature. Wherever it conjoins, the mind exists accordingly;
yet it is not located within, without, or in between—none of these three places.

Although one recognizes the substance of thought and deliberation, while remaining in delusion, one cannot turn back of one's own accord; it remains a state of discursive preoccupation (*ālambana-cintā*).

It exists in accordance with its conjunction and ceases to exist when there is no such conjunction; this is the very proof of its being discursive preoccupation. The "three locations" refer to the internal and external, as well as the latent sense-faculties (*indriya*).
2. Exhaustively Investigating that it Does Not Follow Conjunction.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have now said—that because dharmas arise, various kinds of mind arise, and that wherever there is a point of conjunction, the mind exists accordingly—if this mind has no substance, then there is nothing with which it can conjoin. If it were possible to conjoin while lacking any substance,"
Thus, the eighteen realms arise from the conjunction of the seven objects; this principle is not so.

If they possess substantiality, then when you prick your own body with your hand, does the mind that perceives it emerge from within, or does it enter from without? If it emerges from within, [how could it perceive the external?]
Returning to see within the body, if [the mind] were to come from without, one should first see the face;

thus, the nineteen realms and seven objects are all metaphors for that which has a name but no substance. Furthermore, by means of internal emergence and external entry, one investigates the knowing mind until it becomes self-aware.
Finally, when the investigation reaches its ultimate exhaustion, the realization of the essence will manifest spontaneously, and the Sage’s intent will be seen of itself.
Ānanda said, "I see with this eye; yet the mind knows that it is not the eye. Therefore, 'seeing' does not have the eye as its referent.
The Buddha said, "If the eye were able to see, then when you are inside a room, would the door be able to see? Furthermore, those who are already dead still possess their eyes;
they should all be able to see objects. If they could see objects, how could they be called dead?"
The mind knows that it is not the eye; thus, although it avoids the difficulty of [the eye] being what sees, the fact that seeing is its function conversely reveals the fault of the root of delusion.
Therefore, it asks, "Can the gate see? This is precisely to reprimand the attribution of seeing to the eye.
At this point, the principle that the mind is not the eye has already been established.
Ānanda, furthermore, as for this mind of yours that is conscious and capable of cognition: if it must have a substance, does it have a single substance or multiple substances?
Now, while residing within your body, does it pervade the entire body or does it not pervade it?

If it were a single substance, then when you prick one limb with your hand, your other four limbs should feel it. If all of them felt it, then the pricking would have no specific location. If [you say] the pricking...
If [the self] were a single entity, then your own identity could not be established. If it were multiple entities, then you would become many people; which entity, then, would be "you"?
If it were a pervasive entity, it would be the same as the previous case of being pricked. If it were not pervasive, then when you touch your head, you would also be touching your feet;
yet while the head has sensation, the feet would be devoid of cognition. This is not the case for you now. Therefore, one should know that according to where [it is located],...
If the mind were to exist in conjunction with these locations, such a thing is impossible.
The previous inquiry into the existence of a substantial entity merely exhausted the possibilities within and without;

this further exhausts the possibilities of unity and multiplicity, pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness, silently indicating that the root of the mind is non-dual, so as to cause one to directly recognize it for oneself. If one points to a specific location where it exists, it cannot be perceived by all.

The "entirety" (the whole body) is not a single entity; if it were capable of being fully aware [of all sensations], it would follow that there are many persons. Nor is the entirety a plurality of entities.

If the entire body were to experience the same simultaneous contact, yet one could not perceive it as such—just as when one is pricked in a specific location as before—it would be impossible for the perception to be universal.
If it were not universal, then even when experiencing contact at the same time, one should not be able to perceive them as identical.
The section on the sixth superior grade, "Wherever One Conforms," concludes. △ Seventh, "In the Intermediate State," divided into two parts. First, the actual adherence to the intermediate state.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when I heard the Buddha and Mañjuśrī and the other Dharma Princes discuss the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), the World-Honored One also said that the mind is neither within nor without."
Not being within, one does not perceive the mind internally; not being without, one does not perceive dharmas externally.
This is the Tathāgata’s pointing toward the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Since this leads to [the conclusion that it] is neither internal nor external, it must therefore reside in the middle.
As I reflect upon this, internally there is nothing seen, and externally there is no mutual cognition. Because there is no internal cognition, it cannot be established as being within;
yet because the body and mind cognize one another, it cannot logically be outside. Now, since they do cognize one another, while there is no seeing internally, it must be in between.
Building upon the previous point that the mind is not within, there is nothing seen internally; nor is it outside, for then it would not perceive external objects.
Now, since there is no cognition internally, internal seeing is established as non-existent, yet the body and mind perceive one another, which demonstrates that [the mind] is not located externally.
Thus, it must reside between the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). 2. Thoroughly investigating that it is not in the intermediate space.
The Buddha said: "Regarding what you call 'the middle,' that which is in the middle must not be confused; it cannot be without a location. Now, as you investigate this middle, where does it reside?

Does it reside in space, or does it reside in the body? If it resides in the body, then being on the periphery it would not be the middle, and being in the center it would be the same as the interior."

"Place" refers to the object (*viṣaya*); "body" refers to the faculty (*indriya*). This section exhaustively investigates the faculties and objects; the following sections investigate them both together to demonstrate their lack of intrinsic substance.

Since the body has a center and periphery, it is said that [the mind] is at the periphery and not in the center; to be in the center would be equivalent to being internal. This first section exhaustively investigates the faculties.

If it were located in a specific place, would it have a fixed representation or no representation? If there is no representation, it is the same as non-existence; if there is a representation, it lacks stability.
Why is this? For example, when a person uses a marker to designate the center, looking from the east it is west, and observing from the south it becomes north.
Since the substance of the marker is thus indeterminate, the mind should likewise be confused and disordered.

The "manifestation" (biao) refers to designating an object to reveal the "center. Since what is seen differs according to whether one is in the east, west, south, or north, that which is manifested has no fixed location;
thus, it is said that the mind should not be distracted by grasping at a center.
Ānanda said, "Among what I have spoken, it is neither of these two. As the World-Honored One has said: 'With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
The eye possesses discrimination; the object of form is without cognition. When consciousness arises between them, that is where the mind resides.'"
The Abhidharma school's analysis of the arising of sense organs, objects, and consciousness as their mutual conditions is not the ultimate truth.
Ānanda, by identifying consciousness as the mind, has already remained in a state of delusion; to further claim that [the mind] exists within the sense organs and objects is even more erroneous.
The Buddha said: "If your mind were within the faculties and their objects, would this essence of the mind encompass both, or would it not encompass both?
By examining whether it encompasses both or does not encompass both, you will find that it does not reside within the faculties and their objects; thus, cause yourself to realize this. He said:
Within these two, there is no essence of mind.

If both were combined, the natures of things would become confused; since the object is not the cognition of its essence, they would stand as opposing entities. How, then, could this be the Middle Way?

"Objects" refers to the sensory fields (*viṣaya*); "substance" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*). One knows and one does not know; hence it is called "confused. Knowing is not non-knowing, and non-knowing is not knowing;
hence it is called "two adversaries standing in opposition. When two stand in opposition, the Center has nothing by which to be manifested.
Furthermore, it cannot be both; it is neither knowing nor not-knowing. Thus, it would lack any essential nature. What characteristic, then, could there be for the "middle"?
Therefore, one should know that the claim that it must exist in the middle is untenable.
Since it does not establish the simultaneous engagement with the faculties, it is not "knowing. Since it does not establish the simultaneous engagement with the objects, it is not "not-knowing.

Both meanings having been refuted, its basis is lost; therefore, it is said that it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). How could intrinsic nature be non-existent? It must simply be realized through self-awakening.
The preceding seven [sections] conclude the intermediate portion. 8. All Non-attachment. This is divided into two parts. First, the actual adherence to non-attachment.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the past I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—jointly turning the Wheel of Dharma. You constantly spoke of awakening to and discerning the nature of the mind."
Since it is neither within, nor without, nor in between, and has no location whatsoever—this state of total non-attachment is called "mind.
Is it not the case that my own non-attachment is what is called "mind"?
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "One should not give rise to the mind dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas.
One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. This "dwelling nowhere" is precisely this "non-attachment to all things."
The point of "giving rise to the mind while not knowing" is settled precisely by taking non-abiding as the mind.
Is this not a mistaken understanding? △ Second, thoroughly investigating that it is not non-attachment.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: "As for your statement that the nature of the mind which perceives, knows, and discriminates has no location whatsoever—consider all things in the world, including empty space, water, land, flying creatures, and all other physical objects;
these are called 'all. If you do not cling to them, do they exist or do they not exist?"
Regarding all that is presently manifest, what is called "non-attachment" involves considering whether the present exists or does not exist.
This clarifies that one who does not recognize their own fundamental mind cannot achieve non-attachment toward anything; it is impossible.
When the World-Honored One questioned the location of the mind, Ānanda was unable to realize it for himself. Even if one were to practice total non-attachment, as for the present...
The intent of the following clarification is as vast as the distance between heaven and earth; how much more so, then, could the subject and object ever possibly cancel each other out?
The underlying meaning becomes even clearer:
if it were non-existent, it would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit—how could one not be attached to such things? Yet, that which is non-attached cannot be called non-existent.

If there is no characteristic (*nimitta*), then there is nothing; if it is not non-existent, then it is a characteristic. If characteristics exist, then they are present. How, then, could there be non-attachment?
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for the mind that perceives and knows all things to be called "non-attached. This cannot be the case.
Turtle hair and rabbit horns are said to be ultimately non-existent. Taking up the previous point regarding whether that which you do not cling to exists or does not exist:
if it were non-existent, it would be the same as rabbit horns; what use, then, would there be in "not clinging"?

Since there is already the characteristic of non-clinging, how could there be no mind of all-encompassing awareness? Therefore, it is said that that which does not cling cannot be called non-existent. Indeed, the mind and its objects cannot...
They are mutually non-existent; their mutual manifestation is ultimately never solitary. Therefore, it is further explained through repeated reasoning:
"Where there is no characteristic, there is nothing; where it is not non-existent, there is a characteristic. When a characteristic exists, it is present; how then can there be non-attachment?

If one can illuminate one's own mind, then the myriad phenomena will manifest in response to whatever is encountered, falling neither into existence nor non-existence. Otherwise, there would be dharmas outside the mind, leading to a state of confusion.
However, both "clinging" and "non-clinging" are merely redundant concepts.
Since the arising of karma through ignorance, this mind has long since lost its original station. All manifestations of its nature arise by adhering to form;
before they arise it is oblivious, once arisen it is bewildered, and while arising it is in turmoil—none of which passes through [the true nature].
Once it has reached its ultimate limit, it is natural that it cannot return of its own accord; thus, it must rely on the "condition of realization" (*jñāna-pratyaya*).
When it dwells within the body, this is what all sentient beings commonly perceive. Any doubt regarding what lies outside the body is universally regarded as crude.
Yet, when the mind encompasses the vast void, all things—sentient and insentient alike—are contained and manifested therein. Such a perspective is rare indeed.
It is rare indeed for it not to exist outside the body. Its roots are hidden within the apertures and cavities, as if they were inside;
yet the substance of its conceptualization arises according to conditions, as if it were outside. It has no attachment within, nor can it be traced from either the internal or the external.
Truly, one may say that karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no fundamental basis upon which to rely. At this point, how could we fail to be struck with awe?

The first section, the inquiry into the mind, is concluded. △ Second, the manifestation of the faculty of sight, divided into eleven parts. First, the regret over mere learning and the request to reach the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
At that time, Ānanda was in the midst of the great assembly; he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground.
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "I am the youngest brother of the Tathāgata.

Having received the Buddha’s compassionate love, although I have now left the household life, I still rely upon his indulgent affection. Consequently, despite my great learning, I have not yet attained the state beyond outflows (*anāsrava*).
I was unable to subdue the *Sāvitra* spell and was turned by it; I fell into the house of a courtesan because I did not know the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
"We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha*, so that all those who are icchantikas may be led to abandon their Mleccha ways.

Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, while the entire great assembly waited expectantly with hearts full of longing and thirst for the Dharma.
I have reverently heard your instructions.
The "True Limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*) is precisely the eternally abiding true mind (*tathatā-citta*). To seek to reach this eternally abiding true mind, one must necessarily follow the path of *śamatha*.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies five meanings of *śamatha*: first, it is "able to extinguish," because it can extinguish the fetters of afflictions (*kleśa*); second, it is able to... [text continues]

1. Discipline (*dama*): because it can discipline the sense faculties. 2. Tranquility (*śama*): because the three types of action (*trikarma*) are tranquilized. 3. Seclusion (*viveka*): because of being secluded from the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).

4. Digestion (*praśamana*): because it can digest [and eliminate] greed and other afflictions. *Yuanjue* (Perfect Enlightenment) translates *śama* as "tranquility," which may be summarized by its meaning.

1. *Icchantika*: *Icchan* is translated as "faith" (*śraddhā*); *tika* is translated as "incomplete. It is also said to mean "one who has severed the roots of goodness" (*samucchinnakuśalamūla*), implying ruin and destruction. *Mili-*... [text ends]
The overturning of the chariot represents the eradication of evil views. △ Second, the emission of light symbolizes the perfect clarity of the faculties and nature.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face; the radiance was so brilliant as to resemble hundreds of thousands of suns.
The worlds of all Buddhas shook in six ways. Thus, the lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions were simultaneously revealed.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, these worlds were merged into a single realm.
All the great Bodhisattvas within those worlds remained in their respective native lands, joining their palms in reverent attention.

Previously, he emitted light from the crown of his head to signify that his essence is beyond verbal expression. Now, he emits light from his face to signify that his faculties and nature are perfectly luminous, with no deficiency either internally or externally.

When the Buddha preaches the wondrous Dharma, there is a great causal condition by which all devas, māras, brahmās, humans, and non-humans—whether filled with joy or struck with awe—experience a trembling of body and mind; thus the earth responds to this. Sixth, the sound and form roar and strike.

Regarding the statement that they arise and surge forth, simultaneously opening and manifesting to merge into a single realm: the lands are originally characterized by both opening and closing, yet sentient beings remain deluded and separated from them.
The Buddha, through his majestic spiritual power, causes them to see this briefly. Thus, one knows that the original land is no different from the ten directions;
only the great Bodhisattvas, having reached the very source of the Dharma, return to dwell in their own land, where seeing and hearing are no different than elsewhere.

He was about to reveal two kinds of fundamental [realms], and first emitted a radiance that simultaneously opened and manifested throughout the Buddha-worlds and the lands of the ten directions, merging them into a single realm.
All the great Bodhisattvas, remaining in their own respective lands, joined their palms and listened attentively.

This was to demonstrate that the birth of the Buddha and his body-land are one and the same; for while in one case opening and closing are performed with freedom, in the other case they are rooted [in the fundamental].
Separated by a world of dust, the vast and the narrow appear inherently different; the circular and the stagnant are divided. Yet the body remains this very body, and the land remains this very land.
It is as the great Bodhisattvas all dwell in their own lands, joining their palms to listen attentively;

they know that spiritual transformations shift suddenly, and they realize that apparent contradictions could never be real. This does not hinder the fact that what is seen is still perceived by the eyes, for the forms remain identical to those directly before one.
It is manifested as follows: When the youth Sudhana reached Maitreya’s pavilion in the *Avataṃsaka*, Maitreya Bodhisattva snapped his fingers and the door opened, bidding Sudhana to enter.
Once he had entered, the door closed again. Within that pavilion, he saw it was vast and immeasurable;
all its palaces and gateways were adorned with the seven precious jewels, and there were all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future.
Their names, lineages, spiritual practices, and lifespans were all fully and completely revealed.

He saw his own body present before each of them, as they paid homage and surrounded him. Having observed them all, Maitreya Bodhisattva withdrew his supernatural power, snapped his fingers, and said to Sudhana:
"Good son, arise! Such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); such is their intrinsic nature."
Like a phantom, like a dream, like a shadow, like a reflection—they are all unestablished.
Thereupon, the youth Sudhana saw his own body once again in its original place. How is it that what Sudhana saw differs from this? And when he arose...

It is just as if one were returning to dwell in one's own country, joining one’s palms in reverent attention. Thus we know that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like an illusion; hearing and seeing are nothing other than this.
Delusion and awakening oppose one another, yet the fundamental capacity of the faculties remains unimpaired. One need only have confidence in this oneself.
△ Third, showing the two kinds of roots to distinguish between delusion and awakening.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions;

the seeds of their karma naturally cluster like *akṣa* berries. Consequently, practitioners are unable to attain unsurpassed Bodhi, and instead become merely Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, or even non-Buddhist practitioners, celestial deities, Māras, or the retinues of Māra—all of this arises from ignorance."
There are two kinds of fundamental [delusions]: practicing in error is like boiling sand in the hope of producing fine cuisine;
even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will never achieve it.
Because beginningless ignorance perfumes the mind to form seeds, they are called "karmic seeds. *Akṣa* (惡叉) here means "beads strung on a thread."
This is the name of a fruit from the Western Regions. Three seeds share a single stem, serving as a metaphor for the three—delusion, karma, and suffering—which are inseparable from one another.

Śrāvakas awaken to the Four Noble Truths and grow weary of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); Pratyekabuddhas contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, performing two types of observation: that of cyclic flow and that of cessation.
Both are deluded regarding the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), as they do not enter the True Teaching but instead follow something else entirely. In total...

These are called "external paths" (*tīrthika*). The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) states: "Knowing that desire is to be loathed, one feels aversion toward the path of karma; abandoning evil and delighting in goodness, one again appears among humans and devas.
*Māra* is translated here as "the Killer," meaning that by indulging in and guarding the objects of desire, one brings affliction and harm to right practice.
For this reason, the Tathāgata specifically designates these two kinds of roots, which are present before us: the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Students should awaken to this with clear realization. "Kalpa" here means a long period of time; "dust-kalpas" refers to calculating the number of kalpas by means of fine motes of dust.
"What are these two kinds, Ānanda? First is the root of birth and death from time immemorial;

this is that攀緣心 (pān-yuán-xīn—the mind of攀缘 [grasping at objects]) which you and all sentient beings now take as your own self-nature. Second is the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvāṇa from time immemorial;

this is that識精 (shí-jīng—the essential clarity of consciousness) which is originally luminous, capable of giving rise to all conditions, yet that which is lost amidst those conditions. Because of these..."
Sentient beings have abandoned this fundamental luminosity; though they act throughout the day, they remain unaware of it and thus perversely enter the various realms of existence.
These two kinds of roots are both pointed out as manifesting from within sentient beings themselves.

Just as one uses daily activities to move about and engage with phenomena, sentient beings lack discernment and take these to be their own inherent nature; this is the root of birth and death. One must know that this is the primordial source.
This is the pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana; it does not transcend the present moment of clear discernment.
While asserting that all conditions arise spontaneously through dependent origination, one merely turns away from this in vain.
Because of this turning away, although one is daily within Bodhi and Nirvana, one is constantly either alert or deluded—what is called the "flowing and wandering of Buddha-nature."

The fruit of bodhi-wisdom and the fruit of the cessation of nirvāṇa—these two fruits of merit reside within the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) and are not associated with deluded defilement;
therefore, it is called the "primordially pure essence. This refers exclusively to the true nature (*tathatā*) of the *ālayavijñāna*.

Within its active functioning, it is termed the "consciousness-essence of primordial luminosity" (*vijñāna-sāra-ādi-prakāśa*). Because it is capable of responding to all things, it is said to "give rise to all conditions."

Since it exists within various conditions and cannot be self-awakened, it is called "neglected" (*yí*). This "neglect" is no different from being caught in objective攀緣 (*pānyuán*, clinging to conditions).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Because one does not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

Ignorance is precisely this lack of self-awakening. This lack of self-awakening applies not only to sentient beings; even those engaged in awakening and cultivation who do not accord with the mark of the ultimate truth are likewise subject to it.
It is all due to a lack of awakening; one must certainly not fail to reflect upon oneself.

One should examine and know with certainty that the mind which clings to objects and the mind which arises in response to conditions are neither two nor different; they differ only in their cessation of conflict between delusion and enlightenment.
When deluded, one cannot manifest the various conditions and is instead turned by them, thereby causing the fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness—
One is constantly present throughout the entire day, yet fails to realize it at that very moment. This allows us to understand the daily functioning of one who has attained awakening.
Master Pang said: "The affairs of daily life are no different; they simply accord with me of their own accord. The meaning of this "accordance" is for each person to know for themselves;
it is not easily pointed out or annotated. △ Fourth: Examining the Mind through Conditions and Perceptions.
"Ānanda, if you now wish to know the path of śamatha and desire to transcend birth and death, I shall now question you further.
At that moment, the Tathāgata raised his golden arm and bent his five fingers, saying to Ānanda: 'Do you see this? Ānanda replied: 'I see it.
The Buddha asked: 'What do you see? Ānanda replied: 'I see the Tathāgata raising his arm and bending his fingers.'"
"The Radiant Fist illuminates my mind and eyes. The Buddha asked, "By what do you see it? Ānanda replied, "I and the great assembly all see it with our eyes."
Previously, you requested to visit the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) and asked for instruction on the path of *śamatha*; therefore, I now set this forth for you.
The *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Visualizing the Buddha with Five Fingers* states: "Upon the tip of a single finger, twelve wheels appear;

at the end of each wheel is a svastika, and within the intervals of these svastikas are the marks of thousand-spoked wheels. When the Tathāgata raised his arm and bent his fingers, he spoke to Ānanda...
[The Master] said, "It is difficult to speak of. Do you see it now? This was the first direct pointing. He raised his arm and bent his fingers, manifesting them for Ānanda to see;
therefore he asked again, "What do you see? This was the second direct pointing. Since [Ānanda] was still confused about the arm and the fingers, [the Master] further pointed to the seer;
therefore he asked again, "By means of what do you see? This was the third direct pointing. And...
Ānanda then said, "I and the great assembly have all witnessed this with our own eyes; it was already missed at that very moment.
Yet you now claim that 'seeing' belongs to the eye," and only then did he offer his submission.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, “Now answer me this: when the Tathāgata bends his fingers into a fist of light to dazzle your eyes and mind, your eyes can see it;
but what do you take to be the mind when my fist shines forth? Ānanda replied, “The Tathāgata is now investigating the location of the mind.
I have used my mind to investigate and pursue it, and that which is capable of such investigation, I shall take to be the mind.”
"You can see it with your own eyes, yet you do not recognize it yourself. What do you take to be the mind? You should shine your fist [upon this].

To savor these words closely is like wishing to point out one's delusion using that very delusion as the finger of instruction. Unable to achieve a sudden awakening (*satori*) here, you merely begin to investigate and mistakenly take that for the nature of the mind.
Although it is not something separate, you remain utterly bewildered from beginning to end; you cannot avoid further [confusion].
This requires careful deliberation. △ [The section] "The five fingers can infer the existence of a substance" is divided into three parts.

First, the refutation of the inferring subject. The Buddha said: "Tsk! Ānanda, this is not your mind. Ānanda was startled, withdrew from his seat, joined his palms, stood up, and addressed the Buddha:
"This is not my mind; what should it be named? The Buddha told Ānanda: "This is a false appearance of the external objects before you."
Perception deludes your true nature. From beginningless time until your present life, you have mistaken a thief for your own son;
thus you have lost your original constancy and consequently undergo the cycle of rebirth.

The "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) are precisely the external objects (*viṣaya*). By grasping those external objects, one forms conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), which is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
This perception is not true; therefore, it is said to be "false and illusory. Within delusion, one clings to this and mistakenly takes it to be fundamentally permanent;

thus, it is said to "delude your true nature. The seven locations discussed in the response all belong to that which is being examined. Now, the very moment [the mind] arises, one is aware of it; this is the "examiner" (*parīkṣaka*). As the *Zongjing lu* says:

One can infer that this deluded mind possesses the function of object-directed contemplation (*ālambana-cintā*), yet it is not the true mind. Furthermore, it is said that the deluded mind is a reflection upon the true mind.
I, the humble writer, consider these descriptions to characterize the state of delusion, wherein one has not yet attained immediate awakening;
thus it is termed "object-directed contemplation" and designated as a "reflection. It does not mean that there exists a separate true mind apart from this object-directed contemplation.

It is merely that which precedes the image; it is external to the reflection itself. Thus, the World-Honored One rebuked it as a false appearance and conceptualization of the external objects (*pūrvadhātu*), and also reproached [the practitioner] for being unable to attain immediate awakening and realization.
As the subsequent scripture states: "I do not command you to grasp this as something other than the mind.
From this, one further understands that in delusion, the son becomes the thief, while in awakening, the thief becomes the son—there is no second person.
...and so forth. △ Second, seeking instruction.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the beloved younger brother of our Buddha, it was because my heart loved the Buddha that he caused me to leave the household life.
Why should my mind be concerned solely with making offerings to the Tathāgata? It would rather travel through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to serve all Buddhas and..."
"Good spiritual friend, it is by means of this mind that one gives rise to great courage and performs all those difficult dharmic practices.
Even if one were to slander the Dharma and forever lose their roots of goodness, it is still because of this mind.

If what you have thus clarified were not the mind, then I would be without a mind and identical to earth or wood. Apart from this awareness, there is nothing else at all. Why, then, does the Tathāgata say..."

"This is not the mind. I am truly terrified, and there is no one among this great assembly who does not harbor doubts. I pray that you will grant us your great compassion and reveal what we have not yet understood.
To serve the Buddhas and spiritual friends, and to practice various difficult dharmic deeds—this is the arousal of bodhicitta."
Regarding matters concerning the mind, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The bodhicitta is not, in reality, the Buddha-nature, because it is impermanent.
Even so, its uninterrupted continuity is called the cultivation of the path; it is like the flame of a lamp, which, though extinguishing moment by moment, is nevertheless able to dispel darkness.
The bodhicitta is also like this. Thus, we know that even while in the state of delusion, it is capable of being generated.
As for the bodhicitta, while one remains in the state of delusion, it has never known its point of return.

Although it is not something separate, it is merely called "the mind of enlightenment" (bodhicitta) and is not yet called the "true, eternally abiding mind. Even if one were to slander the Dharma and fall into eternal regression, such a person is merely termed an icchantika.
Nor is it something that exists separately. This is why we maintain that even icchantikas possess buddha-nature.

When one has thoroughly investigated through the seven points of inquiry and all objects of conceptual grasping have been suddenly exhausted, and yet one continues to press further, the moment one begins to search, one suddenly strikes upon it.
If one can achieve this "shattering like tiles and melting like ice," then even if one were to utter a thousand rebukes, it would be of no avail.
"Ten thousand faults! It is simply that no one is able to take it up. Thus, upon hearing 'the noble' designated as 'the base,' one immediately gives rise to a web of doubt;
the unsurpassed true nature is thereby turned into deluded thought. Now, how could the cycle of rebirth belong to external objects? If one knows where to return, why discuss the path?
Therefore, it is said that seeking through investigation has not yet escaped the duality of subject and object; this is still what the Tathāgata has condemned. △
Third, the direct demonstration of the complete nature.

At that time, the World-Honored One revealed this to Ānanda and the great assembly, desiring to cause their minds to enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).
On the lion throne, he stroked Ānanda’s head and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has constantly taught that all dharmas arise."
All is manifested by the mind alone. All causes and effects, and even the minute particles of the world, derive their substance from the mind.
Ānanda, if one examines the fundamental source of everything that exists within all worlds—even down to a blade of grass, a leaf, or a single thread—each possesses its own inherent nature.
Even empty space has its name and appearance; how much more so the pure, wondrously pure, and luminous nature of the mind, which is fundamentally one?
When one thoroughly examines the mind, it is found to have no inherent substance.
This is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences," states in verse:

"Observing all phenomena, They all arise from causes and conditions. Because they do not arise, they do not cease; Because they do not cease, they are inexhaustible. This patience is the most supreme; It is the thorough understanding of phenomena."
There is no exhaustion. When a bodhisattva abides in this patience, they universally behold all Tathāgatas, who simultaneously bestow upon them the prophecy [of enlightenment].
This is called the title of "Buddha" and the name of the "Lion Throne. Regarding the place where any Tathāgata sits—whether it be a couch or the ground—it is all termed the "Lion Throne.
As for the phrase "the pure, wondrously pure, and luminous mind," Dinglin says: that which is pure by being free from defilement is called "pure."
"Purity" means that being pure while remaining within defilement is called "wondrous purity. It is both identical to and separate from [defilement];

This is why the ordinary person’s attachment to a self is so difficult to shatter, and why even those of the Two Vehicles still harbor the notion of dharmas. This is what is meant by:

Moment by moment there is arising and ceasing; one constantly takes the impermanent to be permanent and fails to realize the loss of the true nature, while taking the impermanent to be permanent, ultimately resulting in the recognition of external objects.
Therefore, the World-Honored One generally censures this as "neglecting the true nature" and "acting with inverted views," whereby one transmigrates within saṃsāra.
One brings about one's own cycle of rebirth.
The preceding chapter used the sensory objects to reveal the seeing, and used the seeing to reveal the mind; now it is said that this seeing is fundamentally eternal and its source is immovable.
Yet, throughout the daily lives of sentient beings, they interact with all objects, coming and going in a state of constant agitation.
As for the inability to abide peacefully: it is not that the water of my mind lacks a place to rest.
The mind is not a guest; the mind is not a dust mote. It has been so for a long time. That the mind becomes deluded by guests and deluded by dust has also been so for a long time.
When deluded, one cannot recognize oneself; as the guest departs, one departs with them; as the dust stirs, one stirs with it. Thus, moment after moment, there is arising and ceasing.
They flow along with the mundane stream together. This is what is meant by taking movement as the self and taking movement as the environment;
they do not realize that within the guest there dwells the host. Remaining unmoved amidst motion, they have never had a single thought of turning back to contemplate their own inherent attainment.
How, then, could they avoid acting in a state of delusion until the end of their lives without ever awakening?

Direct Pointing to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, the Cultivation and Realization of the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume One:
Phonetic Explanations.

Miǎo (pronounced miǎo): the appearance of water being vast and boundless. Huǎng (huàng with the entering tone): brilliance and radiance. Shěng (shěng with the upper tone): an eye ailment. Cuì (pronounced cuì): a bird eating. Mì (pronounced mì): tranquility and peace.

Chè (pronounced *chè*, meaning to remove). Sào (pronounced *sāo*, meaning the stench of fat). Lǒngtóng (Lǒng pronounced *lǒng*; Tóng pronounced *tóng*; meaning not yet perfected as a vessel). Wǎn (homophonous with *wǎn*). Zhǐ (pronounced *zhì*, meaning to poke or thrust).

Mèng (pronounced *mèng*, meaning unclear or ignorant). Huī (pronounced *huī*). Jué (pronounced *jué*, meaning a look of hurried or startled observation). Zá (with the entering tone of *zàn*, meaning to press or crowd). Lìn (pronounced *lìn*, meaning stingy or parsimonious).
Miù (with the departing tone of *miù*, meaning erroneous or mistaken). Yù (pronounced *yù*, meaning sunlight). Xì (pronounced *xì*, meaning a great red). Chù (pronounced *chù*).

Dharma-heir of the Successor: Jìn Shì Dànguī (今釋澹歸) has read Jīnbiàn’s *Lèshuō* (樂說), comparing it with the preceding "Seven Proofs" (*qī zhēng*) regarding the two meanings of "guest-dust" (*kè chén*).
This concludes the section on "Bringing forth the Subject and Manifesting the Vision as Empty. △ Eight: Revealing the Nature of Vision.
It is not extinguished. It is divided into six parts. First, seeking the demonstration of what is subject to arising and ceasing, and what is not subject to arising and ceasing.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, felt their bodies and minds become tranquil and composed. They reflected upon the beginningless past.

Having lost my original mind, I falsely identified with the shadows of conceptualization arising from conditioned objects. Today I have attained awakening, like a child who has lost its mother suddenly encountering her again.
With palms joined, I pay homage to the Buddha and pray to hear the Tathāgata reveal the truth and falsehood, the reality and unreality of body and mind.
The manifestation of arising and ceasing versus non-arising and non-ceasing both clarify the nature of the mind.
Although Ānanda has realized that this nature exists apart from sense objects, he has not yet investigated the source of whether the essence of this nature is true or false;
consequently, he cannot discern the reality or unreality of its active functions before his eyes. Thus, this mind of arising and ceasing continues to circulate in the present.

Regarding the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, one still remains hesitant and unsettled. This is truly because, having only recently attained knowledge of the ultimate refuge, consciousness and wisdom have not yet been distinguished.
Therefore, the Tathāgata further points it out from the very source, so that one may know the clear realization that is free from hatred and love.
Without relying on discursive thought, the entire mechanism of non-arising and non-ceasing is present within this very moment. This is what is referred to below as "the vision of the river."
This is what clarifies the source [of the teaching]. △ Second, King Prasenajit’s request:
At that time, King Prasenajit rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In the past, before I had received the instructions of the Buddhas, I encountered Kātyāyana and Vairāṭīputra, both of whom claimed that after the death of this body, its total cessation is called nirvāṇa. Although I encountered them..."
"Buddha, we still harbor doubts. How can you manifest and provide proof that this mind is a ground of neither-arising-nor-ceasing?
All those present in this great assembly who still possess outflows now wish to hear."
Kātyāyana is fully called Kālakātyāyana; this means "Shorn-Haired.
This non-Buddhist teacher asserts that killing all beings does not lead to falling into hell if one lacks shame and remorse, just as empty space does not receive dust or water.
Pūraṇa should be called Sañjayin Vairaṭiputra; *Sañjayin* here means...
Sañjaya is his name. Vīrāṭī means "Non-action" in this language; it is the name of his mother. He is abbreviated as Vīrāṭīputra.

This non-Buddhist teacher claims that the path does not require seeking, for when the kalpas of birth and death are exhausted, suffering ends naturally—like a ball of thread unwinding from a high mountain until the thread is spent and it stops of its own accord.
These views all belong to the nihilistic school (ucchedavāda), which repudiates cause and effect. Among the six masters...
Second: Since it is not yet granted that Śrāvakas in *nirvāṇa* have seen their nature, what they see is but the partial truth (*parīttasatya*). This still belongs to the seven consciousnesses;

as they have not yet attained the permanent and abiding, these are all termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). Thus, one cannot help but harbor doubts. △ Third: An inquiry into the transformation of the physical body.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "Your body is present now. I ask you again:

does this physical body of yours abide eternally and remain indestructible like a diamond, or will it eventually decay and perish? "World-Honored One, this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and destruction. The Buddha said:
"Great King, this body of yours has never yet perished; how then do you know it will perish?

World-Honored One, although this impermanent and decaying body of mine has not yet perished, I observe that before my very eyes its moments are shifting and passing away, renewing themselves without staying, like fire turning to ash."
Gradually it wastes away; its decay continues without ceasing. You can know with certainty that this body must eventually reach total extinction. The Buddha said: "It is so.

Because the physical body is subject to change and extinction, you give rise to the thought that within the body there is something that does not change or perish. Yet you have never experienced such non-extinction; how then can you know of it?

It is precisely by observing the movement of your own self-awareness as thoughts shift and pass away that you hope for a moment of awakening and realization. But when you turn back to observe [the source], you do not..."
Far removed. △ Fourth, comparing youthful appearance with old age:
"Great King, your current age has already reached senescence; how does your countenance compare to that of your youth? "World-Honored One," [the King replied].
In my past childhood, my skin was smooth and lustrous; as I reached adulthood, my vital energies were full and robust; yet now, in my declining years—
Pressed by old age and infirmity, my physical form is withered and haggard, my spirit is clouded and dim, my hair is white and my face is wrinkled;
as my end approaches, how can I compare myself to those times of fullness and vigor?
Comparing the features of childhood with those of old age, one observes the changes in the body to demonstrate that within the body there is that which does not change.
At birth, one is called a *hai* (infant); when first able to walk, a *ru* (child). The outer skin is called *fu*; the patterns of the skin's texture are called *tian*. *Ling* refers to years;
having reached sixty years of age, one is said to be *tui*. *Tui* means to decline and decay. At eighty, one is called *mao*, meaning to be approaching [the end].
It is near. △ Fifth, examining the subtle transition of transformation.
The Buddha said: "Great King, your physical form must not have decayed all at once. The King replied: "World-Honored One, change and transformation shift subtly."
Truly, I was unaware that as the cold and heat shifted and flowed, I had gradually reached this state. Why is this?
At twenty, though I was called young, my countenance was already aged compared to when I was ten. At thirty, I was further declined than at twenty;
now, at sixty-two, looking back at the time I was fifty, I appear just as robust and strong. World-Honored One, I have observed this closely.

It shifts. Although this process of decay and transformation occurs within a limit of ten years, if I were to contemplate it with subtle discernment, its changes would surely not be limited to one or two decades;
they are truly changes occurring year by year. Yet these are not merely annual changes; they are also transformations occurring month by month.
These are not simply monthly transformations; they involve shifts day by day. Upon deep reflection and careful observation, [one sees that] at every kṣaṇa, at every thought-moment—
One cannot remain stationary for even an instant; thus we know that this body will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.

The previous [section] concluded with the transformation of the body, while this concludes the transformation of the years. When it comes to the *kṣaṇa*, one is already close to the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
Thereafter, the phrase "that which does not perish within the body" emerges. Worldly people are coarse and vulgar, and are unable to perceive this; therefore, [the text] below states:

This is shown by means of the characteristics of the faculties and natures. The four lines regarding "subtle transformation and secret shifting" collectively lament the ease with which conditioned fluxes change.
That one is not aware of this subtle shifting is the ultimate height of delusion. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Vigorous physical form does not remain, comparable to a galloping horse;
human life is impermanent, passing away faster than water over a mountain. Yet, people still play like children within the burning house—this is truly to be pitied. At the beginning...
From decades, one is limited by ten years; from ten years, one is limited by one year; from years, one is limited by months; from months, one is limited by days;
until reaching the *kṣaṇa*, where every thought-moment does not abide. If one is not aware of this, then one is truly unaware.
△ Sixth, the correct demonstration of the nature of non-arising and non-extinction, divided into two parts. First, questioning the non-extinction within the body.
The Buddha told the Great King, "You see that transformations and changes ceaselessly shift; you have realized and known your own extinction.
At the time of this extinction, do you know that within your body there is something that does not perish? King Prasenajit joined his palms and said to the Buddha, "I truly do not know."

The years pass and the body transforms until it reaches the point of a single kṣaṇa; every thought-moment shifts and fades away. If one were to suddenly turn back and reflect upon this, how could one be the same as mere earth or wood?
If one does not awaken to this, then it would be necessary for the Tathāgata to appear once more to provide further instruction. II.

Questioning the similarities and differences of seeing water, in order to illustrate the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. This is divided into four parts. First, questioning the seeing of water.
The Buddha said, "I shall now demonstrate to you the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. Great King, at what age did you first see the waters of the Ganges?
The King replied, "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother took me to visit the deity Jīva.
As we passed by this flowing stream, I immediately recognized it as the waters of the Ganges."
Jīva—here translated as "Longevity"—is a deity from the Western Regions. Whenever a child is born there, they must visit this deity.

Having passed many years, one looks back upon them as if they were only yesterday; one sees and knows them immediately, without the need for deliberation. II. Examining the similarities and differences in seeing water.
The Buddha said, "Great King, it is as you have said. At twenty, one declines from the state of ten; this continues until sixty.
As days, months, years, and seasons pass, moment by moment there is change. Thus, when you were thirteen years old and saw this river, compared to when you were three..."
"What was that water like? The King replied, "It was exactly as it was when I was three years old; there was not the slightest difference.
Even now, at the age of sixty-two, it remains unchanged."
Furthermore, because years and seasons change, he limited the period to ten years. He questioned him regarding his perception of this river during those ten years:
"How did it differ or remain the same? This was intended to cause him to awaken to himself—that which is called "not blocking the gate of enlightenment.
The two characters "wǎn rán" (as it is) may be said to have been suddenly picked up from amidst the filth; they are not easily explained to others. △ Three: Single [Case].

The King was asked to observe the similarities and differences [between his current state and his youth]. The Buddha said, "Now you yourself see that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled; your face must certainly be more wrinkled than it was in your childhood.

As you now look at this Ganges River, is there any difference between this vision and the vision with which you looked at the river in your childhood—any distinction between being a child and being an old man? The King replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
It is exactly as it was, without any difference. I have already understood and awakened to this myself. This is to further examine the distinction between youth and old age;
it may be called a repeated and earnest instruction. 4. Showing that the seeing-essence is unchanging.

The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face is wrinkled, this essence of seeing has never been wrinkled in its nature. That which is wrinkled undergoes change; that which is not wrinkled does not change.
That which changes is subject to extinction. As for that which does not change, it fundamentally has no arising or ceasing.
How could birth and death affect it? Yet you still cite those such as Maskarin Gośālīputra, who claim that after the death of this body, there is total annihilation."

Upon hearing these words, the King believed and understood that after death one leaves this life to transition to another. Together with the great assembly, he leaped for joy and was filled with unprecedented delight.

This clearly demonstrates that within the body there exists an indestructible nature; while the present manifestation of birth and death is like that [illusory appearance], its [true] nature is not so.

Arising and ceasing are thus: the true exists within the delusory, and the real resides within the void. Through discernment that accords with conditions, one knows that the horse’s reflection is nothing other than itself;
seeing that the nature is without transition, one awakens to the fact that the ox’s nose is held in its own hand.
Māgandiya—here translated as "One Who Does Not See the Way"—refers to those non-Buddhists who hold views of annihilationism; this term generally indicates the six heterodox teachers.
Annihilation and non-annihilation: this is the point of divergence between our True Dharma and that of the heterodox paths.
Ānanda’s request was, from its inception, intended as a mirror for the world and future generations. Previously, it was stated that his vision was unimpaired and his vision was unshakable;
he clearly understood the nature of the faculties and did not follow the shifting changes of external objects. Yet, he still harbored doubts regarding annihilation after death. This—
These are the common ailments of all sentient beings. Therefore, from childhood to old age, one can easily verify this through what has been personally experienced and witnessed;
yet, it is only by relying on the words of the Sage to suppress and exalt [the truth] that one finally attains self-recognition.

Thus we know that the unsurpassed secret is right before our eyes, yet we fail to perceive its transformative influence as it flows and shifts through successive kalpas. Indeed, the eye must see, and the ear must hear...

There is such a teaching. One person turns their gaze inward; a thousand sages follow the same track. You should maintain this mindfulness with self-confidence, for it remains unchanged through ten lifetimes.
Why wait until you have abandoned one life and entered another before realizing that the self is not extinguished?
King Prasenajit said: "Moment by moment, from thought to thought, there is no staying still. Therefore, I know that my body ultimately undergoes transformation and extinction."

Now, if every thought-moment does not cease, is this not precisely the arising and ceasing of the mind? When the mind is deluded regarding body and world, it follows along with their shifting flux, finding no leisure for abiding.
At such a time, to be pointed directly at the face and have one's life-essence extracted—if one lacks innate wisdom, how could one possibly grasp it?

It was not easy for him to awaken suddenly. Yet the World-Honored One said: "As you now look at this Ganges River, is there any difference between this vision and the vision you had when you were a child looking at the river?
Is there any distinction of youth or old age? That which is revealed by the true nature does not fall within the realm of discursive thought;
it is known as it is seen. How could it differ from the past or the present? This is what the Tathāgata does for sentient beings amidst their delusion—he selects [the truth] for them.
That which is necessarily incapable of being deluded is the self-awakening within a single locus, wherein the whole body is perfectly manifest.

What is called the five sense-faculties of direct perception functions in concert with the eight consciousnesses; it is ever present before one's eyes, yet one fails to awaken to it. Upon encountering a condition for realization, [it is suddenly revealed].
This is identical to what was originally obtained.
The preceding eight sections have concluded the demonstration that the nature of seeing is indestructible. △ Ninth, pointing out the location of the inversion; this is divided into three parts.
First, questioning the loss of the inversion.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and knelt on one knee to address the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, if this seeing and hearing are necessarily neither produced nor extinguished, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of perversion?"
I pray that you will give rise to compassion and wash away my defilements.
Although I have realized that what is seen and heard is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished, the four elements remain distinct and the five aggregates appear vividly before me.
I am deluded regarding form and emptiness right before my eyes, grasping at a floating bubble as my own essence; inverted and unaware of its true location, who can reveal the authentic nature?
To understand the partial and the complete: were it not for the great elucidation of the unobstructed, how could one enter and realize the *dharmadhātu*?

While the Tathāgata’s revelation points solely to the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), Ānanda’s present request cites both seeing and hearing. The *Zongjing* [Lu] states that among the six sense faculties—
Seeing and hearing alone are ever-present according to their function and are easy to manifest clearly;
thus, Rāhula struck the bell and Mañjuśrī chose the ear, both acting with this same intent. △ Second, the Tathāgata shows his arm to investigate perversion.
Immediately, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm; with his wheel-marked hand pointing downward, he showed it to Ānanda, saying:
"Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted? Ānanda replied: "Worldly beings consider this to be inverted, yet I do not know who is upright and who is inverted.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If worldly people consider this to be inverted, then..."

"What do people of the world consider to be correct? Ānanda replied, "When the Tathāgata extends his arm, with hands as soft as tūla-cotton pointing upward toward the sky, that is what they call correct."
The Tathāgata extended one arm downward; this was intended to trigger the realization of the "sword of the eyebrows" and thereby manifest the state of overturning [the world].

Ānanda did not understand and instead took it literally, asserting that according to worldly convention this constitutes being "upside down," and further asserting that what is upright is considered "correct.
This may be called missing the mark right before one's face. *Mudrā* is translated here as "seal" (*in*). (From the *Zhengzhen Chao*)
[The Buddha] said: "This is the hand-gesture for forming a seal (*mudrā*). It is used to subdue demons and outsiders.
The Buddha then raised his arm and addressed Ānanda, saying: "If this [seal] were inverted, with the head and tail exchanged, then all people of the world..."

To look at things with a single-minded partiality—if such is this perversion, it is entirely the Tathāgata’s own arm; it is merely a matter of exchanging the head for the tail or the tail for the head.
What difference is there? The people of the world look with such one-sidedness, yet they do not realize it, each giving rise to their own [delusions].
This is a divergent view. If one were to awaken to this, the beginning and end would naturally shift;
though the single arm remains no different, the inverted names directly beneath it find no place to rest. It is the person alone, yet it is also many times more than that.
Thus you shall know that your own body and the pure Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas are revealed through comparison.

The body of a Tathāgata is called "Right Universal Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*), whereas your bodies are termed "inverted by nature. Examine your own body and the Buddha-body with earnest attention.
Regarding what is called "inversion": in what sense is it designated as inversion?

The Tathāgata’s pure *dharmakāya* is undifferentiated from its *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*. When the thirty-two marks manifest before one, they are identical with all responsive bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) according to the various types of beings;
they are the identity of form and nature, and the identity of existence and emptiness. To realize that which is manifested by one's own mind is to attain the correct [view].
To know that what appears is merely mind is "universal knowledge" (*parijñā*); this is what is called "Perfect Universal Knowledge" (*samyak-parijñā*).
If one clings to the mind as being inside the body, while mountains, rivers, and the great earth all reside outside the body, then there would be phenomena external to this mind;
this constitutes a state of inversion. Therefore, based on this condition, it receives its name, being termed "inverted nature. As for the analogy, it is like the Tathāgata.
One arm hangs down vertically, yet worldly people each perceive it as either inverted or upright; this is merely an inference drawn from analogy to clarify the point.
Therefore, know that the body of the Tathāgata is not "inverted," and it is by virtue of this that he is named "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly Enlightened One).
