Your own bodies, however, are by nature inverted, and it is because of this that you receive your designation. Though called "inverted," they are in fact not inverted at all. Thus it is said.

It is said: "Your body is the Buddha-body. As for what is termed "inversion," where do these names reside? What is designated as "inversion"? Holy names and mundane appellations are all merely sounds;
extraordinary features and inferior forms are all illusory substances. My foolish views differ from various interpretations;
yet, when measured against the intention of the Sages, there must be some subtle truth therein. I dare not conform blindly, but await the judgment of the wise and enlightened.
△ Third, the correct demonstration of the inversion.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly gazed fixedly at the Buddha with unblinking eyes; they did not know where the inversion of body and mind lay.
The Buddha gave rise to compassion, taking pity on Ānanda and the great assembly, and uttered a voice like the tide of the ocean.
He addressed the entire assembly: "Good sons, I have often said that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and the objects of cognition, are manifestations of mind alone.
Your bodies and your minds are all things manifested within this wondrously luminous, true essence, the wondrous mind.
Why, then, do you all lose sight of this fundamentally wondrous, perfectly wonderful, and luminous mind, and this jewel-like, brilliant, and wondrous nature?"
"Recognizing awakening within delusion":

"Form" refers to the eleven types of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*); "mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses; "various conditions" refers to the twenty-four dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*);
"mental factors" (*caitta*) refers to the fifty-one mental concomitants; and "various objects of cognition" refers to the six kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). Five.
In total there are one hundred dharmas, which encompass all things. All these dharmas are manifestations solely of the mind.

When it is said that "your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously bright, true essence of the wondrous mind," this refers to Ānanda’s present conceptualizations as his body and his confusion as his nature;
both are manifested together within the wondrously bright, true essence.
Yet, failing to realize this oneself, one mistakenly treats it as lost. This is what is meant by "delusion within enlightenment.
When the wondrous mind is called the "wondrously luminous true essence," it is fundamentally wondrous and luminous. This luminous true essence is distinguished from that which is false and illusory.

When it is called the "fundamentally wondrous, perfectly wondrous, and luminous mind," this fundamentally wondrous mind is a perfect fusion of stillness and illumination; it is distinguished from [mere] cognition.
It is clarity. That which is called the "wondrous nature of precious clarity" is this very clarity that is wondrous; its function is entirely returned to its essence.
To stare fixedly is the appearance of being dazed and ignorant. Obscurity becomes space.
Within the obscurity of space, the accumulation of darkness becomes form. Form is intermingled with delusive thoughts; these conceptual appearances become the body.
Aggregating on objects, it wavers within; rushing outward, it scatters in flight. This state of confused and turbulent appearances is taken to be the nature of the mind.
Once deluded, they take this as their mind and are firmly convinced that it resides within the physical body.
Obscurity and darkness are the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). When ignorance is obscured and darkened, the original nature becomes utterly desolate;
this is what is meant by "through delusive confusion, empty space arises. Within this space, darkness coagulates; this is the ignorance that acts as the transformative agent.

Relying upon space, it gives rise to views; this is what is meant by "the clarity of thought forms the land. Furthermore, because the color-form produced [by ignorance] reflects back upon the capacity that produced it, it is said:

Form is a mixture of false conceptualizations; the characteristics of these conceptions constitute the body. Once the sense-faculties and the physical body have been formed, this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) then gathers those six objects of perception (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) to form the other four aggregates (*skandha*).
Internally agitated and externally distracted—what is called "turbulent confusion"—is precisely the moistening branch of ignorance (*avidyā*).

When one is deluded once and takes this as the mind, one will inevitably be confused about what constitutes the interior of the body. From this point on, the great masses of sentient beings fall into perversion.
He clung to them, and so they were lost together with him.
He did not know that his physical body, as well as the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, are all things within the wondrously luminous true mind.

It is like setting aside hundreds of thousands of vast, clear oceans and instead identifying with a single floating bubble, claiming that this tiny bubble represents the entirety of the tide and the full extent of the great seas.
You all are people who are doubly lost in delusion; you are no different from those who stand with their hands hanging down.
The Tathāgata calls them objects of compassion.

The physical body is the *indriya-kāya* (the body of faculties), while empty space and the great earth are the *bhājana-loka* (the receptacle world). Both the body of faculties and the receptacle world are transformations manifested by internal consciousness;
they originally lack self-nature and are solely the One Mind. Therefore, it is said that all are the wondrously luminous true mind.

It is an object within [the sea]. The hundreds of thousands of great oceans are a metaphor for the wondrously luminous true mind. The substance of a single bubble serves as a metaphor for the deluded mind that constitutes the body;
this is precisely what was previously referred to as "your body and your mind. To "discard" means to lose or cast away.

One who views things with a twofold perspective is simply one who views them with a singlefold perspective; it is merely said that this singlefold person is deluded. It is like my hanging down my hand:
each person sees it as either inverted or upright, yet there is no difference between them.

The person is deluded regarding the external objects before them because they fail to distinguish between the objective realm and the seeing faculty. Consequently, when the object is present, the seeing arises;

when the object subsides, the seeing ceases. Although this arising is not true arising, and this ceasing is not true ceasing, the nature of the mind within this delusion exists only by depending upon causes and conditions.
Thus, that which is currently manifest before one becomes non-existent as it pursues the objects of the environment. This is capable of being investigated.

This is the mind that is free from the nature of discrimination regarding external objects (*viṣaya*). Since adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*) do not abide, the sovereign emptiness remains tranquil.

Though the body is constrained by years and seasons, one perceives no distinction between childhood and old age; thus, one may realize that what is seen and heard is necessarily devoid of arising and ceasing.
Nevertheless, although this mind that has suddenly turned back can detach from the conditions of the world and the self, it has not yet departed from the dust.
It is not easy to dissolve the anxieties of conceptual discrimination; one considers one's own nature to be ultimately absolute and nothing else.
How could one know that such inversion is truly difficult to awaken from? In the Dharma-realm, there is fundamentally no "self" or "other. The Bohai Sea does not abide in its floating bubbles.
Thus, one takes that which is within the body as the mind. How could one believe that what appears before the eyes is not a thing, but rather a manifestation of one's own mind?

The ocean of nature is inherently endowed with waves; what is manifested is but the mind itself. The moon in the water is entirely returned to the sky. The essence of the myriad phenomena is profound; the light of the mirror is naturally full.
Yet, by regarding them through delusion, one creates intimacy and distance, ultimately resulting in notions of sameness and difference. Is this not, indeed, to have lost the true nature?
This is acting with inverted views. Ānanda, you merely claim that what is seen and heard is fundamentally without arising or ceasing;

yet you must know that delusion and enlightenment are still separated by the partial and the perfect. To awaken is to awaken completely, wherein one realizes all phenomena as oneself—how could there be two or three within a mirror?
To be deluded is to remain deluded forever, clinging to what has been attained while severing connection with the sensory realm; thus, it is difficult to forget each and every thing within the void.
Those lost in delusion are doubly so; it is not merely the case for the sages of old alone.
This concludes the section on the ninth line, which points out the locus of inversion. 10. Distinguishing the conditional mind to demonstrate that the nature of seeing has nothing to return to.
This is divided into three parts. First, [Ānanda] sets forth what he has realized, yet does not dare claim it for himself.
Having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, Ānanda wept and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha and have awakened to the wondrous, luminous mind—the originally perfect and eternally abiding ground of the heart—I have realized the Buddha’s..."

You now manifest the sound of the Dharma; you now manifest with a responsive mind that accords with our gaze. We have merely obtained this mind, yet we dare not recognize it as the fundamental source of the mind-ground.
We pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim the perfect voice to uproot our doubts and lead us back to the Unsurpassed Way.
This refers to the mind that has attained awakening, which is fundamentally wondrously luminous, perfect, and eternally abiding.

Yet the mind capable of attaining this awakening presently perceives the Dharma-sound, arising in dependence upon conditions. When one turns back to examine what has been awakened to, nothing truly real is seen;
therefore, it is said that one has "merely obtained it but does not dare to recognize it. "Perfect sound" means that all sounds are but a single sound, and a single sound is but a single [sound].
"Qie-yin" (phonetic transcription). Furthermore, it is a single word that exhaustively expresses everything; moreover, each [sound] is identical to all others.
△ Second, the reprimand and recognition of the pointing finger to distinguish and return the discriminating mind.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and the others still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind; this Dharma is likewise a condition, and you have not attained the nature of the Dharma (*dharmatā*).
The wondrous, perfect, and eternally abiding state spoken of by the Buddha points directly to your own original ground, the mind-ground—this is the nature of the Dharma.
If Ānanda, upon hearing this teaching, immediately understands the Buddha’s pointing, he will recover his original mind without relying on discriminative cognition."

[He] saw this; this is the attainment of the *dharmatā*. Now, if one uses the presently objectifying mind to take the Buddha’s Dharma-sound as its object, then this Dharma also exists or does not exist in accordance with that objectifying mind.
Therefore, it is said that this is not the attainment of the *dharmatā*. The *Zongjing* says:
"Even Ānanda still recognized the objectifying mind that hears the Buddha’s Dharma-sound as the eternally abiding true mind; he grasped the Buddha’s definitive intent [in this way]. How foolish!"
This means that although Ānanda had grasped the Buddha’s definitive intent regarding the eternally abiding true mind, he did not yet dare to acknowledge it as his own.

This was because he knew that his present state of mind—which was still a conditioned mind (緣心) directed toward what he was contemplating—had never merged with the mind that realizes [that truth]. Thus, he harbored a doubt.
It is like a person pointing out the moon to another with their finger, intending for that person to look at the moon because of the finger.
If, however, that person looks at the finger and takes it to be the substance of the moon, would this person not only lose sight of the lunar disc, but also lose the finger itself? Why is this?
Because they have taken the finger used as a sign to be the bright moon. Would they not only lose the finger, but also fail to distinguish between light and darkness? How much more so...

For this reason, the substance of the finger itself is taken as the nature of the moon’s radiance. Since the two natures of light and darkness cannot be apprehended [independently], the Tathāgata’s teaching is like the finger and the nature of the mind is like the moon.
Pointing with the finger is intended to cause one to see the moon; establishing the teaching is for the sake of pointing toward the source of the mind.
By means of the teaching, one recognizes the mind, and only then does one know that the three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are merely traces left by the pointing finger.

Discourse. If one relies on the teachings as the ultimate meaning, and merely takes what is realized through mental conditions as being vividly present before one's eyes, this is entirely to mistake the finger for the moon.
This is because the teachings are merely that which manifest the truth. Therefore, what is most valued is the immediate dissolution and return [to the source].
The principle manifested by the teachings and the mind of the listener remain ultimately distinct; the finger pointed out and the moon it points to are likewise separate.
Light and darkness are distinct from one another; thus, there is also the analogy of losing one's finger.

You are just like this: if you take the discriminative sound of my preaching the Dharma to be your own mind, then this mind should inherently possess the nature of discrimination even apart from the discriminative sound.
Because one gives rise to discrimination through the teaching of the Dharma, this discriminating mind must possess an inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

Even when free from discrimination, it remains profoundly still and eternally abiding, not arising or ceasing in accordance with the objects of sound. If it lacked an inherent nature, then discrimination would be entirely non-existent, and one would fall into the *tattva* (Primal Principle) of the heterodox paths;
it is largely due to this that the confused practices of externalists arise. This will be explained further in the following text.
"Clear!

It is like a traveler who stays at an inn; having rested for a short while, he departs and does not remain permanently, yet the one who manages the inn never leaves and is called the master of the inn.
This is also like that: if it were truly your mind, it would have nowhere to go."
What is meant by the nature of non-discrimination apart from sound?

This is not merely the case where the discriminating mind regarding sound ceases its discrimination of my own appearance and becomes non-discriminatory with respect to all forms and marks; it extends even until discrimination is entirely absent—neither form nor emptiness.

The Kosalas and others take "taste" as the principle of ultimate darkness (*tattva*). If one is detached from the conditions of all phenomena and possesses a non-discriminative nature, then your mental essence will each have its own place of return; how then can it be considered the master?

This refers to the discriminating mind. If it does not realize the full nature, then the principle that is the object of cognition and the mind that is the subject of cognition will ultimately be unable to abide together, just as a traveler stops only briefly before departing.
Why, then, [does this mind not abide] before the sound of the Dharma is perceived, after the sound of the Dharma has been perceived, and while the sound of the Dharma is being perceived?
In a fleeting moment, turn back and observe: who is the host of this pavilion? This requires a single awakening.

If you merely recognize the discriminating mind that perceives sounds and forms, then once sounds and forms have vanished, discrimination will also perish. Regarding this state that is neither form nor emptiness, few do not savor it as the "dark principle" (*tattva*).
This is precisely what Kūśala and others did—this is a confused and erroneous practice. Apart from conditions, there is nothing.

As for the statement that "each returns to its nature, which has no master," this is because the nature of discrimination takes the conditions of sensory objects as its guests and fails to realize its own essence;

when separated from these objects, it attains its own self and thus becomes the master. This is merely an arousal of self-recognition within a state of non-awakening; it does not mean that there is truly no master.
△ Section Three: Demonstrating that the Essence of Vision Has No Place of Return; Part Five: First, the Question Regarding the Absence of Return.
Ānanda said: "If my mind-nature has various places to which it returns, then why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, luminous, original mind has no place of return?
I pray only that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."

This "returning" is precisely the "returning" of the eight returns discussed below. This "non-returning" is also precisely the "non-returning" of the phrase "who then would there be to return? mentioned below.

Ānanda, although you have already realized through the teaching on the adventitious dust that it is erroneous to have long since falsely identified with the reflected images of conditions, you still employ this conditioned mind while listening to the Dharma at present; therefore, what you have awakened to remains merely grasping.
The Buddha’s definitive intent has not yet been resolved within one's own self; thus, this mind-nature would have to return to the Dharma-sound and could not abide permanently.
Therefore, he again requests the place where the wondrous, luminous, original mind has nothing to return to. △ Second, showing that the essence of vision is not a reflection.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, as for the fundamental source of the clarity of seeing that you perceive in me—although this seeing is not the wondrous, subtle, and clear mind, it is like a second moon;
it is not a reflection of the moon."
Furthermore, when I say "the essence of the seeing-clarity that you perceive," I am referring to the essence of the seeing that Ānanda perceived at that time when he was looking at the Buddha.
This essence of seeing is called the "bright source" (*mingyuan*) because it illuminates within the sense-organ without giving rise to aversion or attachment;
it is truly the original source of the nature's awakening. However, as it has not yet been fully manifested, it cannot yet be called the "wondrously bright and pure mind. Therefore, it is said:
It is like a second moon. If one discriminates based on an object, it arises when the object is present and ceases when the object departs;

this is what is called a "moon-reflection. Although Ānanda has already realized that the reflection is not the true object, his mind that clings to conditions has not yet been resolved, and he still lingers in discrimination.
Therefore, [the Buddha] again uses the nature of seeing present before him—which does not fall into conceptual calculation—to lead him to recognize it for himself. If...
When illumination is manifested right where it is, that itself is the wondrous, subtle, and brilliant mind; it has no other substance apart from this. III.
Listing the Eight Kinds of Phenomenal Objects:
You should listen attentively. I shall now show you the ground from which there is nothing to be returned. Ānanda, this great lecture hall is wide open.
In the east, when the sun rises in the heavens, there is bright radiance; at midnight during the dark fortnight, when clouds and mist obscure the sky, it is again dark and murky.
Through the gaps of doors and windows, one perceives openness; within the spaces between walls and buildings, one observes obstruction.

In places where distinctions are made, one perceives conditions; throughout the vast emptiness, there is everywhere the nature of space. When the appearance of dense mists gathers, it becomes winding and obscured.
The turbid dust settled and the atmosphere cleared.
He then observed the purity and said, "To seek the nature that cannot be returned, one must first point out the characteristics that can be returned. △ Fourth, showing the eight returns.

Ānanda, you have all observed these various manifestations of transformation. Now I shall cause each of them to return to their original source. What is the original cause? Ānanda, these various transformations:
clarity returns to the solar orb. Why is this? Without the sun there would be no clarity;

clarity is dependent upon the sun, and therefore it returns to the sun. Darkness returns to the dark moon. Penetration returns to doors and windows. Obstruction returns to walls and buildings. Conditions...
When the distinctions dissolve, the stubborn void returns to emptiness; the dense mists return to dust; and the clarity returns to a cloudless sky.
Thus, all that exists within the various worlds does not transcend these categories.
This concludes the enumeration of the eight kinds of returning characteristics, by which the essence of seeing is revealed. △ Fifth, the direct demonstration that there is nothing to return:
"As for the nature of the clarity of your seeing within these eight kinds, toward what would you wish to return?

Why is this? If it were to return to light, then when it is not light, you would no longer see darkness. Although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, your seeing is without distinction. All...

That which can be returned naturally does not belong to you; that which cannot be returned by you—since it is not you, who else could it be? Thus you should know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure.
It is because you have become deluded and distressed that you have lost your original nature and undergone cyclic existence, constantly drifting and drowning within birth and death.
For this reason, the Tathāgata calls you "worthy of compassion."
When you wish to know who it is that should return, point directly and clearly; only then can one speak of various distinctions.
To see no distinction is itself the return of all distinctions. That state of non-distinction—how could it be anyone else? Your own mind is precisely the pointing out of the nature of seeing.
The term "original" (ben) refers to the nature of seeing. Tracing this nature of seeing back to its source, it is originally that which is revealed as wondrous clarity.
If one recognizes its point of return in the very place where it is, one will not be misled by discrimination. To miss this point is to lose one's original ground;
thus, one is constantly adrift and submerged, and is therefore to be pitied.

Upon hearing this, Ānanda realized that the natures of his mind and heart each had their respective points of return; he was suddenly enlightened and saw that these very discriminations also returned to the sound of the Dharma.
Because he knew for himself that what he was currently manifesting was but a mind conditioned by objects, he deeply felt the root of doubt within him.
Being unable to obscure itself, he again requested instruction regarding the wondrously luminous, primordial mind. The World-Honored One said:

"As for the eight kinds of seeing you perceive—the clarity and essence of seeing—whom do you intend to return them to? This is to manifest the nature of the sense-faculties by departing from all marks;
it may also be to point to the consciousness-mind by departing from discrimination. Yet you say that the natures of these minds each have a place to which they must return. Why is this?"
One should know that there are eight kinds of seeing-nature. As one sees, so one knows, without falling into discursive thought.

Although none of these have yet been brought to full illumination or resolved into their ultimate source, they are nonetheless direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) within the context of those various deluded consciousnesses. What the Sage intends to grasp is precisely this:

its essence and function resemble the wondrous, subtle, pure, and luminous nature. This is intended so that it may be recognized spontaneously in the present moment, thereby being identical to the Original Source.
It can be said that with a slight application of skillful means, one may swiftly realize Bodhi.

Inferring from this, we know that what the world calls "attaining" within the mind while acting upon phenomena consists of two divergent paths—clarity and obscurity, expansion and contraction—resulting in a chaotic state of interruption and continuity.
These are all instances where the mind-nature has its respective objects of return.
The above ten points have finished examining the conditioned mind to demonstrate that the seeing-nature has no object of return. △ Eleven: Examining the sense-objects to reveal the seeing.
This is divided into six parts. First, distinguishing that the object is not the self:
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no source from which it returns, how can I know that it is my true nature?"
Previously, you refuted the notion that the perceiving mind is the object of awakening; now I request to know the wondrous clarity that is awakened to.
How can this very essence of seeing immediately be the wondrously luminous true nature? Please let me understand this, for I still do not dare to identify it as such myself.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "I now ask you this: at present, you have not yet attained the purity of the outflows-free state (*anāsrava*).
Yet, by relying on the Buddha's spiritual power, you see the First Dhyāna without obstruction. Aniruddha sees Jambudvīpa as if looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of his hand;
the various Bodhisattvas see hundreds of thousands of worlds; and the Tathāgatas of the ten directions exhaustively perceive even the finest motes of dust."
The pure land is such that there is nowhere it does not illuminate; yet sentient beings, though seeing through with clarity, do not exceed a mere inch or two.

The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "According to the Lesser Vehicle, a *śrāvaka* arhat sees a small chiliocosm. Now, Ānanda has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), which is precisely the limit of a small chiliocosm.

That one who has attained the first fruit is able to see [so far] is due to the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*). If he were to see by his own power alone, he would see only a single realm of the first dhyāna."
It can indeed be accomplished through one's own power. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Aniruddha replied to King Śuddhāvāsa:
'I see this Sahā world-system of Śākyamuni Buddha, a trichiliocosm, as clearly as one gazes at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand.
This refers to Jambudvīpa; it refers to all Jambudvīpas. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "All Jambudvīpas..."
In Jambudvīpa, everyone says that the Buddha is therein. Jambudvīpa derives its name from the *jambu* tree.
The *āmala* fruit resembles a peach or a crabapple; at that time, this was held as the standard for comparison.

One sees a hundred buddha-fields on the first stage (*bhūmi*), a thousand buddha-fields on the second stage, and immeasurable buddha-fields on the tenth stage. Vimalakīrti said: "There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One."
He has attained the true divine eye and constantly abides in samādhi, perceiving all Buddha-lands without dualistic marks.
While those of the two vehicles see while in meditative concentration but do not see when they have emerged from it, the Tathāgata is never not in samādhi and never does not see;
therefore, it is said that he "constantly abides in samādhi. Sentient beings, obstructed by the film of ignorance, do not see external objects; this is because of the multitude [of afflictions].
We were born as peers; thus we have demonstrated that while the breadth and narrowness of what is seen differ, the faculty of the root-nature that perceives remains no different.
Ānanda, let us first observe with you the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings reside, and in the meantime, survey everywhere the waters and lands between them.
Moving through the air, although there are various forms and images of darkness and light, none of them are anything other than the obstructions left behind by the discrimination of external objects.

You should, within this, distinguish between self and other. Now I shall lead you to select, from within the faculty of seeing, what constitutes your own essence and what constitutes external objects.
Ānanda, push to the very source of your vision: from the palaces of the sun and moon, which are external objects and not you, down to the seven golden mountains.
Observe thoroughly and with discernment: although there are various kinds of light, these things are not you. Gradually observe further:
the rising clouds, the flying birds, the moving winds, the stirring dust, the trees, the mountains and rivers, the grasses, the weeds, and all humans and animals—none of these things are you.
"Discerning within what is seen" means discerning among the objects that are perceived. The substance of the self and the forms of things are distinct from one another;
the substance of the self is precisely the nature of seeing. Who is it that causes this discernment? It is the self that discerns for itself.
When it reaches the point where "this object is not you," then it is discerning on your behalf—this is merely the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata. 2. Revealing that Seeing is Not an Object.
Ānanda, although all these various natures of things, whether near or far, differ from one another, they are equally beheld by your faculty of vision, which is pure and clear.

Thus, while the various categories of objects possess their own distinctions, the nature of seeing is without difference. This subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence is truly your own nature of seeing.
Previously, I clearly distinguished the substance and characteristics within my own being; this was intended to lead you back to the realization of your nature.

Furthermore, when I said, "Truly, you have realized your nature," I was causing you to personally take responsibility for it. When you said your vision was "pure and clear," you were merely distinguishing it from the defiled consciousnesses.
Although Ānanda knew that the nature of seeing does not return [to the external], he still did not know it to be his own true nature.
This was because he had not distinguished between the object and the self; thus, he could not suddenly attain realization regarding the essence of seeing.

Indeed, in the daily activities of sentient beings, the body dwells amidst objects, and all that is seen is an object. Even when one attempts to turn back and observe, this is again mixed with deluded consciousness.
Therefore, our World-Honored One specifically pointed to all the phenomena presently before us and said, "These things are not you," decisively forbidding any further perception of them as objects.
He then stated that although the natures of all these phenomena differ, they are equally what is beheld by your pure seeing-essence (*darśana-viśuddha*).
He further caused [you] to know that this seeing-essence is itself pure.
The seeing-nature does not mingle with objects; its fundamental wondrousness is thus.
When both conceptualization and appearances are exhausted, the single, pure true mind is internally realized and known in a single kṣaṇa, without following after discursive discrimination.
If you see this object, then you can also see my seeing. If you see it as being the same [as my seeing], that may be called "seeing me.
When I am not seeing, why do you not see the place where I am not seeing? If you see this non-seeing, it is naturally not the characteristic of that non-seeing.
If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, it is naturally not a material thing; how could it not be yours?
This statement shows that seeing must not be a thing; therefore, it points out that Ānanda is the seer, and because of this, even his non-seeing is likewise Ānanda—it is in no way another entity.
If seeing were a thing, then you would also be able to see my seeing.
It is said that each person has their own seeing and it is impossible for them to see one another's, precisely because that which is visible becomes a thing.
Therefore, [the Master] provisionally grants [Ananda's point] by saying: "If you see this object together with me, then that which sees together with me is what I call 'seeing me.

This, conversely, occurs at the time when I do not see, thereby exhausting the notion that seeing must necessarily be an act of seeing. Thus, he proceeds to discuss both seeing and non-seeing, yet these are all ultimately Ananda himself.
Therefore, he again provisionally grants [the point] by saying: "If you see my non-seeing, then naturally it is not that non-seeing of yours."
This characteristic of seeing—this locus of Ānanda’s vision—is none other than another person. The Master finally concludes by saying:
"If you do not see the place where I do not see, then this place where Ānanda does not see is likewise entirely none other than another person.
The World-Honored One speaks of himself as "I," while speaking on behalf of Ānanda, he refers to him as "that. △ Third, revealing that the object and the self are not intermingled.
Furthermore, at the present moment when you see an object, if you have seen the object and the object has also seen you, their essential natures would become intermingled;
thus, you, I, and all the world would fail to be established as distinct entities.

This statement means that the object and the self are not intermingled; this is proven by the fact that seeing must necessarily not be an object. If seeing were an object, then the object would also be seeing.
You would be able to see the object, and the object would be able to see you. Self and other would be undifferentiated, and their essential natures would become confused and entangled.

Consequently, the distinction between sentient beings and insentient things could not be established. What the world refers to as "sentient beings" and the "receptacle world" (the environment) would simply point to existence [without distinction].
"Sentiment is insentient.
Ānanda, when you see, it is you who see, not I. This seeing-nature is all-pervasive; if it is not you, then who is it?
These are the words of direct instruction. It means that although the nature of seeing is the same, each person experiences it individually, like the single moon reflected in a thousand rivers."
Ten thousand reflections are equally round; you should know this for yourself, as they do not borrow from one another.
Why then do you doubt your own true nature? If you consider your own nature to be unreal and seek reality by relying on me, you are mistaken.
These are words of reproach. When you say your nature is not true, you mean that within your nature there is you, like waves upon the sea, never having been separate or different.
You reside within this nature, yet like a wave looking back toward the sea, you immediately become suspicious.
If you knew that you and I share the same source, each would simply grasp the reality for oneself; with mind and eyes bearing witness together, why should one need to ask others?

It is because, after the arising of the seeing and the seen from self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*), there subsequently appear form and mind. Mind consists of the eight consciousnesses and belongs to the seeing;

form consists of the sense organs and their objects and belongs to the seen. Thus, one knows that the seeing and the seen originally share a single source, and the distinction between object and self is difficult to maintain.
This has been so for a long time. Ānanda was unable to recognize the nature of seeing for himself; this is what is grasped through innate clinging, which has been thus from antiquity to the present.
By attaching to objects, one abandons one's own mind; by turning back to see [the object], one still retains conceptual discrimination.
Unless one thoroughly knows where to return, one will certainly be unable to transcend all phenomena with ease and solitude, like water and stone, appearing as if they were mere forms.
Cast into the void; fundamentally they are not separate, nor do they enter into one another.
This is indeed the realm realized solely by the Great Sage, yet it exists within the daily activities of ordinary people. In what way are seeing forms and hearing sounds different?
The faculty of sight is perfect and complete, manifesting right before one; the nature of hearing is profoundly penetrating, with sounds unmixed. Although this does not rely upon—

In its cultivation and practice, one must also attain it once for oneself. That the Tathāgata repeatedly sets forth these words is because he perceives the difficulty [of realization] and thus emphasizes the ease [of the path].
△ Fourth, the doubt that there are differences in the magnitude of views and whether they are intermittent or continuous.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing must be I and nothing else, then when I and the Tathāgata were observing the precious palace of the Four Heavenly Kings' Supreme Treasury and dwelling in the palaces of the sun and moon, this seeing was all-pervasive, encompassing the entire Sahā world.
Yet when we returned to the vihāra, I saw only the monastery; entering the hall with its pure mind, I beheld only the eaves and corridors. World-Honored One, this seeing is like..."
"It is so. Its substance is originally all-pervasive throughout the entire realm; yet now, within this room, it fills only the room.
Is this a case of shrinking the great into the small? Or is it that the walls and roof have constricted it until it was severed? I do not know where the meaning of this lies.
I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and expound it for me."

Having perceived that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, one must realize it is certainly not something other than oneself. This further leads to doubt regarding the expansion and contraction of the nature of seeing, based on the width or narrowness of what is seen.
"Saha" is translated here as the Land of Endurance; "Gārama" is fully rendered as *saṃghārāma*, which is translated as the Garden of the Assembly.
△ Fifth, showing how external objects leave obstructions, divided into two parts: first, the analogy of the emptiness of a vessel.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All worldly activities, whether great or small, internal or external, each belong to the objective fields before one.
One should not say that the faculty of seeing expands or contracts."

The phrase "each belongs to the external objects" has already resolved the doubt; it serves as an illustration that sentient beings are unable to turn back and see because they are all obstructed by external objects.
What follows below elucidates this principle.
It is like a square vessel, within which a square void is seen. I ask you again: is this square void seen within the square vessel fixedly square, or is it not fixedly square?
If it were fixedly square, then when a round vessel is placed there instead, the void should not become round.
If it were not fixed, then when placed within a square vessel, there would be no "square space. You say that you do not know where this principle resides;
yet such is the nature of principles—how could they have a location?
If it were fixed in one direction, it would be limited by its own vessel-like boundaries. If it were not fixed in one direction, then emptiness would have a substantial body.

By this analogy, one sees that the nature of seeing is not obstructed by objects; it can also conform to objects to establish its norms. How could it be restricted by the dimensions of the dharma-realm?

The "nature of meaning" (*yìxìng*) is precisely the meaning of the "nature of seeing. Why is it said that when the nature of seeing is thus, it does not abide according to objects? It does not abide [in accordance with them].
...Furthermore, △ Second, regarding the removal of the squareness or roundness of the vessel:

Ānanda, if you wish to cause [the space] to enter into a state that is neither square nor round, you need only remove the squareness of the vessel; the substance of space itself has no directionality.
One should not say that one must further remove the location of the directional characteristics of the empty space.
That which has no squareness or roundness is emptiness; this serves as a metaphor for seeing one's nature. "Entering" carries the meaning of realization and entry.
If you wish to realize and enter into seeing your nature, you need only remove the perceptions of external objects (*pratyaya*), and seeing your nature will be as it naturally is.

There is no need to further eliminate the location of the square or round characteristics of empty space, because empty space exists within square or round vessels and is always manifested in conjunction with those square or round forms.
One doubts the void. The so-called "Mind-Seal" is to discard both the false and the true simultaneously. How could one know that seeing manifests in response to objects?
Objects come and go of their own accord; it is not that seeing itself has existence or non-existence. Since there is neither presence nor absence, there is no need for removal.

If, as you ask, when entering a room the seeing faculty contracts and becomes small, then when looking up at the sun, would you not have to stretch the seeing faculty out to equal the face of the sun?
Furthermore, if walls and houses can obstruct and sever the seeing faculty, yet a small hole is pierced through them, how could there be no trace of its continuity?
This interpretation is not correct.
These words show that what is seen cannot be contracted, nor can it be extended; what is seen cannot be severed, nor is it continuous.
The above five points conclude the demonstration of the obstructions left by external objects. △ Sixth, the demonstration of the transformation of objects.
All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded by taking themselves to be external objects; they have lost their original mind and are turned about by those objects.
Therefore, within this state, they perceive the great as small.

The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, once it falls into the cycle of manifestation, appears as both mind and form. Being deluded regarding original luminosity, all that is perceived becomes mere objects.
At first, the environment arises from the mind; subsequently, the mind follows the environment. Thus, the nature of empty space remains in vain.
The views of squareness and roundness are difficult to eliminate; such perceptions of large and small have existed from the very beginning.

If one can master objects, then one’s body and mind will be as perfectly luminous as those of the Tathāgata; remaining unmoved within the site of enlightenment, one can, upon the tip of a single hair, universally contain the lands of the ten directions.
To "transform objects" means to transform all things into oneself. All phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind and lack inherent nature;
they are but the single mind. To simply be free from conceptual discrimination is itself *prajñā*. When *prajñā* is all-pervasive, body and mind are perfectly luminous.
When the mind is perfectly luminous, phenomena are subsumed within principle; it is eternally clear and eternally tranquil. [Thus one is unmoved by] the eight winds.
Without wavering, the body is perfectly luminous; thus, essence and principle are entirely phenomena. One is all, and all is one.

The lands upon the tip of a single hair appear vast and expansive before one, not through the employment of supernatural power, but because the Dharma-nature naturally accommodates and encompasses them.
In short, Ānanda, the inability to recognize the nature of seeing for oneself is entirely due to being obstructed by external objects.
When the World-Honored One previously pointed out that "seeing is you," he was now clarifying that the four characters "being turned by objects" constitute the root cause of this ailment.
Once this ailment is removed, the nature of seeing becomes all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing the entire Dharma-realm; it is attained through a single act of inward reflection.
It is so. Only because one cannot turn the gaze inward, this seeing-nature sees only what is before one. When what is before one is vast and empty, one takes it to be seeing the great;
when what is before one is narrow and confined, one takes it to be seeing the small. Thus, one does not realize that it is the objects themselves that are vast and empty or narrow and confined.
All belong to the external objects before one. It is like seeing the void within a square vessel as square; when another round vessel is placed there, one sees the void as round.

Yet one does not realize that both squareness and roundness belong to the vessels themselves, for the void has neither square nor round. Thus, one should awaken to the fact that knowing and seeing have no size;
simply being able to refrain from following the knowing and seeing that arise from external objects is called "transforming things. This is immediate and perfect.
[The Master] said: "It is clear. Although it resides within the bodies and minds of sentient beings, it is no different from that of the Buddha.
The above two sections have concluded the manifestation of the faculty and the vision. △ Third, the designation that the nature of vision is free from "is" and "is not," divided into five parts.
First, the doubt regarding the presence of the nature of vision before one.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this essence of vision is necessarily my wondrous nature, and if this wondrous nature is now present before me, then this seeing must be my true self. What, then, are my current body and mind?"

This wondrous clarity that has been realized is as yet not presumed by me to be my own, for it arises entirely from the discerning causal mind of the one who realizes; its discrimination remains unsettled.
Although I have received the Tathāgata’s pointing out that the nature of seeing is non-reverting, the sensory objects still present obstacles, and the body and mind of discrimination persist.
Thus, the nature of seeing before one is merely suspended in abstraction. If one were to grasp at what is presently manifest, on the contrary—

As for the rest—my current self—the illness lies in the fact that the "thing" and the "self" have not yet merged. When right and wrong alternate, there are various capacities for entry, which immediately contravene the pure awakened mind.
Once one is free from views and conditions and arrives at the single true Dharma-realm, wishing to bestow ultimate [realization], I shall briefly borrow this to meet the needs of those present.

Now, you claim that the mind and body are distinguished as having reality. Yet, in your view, there is no distinct differentiation of my own body. If my mind were truly real, it would cause me to see it;
if the nature of seeing were truly the self, then the body would not be the self. How does this differ from the objection raised by the Tathāgata earlier?
Objects are able to see me; I only pray that you will bestow great compassion upon me to enlighten my unawakened state.
Being unable to recognize my own wondrous clarity, I continue to differentiate between body and mind, still acting as a sovereign master—what is called "having a substantial self.

Although I have realized that the nature of seeing has nothing from which it can be returned, it manifests in response to objects; yet, lacking non-discriminative lucidity, it does not function as its true utility.
The nature of seeing that has been awakened is the guest, while the discrimination of body and mind remains the host.
The host can discern the guest, but the guest cannot discern the host. To take this [discrimination] as the self means that the body and mind are not the self;
thus, the seeing and the body and mind are divided into two entities. This is what is meant by saying that "objects can see me," which most clearly demonstrates its inability to recognize itself.
[End of section on] the ear. △ Second, pointing out that there is no such seeing. This is divided into two parts.
First, indicating the characteristics and interrogating the seeing. The Buddha told Ānanda: "Now, what you say—that 'seeing' is in front of you—is not true.

If it were real and you truly saw it in front of you, then this essence of seeing would have a specific location and could not be without a point of indication. Furthermore, right now, as for [the space] before you..."
Seated in the Jeta Grove, he surveyed the groves, the streams, and the halls, reaching upward as far as the sun and moon, with the Ganges River directly before him.
Now, in the presence of my lion throne, you point out and describe these various signs: that which is "grove" refers to the forest.
That which is luminous is the sun; that which obstructs is the wall; that which is unobstructed is space. Thus it extends even to grass, trees, and the finest hairs;
though they differ in size, as long as they possess form, there is nothing to which one cannot point. If you insist that this seeing must be present before you now—
"You should point it out clearly with your hand. Ānanda, you should know this: if space were the seeing, since it has already become the seeing, what then is space?
If a material object were the seeing, since it has already become the seeing, what then is the material object?"
"You may minutely peel away and analyze the myriad phenomena to extract the essence of the brilliant, pure, and wondrous faculty of seeing.
Point it out and show it to me, so that it is as clearly understood and free from confusion as those other objects."

The prior view is exhausted by the realization that there is no "is. One then seeks to strip away what has been awakened to by exhausting the notion of "no-not-is," ultimately stripping away the capacity for awakening itself.
When the perceived nature of awakening is suddenly forgotten and the discrimination of the one who awakens ceases, the Dharma-realm manifests before one;
with neither "is" nor "not-is," this is finally the ultimate consummation. This is the initial exhaustion.
This refers to the view previously mentioned. "To peel open" means to analyze and dissect. **2. Answering that there is no such view.** Ānanda said:

"World-Honored One, here in this multi-storied lecture hall, reaching as far as the Ganges River, looking up at the sun and moon, pointing with my hand, and wherever my eyes gaze—everything I point to is an object;
there is nothing that is the 'seeing' itself. World-Honored One, it is as the Buddha has taught.

[The Buddha] said: "How much less could I—a disciple with outflows who is but a beginner—and even up to a Bodhisattva, discern from before the myriad phenomena a refined vision that is distinct from all things and possesses a separate self-nature? The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is."

In the daily activities of people, whatever is seen or heard appears momentarily based upon sound and form, like a flash of lightning that enters the mind and is clearly perceived with distinct discrimination.
This nature of discrimination has long been clung to as the "self-mind" and as the "substantial self.
Yet, when one suddenly causes it to depart from all such discriminations and turns back to point toward what is seen and heard—though [the process continues]...
That which was attained through awakening remains as it was before. Though one wishes to relinquish body and mind, they are difficult to forget as they persist within me.
If one intends to investigate this "me" that discriminates and is nothing other than this, one must first suddenly set aside the previously taught view of the nature of seeing.

Only after the Tathāgata’s actions have been exhausted and all indications have ceased will body and mind immediately settle into their former state, becoming tranquil as they were originally. As for all things...

All phenomena and forms exist solely through seeing. If this seeing were itself pointed out as being the same as the objects, then from what would the objects manifest, and to what would the seeing adhere?
To point to anything at all is simply to point to an object; it is precisely because the whole is contained within the object that such seeing does not exist.
If one remains within delusion, one cannot see for oneself; even if one attains profound awakening, it may still be no different from that of ordinary beings. This principle is subtle and profound;
were it not for a Bodhisattva, one could not realize or know it. Although Ānanda outwardly appeared as a Śrāvaka, if he had [truly understood] this...
Can this not be seen in general?

Regarding the first two fingers, there is no such "seeing" at all. △ Third, regarding the third finger, there is no "non-seeing. This is divided into two parts. First, granting that there is no "seeing," one further interrogates why it is not "seeing."
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda: "As you have said, there is no visual essence that exists apart from all objects with a separate self-nature;
thus, among the objects you point to, there is no such thing as 'seeing. Now I tell you further:
as you and the Tathāgata sit in the Jeta Grove, look again at the groves and gardens, even down to the sun and moon and their various distinct forms—therein, there is certainly no 'seeing'."
I have carefully accepted what you have pointed out. You have further clarified which among these various things is not "seeing.
This first confirms that there is no such thing as "is-ness" (being). Only then do you interrogate again regarding the absence of "non-is-ness" (not-being).

When there is no "is-ness" of seeing, that which was realized is dissolved; when there is no "non-is-ness" of seeing, the conditioned mind is suddenly exhausted. This unsurpassed Dharma-seal will be evident from the following text.
△ Second, the answer that there is nothing which is not seeing.
Ānanda said: "I truly see this entire Jeta Grove, yet I do not know what within it is not seeing.
Why is this? If the trees were not seeing, how could one see the trees? If the trees were themselves seeing, how then could they be called 'trees'? Thus it was said.
"Furthermore, if emptiness were not seeing, how could one see emptiness? If emptiness were itself seeing, how could it be empty?
I further reflected that within these myriad phenomena, there is nothing that does not manifest through seeing. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
It is like what is seen in a dream, which one takes to be truly existent things; yet upon waking, one realizes it was all a manifestation of one's own dream.
How could one say that what has not yet been awakened to is "self" and not "things"? It is simply that there is no one to perceive them.
The world appearing before us is likewise like a dream; it is certainly nothing other than this. Upon examining it closely, there is nothing further that confronts or corresponds with a self.
It is not that being fully awakened precludes being within the midst of a full dream; rather, it acts as the causal condition for awakening from all dreams.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata clearly perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they are seen by those within the triple world, without any error.
If one can clearly perceive that there is nothing that is not seeing, then regarding the triple world manifest before one, what should be done?

Contemplate this: there can be no further names or models. First, exhaustively investigate that which is "not the view" (*na-asti-dṛṣṭi*) in order to dissolve the views that stand before you, so that they are not seen as distinct from things.
Then, exhaustively investigate that which is "not non-view" (*na-na-asti-dṛṣṭi*), so that one may know that these distinct discernments are not separate from oneself.
If one can, at this moment, let go of everything all at once, then one will be established in the very place where it is.

The mind is fundamentally non-dual with [the nature of reality]; both are for the purpose of the subsequent text’s statement that there is neither "is" nor "is not. First, this single point clears away all obstructions.
The above concludes the three points indicating that there is nothing that is not seeing. △ Fourth, Mañjuśrī’s request to clarify the two kinds [of seeing], divided into three parts.
At first, the great assembly was struck with awe and trepidation.

Among them were those who were not yet *aśaikṣas* (those beyond training); upon hearing these words from the Buddha, they were utterly bewildered, unable to comprehend the beginning or end of their meaning, and for a moment they were seized with fear, losing their composure.
The self that perceives nature is suddenly eliminated, and the objects of discrimination are likewise transformed.

Being neither self nor object, this is what is realized by great wisdom; it cannot be discerned by a beginner. Therefore, there is a state of bewilderment where one does not know the beginning or end of this meaning.
This is precisely what the following text says: "If it were something seen, there would be something pointed out; if it were not something seen, there would be nothing gazed upon. (2)
Section Two: The Buddha Comforts Them with Words of Truth.
The Tathāgata, perceiving that their spirits were distressed and trembling, gave rise to a heart of compassion and comforted Ānanda as well as the great assembly.
"O sons of good family, the Unsurpassed Dharma King speaks words of truth; he teaches according to reality, without deception or falsehood.
This is not the fourfold evasive discourse on immortality of Makkhali Gosāla. You should contemplate this with careful attention, so as not to fail in your sincere longing."

About to expound the Great Dharma, he first extols the Buddha’s words to strengthen their faith. The Tathāgata has five modes of speech. Zizhong says: that which is without falsehood is called "true" (*satya*);

that which accords with principle is called "real" (*bhūta*); that which does not change is called "thus" (*tathā*); that which corresponds between mind and object is called "non-deceptive" (*amṛṣā*);

and that which foresees what is yet to come is called "non-false" (*ananyathā*). The four kinds of evasive equivocation refer to such claims as "both changing and constant," "both arising and... [and so forth].
It is also extinguished; it both exists and does not exist; it both increases and decreases. To maintain both sides is to lack decisiveness.

To clarify the Buddha’s intent, one must transcend both affirmation and negation, and cast away both mind and objects to reveal the true, wondrous nature, which is fundamentally free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Those who feel deep longing should grieve for their own yearning and reflect with utmost sincerity; do not bring disgrace upon the vision of the Tathāgata.
Out of compassion for them. △ Thirdly, Mañjuśrī formally requests the revelation of the teaching.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, out of pity for the fourfold assembly, rose from his seat amidst the great multitude, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, this great assembly...”
Wu (Awakening) explains that the Tathāgata revealed two kinds of refined vision (*prajñā-dṛṣṭi*) regarding the meaning of whether form and emptiness are "is" or "is not.

This passage originates from Mañjuśrī, who borrowed great wisdom to assist in elucidating the Great Dharma; it is not something that can be achieved by the provisional, limited capacity of the Śrāvakas.
"Refined vision of form and emptiness" refers to the discernment of vision upon form and emptiness mentioned above. "Two kinds" refers to "is" and "is not."
This is not the meaning. This means that there is no such thing as "seeing. As it says below: "If it were seeing, there should be something pointed out.
This is not the meaning of "not-seeing" being non-existent. As it says below: "If it were not seeing, there should be nothing beheld. Yet, when looking at each other, one sees.
World-Honored One, if these previously mentioned objects such as form and emptiness are what is seen, there should be something pointed out;
if they are not what is seen, there should be nothing beheld. Yet now we do not know where this principle leads, and thus we are filled with alarm and fear.

It is not that our past roots of goodness are meager or slight; we only pray that the Tathāgata’s great compassion will illuminate whether these various objects and phenomena are [identical to] this...
As for this seeing-essence, what is it originally? Within it, there is neither "is" nor "is not. What is it originally?
It silently contains the fundamentally pure, wondrous, and luminous essence of Bodhi. To know that [all] is of one single substance, then object and self are merged into a whole;
it cannot be expressed by words and cannot be known by consciousness. Therefore it is said: "Within it, there is neither..."
"Neither 'is' nor 'is not'.

The above four sections conclude Mañjuśrī’s request for the revelation of these two aspects. △ Fifth, the correct demonstration that the nature of seeing is devoid of "is" and "is not," divided into three parts.
First, reconciling that the characteristics of seeing are fundamentally *bodhi*.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly: "The Tathāgatas and great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, while abiding in their own *samādhi*, [realize this].
The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) says: "If one has not yet abided in *samādhi*, one does not believe that there are no phenomena outside the mind, because of conceptual discrimination."

Wisdom: although the mind of understanding does not perish, it merely takes external objects as its condition and has not yet abided in its own ground. "Great Bodhisattvas" refers to those from the tenth ground onward.

The *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* states: "The Buddha says that this samādhi cannot be known by those below the ninth ground or by the followers of the Two Vehicles. This samādhi is precisely the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*.
The seeing and its objects, as well as the perceived characteristics, are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.
This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. How could there be "is" or "is not" within them?

Seeing the sense organ (indriya) is like pointing at the root; seeing the object (viṣaya) conditioned by it is like pointing at the dust; perceiving the characteristics is like pointing at consciousness (vijñāna).

These three—the organ, the object, and consciousness—are like an illusion, devoid of arising and ceasing, because they lack both intrinsic nature and the absence of nature. All things in their totality are but mind alone; this is what the wise have realized. Within this, there is no conceptualization;
it is entirely free from speech and thought. 2. The instruction to Mañjuśrī to manifest the non-dual characteristic.
“Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: Is there another Mañjuśrī like you who is also Mañjuśrī, or is there no such Mañjuśrī?
“Thus it is, World-Honored One. I am the true Mañjuśrī; there is no such Mañjuśrī. Why is this?
If there were such a one, there would be two Mañjuśrīs. However, today I am not without being Mañjuśrī; within this, there is truly neither ‘is’ nor ‘is-not.’”

By this analogy, when the true, essential, wondrously enlightened nature of clarity first falls [into conceptualization]...
To speak of "mind" is itself to fall into delusion and falsehood. △ Third, the correct elucidation of the nature that transcends right and wrong. The Buddha said:
"This wondrous clarity of vision and these various empty objects are likewise so. Originally, they are the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind.
It is through delusion that they appear as form, emptiness, hearing, and seeing, like a second moon. Who created it?"
Regarding this moon, who then is not the moon? Mañjuśrī, there is but one true moon; within it, there is inherently neither "this moon" nor "not this moon.
Sight, emptiness, and dust are fundamentally the wondrously luminous true mind. Thus, to point to them as "form and emptiness" or as "hearing and seeing" is entirely a sudden, deluded outburst.
Since you speak of a "second moon," and ask who is right and who is wrong, then—
Know that sentient beings manifest before you; as faculties and objects interact, they are clearly apparent in their very place. Who can determine right from wrong?
A blink of an eye and it is missed—this is what constitutes "pressing one's eyes."
Therefore, when you now observe the eyes and their objects, and variously manifest them, this is called deluded thought (*vikalpa*). You are unable to discern within them what is and what is not.
These various manifestations are like saying, "This is form and emptiness," or "This is hearing and seeing. Since it is not thus, it should...
What kind of contemplation should be practiced? The wise person, regarding this matter, should naturally understand it clearly beyond the distinction of right and wrong.
Because of this truly refined, wondrous, and luminous nature of awareness, you are able to transcend the distinction between "this" and "not-this."
Wang Dingshun said: "To say that pointing out the finger is not the finger is what is meant by 'seeing the moon and forgetting the finger.

Wēn-líng and Xuě-làng both explain this by taking the finger as a metaphor for the finger, which only increases entanglement. How could the *Zhuāngzǐ* serve as an analogy for the unsurpassed true exposition?
It is evident that they have simply lost their mindfulness."
The seer and the objects of seeing are like flowers in the sky. This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi.
For all Tathāgatas and great Bodhisattvas dwelling in samādhi, their essence is inherently thus;
it is originally devoid of the two characteristics of right and wrong. Ānanda was unable to recognize the nature of his own seeing; thus, at the outset, he was obstructed by external objects.
Since the seeing of one's nature has already occurred, this seeing and its objects of perception cannot be like flowers in the sky.
Because they cannot be like flowers in the sky, hearing and seeing are not exhausted; form and emptiness clash together.
Furthermore, how could one then dwell securely in the pure clarity of Bodhi, like a flower in a mirror or a tree reflected in water, remaining vast and detached beyond right and wrong? This—

As the ancients have said: "The mirage and the flower in the sky do not fall within the categories of existence or non-existence. This profoundly mysterious principle must be realized through a single moment of awakening;
it cannot be conveyed through words or speech.

The preceding three sections have concluded the demonstration that the nature of seeing is free from being and non-being. △ Fourth, the refutation of causality and spontaneity to reveal that seeing perceives the true reality.
This section is divided into seven parts. First: the doubt that the nature of awareness is identical to the spontaneity of the *puruṣa* (the divine self).
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma King has said: that which perceives conditions pervades the ten directions;
it is profoundly still and eternally abiding, its nature being neither arising nor ceasing."

Wenling says: "Awakened cognition (*jueyuan*) is precisely the seeing-nature (*jianxing*). Its ability to perceive light and darkness, penetration and obstruction, and its universal engagement with all things, is what was previously called 'the seeing-nature is all-pervasive,' and also 'the body and mind are perfectly luminous, universally containing the lands.
This awakened cognition pervading the ten directions is that which is profoundly still and eternally abiding."
What difference is there between this and the "Ultimate Truth" (tattva) discussed with the former brahmin Śvāgata, or the various non-Buddhist schools such as those who smear themselves with ashes,
who claim that a true self exists and pervades the ten directions?

The non-Buddhists do not penetrate the true nature of Consciousness-Only. They mistakenly take that which is manifested as an object-like appearance through the transformation of consciousness to be a real self—the sovereign of the seventh [consciousness] and the perceiver of objects by the sixth—pervading all places.

This is like confusing it with the True Awakening that encompasses the ten directions. They do not realize that their posited "Primordial Darkness" (*ādikṣaya*) from which awakening arises is none other than these eight consciousnesses.
Failing to realize the state of deluded movement as the mark of karma, they take this non-awakening to be the "Dark Principle" (Tattva) and this deluded movement as the "Divine Self" (Ātman).

Thus, they are deluded regarding the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature and fall into the affliction of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi). Wandering and shifting everywhere, they are nothing more than subject to birth and extinction;
their practice of self-immolation is merely the survival of the lineage of Śabikāra.
The World-Honored One also once expounded this meaning on Mount Laṅkā for the sake of Mahāmati and others.
Those non-Buddhists always speak of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), whereas I speak of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); it is not within their realm.
In the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the Buddha taught that dharmas arise through causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in order to refute the heterodox views of spontaneous origination (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, this was taught in accordance with the capacities of worldly practitioners and does not pertain to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, there subsequently arises further doubt regarding these causes and conditions.

I now observe that this nature of awakening is spontaneous; it is neither born nor extinguished. It is far removed from all false and inverted views, appearing as if it were not produced by causes and conditions.

How may I instruct others regarding this spontaneity so that they do not fall among the various heterodox paths, but instead attain the wondrous, luminous nature of true awakening and the authentic mind?
Regarding the phrase "How can one show this to that spontaneity so that it does not enter among the various heterodoxies," it should be read as a single breath [of thought].
This means that this seeing-nature is naturally all-pervasive and appears not to be produced by causes and conditions; the intent is that it is identical to spontaneity itself. Therefore, it says:
"How can one show this to that spontaneity so that it may be distinguished and not enter among the various heterodoxies? △ Second.

"To demonstrate that it is not spontaneous, the Buddha told Ānanda: 'I have now thus revealed these skillful means and spoken the truth to you. Yet you still do not realize it, and you remain deluded, taking it to be spontaneous.
Ānanda, if it were truly spontaneous, one would necessarily be able to clearly discern the essential substance of that spontaneity.'"
To cite collateral examples and employ indirect metaphors is called "expedient means" (*upāya*); to reach the ultimate non-duality is called "reality" (*tattva*).

To say that the Buddha reveals them is to state that both the provisional and the real are fully present. This refers to discernment; it means one should investigate the essence of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). If this self-essence were non-existent...
Thus, the existence or non-existence of the *puruṣa* (the divine self) is established or refuted.
You should now observe within this wondrously luminous vision: what constitutes its own nature? Does this vision take light as its own nature?
Does it take darkness as its own nature? Does it take space as its own nature? Or does it take obstruction as its own nature? Ānanda, if light were its own nature, it should not...
One sees darkness. If, moreover, space were taken as its own essence, one should not see obstructions.
Likewise, if the various characteristics such as darkness were taken as its own essence, then at the time of light, the nature of seeing would be annihilated; how then could one see the light?
This statement shows that the nature of seeing has no self-substance. If it had a self-substance, it could not enter into others;
if it did not enter, it could not be pervasive; and if it entered everything, it could not constitute itself as a self. △ Third, the doubt regarding causes and conditions.
Ānanda said, "If this wondrous nature of seeing is certainly not spontaneous, I have now discerned that it arises through causes and conditions.
Yet my mind is still not clear; I ask the Tathāgata: how does this principle accord with the nature of causes and conditions?"
Ānanda had originally doubted that things arise spontaneously; now, having seen this refuted, he raises the principle of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Since the Tathāgata has previously taught the meaning of causes and conditions as being established as a matter of course, he asks: "In what sense does this accord with the nature of causes and conditions?
△ Fourth, showing that it is not [arisen from] causes and conditions, and concluding by demonstrating the detachment from names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
The Buddha said, "You speak of causes and conditions. I shall ask you again: as you now see, this seeing-nature manifests before you.
Does this seeing exist because of light? Does it exist because of darkness? Does it exist because of space? Or does it exist because of obstruction? Ānanda, [the Buddha asked].
If it exists because of light, one should not perceive darkness; if it exists because of darkness, one should not perceive light.
This applies even further to space and obstruction, which are analogous to light and darkness. Furthermore, Ānanda, this seeing also depends upon light in order to exist.

There is seeing conditioned by darkness; there is seeing conditioned by space; there is seeing conditioned by obstruction. Ānanda, if seeing existed conditioned by space, it should not see obstruction.
If seeing existed conditioned by obstruction, it should not see space. This applies likewise to being conditioned by light or darkness, which are the same as space and obstruction.
You should know that this wondrously bright, essential awareness is neither caused nor conditioned, nor is it spontaneous, nor is it non-existent.
It is spontaneous. There is neither "not" nor "not-not," and there is neither "is" nor "is-not. It is free from all marks and is identical with all phenomena.
Why do you now attempt to apply your mind to it, seeking to differentiate it through the conventional, worldly names and signs of conceptual proliferation?
It is like trying to grasp and rub empty space with the palm of your hand; it only increases your own fatigue. How can empty space ever be seized according to your grasping?
What you now call the "seer" is precisely the nature of seeing manifest before you. Is it the cause or the condition?
This is posed for the purpose of investigation and refutation; therefore, it is asked: does this seeing exist because of light and so forth, or does it exist conditioned by light and so forth?
If this illumination does not exist because of light, nor does it depend upon light, then this seeing is clearly neither caused nor conditioned.
Even when one exhaustively investigates causes and conditions, it is also not something that arises spontaneously. It is free from all marks yet identical to all phenomena;

like a mani jewel reflecting the five colors, it is neither identical to them nor separate from them. Within the single truth of the Dharma-realm, there remains only the obstruction of this [subject-object] seeing.
△ Five: Further Doubts Regarding Causes and Conditions.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if the wondrous nature of awakening is neither cause nor condition, why does the World-Honored One constantly proclaim to the bhikṣus that the nature of seeing possesses four kinds of conditions—namely, the condition of space, the condition of light, the condition of the mind, and the condition of..."
"The eye. What is the meaning of this?

Ānanda initially suspected it was spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Having received this instruction, he considered that the teaching on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is based upon the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and must be without error.
Now, having again received this refutation, he cites the words of the Sage to seek definitive discernment. △
Sixth, he again refutes both causes-and-conditions and spontaneity to demonstrate that the nature of seeing is free from the four marks.
The Buddha said: "Ānanda, what I have spoken regarding the various characteristics of worldly causes-and-conditions is not the ultimate truth."

Because they do not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they fail to clarify the mind's eye within emptiness, thereby establishing themselves within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not realize this;
they believe that all worlds exist spontaneously through a primal nature (*pradhāna*), and that their essence is inherently so.

The Tathāgata specifically refutes this by means of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), asserting that existence arises from delusion and does not exist by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*). However, awakening lies in...
Within delusion, even when manifesting illumination, there is neither the ultimate nor the conventional.

Therefore, what follows uses the faculty of seeing to repeatedly investigate and clarify that seeing has no cause and seeing has no object; only then does it lead one to self-awakening at that very spot—what is called "seeing the seeing."
"Ānanda, I ask you again: when people of the world say, 'I am able to see,' what do they mean by 'seeing' and what do they mean by 'not seeing'?
Ānanda replied: People of the world rely upon the light of the sun, the moon, or a lamp to perceive various forms; this is called 'seeing.
