If these three kinds of light were absent, then one would be unable to see."
The sun, moon, and lamps are what make seeing manifest; it is not that seeing exists only after the sun, moon, and lamps.
If non-Buddhists cannot produce vision independently of light, they are the same as worldly people and consequently fall into the error of nihilism.
Ānanda, if it were called "not seeing" simply because there is no light, then one should not see darkness. If one necessarily sees darkness, this is merely the absence of light;
how can it be called "not seeing"? Ānanda, if it is when it is dark that one does not see light, it is for this reason that it is called "not seeing."
Now, when in the presence of light, one does not perceive the characteristic of darkness; this too is called "not seeing. Thus, both of these characteristics are equally termed "not seeing.
Furthermore, if these two characteristics were to mutually suppress one another, it would not mean that your nature of seeing momentarily ceases to exist within them.
If this is so, then you should know that in both cases it is actually "seeing"; how then could it be called "not seeing"?

Brightness and darkness alternate and supplant one another; it is not that seeing momentarily ceases to exist. This demonstrates that seeing is not caused by conditions. This is analogous to a blind person perceiving darkness:
the former demonstrates that seeing does not belong to the eye, while this demonstrates that seeing does not depend upon objects. The intent in each case is revealed through its manifestation.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should now know this: when seeing light, the seeing is not the light; when seeing darkness, the seeing is not the darkness;
when seeing emptiness, the seeing is not the emptiness; and when seeing obstruction, the seeing is not the obstruction.
This is not a matter of clarity or darkness, penetration or obstruction; it is intended altogether to demonstrate that seeing does not exist through causes and conditions.

Since it is not produced by causes and conditions, this nature of seeing does not arise from external objects. Furthermore, one perceives darkness as being the same as light, which further confirms that seeing does not follow the sense organs.
When seeing is manifested by relying upon the organs, then all appearances of darkness can never obscure it. Regarding this, the wise person—
This can give rise to awakening. Therefore, the text below immediately presents the "seeing of seeing. 7.

Directly showing the true mark of the seeing of seeing, which accomplishes four meanings: You should further know that at the time of the seeing of seeing, seeing is not [ordinary] seeing; seeing is already free from seeing.
"Seeing" (*jian*) cannot be reached by [ordinary] vision.

The upper "seeing" (*jian*) refers to awakening; this is what is called "initial awakening" (*shijue*). The lower "seeing" (*jian*) refers to seeing light, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction, yet that which is neither light, nor darkness, nor empty, nor obstructed.
This is the fivefold direct perception (*pañca-pratyakṣa*). Since it is not restricted to the sense organs, and yet is not...

As for the objective realm, it is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; how could it not be manifest? Yet, as long as one has not attained awakening, even though it still dwells within the faculties while detached from sense objects, it remains merely a conventional flow.

How can the dwelling within the faculties and detachment from sense objects of one who has awakened be equated with the dwelling within the faculties and detachment from sense objects of one who has not yet awakened?
Since this dwelling within the faculties and detachment from sense objects of one who has awakened is still...
If one is separated from the sense-bases (āyatana) and objects (viṣaya) that have not yet awakened, then those unawakened sense-bases and objects can never be reached.
It is therefore appropriate that one should always remain within liberation, yet instead remains confined to the sense-faculties grasping at objects.
Thus we know that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is constantly manifest before us; yet, in a mere flash, it is missed, and one immediately enters into conceptual discrimination. Suddenly—

Upon encountering conditions that bring realization, one immediately attains the awakening to the nature; this awakening to the nature is none other than original awakening. Since the beginning [of practice] has already merged with the original, the original itself is without name.
How could the single true Dharma-realm be equated with frivolous conceptual proliferation?
Why, then, do you speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and the characteristics of combination? You śrāvakas are narrow-minded, inferior, and lacking in wisdom;
you are unable to penetrate the pure, true reality. I now instruct you: you should contemplate this well and must not grow weary on the sublime path to bodhi.
This is a reprimand and instruction. The true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is according to its own nature: it is neither internal nor external;
it is neither known nor unknown; it is the single nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), beyond both speech and thought.
Regarding the meaning of "seeing seeing," various commentaries hold that the upper seeing constitutes the essence (*tǐ*) and the lower seeing constitutes the function (*yòng*).

From the perspective of the sense organs (*indriya*), it may seem plausible that the lower seeing is the function; however, while in the state of delusion, one is lost to the true nature (*bhūtatathatā*).
How, then, can there be what is called an "essence"? There are also those who hold that the upper seeing is the function and the lower seeing is the essence; yet, within the midst of delusion—
How could its root be designated as its substance? Furthermore, if its substance is currently deluded, how can it possess the function of purity?
Moreover, some take superior views to be true and inferior views to be false; yet if there is that which is true, what exactly is false?
In sum, all [these positions] take the preceding and succeeding passages of the scriptures as their definitive interpretation. For instance, according to this [text], seeing is not illumination.
One then claims that seeing is fundamentally detached from objects. Since seeing is already detached from objects, by reasoning upward from this, there must be an "intrinsic awakening" (xing-jue).

Thus, one takes this superior seeing as the essence (*tī*). Alternatively, if the seeing that is detached from objects and entrusted to the faculties is already identical to true awakening, then there should be the functional activity of wisdom-illumination (*jìzhào*) that reflects back upon its own essence. This, again, takes the superior seeing as the function (*yòng*). Below...

[They claim] that "seeing" is the essence. Or they say that seeing apart from objects is still not the fundamental awakening (xing-jue). [They argue] there must be a true nature to reflect its delusion.
All of these are based on a literal reading of the scriptures to fix the stages of practice, yet they fail to comprehend the principle of delusion and enlightenment.
How could they know that the true nature fundamentally has neither essence nor function? For the awakened, the function resides within the essence; whereas for the deluded—
The essence resides within its function; for that perfect, luminous awareness does not depend on mental ideation. This is what is meant by "function residing within essence.
All sentient beings have lost this fundamental luminosity; though they act all day long, they do not realize it themselves.
This is what is meant by "essence residing within function. If one awakens, one is entirely true in that very place; even if one has not yet awakened, it is ultimately nothing other than this.
There is. The preceding passage concerned vision as distinct from the eye; now it is revealed that vision does not depend on light.

Both are simply the sensory faculties present before sentient beings, which are non-dual in essence with the original awakened nature and non-dual in function. Yet, while within delusion, they exist but are not realized;
for a time they are pointed out as non-existent and further termed "delusive. Therefore, this is now revealed so that awakening may be awaited.
What is called "seeing the seeing" refers to seeing the nature of seeing that is present before one; it fundamentally does not belong to the eye and is inherently detached from sensory objects.

This delusion is considered the point from which initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*) arises. Now, when initial awakening occurs while one is still in a state of non-awakening, it is merely false awakening.
This is because one fails to see that the nature of the faculties present before one is primordially pure, and instead engages in conceptual discrimination based on conditions. This is...

This is called delusion. If one follows this instruction and exhaustively investigates that seeing does not follow the sense organs and that seeing does not depend on objects, then discursive thought will suddenly cease.
Taking this very discursive thought, one returns to discern the nature of the faculties; by harmonizing them according to each situation, one achieves wondrous observation.

Regarding what is called initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*): if one traces its origin, it arises entirely from the fundamental source. When deluded, it is termed "false"; when awakened, it is termed "initial.
Even while not yet awakened, this discerning faculty is certainly not a separate person. It is like being in a state of intoxication, held fast by wine;
suddenly one awakens, yet the person is not something else—the only difference is that the confusion of intoxication has been lost. It is also like a dream, where [the false]...
When one perceives an external object and even reaches the state of cognition, where has that object gone? The person remains upon the bedding, without any increase or decrease.
True nature (*tathatā*) is likewise so. When deluded, the entire body is illusory; yet this illusion does not arise because of the True. When awakened, the entire body is the True;
yet this Truth does not arise because of the illusory. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The non-Buddhists speak of a 'streaming cause of birth,' which is not the visual consciousness perceiving form."
It is said that they arise from the assembly [of conditions], yet there is another cause. As for that other cause, it is described as being "supreme and wondrous.
This "supreme and wondrous" is what the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) take to be the primal nature (*svabhāva*). They claim that this primal nature acts as the cause of its own production;

thus, all sense faculties, bodies, and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) are born from this nature. This nature is the root of delusion, and this delusion cannot be fully comprehended. Such is the mind and its objects.
All things belong to the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). This mind of spontaneity is itself the divine self (*ātman*), pervading the worlds of the ten directions.

These lands of dust throughout the ten directions envelop what is outside the mind; yet if there were phenomena outside the mind, the mind would become pervasive by means of those phenomena and would further become their causal condition.
The theories of spontaneous causality (*svabhāva-hetu*) and the two-fold mutual dependence (*anyonya-āśraya*) both belong to erroneous conceptions.

This is because they fail to realize the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; failing to awaken to it, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is formed. From consciousness arise the seeing (*darśana*) and the perceived (*nimitta*); "seeing" is discrimination, and "perceived" refers to the sense organs and their objects.

With a discriminating mind, one relies on the organs to grasp objects, failing to distinguish between self and non-self, which makes it difficult to bring forth illumination. Only the fundamental nature of the organs... [is present]. Before—
When the objective realm manifests before one, it is non-conceptual and luminous, briefly revealed for a moment; therefore, the Tathāgata has pointed this out repeatedly.
If one can awaken to it, there will be no further distinction between essence and function from the *tathāgatagarbha*. Nevertheless,
This is also stated with reference to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) before it has reached clarity, so that its nature may be easily recognized;

it does not mean that there is any further identity or difference between it and the seven, six, or two consciousnesses. Indeed, discrimination within delusion has no real self-nature; it arises solely from non-awakening (*abodhi*).

One falsely clings to them as one's own, yet even this clinging has no substantiality. Its nature is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*). When objects depart, clinging dissolves; the true nature is spontaneously free.
All that was previously explained in the preceding text is nothing other than this seeing. Even if the myriad things were to manifest in full array, they would still not constitute a separate entity.
The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and the seven great elements are permitted to be of a single nature; all are self-realized at the moment of awakening.
The realm [of this vision] is almost impossible to fathom through intellectual understanding or the measure of a conch-shell.
The preceding four sections have refuted both causal conditions and spontaneity to reveal that the seeing of seeing is the true mark (dharmatā).
△ Fifth, the manifestation of false seeing to reveal the truth, divided into four parts. First, the request for instruction on the meaning of "the seeing of seeing" as being non-seeing.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has for our sakes proclaimed the nature of causes and conditions, as well as spontaneity, the characteristics of all harmonious combinations, and those that are not in combination, my mind remains unenlightened.

Now, hearing further of ‘seeing seeing’ and ‘not seeing,’ my confusion and distress increase all the more. I prostrate myself, entreating Your Great Compassion to bestow upon us the eye of great wisdom and reveal to us the path of awakening.”
The mind becomes clear and pure. Having spoken these words, he prostrated with tears of sorrow and received the holy instruction.
If one doubts the principle itself, then the mind currently manifest before one still exists; if one doubts the causes and conditions, then the objects presently before the eyes still remain.
This is precisely why one cannot suddenly comprehend that "seeing" is neither seeing nor non-seeing. The following text correctly clarifies the sense-faculties.
The objects of perception are the beginning of delusion regarding sensation. Once this initial delusion is cleared away, one will immediately attain liberation.
△ Second, about to expound the *dhāraṇī*, he exhorts them to listen attentively.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly, and desiring to expound the path of sublime practice for the various samādhis of the Great Dhāraṇī, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Although you possess a powerful memory, it only serves to increase your erudition."
Regarding the subtle and profound contemplation within *śamatha*, your mind has not yet fully understood it. Listen attentively now;
I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so that all future beings subject to outflows may likewise attain the fruit of Bodhi.
"Great Dhāraṇī" (大陀羅尼) is here translated as "Total Retention" (總持). There are distinctions between single-syllable, multi-syllable, and syllable-less [dhāraṇīs].

The divine mantra indicated below is the multi-syllable type. If it reveals the true nature of reality (實相), it carries the meaning of being "without syllables. This is the Dhāraṇī of the True Nature of Reality (實相陀羅).
This is the true samādhi that encompasses all samādhis; therefore, all the pure and wondrous adornments of all bodhisattvas are accomplished by relying upon this.
Contemplative observation is called *śamatha*; it refers to tranquil illumination free from all conceptual discrimination, and is thus termed "subtle and profound" (*weimi*).
△ Third, showing the two kinds of false views, divided into three parts. First, showing the two [kinds of false views].
The general characteristic of perversion:

Ānanda, all sentient beings transmigrate through the world due to the deluded views of dualistic perversion. These arise in their respective places, and they revolve according to their respective karma.
What are these two views? First, the deluded view of the individual karma of sentient beings; second, [the deluded view of the common karma of sentient beings].
The commonality of sentient beings (*sabhāgatā*) is a false perception.
This deduction shows that saṃsāra arises from two inversions. These two inversions are fundamentally based on discrimination (*vikalpa*).

Discrimination is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*), the non-awakening wherein the mind moves. Because it moves, there is seeing; this is the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*). Since this seeing has no substantial essence, it is called "false."

The two inversions belong to the aspect of characteristics (*nimitta-bhāga*). They are that upon which the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) depend; the aspect follows from the seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) and manifests through it. Since the seeing is already false, the aspect must likewise be false.
When the aspect is false, the faculties and objects immediately become like flowers in the sky. Thus, the true nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) manifests before one.
This is the direct method for awakening, given as an answer to the previous question. It is "right where one is. Is this not so?
Wherever the awakened mind moves, that deluded movement is karma; karma is itself suffering. Therefore it is said: "Karma revolves.

Individual karma refers to the root-body (*mūla-kāya*), while common karma refers to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). Deluded vision is one, yet in terms of its objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*), it is twofold.
Thus, it is said below: "For example, today when you observe with your eyes the mountains, rivers, lands, and nations, as well as sentient beings, they are all..."

This is formed by the disease of beginningless views. The *Zongjing* [uses] "distinct karma" (*biye*) as "discriminative affliction" (*fenbie fan nao*) and "common karma" (*tongfen*) as "co-emergent ignorance" (*jusheng wuming*).
This has not been seen to accord with the essential purport of the root sutra. △ Second, showing the false vision of distinct karma.
What is meant by "delusive vision caused by individual karma"? Ānanda, it is like people in the world who have a red film over their eyes;
at night, when they look at a lamp, they see a separate circular shadow with five overlapping colors.
The eye is a metaphor for true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*); the lamp is a metaphor for true reality (*tattvārtha*). True wisdom has no seeing; true reality has no object.
When one sees the circular shadow appearing separately from the lamp's light at night, this is the arising of conceptual discrimination due to the deluded movement of true wisdom.
Thus, upon true reality, there falsely arises the faculty that is able to see—the five colors being the five faculties. True wisdom becomes localized in its seeing.

The faculties are the truth, while delusion is empty and constitutes form; both arise from the same false view. Delusion divides the faculties and their objects, creating distinctions between what is proximate and what is remote.

Upon awakening, one realizes that delusion has no cause, for the nature of the faculties is present right now. Thus, the subsequent text says: "However, as for the one who perceives the optical aberration..."
Ultimately, no fault is to be seen.
What do you think? Is this circular light manifested by the lamp’s brightness the color of the lamp itself, or is it the color of what is being seen?
Ānanda, if this were the color of the lamp, why would those who do not have the visual ailment not see it as well? Yet this circular shadow is seen only by those with the ailment.
Regarding this contemplation: if one perceives form, and that which has already been perceived becomes form, then what would one call that person with the eye disease who sees the circular shadow?
This means that true wisdom and ultimate reality are fundamentally free from fault; the fault lies in deluded movement, which gives rise to its own conceptual discrimination.

Furthermore, as for those who see the circular shadow, what is it called? Although they are within the optical aberration, even one who sees that the shadow is not circular can realize for themselves that it is not the fault of the person.
This is analogous to the Buddha-realm; the visible form is precisely the shadow.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular reflection existed separately from the lamp, then when one looks at a screen, a curtain, or a table from the side, a circular reflection should likewise appear.
If it existed separately from the act of seeing, it should not be within the range of visual perception. How then can a person with cataracts see this circular reflection?
Therefore, you should know that form actually resides in the lamp; the perception of it as a cataract is the shadow. Both the shadow and the perception are defects of vision.

While perceiving the defect is not itself a disease, one must ultimately never say that this [perception] is the lamp or that it is the vision. Within this, there exists neither the lamp nor the vision.
These words also indicate that false manifestations do not exist apart from true wisdom and true reality. Thus, one knows that true wisdom is without intrinsic nature;

through non-awakening, it falsely moves. True reality is fundamentally empty; through false perception, it manifests as form. Wisdom does not give rise to delusion, yet delusion is not separate from wisdom.
Emptiness does not give rise to form, yet form is not outside of emptiness. To realize that delusion is originally void, one finds that the principle and wisdom are naturally so. Because...
This is called "not. It ultimately deviates from the fundamental abiding; therefore, it is further said that seeing the optical defect is not the illness itself.
One should never say that this is the lamp or this is the seeing; within this, there is neither lamp nor seeing.
It is like a second moon: it is neither the substance nor the reflection. Why? Because the perception of a second moon is produced by pressing [the eye].
No wise person should say that this source of the pressed organ is a shape or not a shape, or something apart from seeing or not seeing.
This case is also like that; it is produced by a cataract in the eye. Now, whom would you name as being the lamp or the seeing? How much less could one differentiate what is not [real]?
The lamp is not the seeing.

This is because the second moon is produced by the cause of pressing [the eye]; how could it be seen as a physical form? It is used as a metaphor for seeing a circular reflection, which is produced by a cataract in the eye;
how could it be the lamp that sees? Since this has no basis and is established without a cause, it serves generally to clarify the Truth.

The principle of wisdom is true; though it exists amidst delusion, it remains perfectly distinct. Awakening to this is identical to what was originally attained; it is not something newly created now.
△ Third, showing the commonality of deluded vision.
What is meant by "common deluded vision"? Ānanda, in this Jambudvīpa, excluding the great oceans, there are three thousand islands upon the level lands in between.
The central great island, measured from east to west, contains two thousand three hundred large countries.
As for the other small islands scattered throughout the various seas, some contain two or three hundred countries, while others have only one.

Or two, up to three, four, five, or ten. Ānanda, if among these there is a small continent containing only two countries, and the people of only one country collectively experience adverse conditions, then the sentient beings of that particular land on that small continent—
They beheld all manner of inauspicious omens: sometimes two suns were seen, or two moons;
therein were even halos, solar spots, and crescent rings, as well as comets, meteors, shooting stars, "burdened ears," rainbows, and halos—various evil signs seen only within this country.
The sentient beings of that land had never before seen or even heard of it.

A "continent" (*dvīpa*) refers to a place where one may dwell amidst water; it signifies a boundary or a measurement. There are two thousand three hundred great nations, which belong to the Five Regions of India as well as this Divine Land (China).
Halos, rings, girdles, and pendants are all black vapors surrounding the sun and moon. "Encompassing" (*huán*) means to encircle.

A halo surrounding [the sun or moon] is called a *yun* (halo). A partial eclipse is called a *shi* (eclipse). "Jade pendants and rings" refers to jade objects shaped like pendants and rings. Comets, meteors, and falling stars are all ominous celestial bodies.
The *Erya* states: "The comet is called *chanqiang*. The form of a *bei* (meteor) is shimmering and spreading, like a broom or a *hui* (sweeping star).
They fly away along their paths; the currents flow on in succession. "Fu-er" (負耳) refers to the calamitous vapors facing the sun, appearing like the character for "fu" (to carry) or "er" (ear).
The rainbow (*indrāyudha*) manifests when the Yin and Yang are in disharmony. The *Erya* states: "The *hong* (rainbow) is the *chidong*; the *ni* (the tail of the rainbow) is the female *hong*.
A country where these are not seen is a metaphor for the absence of seeing delusions—like clear, bright eyes gazing upon a cloudless sky.
The preceding three sections have concluded the demonstration of the two kinds of false vision.

△ Fourth, the analogy of the present observation and vision is presented to reveal that the seeing of seeing is not seeing, thereby distancing oneself from conjunction and perfecting Bodhi. This section has three parts. First, the individual karma is used as an analogy for the present observation and vision to establish the seeing of seeing.
Ānanda, I shall now clarify these two matters for you by examining them from both their progressive and regressive aspects.

Ānanda, it is like those sentient beings who, due to the deluded vision of their individual karma, perceive a circular shadow appearing within a lamp’s light. Although it seems to be an external object, it is ultimately produced by the cataract in the eye of the observer.
This cataract is simply the exhaustion of seeing; it is not created by the color itself. Yet, for one who perceives this cataract, there is ultimately no fault in the act of seeing.
Using the same to illustrate the different, and using the different to illustrate the same, it is therefore called "advancing and retreating.

To appear as an object is not [the truth]; truly, there is that which is not produced by form. This further clarifies the exhaustion of seeing. That which is called the True Principle is fundamentally empty; emptiness does not give rise to form.
Altogether, this brings one out of the delusion of seeing, like a cataract. By realizing that the cataract is not the seeing itself, one is free from the fault of seeing.
For example, as you observe today with your eyes the mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings, these are all produced by the disease of vision that has existed since beginningless time.

Vision and its conditions appear to be present objects, yet they are fundamentally the delusions of the visual faculty within my enlightened awareness. They are like the optical distortions seen when looking at a lamp.

That which is observed by the eyes is the sense organ (*indriya*). The mountains, rivers, and lands are the container world (*bhājanaloka*). Sentient beings are the sentient-being world (*sattvaloka*).
Both of these refer to objects (*viṣaya*). The union of the organ and the object arises entirely from the disease of vision since beginningless time.

This means that through the non-awakening of ignorance, there is deluded movement, giving rise to the "seeing portion" (darśana-bhāga). This refers to the previously mentioned delusion of the discerning seeing.
"Seeing" refers to the act of seeing; "the objects of seeing" refers to the lands and sentient beings. Both this faculty (the organ) and its environment belong to the "image portion" (nimitta-bhāga).

It originally arises from the deluded manifestation of the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), and thus appears as if present before one; yet it does not truly exist. "Awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*) refers to the subjective aspect.
"That which is seen by the seeing" (*jian suo-yuan*) refers to both the seeing and its object.

Furthermore, to trace the origin of this defect (*sheng*) whereby the seeing and its object arise, one must begin with awakened clarity, thereby demonstrating that neither the sense organ nor the objective field is at fault. This will be clarified in the subsequent text.

To perceive [the visual distortion] is itself the cataract. The fundamentally enlightened, luminous mind perceives conditions, yet this perception is not a cataract. It is the perceived object that is the cataract;
the perceiving subject is not within the cataract. This is truly the seeing of seeing. How, then, can it again be called "perceiving, hearing, knowing, or seeing"?

"Awakened seeing is precisely awakened clarity; awakened seeing is precisely the cataract. This summarizes the aforementioned "awakened clarity" and the "cataract" perceived by that seeing, yet it specifically singles out "awakened seeing.
Therefore, the text immediately clarifies below: "The fundamentally awakened, luminous mind—its awakening to conditions is not a cataract.

This indicates that the original fundamental awakening is the *tathāgatagarbha*, and that both this and the sensory faculties manifested in response to conditions belong to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); they are originally [so].
There is no fault; it is simply that the entire matter is attributed to the delusion of the perceiving vision. That which is perceived refers precisely to this perceiving vision.
To perceive this perceived object as a delusion is itself "the seeing of seeing. How, then, could it still be called "awakening, hearing, knowing, and seeing"?
Because sentient beings in their daily activities possess this deluded vision, even when their eyes are bright and clear, they cannot awaken to themselves; thus, they are confused.
Form is called "seeing," and its confusion with sound is called "hearing. To know the destination in a mere flash—how could one distinguish between the fundamental and the derivative?
This is what the Tathāgata has three times emphasized.
Therefore, you who now see me, yourself, and all the ten classes of sentient beings in the world—all this is simply the seeing of a cataract.
One who is not the observer of the cataract perceives the true essence; since its nature is not that of a cataract, it is not called "seeing.
This knot, Ānanda, and the present seeing and its objects are all merely the disease of the cataract.
That which is able to see this disease is, moreover, the very faculty of the senses present before you, which knows itself and awakens to itself; therefore, it is said:
That which is not of the nature of an optical aberration is what is called "awakening to the delusion as the truth"; therefore, it is not termed "seeing.
△ Second, using the common karma (*sabhāga-karma*) to further illustrate individual karma (*pratyeka-karma*), the principle is established for all ten directions.
Ānanda, just as those sentient beings share a commonality of deluded vision, so too may one person with a distinct karmic lot be compared to that deluded vision.
A single person with diseased eyes is like that entire country; the circular shadow he sees is produced by the delusion of his cataract.

This inauspicious manifestation appearing to this collective group is likewise produced by the miasmic evil within their shared karma. Both are born from the beginningless delusion of seeing. To take Yama as an example: [text continues]

Throughout the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa, including the four great oceans, the Sahā world, and extending to all the realms of outflows in the ten directions, as well as all sentient beings, they share this same enlightened clarity—the immaculate, wondrous mind.
Their seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing arise through false and illusory conditions;
they are falsely born from these conjunctions and falsely die from these conjunctions. If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction, as well as...
Through this unification, one further eliminates all causes of birth and death, perfects the nature of bodhi which is neither born nor extinguished, and realizes the pure fundamental mind,
wherein original enlightenment is eternally abiding.

To summarize the preceding discussion on the two views—of identity and difference—we shall clarify them through both progressive and regressive analysis, using the single continent of Jambudvīpa as an illustration, and further extending that from Jambudvīpa to the ten directions. All are equally the beginningless, enlightened clarity;

yet this causes the untainted, wondrous mind to falsely manifest as seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, resulting in a delusory conjunction. If one can awaken to this knowledge, one will immediately transcend it.

When harmony and disharmony are [discerned], deluded views are suddenly eliminated; arising and ceasing are forever stilled, and the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing remains perfectly and eternally present.

When the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, through lack of awakening, moves delusively, the "seeing-portion" arises, and consequently, the appearance of forms occurs as the sense organs and their objects confront one another.
They manifest and mutually increase, flowing and turning without end; for all sentient beings, from time immemorial until this day, they have never ceased for even a moment.
Yet the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment is ever-present within the sense faculties; though it is confined by the faculties, it remains constant therein.

It likewise shifts according to objects, yet its non-conceptual clarity has never undergone change. What it manifests by relying on the sense organs appears clearly; when separated from sensory dust, it possesses its own essence.
Its nature is fundamentally thus. Once awakened, it does not follow after effortful application; even before awakening, it is likewise free from deficiency or defilement.
It is simply that while in the state of delusion, no one realizes this, and so it needlessly undergoes flux. It is, for example, like...
"The clouds move and the moon travels; the boat moves and the shore shifts. These are not actual facts, yet having long been driven by them, habituation has become one's nature.
Among ordinary beings, they transmigrate through the six realms, regarding these as empty and false. To those of the Two Vehicles, they appear as lingering in the state of transformation;
their minds are timid toward partial emptiness. Even for those on the ten stages, there remains the subtle object of knowledge, still separated by a fine silk veil. This...

How could there truly be any difference in their status? It is because delusive views have accumulated through habitual perfuming that they are difficult to sever, even when one attempts to maintain mindfulness.

Thus, while the grass hut has long been pitched, the place of jewels remains distant in vain. This sutra points directly to the fundamental nature; it requires only awakening to what is before one’s eyes.
It is precisely the same as the *Avataṃsaka*’s direct transmission to the beginner—how could it require diligent toil over many kalpas? They share the same essential intent; how can they be divided?
Thus, sudden and perfect [enlightenment] are realized. Therefore, one knows that the substance of the single Dharma-realm is sovereign within each person;

all beings on the great earth have fundamentally attained the Buddha-way, yet it is only through realization that this is known. Their wisdom and virtuous marks are fully present even while manifesting in an ordinary body; this does not depend on tracing back to the source, for such would be a mere matter of intellectual faith.
For this reason, Ānanda did not understand the "seeing of seeing," whereas the Tathāgata clarified only the delusion of seeing, knowing that it is delusion.
Movement begins with non-awakening; fundamentally, it is not truly existent. Thus, the nature of seeing is inherently and spontaneously perfected; one need only awaken to it.

This is what is called the luminous mind of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). Awakening to conditions is not an aberration; this imperial decree is manifest and clear—one need only have confidence in it.
Do not obstruct the long journey; let time and years pass in vain. This has been so throughout all ages, past and present.
△ Third, the refutation of harmony and disharmony, divided into three parts. First, a general restatement of harmony and disharmony.
Ānanda, although you have previously realized that the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment is neither of the nature of causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature,
you have not yet clearly understood that this source of enlightenment is neither produced through combination nor through non-combination.
The "origin of awakening" (*jueyuan*) is precisely initial awakening (*shijue*), which is to say, *prajñā*. Regarding the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*:
first, the *dharmakāya*; second, *prajñā*; and third, liberation (*vimukti*). The *dharmakāya* is the wondrous luminosity of original awakening (*benjue*); *prajñā* is this very initial awakening.
Now, to further clarify the initial awakening that realizes *bodhi*, it is neither a combination nor a non-combination. Combination is identical to—

Regarding causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*): if they were not in harmony, they would be identical to the spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it is necessary to discern this. A verse from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:

"It is neither a combination nor a non-combination; its nature is discerned as quiescent and devoid of all marks. The commentary says: "It should accord with conditions, yet it is not a non-combination."

The essence of abiding is not a composite; yet, that which is accomplished through the cultivation of dependent origination is not non-composite. Because it accords with the true mark and exhausts all phenomena, it is not a composite;
furthermore, because the mark of conjunction is absent, there are no marks at all. Being neither conjoined nor separated, this elucidates quiescence.
△ Second, the refutation of conjunction.
Ānanda, I shall now question you again regarding the objects before you.

You still harbor doubts because you believe that the nature of all causes and conditions—which are but the conjunction of the deluded thoughts of the entire world—gives rise to the mind of Bodhi through their combination.
Bodhi is initial awakening (*ādi-bodha*). Bodhi arises from original awakening (*mūla-bodha*) and returns to realize that original awakening;
this is precisely the essence of seeing manifest before one. While unawakened, it is the nature of the sense-faculties; once awakened, it is bodhi.

Since the essence of seeing manifest before one is the outflow of original awakening, although sentient beings employ it in their daily lives without realizing it, it appears as if dependent on external conditions; yet in reality, it arises from the original.

Because it is perfumed by awakening, there will eventually come a time when one is within delusion. That which is called "perfected through the cultivation of dependent origination" is not a lack of harmony;
that which accords with the true aspect and exhausts all phenomena is not a state of conjunction.

If delusive thought were to combine with various conditions to form the mundane world, then while conditions persist, appearances would seem to arise in succession, and when conditions disperse, the shadows of dust would dissolve and sink away. Delusive thought has no [independent existence].
How could its nature possibly be confused with the source of cognition? This can be fully understood through a single pair of distinctions.
Thus, as for this wondrous, pure essence of seeing that you now possess: is it conjoined with light, conjoined with darkness, or conjoined with openness?

Regarding the blending of light and darkness: if you say they blend with light, then observe this light. When the light appears before you, where is the visual faculty mixed? Can the characteristics of the visual faculty be distinguished from the light?
What kind of form would such a mixture take? If it were not the visual faculty itself, how could it see the light? If it were identical to the visual faculty, [how could it be called a mixture?]

What is meant by "seeing seeing"? It must be that seeing is complete. Where do clarity and seeing harmonize? If clarity is complete, it cannot harmonize with seeing. Seeing must be distinct from clarity;

if they were mixed, the names of their respective natures—clarity and seeing—would be lost. If clarity and seeing were mixed, the nature of clarity would be lost; thus, the notion of their "harmonizing" is not tenable.
It is the same with darkness and light, as well as with all various obstructions.

Where is there a mixed perception? This inquiry concerns the place of mixture; if one perceives the characteristics of phenomena, that is precisely the characteristic of clarity. Mixed with what kind of form?
This inquiry into the state of mixture shows that since it does not constitute a mixture, nor do they interpenetrate, it is said: "If it is not the seer, how can it [be seen]?"
Regarding "seeing clarity": if seeing were identical to clarity, how could seeing see? This means that since clarity is already identical to seeing, one cannot use seeing to further see seeing.
Even if they are not identical, each is nonetheless complete in itself. These two difficulties are combined here.
This is simply to clarify that they do not constitute a mixture. Therefore, it concludes by stating: "Seeing must be distinct from clarity.
This is precisely saying that the nature of seeing is different from the external objects before one. If they were mixed, each would lose its name;
where else, then, could there be a distinction between clarity and seeing? "Nature" here refers to the nature of seeing.
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for this wondrously pure essence of seeing within you now: does it unite with light? Does it unite with darkness?

Does it unite with openness? Or does it unite with obstruction? If it united with light, then when darkness arrives and the appearance of light has already ceased, [the essence of seeing would likewise cease].

This seeing does not conjoin with darkness. How, then, can it see darkness? If, when seeing darkness, it does not conjoin with darkness, yet it does conjoin with light, then it should not be seeing light.
Since it does not see light, how can it be said that by conjoining with light, it perceives light and not darkness?
It is the same with darkness and its penetration, as well as with all obstructions:
if they were combined with light, one should not perceive darkness; yet if one perceives darkness while it is not combined with light, then when perceiving light, [the same logic would apply].

If it were already conjoined with light, one should not perceive light. That is to say, if one can perceive darkness without being conjoined with darkness, then one should likewise not perceive light when conjoined with light.
This shows that although there is conjunction with light, one still discerns light rather than darkness;
thus, it is established that the nature of seeing does not conjoin with objects individually, only then being able to see each of them individually. △ Third, refuting the notion of non-conjunction.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as I contemplate it, this wondrous source of awakening is not a composite of the various sense objects and the mental deliberations of the mind?"
The capacity to perceive is the faculty; the object perceived is the field; and the act of cogitation is consciousness.

This is because one perceives that this wondrous fundamental awareness is eternally in mutual conjunction with these three, thereby regulating itself. Now that it has been revealed, it should no longer be in conjunction.
Thus one harbors doubts, not realizing that their essence is fundamentally non-conjoined. Illusions arise from conditions; that which arises from conditions is itself non-arising.

Both mind and objects lack intrinsic nature. The *Ocean of Meanings in a Hundred Gates* states: "One who realizes non-arising understands that objects are the conditions for the mind, while the mind has no cause apart from objects.
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, illusory appearances arise. Because they arise from conditions, they must..."
They lack intrinsic nature. Why is this? Now, objects do not perceive themselves; their arising depends upon the mind. The mind does not perceive itself; it must depend upon conditions.
Because they are obtained through mutual characteristics, there is no fixed attribution. That which arises from conditions is called "non-arising";
it is not that one negates arising from conditions by asserting non-arising.
The Buddha said, "You have now further stated that awakening is not a composite. I ask you again:

this wondrous essence of vision, which is not a composite—is it not in harmony with light? Is it not in harmony with darkness? Is it not in harmony with openness? Is it not in harmony with obstruction?
If it were not in harmony with light, then there would necessarily be a boundary between vision and light. You should observe closely: where is the light, and where..."
This is seeing. It exists within seeing and within light. From what does its boundary arise? Ānanda, if within the limit of light there were no seer, then [seeing] would not reach it;
one would not know where the characteristic of light resides. How, then, could a boundary be established? That same applies to darkness and openness.
It is likewise with all the various realms of beings.
This is because they are boundless, inexhaustible, and not a composite whole; thus, by their mutual containment, they are proven to be boundless.

Furthermore, as for this wondrous seeing-essence, if it were not a product of conjunction, would it not be conjoined with light? Would it not be conjoined with darkness? Would it not be conjoined with openness?

Would it not be conjoined with obstruction? If it were not conjoined with light, then the nature and characteristics of seeing and light would be mutually contradictory, just as the ear and light are.

They do not touch one another at all; even their sight does not know where the characteristic of light resides. How, then, can one distinguish between what is reasonable for them to conjoin and what is unreasonable?
It is the same with darkness and openness, as well as with all various obstructions.
This distinguishes the characteristics of seeing from the nature of luminosity; by tracing them back, one finds they are not conjoined. This is brought forward to provide clear evidence:
if seeing were like hearing, it would not know luminosity for itself; how, then, could it discern the meaning of conjunction and non-conjunction?

The preceding five sections have concluded the exposition on the emergence of false views to reveal the truth. △ Sixth, the general subsumption of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), elements (dhātus), and the seven great elements into the Tathāgatagarbha to initiate true awakening.
This is divided into seven parts; first, the general subsumption.
Ānanda, you have not yet clearly understood that all these superficial, floating, illusory, and transformative phenomena arise in their very place and perish in their very place.
These illusory and false things are called "phenomena," yet their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity.

This refers to the source of Ānanda’s illness. It arises fundamentally from not knowing that all superficial, illusory, and transformative phenomena are produced right where they are and perish right where they are.
"Place" (chu) refers to the substance of the mind. Not knowing that they are produced right where they are leads one to perceive dharmas as existing outside the mind;

thus, one is neither "detached" nor "joined. To be detached is to delude oneself into thinking these phenomena are spontaneous (*svabhāva*); to be joined is to delude oneself into thinking they have a cause.

Regarding conditions: if one does not know that they cease and vanish right where they arise, then there is a mind apart from phenomena (*dharma*). Thus, movement and stillness interfere with one another.

In movement, self and objects become mutually dependent; in stillness, discrimination stands before one. This is the common obstacle for both ordinary people and those of the Two Vehicles—they are all hindered by phenomena.
Only when one is born right where it arises and ceases and vanishes right where it occurs can one further believe that all myriad phenomena are manifestations of the mind alone. Manifestation...
There is no self-nature; it is solely the One Mind. All delusions are like illusions, possessing only names and appearances;
their nature is entirely the wondrously enlightened, luminous essence. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All phenomena are unborn; all phenomena are unceasing.
If one can understand in this way, the Buddhas are ever present. Shitou said: "One who realizes that the myriad things are themselves..."
"It is only the sage who [is thus]. It is further said: 'The sage has no self; there is nothing he does not do.
One who knows this understands that all phenomena (*dharma*) are thus, every mind is thus, and the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are likewise thus.

Yet, according to each individual, they establish various distinct marks and give rise to various distinct conceptions; thus, the Great Sage must labor to provide many skillful means, for all are without [intrinsic nature]."
They are merely real dharmas.
Thus it extends from the five aggregates and six sense bases, through the twelve entrances, to the eighteen elements. Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is illusory arising;
through the separation of causes and conditions, there is illusory cessation. They are utterly unable to know that arising and ceasing, coming and going, are but illusions.
This Tathāgatagarbha is eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading—the wondrous nature of True Suchness.
Within this true, eternal nature, if one seeks for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death, nothing at all can be found.
All of these fail to realize that the various sensory objects are illusory transformations; they mistakenly take them to be real and, following conditions, fall into inversion.

They appear to have conjunction and separation, and appear to have arising and ceasing, yet none of these are actual facts. Furthermore, this arising and ceasing, as well as coming and going, do not exist separately [from the objects themselves].
The *Xinyin lun* says: "When the mind does not give rise to consciousness, it is eternally in nirvāṇa amidst the continuous flow;

when consciousness does not depart from the mind, one merely undergoes birth and death within the ever-abiding. That arising and ceasing, departing and arriving, are all the Tathāgatagarbha is easy for people to know;
yet that departing and arriving, delusion and awakening, and birth and death are utterly ungraspable is truly difficult to verify for oneself. This is because...
One has never yet dwelt securely within the nature of true permanence, nor realized the principle of cessation at its very locus;
this refers precisely to the stage of faith, whereas the human stage is not yet it.
In brief, there is only the single Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This single Dharma-realm is the non-dual true mind, which constitutes the one Dharma-realm.
"One" means that it is as the principle is: empty, pervasive, equal, and without duality.

It is truly because one fails to recognize this single Dharma-realm that, regarding an object that fundamentally does not exist, one falsely perceives an object; and thus, regarding the true mind that fundamentally does exist...

One falsely gives rise to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). The false object does not exist, yet the discrimination is not non-existent. Having become deluded into thinking it exists, one falsely becomes attached to it;

following one's own emotions, one creates karma and wanders through the cycles of ascent and descent. Seeking liberation out of weariness with suffering, one falsely views [reality] as non-existent and focuses the mind on distancing oneself from it;

thus, one becomes increasingly estranged from the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Seeking emptiness within emptiness, one establishes a separate principle of emptiness, attempting to dispel existence by means of existence—this is mere delusion.
The practice of arising dharmas proceeds. Thus, once the ordinary person’s grasping at the aggregates (*skandha*) has ceased, the non-self (*anātman*) of the two vehicles arises again.

While the ultimate fruit is easily equated with the initial resolve, the full extent of what is to be known is difficult to exhaust. All of this stems from being deluded regarding the *tathatā* (suchness) of the single Dharma-realm;

it consequently causes one to mistake the transformation-city for the precious destination. To perceive that there is a substantial entity apart from dust is an error committed by taking [the provisional] as the self.
However, all such discriminations are but the mind; when delusions form a confluence, how can one know that true wisdom is without substance?
It is like the waves upon the great ocean. True reality is eternally serene, like the moist nature of the myriad rivers. Waves exist within the great ocean without ever departing from it;
the moist nature accommodates the myriad rivers without ever being lost. To enter the great ocean is to still the waves; to abandon the myriad rivers is...
Seeking moisture, even those with wisdom find it difficult to achieve success; it is better to be like a fool who remains at ease in non-action.
Thus, the "cat" and the "white ox" manifest the true permanence of self-enjoyment, yet they mock those of the Ten Stages and Three Worthies for grasping at external realms as their own realization.
The three aggregates are all provisional, and even the single mind perishes; birth-and-death and nirvana are fundamentally...
The limit is non-dual. Whether it be bodhi or afflictions, one should maintain mindfulness without shifting; simply let go of what is known, and the vast Great Way will manifest.
△ Second, the five aggregates, divided into five parts. First, form.
Ānanda, why are the five aggregates fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
The five are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "Aggregate" (skandha) means "to cover. This means that these five cover and conceal the true nature.
First, there is a general inquiry regarding the five [aggregates]; subsequently, they are explained individually. All are said to be illusory and false.

If one knows that the five aggregates are illusory and false, then their very substance is entirely true, without the need for transformation; therefore, it is called the "primordial Tathāgatagarbha."
Ānanda, it is like a person with clear vision who gazes at a bright, cloudless sky. There is only a vast, empty clarity, utterly devoid of anything.
Without cause, this person does not move their eyes, but stares until they become fatigued; then, within that empty space, they see illusory flowers and all manner of other delusory, distorted forms.
You should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exactly like this.
The eye is a metaphor for true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*); emptiness is a metaphor for ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). True wisdom has no seeing; ultimate truth has no object.

Because they do not exist [as dualities], they are unmoving—this is a metaphor for beginningless non-awakening and deluded movement, as there is no cause for such existence. The act of staring fixedly represents the state of exhaustion.
Where there is no seeing, it appears as seeing; where there is no object, it appears as an object. Therefore, the following inquiry seeks to exhaustively investigate this to clarify its falsity.
Ānanda, these various wildflowers do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the eyes.
It is thus, Ānanda: if they came from space, having come from space, they would return to space. If there were such coming and going, then it would not be empty space. If space...
It is not empty; it cannot by itself allow the arising and ceasing of its own illusory manifestations, just as Ānanda’s body cannot contain Ānanda himself.
Here, the "wild flowers" are used as a metaphor for form (*rūpa*). The phrase "not from the empty eye" means that true emptiness is devoid of form and true wisdom is devoid of seeing.
If they were to arise from the empty space, there would have to be an entering and exiting; if there were such entering and exiting, it would not be empty space. It cannot by itself...
The arising and ceasing of forms and appearances are, on the contrary, metaphors for emptiness and the absence of intrinsic nature; how could there be an extrinsic nature?
Within true emptiness, form is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent; how then could there be arising and ceasing? Those who perceive arising and ceasing do so only through delusion.

If it emerges from the eyes, then having emerged from the eyes, it must also enter back through the eyes. Since this nature of the flower emerges from the eyes, it ought to possess the faculty of vision.
If it possesses vision, then as it departs into the empty space of the flower, it should, upon returning, see the eye itself. If it lacks vision, [then it cannot have emerged from the eyes].
Since it emerges to obscure the sky, it must in turn obscure the eyes. Furthermore, when one sees flowers, the eyes should be free of obscuration; why then is a cloudless sky called "clear vision"?
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
If vision arises from the eyes, then because one has obtained the functional essence of the eyes, there ought to be seeing. If there were seeing, it would turn back to see the eyes themselves;
if there were no seeing, yet the sky were obscured by cataracts, then those cataracts would likewise turn back to obscure the eyes.
Since the eyes are not themselves obscured, when one sees flowers [in the sky], the eyes should be faultless. Why is it that only when one sees a clear sky is it called "clarity and brightness"?

Is it the eye? This concludes the summary of delusion: by means of true wisdom perceiving the emptiness of reality, one sees that the currently manifest aggregate of form has never shifted or changed;
it is like flowers appearing in the sky, which are but the sky itself obscured by cataracts. △ Second, the aggregate of sensation.

Ānanda, it is like a person whose hands and feet are at ease, whose hundred members are in harmony, who has suddenly forgotten his very existence, and whose nature is free from both aversion and compliance.
For no reason, this person rubs his two palms together in the air, and within his hands, he falsely perceives various sensations such as roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat.
You should know that the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is exactly like this.
The four lines on "tranquil ease and harmonious adjustment" collectively describe how various sensations have not yet arisen.
The four lines on "the two palms" speak to the extreme point that false movement occurs without cause, giving rise to contact and sensation spontaneously.
Ānanda, these illusory touches do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the palm. It is thus, Ānanda:
if they came from space, since they can touch the palm, why do they not touch the body? Space ought not to choose selectively whom it touches.

If they emerged from the palm, they should not depend upon contact; furthermore, because they would emerge from the palm, the palm would perceive them when in contact, but the touch would enter the arm and wrist when separated.
The marrow likewise should perceive the traces of its entry; there must be a perceiving mind that knows the exiting and the entering.

There would naturally be a thing within the body coming and going—why wait for the convergence of conditions to be called "contact"? Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and false;
it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

Feeling exists because of contact; therefore, one must investigate whether this contact arises from space or from the palm. If it arose from space, it would not distinguish between the hand and the body.

If it arose from the palm, it would have points of entry and exit. Since there are points of entry and exit, then when [the hand] joins [the object], the palm should perceive it, and when [the hand] separates [from the object], the body should feel it.

If one is already aware [of it], it does not require contact for it to become a sensation; this demonstrates that the nature of touch is fundamentally non-existent, thereby clarifying that the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is illusory.
III. The Aggregate of Perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Ānanda, it is like a person who speaks of eating sour plums, and water flows from their mouth; or one who thinks of treading upon a precipice, and the soles of their feet [tingle].
It is astringent and sour. You should know that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is likewise so.

To speak of the thought of a plum on a cliff—though it is not a real thing—it causes the saliva to flow and the feet to ache. One must fully understand how such false imaginings pervade all categories of existence.
Ānanda, this sourness you speak of does not arise from the plum, nor does it enter through the mouth. In this way, Ānanda, if it arose from the plum, the plum ought to speak of it itself;
why wait for someone else to say it? If it entered through the mouth, the mouth ought to hear it itself; why need there be the ear?
If it were heard by the ear alone, why would this water not emerge from within the ear? It is like the thought of treading upon a precipice, which is no different from speaking of it.

These are analogous cases. Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
The plum does not speak of itself, and the mouth cannot hear; water does not emerge from the ear. All such delusions are without cause and cannot be traced to their origin.
△ Fourth, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
Ānanda, it is like a violent torrent where the waves succeed one another, such that the preceding and succeeding limits do not overstep each other;
you should know that the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is likewise.
This explains the meaning of the deluded mind’s shifting and flowing: in its preceding, succeeding, and intermediate moments, each thought-moment fails to reach the next;

yet it appears as a continuous succession, like a violent torrent. As these moments push and pull one another forward, they seem to possess a sequence that does not allow for mutual transgression—this is what is meant by "sequence."
Ānanda, such a nature of flowing does not arise because of space, nor does it exist because of water; it is neither the nature of water, nor is it separate from space and water.

Thus, Ānanda, if it were to arise because of space, then the inexhaustible empty space of the ten directions would become an inexhaustible flow, and the worlds would naturally all be submerged and drowned.
Space is a metaphor for ultimate truth; water is a metaphor for true wisdom. This statement means that ultimate truth does not give rise to delusion.
If delusion were caused by the principle [of truth], then from antiquity to the present day, there would not have been a single person capable of realizing that principle.
If [the flood] exists because of water, then the nature of this flood should not be water; it would possess its own characteristics and should now be manifest.

This analogy shows that the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) does not depend on true wisdom. If it were to depend on true wisdom, then wisdom would be the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and formations would be the characterized object (lakṣya);
these two characteristics would have to be distinct and could be pointed out as such in the present.
If it were identical to the nature of water, then when the water is clear and still, it would not be the substance of water;
this illustrates that true wisdom has no active characteristics (*ākāra*). If it were identical to the active characteristics, then when those activities cease, there would be no substance of wisdom.

If one is separated from space and water, space does not exist apart from them, nor is there flow apart from water; therefore, one should understand that the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is empty and false, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature.

This is a metaphor for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It does not depart from the principle of wisdom; while the principle of wisdom is eternally abiding, the flux of phenomena remains manifest.
Such is the nature of delusive appearances from the very beginning. △ Five: The Aggregate of Consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who took a *piṅgala* jar, plugged both its openings, filled it with empty space, and carried it a thousand li away to present to another country.
You should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exactly like this.

The person is a metaphor for sentient beings; the jar is a metaphor for karma; and the space is a metaphor for consciousness. Sentient beings are led by karma, and consciousness follows karma as it departs, just as a jar carries space.

The present *skandhas* (aggregates) are a metaphor for one’s own country; the intermediate and subsequent *skandhas* are a metaphor for another country. The two holes are a metaphor for wisdom and principle.
Sentient beings do not penetrate this wisdom and principle, and thus they falsely follow the transitions of karma, just as if one were to block both holes while carrying space far away.
It proceeds thus, Ānanda:
this empty space does not come from that direction, nor does it enter from this direction.

That direction is a metaphor for the preceding aggregates; this direction is a metaphor for the middle and subsequent aggregates. Consciousness manifests according to karma; there is no such thing as "that" or "this."
Nor is there any coming or going.
Thus it is, Ānanda: if that space were to come from elsewhere, then the original flask would have been empty when it departed; therefore, it remains in the place where the original flask stood.
There would have to be a small amount of empty space. If one were to enter this side by opening a hole and overturning the jar, one should see the empty space exit.
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of consciousness is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

This metaphor illustrates that consciousness does not migrate from the preceding aggregate (pūrvānta-skandha) to the succeeding aggregate (aparānta-skandha). The original jar and the ground represent the locus where the preceding aggregates perform karma;
the jar with its hole opened and overturned represents the place where the succeeding aggregates are drawn by karma. In sum, it is said that consciousness manifests in accordance with karma.
There is no coming or going, nor entering or exiting; it is only through deluded vision that the world appears as if it exists in such a way.
The five aggregates (pañca-skandha) encompass all phenomena, both material and mental. The aggregate of form comprises the eleven types of material dharmas;

sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness comprise the sovereign mind and all mental factors (caitta). To speak of them collectively, they consist of the three categories of sense faculties, objects, and consciousness. Regarding these:

When one is within the aggregates (*skandha*), it begins truly with the arising of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) from ignorance (*avidyā*). As these formations increase, they give rise to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which serves as the condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Being deluded regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*, one takes it to be the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); falsely perceiving the existence of form, one grasps at form to constitute the sense faculties (*indriya*).

With the faculties facing external forms, sensation (*vedanā*) arises; sensation receives the reflections of sensory objects to form perception (*saṃjñā*); and the characteristics of perception flow on continuously.
It functions without interruption. Through the accumulation of karma and the fueling of delusions by its activities, it returns to consciousness, manifesting all at once in a sudden flash.
This cycle revolves without end; the whole is delusion, yet this very delusion is itself the truth, for delusion has no inherent nature while the principle of wisdom remains eternally present.
It is like the sun shrouded by heavy clouds that obscure the entire sky; yet the essence of the sun does not move, and when it encounters the wind...
Due to causes and conditions, the sky suddenly becomes clear; was the sun newly suspended? So too is it for one who has lost their way but attains awakening:

relying on the cause of weariness with suffering and riding upon the condition of teachers and friends, they come to realize that all is illusory, just as clouds disperse. The dispersal of clouds is like a condition.

Japan remains as it was; True Suchness (Tathatā) has no substance. It accepts sense organs and objects without rejection, and allows for the transformations of consciousness while remaining ever thus.
The attainment of Buddhahood by all sentient beings cannot be obstructed by the entry into the realms. If Buddha-nature were subject to flux, how could it be the creation of the One Reality?
Though constantly amidst birth-and-death and coming-and-going, Great Wisdom is brilliantly clear and the Ultimate Principle is limpid and tranquil. Truly...
This may be explained to the ignorant.
*The Direct Pointing to the Heart of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*,
Fascicle Two.

Phonetic Explanations: Yǔn (pronounced yǔn): to die. Cú (pronounced lí): to pass away. Guǎng (pronounced gǒng): a coarse and wicked appearance. Lú (pronounced lú): to set forth or enumerate. Dèng (pronounced chēng): the manner of staring with wide-open eyes.

Mèng (pronounced méng): the lack of clarity in the eyes. Shùn (pronounced shùn): the frequent flickering of the eyes. Bèi (pronounced bèi): the rising of dust. Qù (pronounced qǔ): to spy or look on. Zhé (zhàn, entering tone): to be terrified. Yùn: a halo.
(Yùn). Shì (pronounced zé). Suì (pronounced suì). Chān (chā in the level tone). Qiāng (pronounced qiāng). Shì (pronounced shì; meaning "swift"). Hú (pronounced hú; fine silk gauze). Zuò (same as cù).

The Direct Pointing to the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume Three.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Huṅshu Tiānrán of the Thirty-Fourth Generation of the Dòng Lineage.
The Dharma-heir, the present-day monk Dan-gui, having read the *Jinbian Leshuo*, completes the comparison with the preceding two sections on the five aggregates (*skandha*).
△ Third, the six sense bases (*āyatana*). Divided into six parts. First, the eye base (*cakṣur-āyatana*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, why are the six sense bases fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
Ānanda, that very act of staring with the eyes until they become fatigued—both the eye and the fatigue—are equally the appearance of exhaustion produced by staring within Bodhi.
The six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are the six sense organs. Because the organs are that into which the objects enter, they are called the "six entrances.

The phrase "that person staring with fixed eyes until fatigue arises" refers back to the preceding text on the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Previously, the eye was used as a metaphor for true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*), and the clear sky as a metaphor for true reality (*tattva*).
That person, for no reason, does not move his eyes but stares until fatigue arises; this serves as a metaphor for beginningless non-awakening (*anādikālikāprabodha*).

When the mind moves, there arise the two aspects of the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*). Now, as illustrated in the preceding passage, we take only the "perceived aspect" (*nimitta*) within this context, which refers both to the eye and its fatigue.

Both are, in fact, the "fatigue-induced appearance" arising from the *bodhi* [of the Tathāgata-garbha]. Here, "eye" refers to the faculty (*indriya*), and "fatigue" refers to the deluded vision within that faculty.
The character "appearance" (*xiàng*, *nimitta*) in the phrase "the fatigue-induced appearance of *bodhi*" precisely traces back to the *Tathāgata-garbha*.
Unconsciously stirred by delusion, one becomes weary of these eyes and perceives their forms.
Thus, based on the two kinds of delusive objects—light and darkness—the faculty of vision arises within them; it draws in these objective images, and this is called the nature of seeing.
This vision is ultimately without substance apart from those two objects, light and darkness.
First, light and darkness were designated as objects to demonstrate that the faculty of sight and its perception have no substance apart from their objects;
that is to say, they flow forth from the nature of awareness, yet the vision itself has no intrinsic essence.
Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that this seeing does not come from light or darkness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced in space.
Since light and darkness encompass all forms, yet seeing is not itself a form within space, it is simply because its emergence is not from the organ; rather, it relies upon the organ to manifest.
It originally has no self-nature; it arises spontaneously through causes and conditions. It is destroyed without being destroyed. Why is this?

If it came from light, then darkness would extinguish it immediately, and one should not perceive darkness. If it came from darkness, then light would extinguish it immediately, and one should not perceive light.
If it were produced from the sense organ itself, there would necessarily be neither light nor darkness. Thus, this essence of vision is fundamentally...

It has no self-nature. If it emerges from emptiness, then when you first gaze at external objects, you should instead see the sense organs upon returning [to the source]. Furthermore, if emptiness observes itself, what concern is that for your sense-faculties?
From light one does not see darkness; from darkness one does not see light; and from the sense-organ, there is no time of either light or darkness.
This essence of vision, however, exists within the floating dust [of the physical eye]; it has no inherent nature of its own and cannot manifest on its own.

If it were to emerge from space, it would simply return to the eye that ought to see. Furthermore, the capacity to observe belongs to space itself; it is not related to the sense organ or its sensory entrance.
Therefore, you should know that the eye-entrance (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is illusory; fundamentally it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

When one exhaustively investigates all illusions, causes and conditions find no basis, and as for further doubting spontaneity, where could it possibly be manifested? △ Second, the ear-entrance (*śrotra-āyatana*).
Ānanda, it is like a person who, with two fingers, tightly plugs their ears. Because the faculty of hearing is strained, sounds arise within the head;
both the ear and the strain are equally the signs of fatigue produced by the fixed gaze of Bodhi.
This is the fundamental root of the analogy: blocking one's ears with a finger causes the ears to become fatigued and produce sounds;

this serves as a metaphor for the delusion of the ear-entrance (*śrotra-āyatana*). The delusions of the ear-entrance present in the unblocked ear are all like the illustrative example. Therefore, it is said:
"These are equally the signs of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi."
Based on the two kinds of false objects—movement and stillness—the faculty of hearing arises within them, absorbing these objective phenomena; this is called the nature of hearing.
This hearing has no ultimate substance apart from those two objects of movement and stillness. Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this hearing...
It does not come from movement or stillness; it does not emerge from the sense faculties; nor is it produced from space. Why is this?

If it came from stillness, then movement would be extinguished along with it, and one should not perceive movement. If it came from movement, then stillness would be extinguished along with it, and there should be no awareness of stillness.

If it were produced from the sense faculties, there would necessarily be neither movement nor stillness. Thus, the essence of hearing is originally without intrinsic nature. If it were to emerge from space... [there would be... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "若於空出，有". The translation reflects the available portion of the text.)
