If hearing constitutes its inherent nature, then it is not empty space. Furthermore, if space itself hears, what does that have to do with your faculty of hearing?
Those who claim that hearing constitutes its inherent nature and that hearing emerges from space argue that space would then become the nature of hearing and could no longer be called "space."
Therefore, you should know that the ear-entrance (*śrotra-āyatana*) is illusory; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This is explained in the same manner as the preceding section. △ Third, the nose-entrance (*ghrāṇa-āyatana*):
Ānanda, suppose there is a person who pinches their nose tightly; after pinching for a long time, they become fatigued, and then within the nose they perceive a sound.
The sensation of cold. By means of contact, one discriminates between penetration and obstruction, emptiness and solidity. Thus it extends even to various fragrant and foul odors;
together with the nose and its fatigue, these are all but the appearance of exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi.

This is also the same as the ear-faculty (*śrotra-āyatana*). It uses the fundamental faculty as a metaphor to reveal the falsity of the present nose-faculty (*ghrāṇa-āyatana*). The remaining three faculties below follow this example.

Because of the two kinds of false objects—permeability and obstruction—the faculty of hearing arises in the center; it draws in these objective phenomena, which is called the nature of smelling and hearing.
This hearing is ultimately devoid of essence when separated from those two objects, penetration and obstruction. One should know that this hearing does not come from penetration or obstruction;
it does not emerge from the faculty, nor is it produced in space. Why is this? If it came from penetration, then upon obstruction, hearing would cease; how then could one know obstruction?
If it existed because of obstruction, then during penetration there would be no hearing; how then could it manifest the perception of fragrance, stench, and so forth? If...
It arises from the sense organ; it certainly has no obstruction or penetration. Thus, this faculty of hearing originally lacks intrinsic nature.

If it were to emerge from space, then that hearing would naturally turn back to smell your own nose. Space itself would possess the power of hearing; what concern would it have with your sense-faculty? Therefore, you should know that the olfactory faculty is illusory;
it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions, nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
This follows the general explanation given previously. △ Fourth, the tongue faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*).

Ānanda, it is like a person who licks their lips with their tongue; by licking repeatedly until they become fatigued, if that person is ill, they perceive a bitter taste, whereas a healthy person perceives a slight sweet sensation.
Through this contrast between sweetness and bitterness, the unmoving nature of this tongue faculty is revealed.
At that time, the nature of blandness is ever-present. Together with the tongue and its exertion, they are equally the appearance of fatigue arising from the fixed gaze of *bodhi*.
Because of the two kinds of false objects—sweetness and bitterness—the faculty of cognition arises within them; it draws in these objective images and is called the "nature of knowing taste.
This nature of knowing taste has no ultimate substance apart from those three objects: sweetness, bitterness, and blandness. Thus, Ānanda, you should know this.

Thus, one knows bitterness and blandness through tasting; it does not come from sweetness or bitterness, nor does it exist because of blandness. Furthermore, it does not emerge from the tongue, nor is it produced from empty space. Why is this?

If it came from sweetness or bitterness, then when the blandness is tasted, that [knowledge of] sweetness or bitterness would cease; how then could one know the blandness? If it emerged from the blandness, then when sweetness is tasted, that [knowledge of] blandness would perish;
how then could one know the two characteristics of sweetness and bitterness? If it were produced from the tongue, there would necessarily be no sweetness.
The perception of blandness and bitterness is the faculty of tasting; know that this faculty has no inherent nature of its own.
From the perspective of the tongue, it is the ephemeral sense-organ (*āśraya-mūla*); the "faculty of tasting" refers to the ultimate sense-organ (*paramārtha*).

That is to say, if this perception of taste were produced from the ephemeral tongue-organ, then this ultimate faculty of tasting would reside within the ephemeral organ. However, when there is neither sweetness nor blandness, [it does not exist].
The original nature cannot manifest itself. Regarding the three—sweet, bitter, and bland—only two types of delusory objects are mentioned:
sweet and bitter belong to the realm of flavor, while bland belongs to the realm of non-flavor; therefore, they are divided into two pairs.

If it emerges from space, then space itself experiences its own flavor; this is not something known by your mouth. Furthermore, if space knows it for itself, what concern is that for your sense-faculties?

Your previous statement that "the name is known as the nature of flavor" merely relies on the premise that space experiences its own flavor and space knows it for itself; thus, the phrasing becomes redundant.
If you find this repetition objectionable and attempt to distribute the application [of the flavor] among the objects and the sense-faculties, then the text will lack coherence and meaning.
Therefore, you should know that the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
This is explained in the same manner as the preceding sections. △ Five: The Body-faculty (*kāya-āyatana*).
Ānanda, it is like a person whose one cold hand touches another hot hand. If the cold power is greater, the hot [hand]...
From cold, if the efficacy of heat is superior, the cold becomes hot. Thus, through this contact of combined perceptions, the knowledge of separation is revealed.
If these forces were to become established, they would arise from the contact of fatigue; when the body and fatigue coincide, both are but the signs of fatigue produced by the fixed gaze of Bodhi.
Both hands are the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*); therefore, cold and heat constitute the tactile object (*spraṣṭavya*). When they are combined and harmonious, separation must be contrary;
when they are combined and contrary, separation must be harmonious. Thus, the perception of conjunction manifests the cognition of disjunction.

When these forces interact as causes arising from fatiguing contact—namely, the force of cold and the force of heat—they are formed through the interaction of the predominant and the superior. This is due to...
Regarding the fatigued touch of the two hands, this perception is illusory;
it serves as a fundamental analogy to clarify that the present body-faculty is likewise so, being equally a sign of visual fatigue arising from the state of *bodhi*.
Based on the two kinds of deluded objects—separation and conjunction—an awakening arises within the center, which inhales these objective images; this is called the nature of cognitive awareness.
This essence of cognitive awareness is ultimately without substance apart from those objects of separation and conjunction, or opposition and compliance. Thus it is, Ānanda.

You should know that this cognition does not come from conjunction, nor does it exist through opposition or conformity; it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it born from space. Why is this?
If it came at the time of conjunction, it would have already ceased upon separation—how then could cognition perceive separation? The two aspects of opposition and conformity are likewise so.

If it emerged from the sense organs, there would necessarily be no four characteristics of conjunction, separation, opposition, and conformity; thus, your bodily cognition would be fundamentally... [non-existent].
There is no self-nature; it must emerge from emptiness. Emptiness is self-aware; what concern is this for your sense-base?
Therefore, you should know that the body-base is illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature.
This follows the general explanation given previously. △ Sixth, the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*).
Ānanda, it is like a person who sleeps when weary; having slept soundly, he awakens. Upon encountering sensory objects, he recollects them; losing this recollection constitutes forgetfulness.
All sentient beings are currently in a state of delusion; they possess "intention" (*manas*) but lack the "mind" (*citta*). When intention arises, the past and future become distinct;
when intention ceases, the present becomes obscure and indistinct. Moment by moment this shifts and changes, yet throughout one's entire life, one remains unaware of it.
This is precisely the fundamental root that is most easily clarified. It can be illustrated by the analogy of sleep, waking, recollection, and forgetfulness—specifically, the state within sleep.
A dream is used as a metaphor for provisional existence; suddenly waking from a dream is used as a metaphor for provisional non-existence.

Failing to understand provisional existence, one perceives the objects of the dream and subsequently recalls them; failing to understand provisional non-existence, one loses the memory upon waking and thus forgets them.
This fully describes the mind entering into falsehood, thereby introducing the mental faculty (*manas*) which is the subject of the following passage.
These are its inversions: arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. They are absorbed and returned into the midst of habitual practice, never exceeding one another.
What is called the faculty of mental cognition, together with the mind and its toil, is likewise a state of visual fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi.
This follows the preceding analogy, using it as an example for all instances of recollection and forgetting, which are like waking from sleep.

Recollection is like arising; forgetting is like ceasing. Arising is not truly arising; ceasing is not truly ceasing; therefore, they are called "inversions. The initial recollection is called arising;
the sustained recollection is called abiding; the initial forgetting is called change; the completion of forgetting is called cessation. To "inhale and practice" means to inhale these four stages.

The characteristics all return to the mental faculty (*manas*). The four characteristics are distinct and clear; in a single moment, they do not intermingle. Therefore, it is said that they do not transgress one another.

"According with the mind" refers to the intention of recollecting or forgetting—this indicates the six consciousnesses. The "faculty" (*indriya*) is the seventh consciousness. The seventh consciousness is the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*);
sentient beings deludedly take it as their own self-substance, which is what is called "toil. Therefore, it is said that they are equally *bodhi*.
The appearance of fatigue arises from staring.

Due to the two kinds of delusory objects—the arising and ceasing—consciousness gathers and dwells within; it draws in and seizes internal objects, causing seeing and hearing to flow against the current.

When this flow reaches a point where it no longer extends outward, it is called the nature of awareness and cognition. This nature of awareness and cognition is detached from those two objects of waking and sleeping, and of arising and ceasing.
Ultimately, it has no substantial reality.
Because of the two kinds of delusive objects—arising and ceasing—the aggregate of cognition abides in the center.

This refers to past external objects that correspond with the mind; when remembered, they appear vividly. These are what are called "fallen shadows," and they constitute internal objects. Thus it is seen.
To hear and follow along with sounds and forms is to flow with the current; to see and hear while grasping at sounds and forms and entering into them is to flow against the current.
To flow against the current is to reach a place where there is nowhere to go; it is that which the mental faculty alone can take as its object, named the nature of awareness and cognition.

Thus, while one is lost in delusion, it exists in dependence upon sensory objects; yet when separated from those objects, it is absent. This is because one is unable to reunite this awareness and cognition and return [to its source].
This is because its fundamental nature is complete; hence it is said to have no substance. This means that awakening and cognition possess no self-substance (*svabhāva*).

"Awakening and sleep" is a metaphorical borrowing from the preceding analogy of sleeping and waking, used to illustrate the provisional existence and provisional non-existence of arising and ceasing; it does not refer literally to the states of sleep and waking.
Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that this faculty of awareness does not come from waking or sleeping; it does not exist through arising or ceasing;
it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it born from space.
Awakening and sleep correspond precisely to the two terms "recollection" and "forgetting. Dreams within sleep are recollection; suddenly losing [the object] upon awakening is forgetting.
When there is correct recollection, it is arising; when recollection is lost, it is ceasing. If the mind does not confront sensory objects, from where could discrimination arise?
If one is apart from the mind, there is no awareness; how could it then emerge from emptiness?
Why is this? If awakening comes from sleep, then as soon as one sleeps, awakening immediately ceases; what, then, would constitute sleep?

If it must exist during birth, then upon death it becomes non-existent; who would then undergo death? If birth exists because of death, then as death ceases, birth is non-existent; who would know of birth?

"What shall one take as sleep? Who shall undergo cessation? Who knows that which is born? These three phrases, by themselves, should naturally awaken one so that one is not detained by the faculty of the mind.
If it arises from the sense organs, then its two states of waking and sleeping would open and close according to the body;

yet apart from these two forms, this cognizer would be like a flower in the sky—ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature. If it arises from space, it would simply be the cognition of space; what concern would it have with your sense faculties?
The two bodies are precisely the two bodies of waking and sleeping. This clarifies that the nature of enlightened awareness is devoid of self-nature;
it manifests through waking and sleeping and cannot arise of itself.
Therefore, one should know that the mental faculty (*manāyatana*) is illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing a spontaneous nature.
The explanation is the same as before.
This includes both the "fixing" (*staimitya*) and the "fatigue" (*klamatha*); these are equally the signs of fatigue produced by the *bodhi*-gaze.

Furthermore, it says that this seeing, apart from the two objects of light and darkness, ultimately has no substance. How then can all that is produced by the gaze be subsumed within the wondrous nature of *bodhi*? And yet, this...
Is it not seen that this, in turn, refutes the claim that [seeing] lacks substance? Now, the statement "this is the mind, not the eye" already clearly points to seeing as being the mind;
thus, this "lack of substance" refers to the fact that seeing lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and its entire essence is the mind.
Therefore, speaking in terms of seeing, it is said to have no self-substance; speaking in terms of the mind, it is said to have no substance of seeing. This directly points to...
Detached from dust and freed from views, one awakens and attains self-mastery; this applies to all six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The first three sets of six sense bases are concluded. △ Fourth, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). This is divided into six parts. First, the two bases of form and vision.
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the twelve bases (āyatana) fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?
Ānanda, you should now observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds. What do you think?
Do these forms arise from the eye’s seeing, or does the eye arise from the appearance of forms?
The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: "Bases (*āyatana*) refer to gates of arising. Because the mind and mental factors arise and grow therein, they are called bases.
This is because the six faculties and the six objects are the places where consciousness arises; whereas the previous section spoke of the faculties, this section speaks of the objects.
Since one investigates by means of the faculty confronting the object, both are presented here for thorough analysis.
Ānanda, if it were the eye faculty that produced the appearance of form, then when seeing empty space—which is not form—the nature of form would have to dissolve.

If it dissolved, everything would manifest as being utterly non-existent. Since the appearance of form would no longer exist, who would perceive the substance of empty space? The same applies to empty space.
This is the ultimate exhaustion of form where no place of arising exists. It begins by stating that the eye does not give rise to form;

for when one perceives emptiness, the nature of the form capable of being produced has already dissolved, and the characteristics of the form produced have likewise perished. What could there be to stand in contrast and manifest the substance of emptiness?

By exhausting form until both the subjective capacity and the objective object are utterly spent, even the act of manifestation itself vanishes. Thus, one gains further knowledge of the present moment before one.

Absolutely. How could one possibly entertain such deliberations? This merely exhausts the analysis of form; the same applies to speaking of emptiness, for emptiness and form are fundamentally inseparable.
Furthermore, if the dust of form gives rise to visual perception, then by contemplating that emptiness is not form, seeing itself will vanish. Once it has vanished, it is utterly non-existent.
Who clarifies that form is empty?
It is said that form, too, does not arise in the eye; for one clarifies that it is like a flower in the sky, unable to produce clarity in the clear eyes.

At the moment of seeing the sky, the form produced by that vision has already dissolved, and the characteristics of the form capable of producing it are entirely exhausted. Thus, both the subject and the object...
Both are extinguished; who can distinguish between emptiness and form? What is called true wisdom has no seeing, and the true principle has no form;
this is what one may conceive therein. Furthermore, the mention of "emptiness" also follows the same principle as before.
Therefore, you should know that seeing and the emptiness of form both have no location; thus, form and seeing—these two locations—are false and illusory.
Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor do they possess an inherent nature.
This statement regarding "location" is thus reduced to a non-location; it thereby becomes a false fabrication.
Since it has become a false fabrication, its causes and conditions arise spontaneously, further constituting frivolous conceptual proliferation. △ Second, the two locations of sound and hearing.
Ānanda, listen further to this: when food is prepared in this Jeta Grove, the drum is struck; when the assembly gathers, the bell is tolled.

Regarding these sounds of the bells and drums, which follow one another in succession—what do you think? Do these sounds come to the side of the ear, or does the ear go to the place where the sounds are?

Sound does not come to the ear, nor does the ear go to the sound; yet hearing and resonance function together. The bells and drums do not intersect, and movement and stillness have no before or after.
Though the words exhaust the sounds, the meaning has already been revealed in mystery. Let the reader contemplate this.

Ānanda, if this sound comes to the vicinity of the ear—just as when I went to Śrāvastī for alms and was at Jeta’s Grove, I was not there [in that specific location]—then this sound must come to Ānanda’s ears. Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it together;
how much less so the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas? Yet, upon hearing the sound of the bell, they all came together.
Regarding the place where food is eaten:
if sounds from all quarters reached one's ears simultaneously, they would have to come individually rather than arriving everywhere at once.

This is illustrated by the proof that when the Tathāgata went into the city to beg for alms, there was no "self" in the Jeta Grove; this is also evident upon observation according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, if your ear were to travel to the location of the sound, then just as when I have returned to reside in the Jeta Grove, there would be no "I" remaining here in the city of Śrāvastī;

yet when you hear the sound of a drum, your ear has already gone to the place where the drum is being struck. Now, when the bell-sound arises simultaneously [with the drum], [which one does your ear follow?]
They should not hear them simultaneously; how much less so the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within? If there were no coming and going, there would likewise be no hearing.
If the ear traveled to the location of the sound, it would have to go alone to the side of the drum and should not further hear the sound of the bell as it comes and goes.
Both are exhausted; this further demonstrates that both hearing and sound are equally false.
Therefore, one should know that both hearing and sound have no location; thus, the two locations of hearing and sound are both empty and false.
It is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature;
this is explained as in the previous passage. △ Third, the two locations of smelling fragrance:
"Ānanda, you are now smelling this sandalwood in the incense burner. If this fragrance were burned from even a single *zhu* (a small weight), [the scent would fill] Śrāvastī..."
Within forty *li* of the city of Raft, the scent is perceived simultaneously. What do you think?
Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree, or does it arise from your nose, or does it arise from space?
This refers to the place where the single atom of dust arises, independent of the contact with the sense organs. Sandalwood is the foremost among all fragrant woods.
As for the *zhu*, twenty-four *zhu* constitute one *liang*.
Ānanda, if this fragrance were produced in your nose, and was designated as being produced by the nose, it would have to emerge from the nose.
Since the nose is not sandalwood, how could there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose? If it is designated that you smell the fragrance, then it must enter through the nose;
yet for fragrance to emerge from within the nose while being called "smelling" is logically untenable.
If fragrance were produced by the nose, then the fragrance should emerge from the nose; yet now it enters through the nose, and only then is it called "smelling fragrance.

The nose is not sandalwood itself, so how could one claim that there is the scent of sandalwood within the nose? To exhaust the meaning of "hearing" (perceiving), one must acknowledge that [the scent] emerges from the nose, thereby proving that it is not produced by the nose.
If fragrance were produced from emptiness, and since the nature of emptiness is eternal and constant, fragrance ought to be ever-present. Why, then, rely upon burning this withered wood in a brazier?
Since the nature of emptiness is eternal and constant, fragrance must depend on the burning of wood; it cannot be that fragrance arises from emptiness alone.
If it arises from wood, then this fragrant substance must become smoke through burning. If the nose were to perceive it, it would have to encounter the scent of that smoke.
Yet, before the smoke has even ascended far into the air, how is it that [the fragrance] is already smelled within forty *li*?
Smoke serves as the sign for wood; the nose perceives only fragrance and does not receive the smoke itself. Although the smoke rises no great distance, it is perceived at forty *li*.
Thus we know that fragrance is not produced by the wood.
Therefore, you should know that the nose and its fragrance, together with the act of smelling, have no location. Thus, both the act of smelling and the fragrance are empty and false;
fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
The commentary on the connection is the same as before. △ Fourth, the two locations where flavors are tasted:
"Ānanda, you constantly carry the alms bowl among the assembly at the two times of the day. During that interval, you may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter, which are called superior flavors.
What do you think? Does this flavor arise from space, or does it arise within the tongue?"
Regarding food:
this also serves to exhaustively investigate the place where the sense-object arises.
Ānanda, if this taste were produced in your tongue, it would be located within your mouth; yet you possess but a single tongue, and that tongue—
At that time, when the flavor of clarified butter has already been experienced, upon encountering black rock honey, it should not shift.
If it does not shift, it cannot be called "knowing the flavor. If it does shift, yet the tongue is not a plurality of entities, how can a single tongue perceive multiple flavors?
Because the encounter with honey makes the taste possible, it is realized that [the taste] does not arise from the tongue.
If it were produced by the food, and the food itself lacks consciousness, how could it know itself? Furthermore, if the food knew itself, it would be the same as another person eating.
How could this have anything to do with your knowledge of the names and flavors [of food]?
Since food lacks the faculty of consciousness, how could it possibly know flavor? Even if one were to concede that it does possess such knowledge, it would still be identical to the food of others;
therefore, it is not produced by food.
If it arises from space, what flavor would you experience as you consume that emptiness?

If that emptiness were to have a salty taste, once your tongue was salted by it, your face would also become salted; then the people of this world would be just like sea fish, constantly experiencing saltiness.

One is utterly unaware of the bland. If one does not recognize the bland, one likewise does not perceive the salty; there would necessarily be no cognition at all. How, then, could this be called "taste"?
Regarding the four lines beginning with "Since it has long tasted the salty," you have already exhausted the point that emptiness lacks such [sensory] activity.

Since it has long been tasting the salty, it is utterly unaware of the bland; if it does not recognize the bland, it likewise does not perceive the salty. Furthermore, the emergence of taste must depend upon cognition, yet emptiness possesses no cognition.
The nature of taste is fundamentally non-existent; it is entirely a transformation of consciousness.
Therefore, one should know that taste, the tongue, and the act of tasting all lack a fixed location; thus, both the act of tasting and the taste itself are equally illusory.
"It is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
This is explained in the same manner as the preceding passage. △ Fifth, the two bases of body and touch.
"Ānanda, you regularly rub your head with your hand every morning. What do you think? Regarding that which is known through this rubbing, who is it that acts?"
That which is capable of touching—does it reside in the hand, or does it reside in the head?

This, too, is a solitary inquiry into the place where the object arises. Since both the subject that touches and the object touched are one's own body, the subject that perceives and the object perceived are likewise identical to external objects.
By examining the capacity for perception, one finds that the locus of touch is not fixed; through careful investigation, one knows that what is seen is precisely what is known.
This is a confusion that will be refuted by the following text.
If [the faculty of touch] were located in the hand, the head would be devoid of cognition; how then could contact be established? If it were located in the head, the hand would be useless.
What is meant by "contact"? If these were separate entities, then you, Ānanda, would have two bodies.

If the capacity for contact resides in the hand, then the head should be devoid of cognition; if the capacity for contact resides in the head, then the hand should be useless—and that which is useless is devoid of cognition.
Since both possess cognition, there must be two bodies.
If contact were produced by the head and hand being one, then the hand and the head would have to be a single entity. If they were a single entity, contact could not be established.

If they were two distinct entities, with which one would contact reside? It cannot reside in the agent, nor can it reside in the object; if it resided in the object, it would not be the agent, and if it resided in the agent, it would not be the object.
Space should not come into contact with you;

yet since both the head and the hands touch it, they must be of one substance. If they were of one substance, there would be neither subject nor object, and thus the meaning of "contact" would not be established.
If they were of two substances, then both substances would be the subject; what then would be the object? Or if both substances were the object, what then would be the subject?
It can touch. It should not be that empty space becomes something that touches you; this would immediately contradict the previous inquiry regarding the arising of emptiness.
Therefore, one should know that both the perception of touch and the body have no location; thus, both the body and touch are equally illusory.
It is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature;
this is explained in the same manner as before. △ Sixth, regarding the two bases of mind and dharmas:
Ānanda, that which you constantly take as objects within the mind—the three natures of good, evil, and neutral—these constitute the laws that give rise to phenomena. These phenomena...
Does it arise from the mind itself, or does it exist as a separate location apart from the mind?
Since "intention" (*manas*) here refers to the mental faculty (*manendriya*), the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—refer to the mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*).

"Dharma" (phenomena) functions like a model or pattern; though dharmas do not themselves produce [the mind], the beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) formed within the mental faculty seem to carve out [its form].

This is not like the case of form and other objects, which possess substantial reality. Since they are manifested through the transformation of consciousness, to inquire whether they are identical to the mind or distinct from it results in faults in either case, as will be clarified below in the text.
Ānanda, if the dharma were identical to the mind, then it would not be an object; it would not be something for the mind to take as its objective support (*ālambana*).

How, then, could it constitute a sense-field (*āyatana*)? It is only when the mind encounters an object that they form an objective support. If the dharma were identical to the mind, it would not be an object. Since there would be no objective support, from what could a sense-field be established?
If there were a separate location apart from the mind, then would the self-nature of that phenomenon be conscious or unconscious? If it were conscious, it would be called "mind";

being distinct from you yet not an external object, it would be identical to the mental measure (*cittamātra*) of others. It would be you and it would be the mind; how could your mind then be dualistic with respect to you?

The intrinsic nature of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is fundamentally without cognition; it is only through the transformation of consciousness that they appear as such, and thus one may challenge whether they are cognitive or non-cognitive.

If they were cognitive, they would belong to the mind. However, since they differ from your own substance and yet are not the characteristics of external objects, they are identical to the mental measure (*citta-pramāṇa*) of another person.
Because they differ [from you], they resemble another; because they are cognitive, they are like the mind. Therefore, this inquiry arises.
Furthermore, if you claim that it is not "other" but is you yourself, then both the sense organs and their objects would be conscious; how could your mind possess two distinct aspects?

If it is not consciousness, then these objects—being neither form, sound, fragrance, taste, texture, nor the sensations of separation, union, cold, warmth, or the characteristics of empty space—are nothing at all.
Where could it possibly exist? Now, within the emptiness of form, there is no indication whatsoever. It cannot be that there is further emptiness outside of the human realm.
Since the mind is not an object of perception, from what could its locus be established?

It is neither cognition, nor is it the same as the five sensory objects of the real realm; it is the ultimate object of mental focus, exhausting both emptiness and form, and is entirely devoid of representation.
In such a state, where could it possibly be established?
Therefore, you should know that both dharmas and the mind have no location; thus, both the mental faculty and dharmas are equally false and illusory.
Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
The commentary on the formation of these bonds is the same as before.

What is seen before one’s eyes is one’s own seeing; form is its own form, and emptiness is its own emptiness. Though the myriad phenomena of the present are arrayed before us, it is said that they all lack a fixed location.
This is truly difficult to understand, for it is because seeing is confined by form and emptiness that it becomes localized and forms a faculty. This faculty—
Dusts depend upon one another; the mind and its objects appear vividly. Emptiness has no substance by nature, and form is likewise subject to change.
At this very moment, when one is in darkness, there is nowhere to return; when seeing occurs, to what can it be attached? Try looking back once:
like suddenly waking from a dream, as you examine the realms of experience, the subject and object fall away abruptly—who, indeed, has established them? All other locations are likewise thus.
The forty-two locations above are concluded. △ Fifth, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). Divided into six parts, first is the element of eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the eighteen elements fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature (*tathatāsvabhāva*) of the Tathāgata-garbha?

The faculties, objects, and consciousnesses each consist of six. According to the ancient commentary, "dhātu" (界) means a lineage or category; each serves as a boundary so that they do not become confused with one another.
Below, these boundaries are broken down to be reunited within the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. This is different from the entry points used to exhaustively investigate the places of birth.
Ānanda, as you understand it, visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions.
Does this consciousness arise because of the eye and take the eye as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of visible forms and take visible forms as its constituent element?

When the sense organs and their objects encounter one another, consciousness arises therein; this is the principle of dependent origination. Ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle regard this as truly existent, so [the text] refutes their attachment to reveal that it is "mind-only.
Whether one speaks of causes and conditions or of spontaneity, both are mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).

The visual faculty (*cakṣurdhātu*) takes up the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of past forms to constitute its elemental nature; it then manifests the nature of seeing by confronting present forms with the present. Form...

Due to what was previously seen by the eye and the predominant power of the present, the characteristic of the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*) is established. Consciousness relies upon the eye and takes form as its object, cognizing it clearly;
because the seeds of perfuming exist within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it immediately discriminates in accordance with what is currently seen.

This is the characteristic of the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*). These [three] are each examined through the eye and form in order to exhaustively investigate their lack of a separate realm (*dhātu*).

Ānanda, if [consciousness] arises because of the eye, then in the absence of form and space, there would be nothing to differentiate. Even if your consciousness were present, what would you have it serve?
Furthermore, your seeing is not blue, yellow, red, or white; since there is nothing to indicate it, from what could its boundaries be established?
When the eye arises, there is no emptiness of form; discrimination has nothing upon which to rely.

This eye is also not blue, yellow, red, or white—this statement that the single eye is devoid of color means it cannot constitute the intermediate realm. "Seeing" refers to the seeing of the eye itself.
If consciousness arises because of form, then when space is devoid of form, your consciousness should cease. How then could you cognize the nature of this void?
If form undergoes change, you likewise cognize that the characteristics of form are shifting; yet if your consciousness does not shift, from what basis would the realms of perception be established?
If it changes along with the transformation [of form], then the characteristics of the realm would naturally cease to exist. If it does not change, then it is constant;

yet since it arises from form, it should not be able to cognize the location of space. When form arises, it should be extinguished within space; thus, it could not know space. Furthermore, when form undergoes transformation, your consciousness should perceive it.
If cognition is known [to be unchanging], then the nature of consciousness does not shift; it stands solitary and isolated—how could it constitute a realm?
As for those who argue for change, they further calculate that consciousness and form undergo transformation together. If they transform together, no realm can be established.
If they do not transform, then the consciousness that gives rise to form would have its subject and object as similar types, and it too should never know emptiness.

If both types [of causes] were involved such that the eye and form arise together, then when they combine, they would separate from the middle; and when they separate, they would join at both ends. Their essential natures would thus be confused and disordered;
how, then, could they constitute a "realm" (*dhātu*)?
If the eye and form combined to produce a middle realm, then the consciousness of that middle realm should be divisible into knowing and not-knowing. Therefore—
It is said that they are separated in the middle. Being separated, one half follows the sense organ and one half follows the object; therefore, it is called "the two joining.
This is what is meant by the confusion of their essential natures, whereby they cannot constitute a *dhātu*.
Therefore, one should know that the eye and forms serve as conditions for the arising of the eye-consciousness element.

Since these three locations are all non-existent, then the eye and forms, as well as the three factors of the form-element, are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

The three—sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—mutually depend upon one another to constitute the realms (*dhātu*). If even one of these is not established, then all three are not established; therefore, it is said that they are "entirely non-existent.

This reveals that [all things] are manifestations of mind alone and lack inherent nature (*svabhāva*). Being manifestations of mind alone, they are not produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Since both lack intrinsic nature, they are not self-originated.
△ Second, the auditory consciousness element. Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the ear and sound as conditions, auditory consciousness arises.
Does this consciousness arise because of the ear, taking the ear as its element? Or does it arise because of sound, taking sound as its element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the ear...

When the two characteristics of motion and stillness do not manifest before it, the faculty does not constitute cognition; there is necessarily nothing known. Since even cognition itself cannot be established, what form or appearance could consciousness have?
It is because of motion and stillness that the faculty’s cognition first appears. If motion and stillness were absent, by what would the faculty’s cognition be made known?
When [the object] is perceived, mental consciousness arises; this faculty of cognition refers exclusively to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

If one takes "hearing" as the basis, since there is neither movement nor stillness, hearing would have nothing to establish it. How then could the ear-form, which is a mixture of visible form and tangible objects, be called the "element of consciousness"?
If so, from what would the "element of ear-consciousness" itself be established?

The sensory organ is formed from the floating particles (rajas). Because there is the ear in its ultimate sense (paramārtha), one knows that hearing occurs even though there is nothing to which it is attached; thus, the ear is a floating-sensory-organ (āyatana).
Furthermore, since it is a composite of various phenomena (dharmas), why is it called the "consciousness-element" (vijñāna-dhātu)? This "ear-hearing" refers to the floating particles;
taken as a whole, it is said that because the two characteristics of motion and stillness do not exist, the ear-consciousness-element is not established.
If [consciousness] arises from sound, and consciousness exists because of sound, then it would have no relation to hearing. Without hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound would vanish;

yet if consciousness arises from sound, you must admit that the characteristic of sound exists because of hearing. Hearing should then hear the consciousness; if there is no hearing, it is not a constituent element (*dhātu*).

When hearing occurs, it is accompanied by sound. Since consciousness has already been affected by hearing, who knows this hearing-consciousness? If there were no knower, one would ultimately be like grass or wood.
When sound arises, there is no nature of hearing; who then perceives the characteristics of sound?

Even if you claim that consciousness arises from sound, you must admit that the characteristics of sound exist because of hearing. Thus, at the very moment of hearing the sound, it is the hearing-consciousness itself, for consciousness arises from sound.
The seed and the sprout are of a similar nature. If there were no consciousness of hearing, it would not fulfill the definition of a "sphere" (dhātu);
that is to say, sound would not be a sphere for the arising of consciousness. Hearing is identical to sound; since consciousness can discern it, sound becomes the object of what is heard.
Who, then, is the knower who knows this consciousness of hearing? If there were hearing without knowing, one would be the same as grass or wood. [This] admits sound...
Because one hears the origin of the characteristics of sound, this serves to remedy the difficulty of sound arising.

When hearing responds to what is heard, consciousness then avoids the sound that is heard, fearing it might be confused with the permanence of the sense-faculties and their objects. Once consciousness has already been "heard," its power of discrimination is further stripped away;
thus, the inquiry into the nature of hearing-consciousness reaches its conclusion. Whether through empty concession or empty withdrawal, all is seen to be empty and false.

The auditory faculty and its object should not be mixed to form a middle element (*dhātu*), for there is no intermediate position within an element. If there is no middle, how then can the characteristics of "internal" and "external" be established?
This is the refutation of the co-arising of the eye and visible forms. Since they cannot be mixed to form a middle, from what would the elements be determined?
Therefore, one should know that the ear and sound serve as conditions for the arising of the auditory consciousness-element (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*).

Since these three locations are entirely non-existent, then the ear, the sound, and the auditory consciousness-element—these three—are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The explanation of the conclusion is the same as before. △ Third, the element of nose-consciousness.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the nose and odors as conditions, nose-consciousness arises.

Does this consciousness arise because of the nose, taking the nose as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of odors, taking odors as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the nose...
Then, within your mind, what constitutes the nose? Is it the physical form of the two nostrils, or is it the nature of olfactory cognition and its movement?
This investigation reveals that neither arises from the nose itself; both the superficial and the ultimate are merely floating dust.

If one takes the physical form of flesh as the substance of the body, then bodily cognition is simply contact; thus, what is called "body" is not the nose, and what is called "contact" is simply the sense-object.
Since even the nose lacks a name [in this context], how can one establish the [distinct] elements (*dhātu*)?

First, I shall refute the notion of the "floating root. The floating root is the body; that which touches the body is called an object. This proves that [the sense of smell] does not arise from the physical nose.
If one were to take olfactory cognition as the criterion, then within your mind, what would you consider to be the knower? If you say the flesh is the knower, then it is the flesh that knows.
The original contact is not the nose.
The following sections all refute the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). First, the cognition of the flesh is refuted; it remains identical to bodily touch.
If one takes space as the cognizer, then space would know itself; thus, the flesh would not be the faculty of perception. If this were so, then space must be you.
Your body is not the knower. Today, Ānanda, you should have no location [of consciousness].
Next, I shall refute the notion that space is the knower. If space were the knower, then space would be you. If the flesh is not sentient, then your body is without knowledge;
in that case, Ānanda, where would your physical presence actually be?
If you take fragrance to be consciousness, then that consciousness belongs solely to the fragrance;

what concern is it to you? Next, [the text] refutes the notion that fragrance is consciousness: "The consciousness of fragrance is not you. This refers to fragrance as being consciousness; [it asks: "Is it the consciousness that perceives fragrance?"
Furthermore, he formulates the following counter-argument:
"If fragrant and foul odors must arise within your nose, then those two types of flowing vapors— the fragrant and the foul— would not arise from the eranda tree and the sandalwood tree respectively."
Because you perceive fragrance and stench through your nose, you maintain the notion that fragrance and stench arise within your nose.
However, this fragrance and stench do not originate from the *eranda* (castor-oil plant) or the sandalwood tree. The *eranda* is a foul-smelling wood;
yet, within an *eranda* thicket, sandalwood trees may constantly grow. Once those sandalwood trees have matured, the *eranda* will forever be devoid of its foul odor.
The two things do not come to you; you yourself smell your own nose. Is it fragrant or foul? If it is foul, it is not fragrant; if it is fragrant, it should not be foul.
You yourself smell your own nose to see if it is fragrant or foul, yet upon investigating whether fragrance or foulness arises, they do not arise from your nose.
If it is foul, it is not fragrant; if it is fragrant, it should not be foul. Furthermore, this provides the basis for the following refutation regarding the simultaneous perception of both.
If you were able to smell both fragrance and stench simultaneously, then you, as a single person, would have to possess two noses.
When I question you, there appear to be two Ānandas before me; which of them constitutes your true self?
If the nose were entirely fragrant, it should not perceive odors; if the nose were entirely foul-smelling, it should not perceive fragrances.
Since it is now able to perceive both, there ought to be two noses. If there were two noses, there would have to be two distinct entities.
If the nose were a single entity, fragrance and stench would not be two distinct things. Since what is foul becomes fragrant and what is fragrant becomes foul, these two natures do not exist;
from whom, then, could the [olfactory] element be established?

Furthermore, if there were but a single nose, one would perceive fragrance and stench simultaneously; thus, fragrance and stench would lack fixity, and how could the element of consciousness be established?

If consciousness arises because of fragrance, then consciousness exists because of fragrance—just as the eye has the faculty of seeing yet cannot see itself; because consciousness exists because of fragrance, it cannot know fragrance itself.
One should not be able to know fragrance.
Since fragrance has already given rise to consciousness, that consciousness is itself the fragrance; therefore, fragrance cannot further know fragrance, just as the eye cannot further see the eye.
Knowing is precisely not arising; not knowing is not consciousness.
Following from the above: if consciousness were able to know fragrance, then consciousness would not arise from fragrance. If it does not know fragrance, [it is not consciousness].
Thus, it is not the essence of consciousness that discerns;
fragrance does not exist through cognition. The fragrance-element would not be established. If consciousness does not know fragrance, then the element cannot be established based upon fragrance.

Building upon the previous point that fragrance and stench arise from your nose, you should know that fragrance exists. If this [nose] were not aware of fragrance, then the fragrance-element (*gandhadhātu*) would not be established.

Furthermore, based on the preceding point that consciousness arises because of fragrance, [the nose] should not be unaware of fragrance; hence it is said that "consciousness does not perceive fragrance.
Regarding the "element" (*dhātu*), it is so called because consciousness establishes the element by depending on fragrance; if it were now unaware of fragrance, then the "element" would not exist.
It is not established from fragrance.
Since there is no intermediate state, neither interior nor exterior can be formed. Those various natures of hearing are ultimately false and illusory;

when traced upward to the sense organs and their objects, they cannot produce consciousness. Thus, there is no intermediate state. Since the intermediate does not stand, neither interior nor exterior exists.
Therefore, it is false and illusory.
For this reason, one should know that although the nose and fragrance serve as conditions for the arising of the nose-consciousness element, these three locations are entirely non-existent;
thus, the triad of the nose, fragrance, and the fragrance-element are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The explanation of the conclusion is the same as before.
△ Fourth, the tongue-consciousness element. Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the tongue and flavors as conditions, tongue-consciousness arises.

Does this consciousness arise because of the tongue, taking the tongue as its element? Or does it arise because of flavors, taking flavors as its element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the tongue...
Then all the sugarcane, *ume* plums, *hāridrā*, rock salt, *śuṇṭhī*, ginger, and cinnamon in the world would have no taste at all.
You should test your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter?
Consciousness arises because of the tongue. If it were not for the five flavors, the tongue would possess both sweetness and bitterness;

why then does it not taste itself? If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste the tongue? Since the tongue does not taste itself, what constitutes its cognition? Thus, the nature of the tongue is not bitter.
Taste does not arise by itself; how, then, can the element [of taste] be established?
If the nature of the tongue were bitter, the tongue would already be a taste; who then would be the knower of taste? If the tongue were not bitter, then there would be no taste;
how could the element of consciousness be established?

If consciousness arises because of flavor, then consciousness itself would be the flavor, just as it is with the tongue-organ; thus, it should not taste itself. How then could consciousness discern whether something is a flavor or not a flavor?

Previously, when [consciousness] arose because of the tongue, the tongue did not taste itself; now, when it arises because of flavor, it is identical to the tongue and should likewise not taste itself.

Furthermore, all tastes do not arise from a single substance. Since tastes arise from many sources, consciousness should likewise possess multiple entities. If the entity of consciousness were one, then that single entity would necessarily be produced by taste;
yet when salty, bland, sweet, and pungent flavors combine and arise together, their various changing characteristics are unified into a single taste.
It should be without discrimination. Since discrimination is absent, it cannot be called consciousness (*vijñāna*). How, then, can it be called the "consciousness-element of the tongue and flavors"?
If flavors arise individually, then consciousness should consist of multiple entities. If consciousness were a single entity, then the five flavors would likewise have no distinction.
That which lacks distinction is not consciousness; if the tongue and flavors were conflated, how could the consciousness-element be established?
It cannot be that space gives rise to your mind-consciousness.
This [consciousness] arises from the exhaustion of space;
it arises from the conjunction of the tongue and flavors, yet within this very process there is fundamentally no self-nature. How, then, could it arise from the elements?

If this [tongue-consciousness] is exhausted through arising from a combination of conditions, then consciousness lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the element (*dhātu*) is likewise not established.

Therefore, one should know that although the tongue and flavors serve as conditions for the arising of the tongue-consciousness element, all three locations are entirely non-existent; thus, the tongue and the flavors— [...are likewise empty.]
And as for the three [elements] of the tongue-element (*jihvā-dhātu*), they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The explanation of their binding and release is the same as before. △ Fifth, the consciousness-element of the body (*kāya-vijñāna-dhātu*).
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand—that the body and touch serve as conditions to give rise to body-consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the body?
That which is produced has the body as its element; that which is produced by contact has contact as its element.

Ānanda, if it were produced solely by means of the body, there would necessarily be no conditions for the two types of mental application—conjunction and separation—and what, then, would the body perceive?

This arises from the exhaustion of the sense faculties (*indriya*). Since there are no conditions for contact (*sparśa*)—neither the two types of "separation" nor "conjunction"—how can body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) manifest?
Gross investigation (*vitarka*) is called "awakening" (*jāgṛti*), while subtle analysis (*vicāra*) is called "observation" (*anupaśyanā*).
If it were produced because of contact, there would necessarily be no body for you; who, lacking a body, could perceive union and separation?
This [consciousness] arises from the atoms themselves; thus, there would be no root-body to perceive union and separation.
Ānanda, objects do not touch cognition; it is the body that knows there is contact.
An object cannot be known through contact itself; rather, the bodily cognition must necessarily depend upon the presence of contact.
This is precisely stated to introduce the subsequent difficulties regarding the two "identities" and two "non-identities."

To know the body is to know contact; to know contact is to know the body. Yet that which is contact is not the body, and that which is the body is not contact. These two characteristics of body and contact are fundamentally without location.
If contact can produce consciousness, it must first be known by the body before it becomes contact; therefore, it is said that "knowing the body is itself contact.
Furthermore, one must know it as contact before it is designated as "my body"; therefore, it is said that "knowing contact is itself the body.

If it has already become contact, then the object (viṣaya) must necessarily not be the faculty (indriya); therefore, it is said to be "not the body. If it is my body, then the faculty must necessarily not be the object.
Therefore, it is said that there is no contact. Is it not the case that the two characteristics of the sense organ and the object originally have no fixed location?
When combined with the body, they constitute the very nature of the body itself; when separated from the body, they are simply the characteristics of empty space and so forth.
When this contact joins with the body, it is entirely the sensation of the body; when separated from the body, it is identical to empty space.
This reaches the point where, both internally and externally, there is no state of contact; this is intended as the reason why the element of touch is not established in the subsequent section.

Since the internal and external are not established, how can the middle be established? Since the middle cannot be established, and since the nature of the internal and external is empty, from whom would your consciousness arise, and by what means would the realms be established?

"Internal and external" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). Since the nature of the sense organs and their objects is empty, and the substance of consciousness is like an illusion, one knows that these three locations are entirely non-existent.

Therefore, one should understand that when body and touch serve as conditions, the element of body-consciousness arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, both body and touch—
And as for the body-element and the three [other elements], they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature;
the explanation of their bondage and liberation is the same as before. △ Sixth, the consciousness-element:
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand—that with the mind and mental objects as conditions, consciousness arises—is this consciousness, moreover, caused by the mind?
That which is produced has the mind as its realm; it is produced because of dharmas, having dharmas as its realm.

Ānanda, if it is produced because of the mind, then within your mind there must be something upon which you reflect, which brings forth your mental activity. If those preceding dharmas were absent, the mind would have nothing from which to arise.
Apart from conditions, there is no form; what, then, would consciousness be used for?

This [consciousness] arises by exhausting the sense-faculties. This means that apart from dharmas, the mind has nothing upon which to rely and thus gives rise to discrimination. "Apart from conditions" refers to being apart from the conditions of dharmas.
If one is apart from the conditions of dharmas, then even the formal segments of the mind cannot be apprehended, let alone consciousness itself.
Furthermore, is this consciousness-mind identical to or different from the various faculties of deliberation and the nature of discernment?
This consciousness-mind, according to the above, should be called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because below it there are these two functions: deliberation and discernment. This is so.
With deliberation as the seventh and discernment as the sixth, both belong to the faculty of mind (*manas*).

Since the fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is originally the eighth, it may be called the "consciousness-mind" (*vijñāna-citta*). When the Tathāgatagarbha, through non-awakening, undergoes deluded movement, the entire mind becomes consciousness;
thus one knows that the essence of mind and consciousness is identical, differing only in their states of delusion and awakening. In delusion, one grasps at phenomena.

When the faculties are established, there is then deliberation and discernment; this investigation of their similarities and differences is intended so that people may awaken to the essence of consciousness without departing from the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses], whereby the Tathāgatagarbha need not be borne as a separate burden.
If "intention" (*manas*) is identical to "consciousness," how can that which is produced be distinct from intention? If they were not distinct, there would be no object of cognition.

If there is no object of cognition, how can intention arise? If there is an object of cognition, how can one cognize intention? Thus, neither identity nor difference between the two natures can be established.
How is the realm established?

If this mental consciousness were identical to the mental faculty (*manas*), then being identical it should not arise again; furthermore, there would be the fault of the confusion between faculties and consciousnesses.
If the mental consciousness were different from the mental faculty, then being different it would arise as something of a dissimilar class. It should...

There is no cognition. Even if there were cognition, it would not correspond to the mind (*manas*). What is meant by "cognizing the mind"? It is as if saying that cognition does not arise from the mind.

Being neither identical nor different, one exhausts the investigation into the arising of the mind; thus, one may grasp the essential principle of the realization or delusion regarding its substance and function.
If worldly phenomena arise from causes, they do not exist apart from the five sense objects.
Observe that the phenomena of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch have distinct characteristics; they correspond to the five sense organs and are not subsumed by the mind.

The five sense-consciousnesses arise from present objects and are not subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas*). Since they are not subsumed under the mental faculty, from what could mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arise?
Your consciousness definitely arises based on phenomena (*dharma*). Now, observe these phenomena closely: what is their form? If they are apart from form and emptiness...
Movement and stillness, penetration and obstruction, union and separation, arising and ceasing—transcending all these marks, one ultimately finds nothing to be attained.

The three characters for "dharmas" (法) refer to internal dharmas (internal sense objects). However, these internal dharmas, if separated from the true reality (實相) of form, emptiness, and so forth, are likewise unattainable;
this serves as the basis for the subsequent text’s investigation into how arising and ceasing lack any inherent substance.
When there is arising, form, emptiness, and all dharmas arise together; when there is cessation, form, emptiness, and all dharmas cease together.

Since the cause itself does not exist, what kind of form or characteristic could the consciousness that arises from it possess? Since no such characteristics exist, how could the realms (dhātus) be produced?
Form and emptiness are the dust of form; movement and stillness are the dust of sound; penetration and obstruction are the dust of smell; contact and separation are the two dusts of taste and touch;

and only arising and ceasing point to the dust of dharmas. Yet arising also occurs because of external phenomena such as form and emptiness, and ceasing also occurs because of external phenomena such as form and emptiness.
These are the shadows left behind when the five dusts fall away; they exist apart from those various characteristics.

There must be no substantial entity. Since the dharma-object (dharmāyatana), which serves as the cause, lacks a substantial entity, how could the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), which arises from it as the effect, possess any form?
If it has no form, from what basis could its realm (dhātu) be established?
Therefore, one should know that with the mind and mental objects as conditions, the consciousness-element arises.
When these three locations are entirely absent, then the mind, mental objects, and the consciousness-element—these three—are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The explanation of the formation [of these states] is the same as before.

Essentially, since the *tathāgatagarbha* has no inherent nature (*svabhāva*), movement gives rise to views; because of these views, there appear characteristics. Internally, these resemble the sense-faculties and the body;

externally, they resemble the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). Gathering from without and absorbing from within, they give rise to what appears to be discrimination. Whether there is some degree of cognition, or...
Alternatively, there may be ignorance. That which resembles the true is not truly true; that which resembles the false is not truly false. When the mind moves, it constitutes an objective realm;

yet since the realm does not exist apart from the mind, one cannot distinguish between what is near or distant. In the interval, there is no master. For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), objects and self are not differentiated;

for a perfected person (*arhat*), form and mind are non-dual. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of things as being produced by causes and conditions for the sake of ordinary people, and for the sake of Bodhisattvas...
The conceptual proliferation of words and meanings is merely a provisional means and does not yet constitute the ultimate exposition.
These eighteen realms are all the *tathāgatagarbha*, yet they conclude with the statement that the three bases (*trivastu*) are entirely non-existent. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"The Tathāgata spoke thus in order to sever the fear of fools regarding the phrase 'selflessness'; it is the realm of non-existence, free from false discrimination."
This refers to the Gate of the Ālayavijñāna (Storehouse Consciousness). Those who aspire to this Way should reflect upon it.

The fifty-eight realms above are concluded. △ Sixth: The Seven Great Elements. This is divided into nine parts; first, the inquiry regarding the combination of the four great elements and the request for instruction.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often taught that all the various transformations in the world arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and are manifested by the combination of the four great elements. Why, then, does the Tathāgata now reject both causes and conditions as well as spontaneity?
I do not yet understand to what this principle refers. I only pray that you will take pity on us and reveal it for the sake of all living beings."
The Way is the definitive meaning, a dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
This world of dharmas is a transformation resulting from the conjunction of the four great elements as causes and conditions.

In the past, the World-Honored One revealed the principle of dependent origination for the sake of ordinary beings and those of limited capacity, enabling them to follow conditions and know how to return to the source. Now, he speaks of the Mahāyāna, the ultimate truth.
This is not mere frivolous discourse. Ānanda still clings to his former assertions and, fearing that sentient beings might fall into this web of doubt, he hopes for an authoritative instruction.
The definitive meaning of the Middle Way is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). II. A general rebuke that the nature of the great elements is not a composite.
This section is divided into two parts. First, a reprimand for being learned without skillful discernment.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Previously, you were weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and you resolved to diligently seek unsurpassed Bodhi. Therefore, I shall now reveal the ultimate truth for you."
Why do you further entangle yourself with the causes and conditions of worldly frivolous discourse and deluded imaginings?

Although you are learned, you are like a man who knows the names of medicines but cannot distinguish them when the actual medicine appears before him; the Tathāgata says such a person is truly to be pitied.
"Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so that those who practice the Mahāyāna in the future may also penetrate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Ānanda remained silent, receiving the Buddha’s holy command.

The delusions of the world follow various causes and conditions to form all phenomena. The followers of the Two Vehicles understand this, thereby realizing non-self and severing the causes for birth within the Three Realms;
thus they eliminate the grasping at a personal self. However, this is not the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna.

Because Ānanda was weary of and detached from the Lesser Vehicle, the Tathāgata, based on that, provided all previous instructions to point directly to Bodhi: the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and the sense-fields (*dhātu*).

The realms are all rejected as empty and false; this is entirely for the purpose of eliminating attachment to dharmas. This is what is meant by "the true medicine appearing before one, yet being unable to discern it.
△ Second, a general clarification that the great nature is not a composite.
Ānanda, it is as you have said: the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world.
Ānanda, if the essential nature of those great elements were not itself a combination, they would be unable to intermingle with one another, just as empty space does not combine with material forms.
Regarding the great elements (*mahābhūta*), they appear to be in a state of combination, yet in essence they are not actually combined; therefore, they cannot be intermingled, just like empty space.

This serves as the basis for the subsequent passage which explains that their combination is a false perception. The four great elements arise from deluded thought and are manifested solely by the mind.
Although they give rise to all phenomena according to various conditions, their nature is the nature of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). It has not...
If one has ever moved toward this realization, it is difficult to speak of it unless one possesses profound awakening.

If things were merely a harmonious combination, they would be like a magical transformation, where beginning and end mutually complete one another and birth and extinction continue in succession—death giving rise to life, and life leading to death.
Birth after birth and death after death, like a whirling firebrand, have never ceased. Ānanda, it is like water forming ice, and ice returning to water;
this is the breaking of the combination, yet True Suchness (tathatā) remains unchanging while following conditions. This is not the same as transformation. At the very beginning of birth...
Beginning is the start; cessation is the end. This beginning and end constitute birth and extinction, which merely take up the two meanings of "forming" and "continuing.
The beginning forms the end, and the end forms the beginning, thus forming a mutual completion. Birth continues death, and death again continues birth.
It forms a continuous succession: death and birth, birth and death, revolving without end like a whirling firebrand that has no beginning or end;

this is a metaphor for the lack of rest in birth and death. When one exhaustively examines all combinations, the phenomena of arising and ceasing manifest in this manner, appearing exactly like magical transformations.
Yet sentient beings are deluded, not realizing that their true nature is not a combination.
In the interim, it is a temporary illusory perception; therefore, it is said to be "like" [a phenomenon]. Just as water becomes ice, and ice returns to water.
The above two sections conclude the general refutation that the nature and substance of the great element [earth] are not a composite. △ Third, the withdrawal of the earth element.
Observe the nature of earth: that which is coarse constitutes the great earth, while that which is subtle consists of minute particles down to the *paramāṇu*.
If one analyzes that ultimate particle of form (*rūpa-paryanta-lakṣaṇa*) into seven parts, and further analyzes those *paramāṇus*, they are nothing but the nature of true emptiness.
By taking the coarse form and analyzing it into subtle parts, one takes the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) and divides it into seven parts; thus it becomes the "proximate void" (*anuvyañjana*).
If one further analyzes this proximate void, it is simply the nature of actual emptiness. This serves as the introduction to the subsequent passage stating that matter and emptiness do not combine.
The "limit of matter" refers to the most subtle state of matter, which is adjacent to emptiness; therefore, it is called the "limit."
Ānanda, if these atoms were analyzed until they became empty space, you should know that empty space gives rise to the appearance of form.

Since form can be analyzed into emptiness, it follows naturally that emptiness can be synthesized back into form. This was first established as a general principle, and is now being investigated through further inquiry.
Regarding what you have now asked—how various phenomenal transformations in the world arise through combination—consider for a moment this single *paramāṇu* (subtle atom).
By how much empty space must it combine to exist? A *paramāṇu* cannot be formed by the combination of other *paramāṇus*.

If you grant that matter is analyzed into emptiness, you must grant that emptiness is synthesized into matter. If it were synthesized from neighboring atoms (*paramāṇu*), it would possess spatial dimensions and thus could not be a neighboring atom.
Furthermore, regarding the neighboring atom-dust that is analyzed into emptiness: by what kind of material characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is space synthesized?
Since you allow that space combines with form to constitute form, you must likewise allow that form combines with space to constitute space.

If, at the time of combining with form, that which combines with form is not space; and if, at the time of combining with space, that which combines with space is not form—then form may still be analyzed [into its constituent parts].
How can emptiness be joined?
That which is joined with form is not emptiness; that which is joined with emptiness is not form. This means that form and emptiness cannot be mutually joined to constitute one another.
To state again that while form may still be analyzed, how can emptiness be joined? This is to say emphatically that emptiness cannot be joined—a point easily understood by people.

[Subhūti] saw [it], yet in reality, form does not necessarily need to be analyzed; only a Buddha knows this. This is intended to repeatedly establish the principle of the following passage concerning true emptiness and true form:
"From the very beginning, you have not known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form; it is pure and fundamental."
Pervading the entire dharma-realm, it accords with the minds of sentient beings and manifests according to the measure of their cognition and their karma.
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, there is no inherent self-nature; therefore, all form is precisely the form of nature, and all emptiness is precisely the emptiness of nature.
Since the form of nature is not [ordinary] form, it is true emptiness; since the emptiness of nature is not [mere] emptiness, it is... [true form].
True color. This is the color of true emptiness; it is originally pure and does not depend on cultivation or effort. Its substance pervades the dharma-realm and is without obstruction.
Sentient beings are deluded regarding this; following their perceptions, they give rise to karma, thereby forming the causes—both tainted and untainted—of the ten realms.
Causes and effects differ; there is nothing that can be exhaustively interrogated.

The world lacks knowledge and is deludedly attached to causes and conditions, as well as to the nature of spontaneity; all of these are merely the conceptual calculations and discriminations of the conscious mind.
There are merely words, yet they possess no real meaning at all.
This ignorance constitutes a failure to comprehend the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Lacking any understanding of the ultimate truth, one gives rise to conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*);

this refers broadly to the provisional beginnings of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), not only to ordinary people and non-Buddhists. It is the mind of consciousness that engages in such discrimination.

Discriminative calculation (*vikalpa*) is precisely the measure of the knowable. This conjunction of causes and conditions arises spontaneously and is also characterized by synthesis; collectively, it is termed "falsehood.
