It is the nature of consciousness that is being held accountable; therefore it is said: "Deluded obscurity is itself ignorance. Yet the true nature of ignorance is precisely Buddha-nature.
If, while in a state of delusion, one can suddenly recognize this for oneself, one is immediately and fundamentally liberated; there are not two distinct entities.

The sequence for unraveling the knots follows a specific order; yet when the six are unraveled, even the "one" perishes. By selecting the faculty of perfect penetration, one enters the stream and achieves true awakening.
This means that although there is a sequential order to the unraveling of the knots, once the six are unraveled, even the notion of "one" vanishes.

In the Mahāyāna, ignorance and the two attachments to self and phenomena are directly shattered, and discursive thought is instantly discarded. If one awakens to the perfect faculty, as soon as one enters the stream, one is immediately equal [to those who have completed the stages].

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the initial mind of the *Avataṃsaka* both allow for equality with the Buddha; as they share this same intent, even though [the *Lotus Sūtra*] suppresses the lower stages to select for those of superior faculties, it nonetheless embodies the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
The *ādānavijñāna*—the subtle consciousness whose habitual tendencies form a violent torrent—is neither real nor unreal; fearing that people might become deluded, I have never openly expounded it.

*Ādāna* here is translated as "grasping and maintaining"; it is an alternative name for the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). This [consciousness] originally takes the root-nature as its basis and is supported by the substance of the eight consciousnesses.
The fundamental nature is inherently profound and secret; however, due to deluded movement becoming habitual, there arise the two divisions of the perceiving subject and the perceived object.

Like a violent torrent, the flow does not know how to return, thus forming deluded movement; in this state, it would seem not to be real. Yet the original store-nature (ālaya-vijñāna) must not be deluded.
Therefore, if one is deluded regarding that which is not delusion, one simultaneously accepts delusion; if one is deluded regarding that which is not real, one simultaneously accepts reality.
And discard them both; it is not appropriate to expound upon this.

The self-mind grasps at the self-mind, whereby that which is not illusory becomes an illusory dharma. If one does not grasp, there is nothing that is not illusory; yet even the non-illusory does not arise.
How are illusory phenomena established?
The sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) belong to the *nimittabhāga* (the objective aspect), while the nature of consciousness belongs to the *darśanabhāga* (the subjective aspect).

Because the manifestation of objects through the organs gives rise to discrimination, it is said that "one's own mind grasps its own mind. Although both are equally the non-discriminative essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*, they are falsely divided into organs and objects.

Dust. Therefore it is said: "That which is not illusion produces illusory phenomena. If the sense organs and their objects appear together yet there is no discrimination, then even the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha does not know itself;
though existing within the organs and objects, it is nonetheless ungraspable. Regarding this, the wise person—
What should this be called as a model?
It is named the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening, the Illusion-like Samādhi, by which one transcends the stage of No-More-Learning in the snap of a finger.
This Abhidharma is the single path to Nirvana for the Bhagavāns of the ten directions.
*Samādhi*—here translated as "right reception" (*zhèngshòu*) and also as "samāpatti"—is the Illusion-like Samādhi (*yàohuàn sānmèi*).
*Abhidharma*—here translated as "incomparable dharma" (*wǔbǐ fǎ*)—also refers to this very samādhi. The Bhagavān is endowed with the six meanings [of the term].
This refers to sovereignty, brilliance, physical excellence, renown, auspiciousness, and nobility. This follows from the preceding point that what is not illusory does not arise;
thus, how could illusory phenomena be established? It is the absolute, unconditioned true mind, which is likened to a lotus flower: emerging from the mud, it remains unstained.
It is also like the precious sword of the Vajra King; whatever it is aimed at, it shatters. This fundamental great wisdom can destroy ignorance;
it is called the Illusion-like Samādhi. This Illusion-like Samādhi is the very form that is free from form, and the very thought that is free from thought—the true cultivation of the Mahāyāna.
It does not fall into gradual stages, but instantly transcends those of fixed nature and the Two Vehicles. Thus do the Tathāgatas of the ten directions [attain it].
Because they follow the same path, they reach the ultimate fruit; there is no longer any divergence between them. To savor the meaning of these verses in detail:
it is only a matter of the presence or absence of the root-nature (indriya). Whether one is a person of the world or a sage, the root-nature is non-dual.

It is only when this nature is obscured by delusion that it is designated as "ignorance" (avidyā); yet when it is revealed and made manifest, it immediately becomes liberation. And in reality, ignorance...
Liberation originates within the roots; therein, nothing at all can be apprehended. Therefore, both the "true" and the "not true" are inexpressible.

This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Here, the wise should fix their own eyes. If one attempts to prevent the error of [clinging to] emptiness as being existent, one has already missed the mark.
Grasping leads to delusion; non-grasping is awakening. Once this object of knowledge is understood, [one is liberated].
Transcendence occurs right where one stands; this is what it means to enter the stream and subsequently achieve perfect enlightenment.

The illusion-like samādhi is the true skillful means. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that there is nothing superior to the illusion-like [samādhi]. Who but those who have transcended all measures could know this?

The first section, which concludes the initial indication of the faculties to point out the delusion, is finished. △ Second, tying the cloth to demonstrate the original source of the knots, divided into three parts.
First, the description of the clarification:
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata in both *geya* and *gāthā* verses, [were moved].
Intermingled yet refined and pure; subtle and clear, penetrating to the core. My mind and eyes opened to clarity, and I marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
*Ge-yā* (Geya) is translated as "repeated verse"; it refers to verses that restate the preceding prose (*gadya*). *Gāthā* is translated as "recited verse" (or simply "verse");
it does not depend on prose but consists merely of verses chanted in praise. The phrase "intermingled yet refined and pure" refers to the aforementioned verses' capacity [to clarify].
The words that explain it clarify and penetrate the principle being explained; they describe what was heard in order to delight the mind and eyes and bring about clear enlightenment.
△ Second, the request to unravel the sequence of the knots.
Ānanda joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him: “I have now heard the Buddha’s words on the unobstructed, great compassionate nature—pure, wondrous, eternal, and true.
Yet my mind has not yet fully realized the sequence for loosening the knots so that the six are resolved and the one is extinguished. I pray that you will bestow your great compassion upon me.”
Again, out of compassion for this assembly and those of the future, he bestows the sound of the Dharma to wash away deep-seated defilements.

There is no restriction in two respects: first, there is no restriction regarding persons, as he does not exclude those of inferior faculties; second, there is no restriction regarding the Dharma, as even the secret teachings are fully revealed.

Regarding the phrase "the nature is pure, wondrous, and eternal": "nature" refers to the faculty-nature, meaning that this faculty-nature is fundamentally pure and fundamentally wondrous, and was originally not...

"Transformation and change" (biànyì) belong to that which is signified (*vācya*). "Ultimate meaning" (*nītārtha*) is called "true" (*zhēn*); being without falsehood is called "real" (*shí*). To say that these dharma-words are "true and real" points to the signifier (*vācaka*).

"To unfold" (*shū*) means to understand. The preceding section opened up and showed the method for untying the knots: "If one establishes cognition within seeing and knowing, this is the root of ignorance;
if seeing and knowing are free from [the notion of] seeing, this is *nirvāṇa*. It further says: "Delusion and obscurity are ignorance."
"Upon realization, one is immediately liberated. He further said: "If one does not grasp at non-illusion, even non-illusion does not arise;
how then can illusory phenomena be established? This may be called a clear and direct pointing-out, yet he has not yet provided a detailed, itemized exposition of each point.
As the subsequent text states: "Because your mind-nature has been deranged since beginningless time, your cognition and vision have arisen falsely," and further:
"When this faculty is first understood, one first attains the emptiness of persons; when the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, it constitutes the liberation of dharmas.
Therefore, it must be requested again. △ Third, showing the knots and inquiring into the origin of the knots.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, upon his lion throne, adjusted his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, gathered up his *saṃghāṭī* robe, and took hold of a seven-jeweled stand.
Reaching out his hand over the stand, he took the flowered cloth offered by the devaputra Kāpila.
*Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* is here translated as "inner garment. *Saṃghāṭī* is here translated as "great robe" (*mahāsaṃghāṭī*).
*Kāpāla* is here translated as "time-portion," which refers to the Yāma Heaven. *Trepā* is a silk fabric from the Western Regions; its value is immeasurable.
In front of the great assembly, he tied the cloth into a single knot and asked Ānanda, "What is this called?

Ānanda and the great assembly together replied to the Buddha, "This is called a knot. Thereupon, the Tathāgata folded the layered flower-cloth and tied another knot, asking Ānanda once more, "What is this called?
Ānanda and the great assembly again replied to the Buddha, "This too is called a knot."
In this manner, he successively knotted the flowered handkerchief until six knots were formed in total.

As each knot was completed, [the Buddha] took the knot that had been formed in his hand and held it up, asking Ānanda, "What is this called? Ānanda and the great assembly likewise replied to the Buddha in succession:
"This is called a 'knot'. The Buddha told Ānanda, "When I first knotted the handkerchief, you called it a 'knot'."
"This folded flower-cloth was originally a single strip. How can you say that a second and a third knot have been formed?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, this precious folded flower-cloth was woven into a handkerchief;

although it was originally a single entity, as I contemplate it, when the Tathāgata makes one fold, it receives the name 'one knot. If it were folded a hundred times, it would ultimately be called 'a hundred knots. How so?
Moreover, this precious *kaṭhina* cloth has six knots; it never reaches seven, nor does it remain at five.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata permit that only the first is called a knot, while the second and third are not? The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This precious flower-cloth—do you know that this cloth originally consists of but a single strand? When I tied it six times, they were called six knots. Examine this cloth carefully."
The substance is the same; it is because of the knots that there are differences. What do you think? When the first knot was formed, it was called the "first.
In this way, up until the sixth knot was produced. Now, I wish to take the name of the sixth knot and establish it as the "first.
"No, World-Honored One. As long as the six knots exist, this name 'sixth' can never be the 'first. Even if I were to exhaust my lives..."
"How can you clearly distinguish these six knots so as to give them different names? The Buddha said, "It is so. These six knots are not the same;
yet when one traces back their original cause, they were all fashioned from a single piece of cloth. To make them disordered would ultimately be impossible.
Thus it is with your six faculties: within ultimate sameness, there arises ultimate difference."
"When I first tied it, you called it a 'knot. This silk scarf was originally but a single strand; why then do you call the second and third [loops] knots?
This is a metaphor for the primordial nature of awakening. Initially, from the luminosity of awakening, delusion arose;
through this delusion, the marks of perception appeared, whereby the six sense faculties manifested simultaneously. Thus, these are the knots of the six sense faculties."

Originally, there was the clarity of self-awakening, yet the delusion of that awakening’s clarity pervades the six sense faculties. Fundamentally, this delusion does not distinguish between essence and function;
even when speaking of awakening, it permeates both the partial and the whole. Since neither bondage nor knots possess the categories of one or six, how could liberation have a beginning or an end?
Yet Ānanda insists on fixed sequences and cannot tolerate confusion; such attachment to the dharmas of the Two Vehicles is not easily forgotten all at once.

Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke only of the first knot being distinct from the other six. This initial point clarifies that the cloth was originally a single strand which suddenly became knotted;
it refers to the "first" in terms of that single strand, not in terms of establishing a sequence of priority among the six knots.
It is further asked: "Do you wish to take the name of the sixth knot and establish it as the first?

This is done so that the sixth may represent all six knots collectively, thereby distinguishing them from the first. It is also said: "The six knots are not the same; yet when one traces back to their original cause, they are all fashioned from a single piece of cloth."
It is further said: "Within ultimate identity, there arises ultimate difference. All of this takes the six to look toward the one, using identity to establish difference;
it originates from a single essence and culminates in names and forms. Delusion gives rise to causes for existence, yet when delusion is understood, it is seen to be fundamentally provisional.
Do not allow expedient means to obstruct the true reality. Let the student reflect upon this.

The two upper strands were tied together to demonstrate the formation of a knot; this concludes the demonstration of the origin. △ Third, demonstrating the sequence of untying the knots. This is divided into four parts.
First, questioning and demonstrating the origin of the knots.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "If you must find these six knots unsatisfactory and wish for them to become one, how can that be achieved?"
Ānanda said, "If this knot remains, disputes will arise in abundance; within it, there naturally arises the notion that 'this is the knot, not that,' or 'that is the knot, not this.
If the Tathāgata were to untie them all today, and the knots did not arise again, then there would be no 'this' or 'that.
One could not even call it 'one,' so how could 'six' be established? The Buddha said, "The dissolution of six and the disappearance of one is likewise so. It is because of you..."
At the outset, the nature of the mind becomes deranged, and false perceptions arise. As these delusions continue without ceasing, the wearying faculty of vision gives rise to dust.
It is like when one strains the eyes, and there appear illusory flowers; within the tranquil clarity of the essence, these arise causelessly through agitation.
All the worlds—the mountains, rivers, and great earth, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana—are but the inverted appearances of those illusory flowers born of frantic toil.
This truly elucidates what constitutes a "bondage. It arises because, from time immemorial, your mind-nature has been deranged, causing deluded perceptions to manifest;

this refers to taking that which is originally awakened and luminous to be false. As the manifestation of delusion does not cease, the wearying faculty of vision gives rise to the dust of sensory objects.

It is like when the eyes are strained, there appear illusory flowers before them; thus, through the interaction of subject and object, distinctions of identity and difference, as well as neither-identity-nor-difference, are produced.

This fundamental clarity and purity has no cause for its arising through disturbance; yet it manifests before us as the world and its sentient beings, like flowers in the sky that have no underlying cause.
If one awakens to this lack of cause, birth-and-death and nirvana will immediately subside of their own accord.

"It was like a dream from yesterday. Furthermore, regarding those who speak of *nirvāṇa*, they submit to the principle of "extinguishing" what follows. △ Second, the inquiry into the method of resolution.
Ānanda said: "This toil is like a knot; how can it be untied? The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth in his hand and tilted it to one side...
He pulled it from the left and asked Ānanda, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One.
He then turned his hand and pulled it from the right side, asking Ānanda again, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I have now pulled it from both the left and the right with my hands, yet I cannot untie it; even though you employ skillful means, how can it be untied?"

The various commentaries on the left and right all use the analogy of empty space and existence. I, the fool, believe they should instead refer to the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

They have not yet clarified that the nature of the sense organs is the locus of the cause of delusion. Even if one leaves the objects behind to seek stillness and closes the six gates, this is not ultimate liberation;
for it serves as the introduction to the meaning of binding the mind at the core. △ Third, granting permission to remove the binding of the mind and dissolve delusion.
He returned to his true state.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, when one unties the knot at its center, it immediately disperses. The Buddha told Ānanda, “So it is, so it is.
If you wish to remove a knot, you must do so at the center of the knot.”
What is called "tying the mind" refers to the fact that the mind is itself the eternally abiding awakened mind (*bodhicitta*). This awakening has no inherent nature;

it is through delusion that it takes what is perceived as an object, thereby initiating the process of bondage. If one can clearly understand, within the presence of the sensory faculties, the state where neither aversion nor attachment arises, then at that very moment one will manifest awakening and accord with original enlightenment.
Thus, one will be able to thoroughly comprehend the falsity of the "awakened clarity" and, regarding the six external sense-objects, proceed as before.
Manifesting before one, it arises from the six sense faculties; discernment is solemn and complete. The understanding of the emptiness of persons and phenomena is not absent in its sequence.

Yet, the fundamental wisdom is luminous, wherein principle and phenomena are without obstruction. From beginning to end, cause and effect are known only through self-realization; they do not depend on being whole or incomplete.
Ānanda, I teach that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp at the coarse, composite characteristics of the world.

The Tathāgata illuminates both mundane and supramundane phenomena, knowing their fundamental causes and how they emerge according to their respective conditions. Thus, even down to a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he knows its number.
Regarding the various things appearing before him—whether pines are straight or thorns are crooked, whether cranes are white or... [the text continues].
The "darkness" (wu-xuan) refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). One must fully comprehend its fundamental source:
the cause is precisely the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), while the conditions are all pure dharmas.

Because the Buddha-nature is devoid of intrinsic nature, one should clearly illuminate what is called the "clear illumination that thoroughly penetrates ignorance. The Buddha-nature is fundamentally pure, for it is empty from the beginningless past.
False habitual tendencies arise from non-awakening; relying upon what is illuminated, they shroud the six sense faculties.

Although one must manifest illumination, it requires the power of purification—namely, the aforementioned Illusion-like Samādhi, which is perfected in a mere snap of the fingers. This serves as the skillful means, differing from the substantial dharmas of the Two Vehicles.
By inferring this, one knows that among both mundane and supramundane phenomena, there is none that does not have its own fundamental source.
Causes each have their respective objects of perception. The Tathāgata has elucidated the fundamental cause for appearing in the world:

by perfecting pure conditions, he attained all-knowledge and possessed correct universal cognition. Spontaneously, his dust-like delusions were exhausted; reaching beyond all realms, he fully understood their original causes.
Therefore, Ānanda, choose whichever of the six faculties you prefer from within your mind. Once the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of sensory objects will naturally cease.
When all delusions have been eliminated, what need is there to wait for anything that is not true?

This gives rise to the discernment of the perfect faculties, which is to say, turning the faculties back toward their source. Although this constitutes an illumination, it still requires the power of purification.
△ Fourth, showing the sequence of the knots being untied: the liberation should follow a specific order.
"Ānanda, I now ask you: regarding this *karpāsa* cloth, when these six knots appear before you, could they all be untied simultaneously?
No, World-Honored One. These knots were originally tied in succession; today they must be untied in succession.

Although the six knots share the same substance, the knots themselves do not arise at the same time. Therefore, when the knots are being untied, how could they be removed all at once? The Buddha [said].
He said: "The liberation of the six sense organs is likewise so.

This statement regarding the 'untying of knots' cannot occur simultaneously; it follows the sequence of the subsequent text, wherein one first attains the emptiness of persons and subsequently accomplishes the liberation from dharmas.
However, while this analogy points to the sequential order of untying the knots, one must know that the subject of the analogy possesses a distinct stagnation regarding the Perfect [Teaching]. But...
Grasp the meaning of this; do not be overly constrained by it.

When these faculties are first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons. When the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, one achieves liberation from phenomena. Once liberated from phenomena, [one proceeds further].
When both are empty and non-arising, this is called a Bodhisattva attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) from within samādhi.
Ānanda himself acknowledged the demonstration of striking the bell; this occurred after he had clarified the nature of his faculties.

Here it is said that he first attained the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which is precisely the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā-svabhāva*). Thereby, he attained the understanding of dharmas (*dharma-prajñā*); for there are no phenomena apart from the mind. However—

One thoroughly understands that which is known; yet there is nothing to be understood. Spontaneous dharmas and all conceptualization are exhausted. This is the direct and swift path of the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-sheng), not the realm of the Tripitaka or the Shared Teaching (Zang-tong).
As stated in the passage below: "First, upon entering the stream, one loses the object.

Once that which is entered is stilled, the two marks of movement and stillness clearly do not arise. From this, one gradually increases [this state] until what is heard and the hearing itself are both exhausted. This corresponds to the present context.
This root is the initial understanding. One first attains the emptiness of persons; hearing is exhausted and does not abide, and that which perceives and the perceived are both empty.

This is the understanding of phenomena (*dharma*). When arising and ceasing have been extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one. This constitutes the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Consider this carefully to see how these stages correspond.

This is also inherently sound and appropriate. However, since the selection of faculties according to the inferior capacities in the subsequent text has already implicitly demonstrated the perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) through skillful means, one should likewise first suppress this principle even within the context of the gradual sequence (*cidi*). Therefore, it is not permissible to treat these as substantial dharmas (*shifafa*).
It merely says that this faculty is first liberated. What is it that is liberated? Generally speaking, one grasps at form to constitute seeing; seeing is itself the substance of the self.

If one can detach from form, seeing does not stand independently. This emptiness, therefore, empties the attachment to the seeing that grasps form, rather than emptying the nature of the faculty that reflects form.
If this distinction is not understood, then the absence of a self apart from seeing is what constitutes nirvana.
This is why the Two Vehicles are not permitted to see the Buddha-nature. Now, form (*rūpa*) is a dharma, and it is seen by a person. Once form has departed, the seeing ceases;

once the person is empty, the dharma still remains dependent. This means that while the seeing that grasps form has already departed, the form that is the object of that seeing has not yet been exhausted.
Because one says there is form that can be departed from, it is not yet exhausted. Since form is not yet exhausted, [the seeing] is not yet...

One may speak of the perfect clarity of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Emptiness is precisely the nature of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Since phenomena arise from the mind, if the mind does not arise, phenomena have no basis to abide.
Therefore, one knows that as long as the grasping at phenomena external to the mind has not been abandoned, the emptiness of persons remains incomplete.
Only when emptiness is perfectly clear can one achieve liberation through phenomena (*dharma-vimokṣa*); this is the vision of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

All this arises from the ultimate realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). When one reaches this ultimate, even the characteristic of emptiness itself vanishes. It is like a person who has first awakened; they do not say, "I have awakened.
This is what is meant by "the six [consciousnesses] being resolved and the one [seventh consciousness] perishing. I have previously examined what is stated in various sutras:

the two vehicles realize the emptiness of persons but have not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). This is said solely with respect to their severing the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). As for the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), if...
[If one must] sever [them], how could mind and objects be tranquil? Therefore, know that persons and dharmas should be simultaneously and suddenly empty;
such talk of "before" and "after" is merely the World-Honored One’s skillful means.
The above three sections conclude the demonstration of the sequence for resolving the knots. △ Fourth, the universal inquiry into the perfect penetration, divided into twenty-seven parts.
First, the presentation of realization and the request for instruction on the perfect faculty.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, attained a wisdom and awakening that was perfectly penetrating; they were freed from all doubt. At that time—
With palms joined, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying: "Today our bodies and minds are radiant and clear; we have attained a swift state of unimpeded ease.
Although we have realized the meaning of the 'one' and the 'six' being lost, we have not yet reached the fundamental root of perfect penetration.

World-Honored One, we have been adrift for countless kalpas, solitary and exposed. With what heart or what concern could we have anticipated becoming part of the Buddha’s celestial kin? We are like infants who have lost their mother’s milk."
Suddenly I have encountered my compassionate mother.
Those who drift and wander are those submerged and floating within the six realms of existence; those who are orphaned and exposed are those who have yet to find a place of rest.

I have already awakened to the realization that the six dissolve and the one perishes, yet I have not yet attained deep entry through the single gate. Recalling my former drifting, I rejoice in what I have now encountered.

If, moreover, through this encounter the Way is realized and the secret mantras obtained are identical to one’s original awakening, then there would be no difference from having never heard them at all.
I pray only that you will bestow great compassion and grant me these secret adornments, so that I may fulfill the Tathāgata’s final instruction.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and withdrew to conceal his profound intent, hoping for the Buddha’s secret transmission.
As for what is called "awakening to the fundamental," the fundamental has never been deluded, and now there is likewise no awakening; therefore, it is said to be equal to not having heard it at all.
This is precisely where Ānanda deeply penetrates the true reality (*dharmatā*). Those of inferior capacity are startled and amazed; yet, in a single moment, all are simultaneously understood.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is the secret and wondrous adornment; by entering deeply through a single gate, the skillful means are perfect and sublime. This is the ultimate finality.
Therefore, one must silently and serenely receive it in contemplative stillness. △ Second, the announcement to the assembly and the inquiry.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the great Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats whose outflows were exhausted within the assembly.
"You Bodhisattvas and Arhats have been born into my Dharma and have attained the state of no-more-learning. I now ask you:
regarding your initial aspiration and your realization of the eighteen realms, which one constitutes perfect penetration? By what skillful means did you enter samādhi?"
The twenty-five sages attained perfect penetration by awakening to the seven elements and the eighteen realms.

Here, the mention of only the eighteen realms is because the element of consciousness is subsumed within the six consciousnesses, the element of seeing is subsumed within the six sense organs, and the five elements are subsumed within the six sense objects.

When investigated to the ultimate conclusion, the seven elements and eighteen realms are all collectively subsumed within the six sense organs. Therefore, it was said above regarding "birth-and-death and peace-and-bliss."
These six sense faculties are all equally pointed out and elucidated as being nothing other than the nature of the faculties themselves. Regarding those born within my Dharma, Changshui says:
"Born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by the Dharma, they obtain a portion of the Buddha-Dharma. △ Third, the perfect penetration of the sense-object of sound.
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“While we were in the Deer Park and at the Kukkuṭārāma, we witnessed the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of the Way. Through the Buddha’s voice, we realized and clarified the Four Noble Truths.
When the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, ‘Who understands? I was the first to declare that I understood. The Tathāgata confirmed my name as Ajñāta. Thus spoke the Wondrous Voice.
Miyuan: "I have attained Arhatship through sounds.
The Buddha’s voice issues from the Buddha’s mouth, yet the sound is not the mouth. The resonance pervades the ten directions;
it does not fall into the dust of audible objects and cannot be conceptually differentiated, yet it is not that there is no sound. This is the true mark of sound. Having realized this, I know."
The Four Noble Truths are likewise so. At the assembly of Nirvāṇa, the Buddha preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for those of the Two Vehicles.
He addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying: "There is suffering, there is truth, there is reality; there is accumulation, there is truth, there is reality;
there is cessation, there is truth, there is reality; there is the path, there is truth, there is reality. The Tathāgata is neither suffering nor truth, yet he is reality. He is empty."
Emptiness is neither suffering nor a truth; it is reality. Buddha-nature is neither suffering nor a truth; it is reality.

That which is called "suffering" is characterized by impermanence and is a characteristic that can be severed; this constitutes a true truth (*satya*). The nature of the Tathāgata is not suffering, is not impermanent, and is not a characteristic that can be severed;
therefore, it is reality. That which is called "origination" (*samudaya*) is that which causes the five aggregates (*skandha*) to harmonize...
That which arises through combination is called suffering and is also called impermanent; it is a characteristic that can be severed.
The nature of the Tathāgata is not the nature of accumulation (*saṃskāra*), nor is it the cause of the aggregates (*skandha*); it is not a characteristic that can be severed. Therefore, it is real.

That which is called cessation (*nirodha*) refers to the cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*). It is both permanent and impermanent. That which is attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles is called impermanent; [that of] the Buddhas—
That which is attained is called "constant" and is also called the "realized Dharma. This is the ultimate truth, the nature of the Tathāgata.
It is not called "extinguished," yet it can extinguish afflictions. It is neither constant nor impermanent; it is not called "realized knowledge," for it is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Therefore, it is real. The Path is that which can sever the afflictions; it is both permanent and impermanent, and it is a dharma that can be cultivated.
This is called the Real Truth. The Tathāgata is not the Path; he cannot sever the afflictions, he is neither permanent nor impermanent, and he is not a dharma that can be cultivated.
It is eternally abiding and unchanging; therefore, it is the truth. These Four Noble Truths of the Mahāyāna are not attainable by those of the Two Vehicles.

Nevertheless, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, there is only the One Vehicle, and no second or third. Sentient beings each receive it according to their own capacities, just as when heaven sends down rain universally, the moisture received by each thing—whether great or small—is distinct.
Furthermore, he secretly conceals [the ultimate] while manifesting [the expedient] outwardly; at this time, there is no obstruction and it is universal.
He showed that there could be no further vehicles.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, [Ānanda] said: "As I have realized it, sound is supreme.
Wēnlíng says: "Among the twenty-five gates, sound is first designated because it is the substance of the teaching in this land. (4)
Upānandasena, whose faculty of the sense-object of form was perfectly penetrating, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I too, when observing the Buddha’s initial attainment of enlightenment, contemplated the signs of impurity and gave rise to great revulsion; thereby I awakened to the nature of all forms, which arises from [the contemplation of] impurity."
Purity. The white bones and subtle dust dissolve back into space. When both emptiness and form are non-existent, one achieves the path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The Tathāgata has sealed me with the name Niṣadha. Once the dust and color have vanished, the wondrous color is subtle and perfect. I attained Arhatship through the characteristics of form.
Regarding the Buddha’s inquiry into perfect penetration, according to my realization, the causal factor of form is supreme.

Beginning with the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), the mind gives rise to weary detachment (*nirveda*). With this mind of weary detachment, one investigates the dust [of sensory objects] until it returns to emptiness.

Form and emptiness are non-dual; thus one attains the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of form. This means that once the coarse form of the dust is exhausted, the wondrous form becomes subtle and perfect. Changshui said:
Having realized that all material phenomena (*rūpa-dhātu*) are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, it is said that one awakens to the nature of all forms.
Contemplating the signs of impurity is the Bodhisattva’s practice of the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā-vipaśyanā*); it is not like the Śrāvaka’s wearying detachment in seeking *nirvāṇa*.
As Nāgārjuna states in his commentary: "Although the nine contemplations are contemplations of impurity, by relying upon them, one can accomplish the Great Matter. Thus, the Bodhisattva...

Out of compassion for sentient beings, and knowing that the three poisons are the causes and conditions for their existence, [the Buddha] taught the contemplation of the bloated corpse (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*) and so forth for those attached to form, in order to destroy the internal and external attachments to the characteristics of the body. This constitutes the Bodhisattva’s practice of the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*).
Zhanran said: "The Bodhisattva, with the mind of Great Nirvāṇa, cultivates the dharma of pure karma, such as the floating bag, the white bones, and the eight [contemplations]."
Because he contemplates [the aggregates] as suffering and so forth, he is not exclusively for the sake of the Two Vehicles. Niṣadha means "dust-nature" (rajas-tattva) in this language;
he received his name based on his awakening. △ Fifth: The Perfect Penetration of Fragrant Dust.
The youth Gandhahastin immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I heard the Tathāgata instruct me to carefully contemplate the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena. At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I was dwelling in quiet seclusion and pure fasting.
I saw bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense; the fragrance was tranquil as it entered my nostrils. I contemplated this scent and perceived that it was neither wood nor empty space."

"It is neither smoke nor fire. When departing, there is nothing to which it clings; when arriving, there is no place from which it comes. By this, my conceptual mind was dissolved, and I realized the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
The Tathāgata conferred upon me the title 'Incense Purity' (*Gandhāra*). Worldly vapors were suddenly extinguished, and wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive.
Through this Incense Purity, I attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the Incense Purity is supreme."
Fragrance is one of the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). It is neither wood nor space; it is neither smoke nor fire.
When departing, it has no place of attachment; when arriving, it has no point of origin. This is what is meant by "being detached from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is itself all dharmas.

Since fragrance is thus, so too are all dharmas. Directly, mental activity dissolves; nature and appearance are eternally abiding, beyond the reach of consciousness. This is the true nature of fragrance.

Xiangziyan took "Awakening" (Wu) as his name. "Childlike Truth" (Tongzhen) signifies the initial entry into the Buddha-dharma and also manifests the entry into the Way through a state of pure innocence, like Mañjuśrī, Sudhana, and other great Bodhisattvas who are all called "youths.
"At ease" (Yanxi) refers to the evening when the light fades.
"Pure chamber" (Qingzhai) refers to a room of purity. △ Sixth: The Perfect Penetration of the Sense-Object of Flavor.
The two Dharma princes, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, as well as the five hundred Brahmās present in the assembly—
Changshui says they are called "Dharma princes" because they are capable of succeeding to the position of a successor and continuing the lineage of the Buddhas so that it remains unbroken.

Five hundred Brahmā deities, who were his followers, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since beginningless kalpas, we have served as skilled physicians for the world."
Within his mouth, he tastes the grasses, trees, metals, and stones of this Sahā world; their names and numbers total one hundred and eight thousand.

Thus he fully knows all flavors—bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent—as well as their combinations, their innate qualities, and their transformations, whether they are cold or hot, and whether they are toxic or non-toxic;
he is able to know them all completely. Serving the Tathāgata, he has thoroughly understood the nature of flavor.
"It is neither empty nor existent; it is neither identical to the body and mind, nor separate from them. By discerning the cause of flavor, I attained awakening.
The Buddha-Tathāgata bestowed his seal of approval upon the names of my brothers, the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. Now, within this assembly, we are Dharma Princes.
Through the awakening to clarity via flavor, our rank has reached that of Bodhisattva. When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, this is what I have realized."
Taste is the cause;
it is because of this cause of taste that there is the cognition of it, which awakens to the nature of taste. Emptiness cannot perceive, therefore it is said to be "not empty.

Existence has no form, therefore it is said to be "not existent. The body is not the cause of cognition, and the mind shares in arising and ceasing; therefore, it is said to be "not identical" [with them].
Body and mind: flavor is not the tasting of emptiness, and discernment is not the flavor itself; therefore, it is said that they are not separate from body and mind.
From this discernment of the cause of flavor, the nature of awakening is revealed, wherein essence and function are fully manifest, serene and perfect.
As stated in the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-sūtra* according to the testimony of Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Vaidūryaprabha. There was a bhikṣu named Sūrya..."

In the land of Zang, the True Dharma was proclaimed. There was an elder named Jyotirprabha who, having heard the preaching of the Dharma, presented harītakī and various medicinal herbs to the great assembly of Sūryagarbha, vowing:
"May I, in the future, be able to cure the two types of illness—those of body and mind—for all sentient beings.
The entire world rejoiced and bestowed upon him the name Bhaiṣajyarāja. His younger brother was named Vidyutprabha, who [offered] the most sublime *sarpis* (clarified butter).
He made offerings of these medicines and was thus named Yaoshang (Medicine Superior). △ Seventh, the Perfect Penetration of the Object of Touch:
Bhadrapāla, together with his sixteen companions who were bodhisattvas, [attained this state].
Bhadrapāla means "Good Protector" (Śubharakṣita). Changshui says: According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Vidyutkhecararāja Buddhas appeared in succession.
During the period of the True Dharma (*śāsana*) of the first of these Buddhas, this person was an arrogant one who reviled the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta;
because of this, he fell into hell and remained there for a thousand *kalpas*. Once his retribution was exhausted, he emerged and encountered the next...
Bhīṣmagarjitasvara attained awakening upon leaving the household life. Following custom, he entered the bathhouse; observing this nature of water, he realized it was ultimately ungraspable.

Since it does not arise from causes, he thereby awakened to the causal nature of water. Regarding the sixteen *bodhisattvas* (kai-shi) who were lay practitioners in the royal city, Master An states that "kai-shi" means "beginning practitioners.
Jingxi states that it is because their minds have first opened, or because they have first resolved to attain enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*).

He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "In the past, under the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, we heard the Dharma and left the household life.
Once, during the time for bathing the Sangha, we entered the bathhouse according to custom; there, we suddenly realized the cause of water: it does not wash away dust."
Nor did he bathe his body; remaining tranquil in the interim, he attained the state of non-existence.

Without forgetting his past habitual practices, even until the present time, he followed the Buddha into the homeless life and attained the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). That Buddha named me Bhadrapāla. Through the manifestation of sublime touch, he proclaimed clarity.
Thus one becomes a son of the Buddha and dwells therein. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, according to what I have realized, the faculty of touch is supreme.
Water lacks the cause for washing; neither the object nor the body possesses the nature of being washed. These three do not reach one another.

"Peaceful and secure in the interim. "The interim" refers to the mind that perceives touch. Once the sensory object of touch is exhausted, wondrous touch is proclaimed and made manifest. "Wondrous touch" also points to the perception of touch;
it means that, directly beneath, there is neither a subject that touches nor an object that is touched.

When the subject that perceives and the object perceived cease, true awakening manifests before one. Therefore, it is said that "wondrous touch is proclaimed and made manifest. As for "past habits," this refers to the former Buddhas at the beginning...

The mind. Now that the Buddha has reached ultimate realization, he does not forget his past causes. Changshui [Zongjing] says that the "dissipation of deluded habits" does not correspond well with the preceding and following contexts.
△ Eighth: The Perfect Penetration of Mental Objects (Dharmas).
Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Jālinīprabhā, and the others immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa."

I have been able to draw near [to the Buddhas], hear the Dharma, and practice it. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I have made offerings to his relics, kept lamps burning to maintain the light, and anointed the images of the Buddha with purple-gold light.
From that time onward, in birth after birth and life after life, my body has always been perfectly formed.
The "Gathering of Purple Golden Light. These bhikṣuṇīs of the Purple Golden Light and others were my own kinsmen who resolved their minds for enlightenment at the same time as I.

Observing that the six sense-objects in the world are subject to decay and transformation, they cultivated the state of extinction through emptiness and stillness; only thus could their bodies and minds achieve it.
Passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas was like the snap of a finger. Through the dharma of emptiness, I attained arhatship.

The World-Honored One declared me the foremost among those who practice dhūta, as I have clearly realized the wondrous Dharma and extinguished all outflows. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, this is what I have realized.
The Dharma-condition is superior.

The shadows of the five sense-objects as they fall away and pass into extinction become the objects of the mind. By contemplating the transformation and cessation of phenomena, mental activity naturally subsides;

thus, with a mind of emptiness and stillness, one achieves cessation (*nirodha*). Although this cessation is the "cessation of sensation and perception" within the nine successive stages of attainment, it is here [the ultimate].

This is a meditative visualization. However, by awakening to and clarifying one's own mind, one suddenly empties the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), and all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever severed;

thus, it certainly is not subsumed under the nine successive stages (*navānupūrvavihāra*). *Śarīra* here is translated as "bone-body" and also as "sacred bone. It is like a precious jewel of five colors;

it is that which has been cultivated through the power of the Tathāgata’s morality, concentration, and wisdom, and is the unsurpassed field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). *Kāśyapa* here is translated as...
Pindola-Bharadvāja. Within the Dharma, there were three Kāśyapas, all of whom were great beings (*mahāpuruṣa*). Among those sharing the same name, this one was the eldest.
He practiced the twelve *dhūta* austerities and difficult ascetic practices; as Mahākāśyapa was foremost among them, he was designated as "Mahākāśyapa.
Having received the Buddha’s final charge, he transmitted the Dharma and the robe, entered meditative absorption at Kukkuṭapāda, and [the nun] Suvarṇaprabhāsā Bhikṣuṇī was... [immediately].
The wife of Mahākāśyapa when he was a householder. △ Ninth: Āniruddha, whose faculty of the eye is perfected.
He rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first left the home life..."
I was constantly fond of sleep. The Tathāgata rebuked me, saying that I belonged to the class of beasts. Upon hearing the Buddha’s reproach, I wept and reproached myself;
for seven days I did not sleep, and consequently lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One then showed me the Vajra Samādhi of Delightful Vision and Illumination.
I do not perceive the ten directions through the eye; rather, my essential purity is transparently clear, as if looking at fruit in the palm of my hand.

The Tathāgata certified me as having attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, to revolve the faculty of sight and return to its source is the foremost method.
"Delighting in seeing illumination" means that by using the essence of vision within the sense organs, one turns back to contemplate one's own nature, thereby manifesting the original radiance.
The Vajra-samādhi refers precisely to this manifestation of the original radiance; it is severed from the sense organs and detached from sensory objects, being firm, solid, profound, and secret.

Therefore, he is able to perceive the ten directions without relying on the eye-faculty. Furthermore, the phrase "the refined and true is transparently radiant" reveals the efficacy of turning the vision back to follow its source;
it is that which has been penetrated by the refined and true, not something attained through cultivation.
Aniruddha—here translated as "Without Poverty" or "As One Wishes"—was the son of King Śuklodana. 10. The Perfect Penetration of the Nose-Faculty.
Cūḍapanthaka: *Cūḍa* means "by the side of the great road.
Formerly, he was the daughter of an elder who followed her husband to another country. She gave birth twice, and both times it was by the side of the road.
The elder son was thus called Cūḍa, which means "by the side of the great road"; the younger son was Panthaka.
This refers to the side of a narrow path. This term "younger brother" (ti) is used inclusively to refer to the elder brother as well; it means the younger brother of Cūḍapanthaka.

In the past, he was a great Dharma master who was stingy and secretive regarding the Buddha-dharma; consequently, he was reborn with dull faculties. Nevertheless, due to his past roots of goodness, he encountered the Buddha and left the household life.
When five hundred bhikṣus taught him a single sutra together for ninety days, he was unable to master it.

He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I lack the capacity for recitation and retention, and do not possess the nature of great learning.
Having first encountered the Buddha, I heard the Dharma and left the household life; I have memorized a single verse of the Tathāgata over the course of one hundred days."

"I would lose what was before while grasping for what was after; I would lose what was after while grasping for what was before. The Buddha, out of compassion for my folly, taught me to dwell in retreat and regulate the inhalation and exhalation of breath.

As I then observed the breath, I saw it as subtle, exhausting the very momentary nature (*kṣaṇa*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. My mind then became suddenly clear."
I attained great non-obstruction, and eventually, with the exhaustion of outflows, I became an Arhat. Abiding beneath the Buddha’s seat, I was sealed as one beyond training.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, by reversing the breath and following emptiness, this is the foremost method.

Regulating the inhalation and exhalation of the breath is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata, intended to cause the mind to take the breath as its object so that it does not become distracted.

Thereafter, one investigates the subtle and the minute until all arising and ceasing is exhausted, reaching the point of a single *kṣaṇa*. One then exhausts emptiness until there is nowhere to return;

looking back at that which was regulating, the outflows (*āsrava*) are simultaneously exhausted. This is not like the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of the Tiantai school, but rather the Dharma of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. Zhang Wujin harbored doubts regarding this.
Regarding the regulation of the breath (*ānāpāna*): it is said that this is not found in the various sūtras. To dare to delete or add words and phrases is the habit of a pedant;
it invites derision from those with true discernment, so one must be cautious. The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states that a *kṣaṇa* is an extremely brief duration beyond the reach of thought.
One *tathatā*-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) contains ninety-nine *kṣaṇas*, and one *kṣaṇa* contains ninety-nine... [moments].
Arising and ceasing. By investigating this through reasoning, one awakens to the knowledge that beyond a single breath, no other breath can be found.
At this very moment, the light of the mind is spontaneously revealed; it is not to be sought from others. The breath belongs to the nose; this is the perfect penetration of the faculty of the nose.
△ Eleven: The Perfect Penetration of the Faculty of the Tongue.
Gavāmpati—this is translated as "ox-chewer" (niuchi) or alternatively as "ox-tongue. Because his tongue resembled that of an ox, he suffered from the ailment of "empty whistling";
even after eating, he would constantly make a sucking sound as if chewing, and thus people of the time called him "the Ox-chewer."
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have committed verbal karma;

during past kalpas, I mocked śramaṇas lightly. Consequently, in life after life and birth after birth, I suffered from the ailment of rumination. The Tathāgata has shown me the Dharma-gate of the Single Flavor of the Pure Mind-Ground.
Having attained this, I have extinguished the mind and entered samādhi, observing that the cognition of flavors is neither a substance nor a thing."
One should contemplate so as to transcend all worldly outflows (*āsrava*). Internally, one is liberated from body and mind; externally, one leaves behind the world.

Far removed from the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), like a bird escaping its cage, one is free from defilement and has dissolved all dust. With the Dharma-eye purified, one becomes an Arhat. The Tathāgata personally certified me as having attained the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized: returning to the flavor and revolving the faculty of cognition—this is the foremost.
When tasting flavors with the tongue, one perceives them through the reflection of those flavors. Upon awakening to this faculty of cognition, one realizes it is neither flavor nor tongue;
thus, one is transcendentally and uniquely liberated. This is what is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Flavor of the Pure Mind-ground.

To be internally liberated from body and mind is to reach the ultimate state where both body and mind are simultaneously liberated by means of non-substantiality. To externally cast off the world is to reach the ultimate state by means of non-objectivity.

The physical realm and its contents are both cast off, like a bird escaping from a cage. Being free from defilement and having dissolved all dust, one immediately attains the intent of transcendence through mindfulness.
The Tathāgata showed me everything down to the entry into *samādhi*, summarizing what is attained;

subsequently, he described how the knowledge that tastes the flavor of contemplation leads to the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Zhang Wujin remarked: "Contemplating the ground of the mind in stillness seems to be a partial [realization]."
Two layers. It should not be based on the original root. △ Twelfth, the perfect penetration of the body-faculty (kāyendriya):
Pilindavatsa. This translates as "Residual Habit.
For example, he called the goddess of the Ganges River a "little slave girl" because in a past life he had been a Brahmin.
"Gate! It is named for the residual habit of *asmimāna* (the conceit 'I am').
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: 'When I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I entered the Path through the Buddha.'"
I have often heard the Tathāgata speak of how all things in the world are not to be relished. While begging for alms in the city, my mind was contemplating the Dharma-gates;
unaware of it, a thorn in the road pierced my foot, causing my entire body to ache. I became aware of this and recognized this profound pain.
Although the awareness was aware of pain, the awareness of the pure mind was free from the awareness of pain. I further reflected:

"In a single body such as this, how could there be two simultaneous awarenesses? Before long, having gathered my mindfulness, my body and mind suddenly became empty. Within twenty-one days, all outflows were completely exhausted.
I attained arhatship, received the seal of personal certification, and realized the state of no-more-learning. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied:
"According to what I have realized, the pure awakening that leaves the body behind is the foremost."
To know the sensation of bodily pain is simply to perceive the awareness that perceives pain; this exists only within delusion and is common to ordinary people.
If one awakens to the awareness that perceives pain, this awareness is pure: no pain can be found, nor is there any perception of pain.

This occurs at the stage of initial awakening, when subject and object have not yet been forgotten; therefore, one must collect the mind and suddenly realize emptiness, only then attaining pure awareness.
This is the relinquishing of the body. At this very moment, it is still the awareness that knows pain, no different from that of an ordinary person.
The cognition that uses awareness to perceive pain arises because of delusion; yet if one awakens from that delusion, even this awareness has no source.
This is not something extraordinary, nor is it easy to speak of. I fear that if one clings to the mind that arose from delusion, it will be difficult to speak of liberation. △ Thirteen.
"Subhūti, whose faculty of mind is perfectly penetrating—
known here as 'Born of Emptiness'— has attained the Samādhi of Emptiness since remote kalpas and has been named for this; he also constantly practices it."
The Samādhi of Non-contention: All people joyfully behold him because he delights in emptiness.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind has attained non-obstruction."
I recall my successive births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. From the very moment I was first in my mother’s womb, I knew emptiness and stillness;

thus it continued until the ten directions became empty, and I also caused sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness. Through the Tathāgata’s awakening of their inherent nature to true emptiness, they were graced.
Emptiness is perfectly luminous; having attained arhatship, one suddenly enters the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of emptiness, sharing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Thus sealed as one beyond training, liberated into the emptiness of nature, I am unsurpassed.
Since beginningless kalpas, his mind has been unimpeded. Even while first in his mother’s womb, he already knew emptiness and stillness.
This demonstrates the entry from emptiness into awakening, clarifying that the nature of awakening is true emptiness. Thus, one suddenly enters the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous sea of emptiness.

Therefore, know that the true emptiness of the nature of awakening is not the same as the emptiness and stillness perceived by the followers of the Two Vehicles, who merely claim to have attained arhatship. Thus it is said: "Suddenly..."
One enters into the Tathāgata. Furthermore, it is said that one is sealed as having attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); thus, this "no-more-learning" refers to the Mahāyāna.
Even a Buddha in *nirvāṇa* may be called a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) or an *arhat*. This is according to the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
If he is called a *srotāpanna*, it is because he emphasizes the initial mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), in the sense that he is no different from a Buddha.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. According to what I have realized: all phenomena enter into non-existence; where there is nothing to negate, negation itself is exhausted. Turning back from phenomena to return to the Unconditioned—this is the foremost.
Changshui says: First, by means of single emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one empties all marks; therefore it is said, "all marks enter into non-being.

Next, by means of double emptiness, one empties the mark of emptiness itself; therefore it is said, "that which is not [the object of] non-being is exhausted. This implies that even non-being is exhausted.

This first statement concerns "single emptiness" in contrast to "marks," meaning that all marks are fundamentally empty. This second statement concerns "double emptiness" in contrast to "emptiness" itself.
This means that even the characteristic of emptiness is empty. "Non-existence is also exhausted" refers to the exhaustion of this very "double emptiness.

As for not concluding with a formal revelation of the awakened nature, it has already been set forth previously; therefore, here we speak only of what is realized, which must be personally understood by each individual.
△ Fourteen: The Perfect Penetration of Eye-Consciousness.
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind and vision have been pure.

Thus, throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have attained unimpeded penetration upon seeing even a single instance of the various transformations of the mundane and supramundane worlds."
Regarding "the purity of seeing with the mind": this arises from the clarity and sharpness of visual consciousness, giving rise to mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*).

To say that one sees all mundane and supramundane phenomena (*dharma*) and penetrates them all without exception is merely a description in terms of names and signs; it does not constitute true penetration of supramundane phenomena.

One must contemplate the subsequent text to realize that the mind is boundless before one can truly be said to have "seen the truth" (*satyadarśana*). These points may be used as mutual corroboration.
On the way, I encountered the Kāśyapa brothers following one another as they proclaimed the teaching on causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), whereby I realized that the mind is boundless.
The verse on causes and conditions says: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions—I declare them to be empty; they are also provisional designations."

This is also the meaning of the Middle Way. If one realizes the Middle Way, it is called "seeing the Truth" (*satyadarśana*). This awakening to dependent origination may correspond to the first fruit [of the path].

Having left the household life following the Buddha, one perceives that the clarity of enlightenment is perfect; attaining great fearlessness, one becomes an Arhat and serves as the Buddha’s eldest son.

Born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma—when the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, as I have realized it, the mind and vision emit light, and when that light reaches its peak, true knowledge and vision arise; this is the foremost.
This is realized through the illumination and discernment of eye-consciousness, whereby one returns to the wondrous clarity and gives rise to the true nature of awakening.

When this light reaches the ultimate limit of knowledge and vision, fearlessness arises—namely, the four fearlessnesses—which means that having thoroughly penetrated the source of all phenomena, there is no longer any doubt or fear. Prajñāpāramitā serves as the mother.
Wisdom arises from the object; wisdom is itself the son. Since wisdom is supreme, he is the eldest son.
Originally revealed by the Tathāgata, he thereby attained what is realized; thus it is said, "from the mouth" and "from the Dharma. △ Fifteen: The Perfect Penetration of Ear-Consciousness.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva:

his practice pervades the entire Dharma-realm, hence he is called "Universal" (Samanta); his rank is adjacent to the ultimate sages, hence he is called "Worthy" (Bhadra). Samantabhadra has three positions:

first, the prior position, which refers to the two stages of the aids to penetration and the preparatory practices prior to the [ten] grounds; second, the actual position, which refers to the ten grounds as well as the two states of Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment.
Regarding the "three stages after": having already attained the fruit, one does not abandon the gateway of the cause.

This means that although one has already become a Buddha, one does not relinquish compassion and vows, but devotes oneself solely to saving sentient beings; Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and other such Bodhisattvas are examples of this.
Master Li said: "Mañjuśrī is the younger son, and Samantabhadra is the elder son; when these two sages unite their bodies, they are named 'Buddha'."

Regarding Samantabhadra being the eldest son: this means that based on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one gives rise to practice; one practices the wisdom of differentiation (*prabheda-jñāna*) and governs the dharma of the Buddha-family.
Because each of the *pāramitās* exists in its own right, one constantly establishes the dharma of the Buddha-family through the gateway of practice.
He succeeds to the affairs of the Buddha’s household; therefore, he is called a Dharma Prince (*dharmaputra*).
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have already served as a Dharma Prince for Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct those disciples who possess the faculties of Bodhisattvas to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra."
They derive their names from me.
For all those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle, once they have first brought forth the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), they immediately give rise to its differentiations;
the practices undertaken based on that wisdom are all called the "Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra. Therefore, it is said that they receive their names from me.
“World-Honored One, I listen with my mind and discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings.

If, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, there is a single sentient being who brings forth within their heart the practice of Samantabhadra, at that time I shall mount a six-tusked elephant and manifest hundreds of thousands of bodies, arriving at that very place. Even if their obstructions are so deep that they do not yet perceive me, I shall—”

That person, in the midst of darkness, has their head stroked and is protected and comforted, enabling them to achieve success. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I spoke of its fundamental cause:
the hearing-faculty of the mind was illuminated and manifested, resulting in sovereign discernment; this is the foremost.
This is the turning back of auditory consciousness from hearing toward the True, giving rise to true hearing of the awakened mind.

It does not depend upon the faculty of the ear or the nature of auditory consciousness to universally hear all the knowledge, views, and the practices of Samantabhadra initiated by all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Just as the thoughts arising within one's own mind are self-arisen and self-awakened, that person personally perceives the Universal [Samantabhadra].
The Worthy One, riding upon the six-tusked elephant, arrives before each person to stroke their heads and offer comfort;

yet, in reality, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva never actually goes before those people. Each person sees him for themselves through the resonance of Samantabhadra’s mental hearing, brought about by his great compassion.
Even if one's obstructions are so deep that they do not see him at that moment, the spiritual resonance has already occurred within the darkness.
This is the concealment of flaws. That is to say, within the single Dharma-realm, there are no two essences and no two functions.
△ Sixteen: The Perfect Penetration of Nose-Consciousness.
Sundarananda: *Sundara* means "handsome";
this is the name of his wife. *Nanda* means "joy"; this is his original name.
When both names are used together with the wife's name, it serves to distinguish him from Nanda the Cowherd, who was the Buddha’s own younger brother.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first left the household life and entered the Path under the Buddha, although I was fully endowed with the precepts, my mind was constantly distracted and agitated regarding *samādhi*, and I had not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).

The World-Honored One instructed me and Cūḍapanthaka to contemplate the white [spot] at the tip of the nose. When I first contemplated it earnestly for twenty-one days, I saw the breath within the nostrils."
The inhalation and exhalation become like smoke; the body and mind are internally luminous. The world becomes a perfect, hollow void, universally pure and clear, like lapis lazuli.
As the appearance of smoke gradually fades away, the breath becomes white. The mind opens and the outflows are exhausted; all inhalations and exhalations transform into radiant light.
I illuminated the worlds of the ten directions and attained Arhatship. The World-Honored One prophesied that I would attain Bodhi. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied:
"Through the cessation of my mental activity, after long stillness, clarity was revealed; through the perfection of this clarity, outflows were extinguished. This is the foremost."
Contemplating the white at the tip of the nose means fixing the mind on a single point. After twenty-one days, body and mind become still and serene;
internally, a perfect luminosity arises, and externally, a void-like purity is achieved. One then says that one sees the breath entering and exiting through the nostrils like smoke.
Such a vision occurs during that state of stillness and serenity; it is not considered a sign of attaining true power. Once internal clarity has been attained...
The exterior is empty; the mind’s awareness arises spontaneously, and suddenly one regains [clarity]. All inhalations and exhalations are transformed into light.
This mental radiance appears simultaneously, illuminating the ten directions; this is not due to the transformation of the breath itself.

What is called "the smoke-like vapor vanishing of its own accord" and "I extinguish the breath through extinction" are all variations of what is perceived before and after the meditation has reached its ultimate state of long-term stabilization. It is just like this.
Within, one perceives perfect clarity; without, one perceives empty purity. The cessation of light and the cessation of white are both realms manifested within meditative contemplation.
Their essential meaning lies solely in the mind’s development of illumination—illumination that is perfect and leads to the exhaustion of outflows. △ Seventeen:
The Perfect Penetration of the Tongue-Consciousness.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Throughout kalpas past, my eloquence has been unimpeded; I have expounded upon suffering and emptiness, deeply penetrating the true mark."
Sentient beings perceive all phenomena as permanent; for the sake of those of the two vehicles, the Buddha teaches impermanence.
Sentient beings perceive that there is a self, and that this is pleasure and purity; for the sake of those of the two vehicles, the Buddha teaches suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The followers of the two vehicles then use these very teachings to guide sentient beings; thus it is said that he proclaims suffering and emptiness, yet in reality [it concerns] impermanence.

The teachings of suffering, emptiness, and non-self implicitly contain the principles of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. This constitutes a profound realization of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*);

it does not mean that there is a true nature existing apart from suffering and emptiness. That Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra kept these truths secret within while outwardly assisting in the propagation of the Buddha’s transformation was not something that began only today.
In this manner, even up to the secret Dharma-gates of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have revealed them subtly within the great assembly and attained fearlessness.
Knowing that I possess great eloquence, the World-Honored One has used the wheel of his voice to instruct me to propagate them.

In the presence of the Buddha, I assisted the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma; through this lion’s roar, I attained arhatship. The World-Honored One certified me as supreme in preaching the Dharma.
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied that by means of the sound of the Dharma, I subdue demonic adversaries and extinguish all outflows (*āsrava*).
This is the foremost.
The Dharma is fundamentally eternal, yet it is spoken of as impermanent; by speaking of impermanence, one reveals true eternity.
The Dharma is fundamentally blissful, yet it is spoken of as suffering; by speaking of the suffering of phenomena, one reveals true bliss. This is the secret dharma-gate.

This is a subtle and profound revelation. By means of the Mahāyāna Dharma, through the provisional and the real, and through opening and closing [the teachings], he proclaims them according to the needs of beings.

Thus, no māras or heterodox teachers can gain the advantage; this is what is meant by "subduing. Regarding the phenomena of outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*), they cannot find any flaw; this is what is meant by "extinguishing.

All of this is achieved through the skillful means of eloquence (*pratibhāna-upāya*), wherein one perceives that perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-prativedha*) is all-encompassing and without exterior. △ Eighteenth Section: The Body.

Regarding the perfect penetration of consciousness, Upāli immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I personally followed the Buddha when he left the city to renounce the world;
I personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity; and I personally saw the Tathāgata subdue all the māras. He then [continued]: “To regulate...”
All these non-Buddhists have liberated themselves from worldly desire and the various outflows (*āsrava*).

Having received the Buddha’s teachings on the precepts—ranging thus from the three thousand modes of deportment to the eighty thousand subtle categories of natural and proscribed offenses—they have become entirely pure. With body and mind in total tranquility, they have attained the state of Arhat.
Among the assembly of the Tathāgata, I am the leader; my own mind has been personally sealed [by the Buddha]. Upholding the precepts and cultivating the person, I am among the multitude...
He is ranked as the foremost.
Upāli—here translated as "Close Attendant"—was the minister who served as an intimate attendant when the Tathāgata was a prince; therefore, he is mentioned first among those who served him closely.
Having personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s renunciation, his ascetic hardships, his subduing of Māra, his overcoming of externalists, and his liberation, [he is thus placed at the beginning].
This refers to the teachings of the Ultimate Instruction. Among the disciples of the Buddha, this is the foremost and supreme view.

Regarding the two hundred and fifty precepts, each possesses the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—resulting in one thousand. When these are further correlated with the three clusters (*triskandha*), they become three thousand.
