Furthermore, by assigning these three thousand to the seven branches of body and speech, they become twenty-one thousand. These are then further assigned to the four divisions.

Afflictions total eighty-four thousand. As for the three aggregates (*saṃgraha*), they refer to the aggregate of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka*), the aggregate of gathering ethical discipline (*vinaya-saṃgrāhaka*), and the aggregate of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka*).
Regarding the four types of afflictions, these are those characterized by excessive greed, excessive hatred, excessive delusion, and those with equal proportions (*sama-bhāga*).

"Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the essential nature (*svabhāva*), meaning that the dharmas subject to precepts are inherently evil by their very nature, such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying.

An offense immediately constitutes karma. This differs from prohibitory karma (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), whose essential nature is not inherently evil, but which is nonetheless forbidden by the Buddha because it opens the door to various evils, such as the prohibition against alcohol and the like.
By means of the Buddha’s precepts, the body attains tranquility; because the body is tranquil, the mind also attains tranquility.
When both body and mind are tranquil, one gives rise to the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*). This is what [the Buddha] has personally sealed for me.
It is the mind. Therefore, know that when body and mind are quiescent and extinguished, pure awakening manifests before one.
This pure awakening is the eternally abiding mind, certified by the Buddhas.

The Buddha asked about the perfection of penetration. By means of grasping the body, I attained mastery over the body; then, by gradually grasping the mind, I attained thorough penetration of the mind.
Thereafter, both body and mind became entirely unimpeded and sharp. This is the foremost method.
To grasp the body and call it "sovereign," and to grasp the mind and call it "penetrating"—this is still merely awakening to the fundamental, profound, and perfect nature.
It enables the body and mind to be like a wondrous lotus flower, conforming to the world while skillfully entering emptiness and stillness. △ Nineteen:
The Perfect Penetration of the Consciousness.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first went along the road to beg for alms, I encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa—and they proclaimed to me the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causal conditions.
I instantly gave rise to the resolve for enlightenment and attained great penetration. The Tathāgata then bestowed upon me a kāṣāya robe to wear."
His beard and hair fell off naturally.
Maudgalyāyana should be called Maudgalyāyana-Kauṇḍinya. "Maudgalyāyana" (目犍連) means "of the clan of beans" (采菽氏);
this is his *gotra* (surname). "Kauṇḍinya" (拘律陀) means "knotless tree"; this is his personal name (*nāman*). "Uruvilvā" (優樓頻螺) means "wood."
Kuālín (Gua-lin), also called Mùguā Lóng (Moguā-lóng). He had a protuberance on his chest shaped like a papaya. *Gayā* means "city" here;
*Nadī* means "river" here. These three Kāśyapas explained the causes and conditions in the same manner as Śāriputra.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one manifests various supernatural powers (abhijñā) based upon the true reality (bhūtatathatā), not by means of dualistic characteristics.

One perceives all Buddha-lands as arising from the ultimate truth (satya) while remaining unmoved from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), pervading the ten dharma-realms. Therefore, by giving rise to this mind, one attains great penetration and mastery.

One immediately penetrates the true nature (*dharmatā*). By realizing that causes and conditions are like an illusion, the discriminating mind ceases, and one naturally arrives at the true nature itself.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana both went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha saw the two men from afar and addressed the bhikṣus: 'Among my disciples, this one is foremost in wisdom; that one is foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). The Buddha..."

As soon as he was addressed with the words, "Welcome, Bhikṣu," his beard and hair fell away of their own accord; dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he was fully provided with the robe and bowl.
Having received the perfected precepts, I traveled through the ten directions without hindrance; my supernormal powers were manifested and proven supreme, and I attained the state of an Arhat.
Not only does the World-Honored One do so; the Tathāgatas of the ten directions also praise my spiritual power as perfectly pure, luminous, sovereign, and fearless.
This is because, relying upon the true reality (*dharmatā*) and arising from that reality, I have attained unimpededness; thus, I am able to reach everywhere throughout the ten directions.
As for the Tathāgatas of the ten directions praising my spiritual power: when Maudgalyāyana wished to know the distance to which the Tathāgata’s voice could reach, he flew—
Passing through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to the west, among the assembly in that land, they saw his physical body was immense;

finding his form so small, they mistook him for a "human-headed worm. That Buddha then said: "This is the foremost disciple of Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One of the immeasurable buddha-lands to the east, who has arrived here following our voices. Do not treat him with contempt or negligence."

The Buddha asked about the method of perfect penetration. I replied: "I attained it by turning back the tranquil light of the mind. It is like settling a turbid stream until, after a long time, it becomes clear and limpid;
this is my foremost method.
'Turning back the tranquil' means turning the mental consciousness back into the perfect stillness. From this wondrous, tranquil, and perfect mind, all spiritual functions are manifested."
Therefore it is said: "It is like settling a turbid stream; after a long time, it becomes clear and limpid. As the water swirls and settles, it becomes as clear as when turbidity was first settled;
once it is clear and limpid, the light of the mind naturally manifests. △ Twenty: The Perfect Penetration of the Fire Element.
Ucchuṣma is translated here as "Fire-Head" (Huotou).
He attained the Way by contemplating the nature of fire, and thus he was named accordingly.
Because he manifests as the Vajrapāṇi deity holding a vajra to serve as a protective attendant, no primary seat is provided for him.
Before the Tathāgata, he joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I constantly recall that in the distant past, during many kalpas ago, my nature was full of lust. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Śūnyarāja, who spoke concerning those of excessive desire."
It became a mass of fierce fire. He instructed me to contemplate throughout my entire body—the hundred skeletal members, the four limbs, and all sensations of cold and warmth.
Spiritual light coalesced within, transforming my many lustful thoughts into the fire of wisdom. From that time on, all Buddhas called me by the name Huotou (Fire-Head).
By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, I attained the state of an Arhat. Thereupon, I made a great vow:
"When all Buddhas attain the Way, may I serve as their powerful attendant and personally subdue their demonic adversaries."

The hundred bones and four limbs belong to the earth element; cold belongs to the water element; warmth to the fire element; and breath to the wind element. Contemplating these four elements thoroughly, one finds no master; there is only deluded thought.
Deluded thought has no basis, and the spirit naturally becomes stilled and tranquil. Once the spirit is stilled and tranquil, [the mind is liberated].
Then the light of wisdom bursts forth; this is the Fire-Light Samādhi.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of dhyāna], I replied: "By observing with clarity that the warmth and touch within my body and mind flow through unimpeded, all outflows were extinguished."
One gives rise to the great jewel-flame and ascends to unsurpassed enlightenment; this is the foremost.
While the preceding section generally contemplates the four great elements, this section alone scrutinizes the tactile sensation of warmth within the body and mind.

Since the nature of lust belongs to fire and one's past habitual tendencies toward it are particularly heavy, one must apply intensive investigation. When [lust] is found to lack intrinsic nature, the fire of the mind naturally subsides; this subsiding is itself the flame of wisdom.
It arises instantaneously. That which is called "the true emptiness of the nature of fire" and "the true fire of the nature of emptiness" flows unimpededly;
it refers to the flames of speech and wisdom pervading the entire body, not to the sensation of warmth or touch. △ Twenty-one: The Great Perfection of the Earth Element.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder (Dharaṇīdhara), Jiaoguang says:
First, one levels the external earth; thereby, one realizes the mind-ground. Consequently, one maintains this fundamental awakening and perfectly realizes the treasury-mind;
for this reason, he is named Earth-Holder.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, when the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu.

Whenever there were roads, fords, fields, or narrow passes that were uneven or improper, causing harm or damage to carts and horses, I would level and fill them all; I would either build bridges or carry sand and earth myself."
Thus, through such diligent toil, immeasurable Buddhas appeared in the world. There were sentient beings who, in the midst of marketplaces, required someone to carry their goods for them;
I would first carry them to their destination, set down the goods, and depart immediately without taking any payment.
During the time when Vipaśyin Buddha was present in the world, there was widespread famine. At that time, I worked as a porter;

regardless of whether the distance was far or near, I would accept only a single coin. Or, if a cart or oxen were mired in the mud, I possessed supernatural power and would push their wheels for them.
He uproots their suffering and affliction.
The above all recounts his past causes. Though he has not yet attained awakening, he already manifests the Bodhisattva’s practice of sacrificing himself to benefit others;
with this body and mind, he dedicates [the merit] toward Bodhi and does not grasp at fields of merit. Therefore, there is the following passage.
This was the response to my aspiration. Viśvabhū means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All. *Shi* refers to a marketplace (*huan*), and *yuan* refers to a city gate (*huai*).
At that time, the Great King of the kingdom invited the Buddha to a vegetarian feast. During that occasion, I leveled the ground to await the Buddha. Thus it was with the Tathāgata Viśvabhū.
He placed his hand upon my head and said, "You should level the ground of your mind; then the ground of the world will all become level.

My mind was immediately opened, and I saw that the subtle particles of my own body were no different from all the subtle particles that constitute the world. Such is the intrinsic nature of these subtle particles.
They do not touch one another; even weapons do not touch them. I have realized the patience of non-arising within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and attained arhatship.
Now, having turned my mind toward enlightenment, I enter the rank of bodhisattvas.
Hearing the Tathāgatas proclaim the ground of the Buddhas’ wondrous Lotus wisdom and vision, I was first to bear witness and served as their leader.
This describes the source of awakening. By leveling the external ground, one awakens to the leveling of the mental ground.

Seeing that both internal and external atoms lack self-nature and are nothing but the single mind, the mental ground becomes level; thus, the ground of the world and all things therein become level as well.
The minds of sentient beings are deluded, obstructed by the four great elements. Internally they perceive that which is created; externally they perceive that which creates.
All manner of permeability and obstruction, movement and stillness, cold and warmth are manifested, mutually contacting and disturbing one another.

When one realizes that all phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind alone, views subside and consciousness is forgotten; then all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent, and the *dharmatā* is spontaneously perfect. As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: [text continues]

This refers to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The "wondrous lotus" is used as a metaphor for this. Originally, he awakened to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within the *dharmatā*.

Furthermore, it is said that he has now "turned his mind and entered. This was a provisional demonstration for the time being; now, however, he is in the actual stage, wherein there is no longer any distinction of depth or shallowness.
The Buddha asked about the perfection of penetration. I have observed with clarity that the two objects—the body and the sensory realm—are equal and without distinction;

they are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, from which delusions arise as sensory dust. When this dust is消 (dissolved) and wisdom becomes perfect, one achieves the Unsurpassed Way. This is the foremost.
The body-element and its two objects are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha; this is the realization that all dharmas are manifested solely by the mind.
Since they are manifested solely by the mind, all dharmas are originally devoid of self-nature. Originally, it was through the clarity of awakening that delusion arose;
yet knowing that delusion has no cause, one realizes that the nature of awakening is fundamentally wondrous. 22. The Perfect Penetration of the Water Element.

Contemplating within the body, one sees that the nature of water is not subject to displacement. Beginning with mucus and saliva, and extending thus to the extremities of lymph, marrow, blood, feces, and urine, as they circulate throughout the body, the nature of water is identical in all.
Seeing this water within the body, one perceives it to be no different from the various fragrant oceans of the Floating Banner King Lands outside the world-system.
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the Flower Treasury Ocean (Puṣpasaṃbhava-samudra) there is a great lotus flower.

Because it was vast, it was called a "king" (rāja).
At that time, I had first accomplished this contemplation; I saw only the water and had not yet attained the bodiless state (*kāya-vigama*).

Seeing nothing at all, the child, being ignorant, picked up a piece of tile or gravel and threw it into the water;

...up to this point. Even if Mount Sumeru were to strike my head, it could not move a single hair on my body.

I have reflected upon this: I have now attained the path of Arhatship and have long been free from the conditions of illness; why then today...
Suddenly, a pain arose in my heart, and I feared that [the Dharma] might be lost. At that time, the youth came quickly before me and related the matter as described above.
I then told him: "If you see water again, you should immediately open the door, enter this water, and remove the tiles and rubble."
The youth followed the instruction. Later, when he entered meditative absorption, he again saw the water; the shards and rubble were as they had been. He opened the door and cleared them out.

Afterward, when he emerged from absorption, his physical form was restored to its original state. He encountered immeasurable Buddhas, continuing in this manner until he reached the Tathāgata Sovereign King of Unhindered Penetration through Mountains and Seas, at which point he finally attained the dissolution of the self.
His nature became one with the true emptiness of all the fragrant water-oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

They are non-dual and without distinction. Now, under the Tathāgata, I have attained the name of "Celibate Youth" (Kumārabhūta) and am included among the assembly of Bodhisattvas. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the faculties], I replied:
"By means of the single flavor of the nature of water flowing everywhere, I attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and perfected Bodhi; this is the foremost."
When one realizes the true self-nature, then the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water. Since water is thus, so it is with the seven elements;

within the true emptiness of the nature, all things are both truly real and truly empty. When you cast a pebble into the heart, the body has not yet perished, and the Dharma remains perfectly present.
By means of the mind entering meditative concentration, that which is non-mind is itself concentration; by means of the mind contemplating water, [one perceives its true nature].

That which is not water is precisely the mind. That it is non-dual and indistinguishable from the fragrant waters of the ten directions means that, according to how they manifest, there is no further sequence of entering or exiting;
this is what is meant by saying that water and its nature flow as a single flavor.

Thus we know that even the Arhats of the Two Vehicles, having realized the emptiness of persons, have not yet forgotten phenomena (*dharma*). My humble opinion is that if phenomena have not yet been forgotten, then...

The emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is likewise not yet perfected or ultimate. The *Lotus Sūtra* calls it a "transformed city" (*nirmita-pura*), and further states that there is only the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), with no second or third.
△ Twenty-third: The Perfect Penetration of the Wind Element.
Regarding the Dharma Prince Vaidūryaprabha, Changshui says: "The full name is Vaidūrya; this translates as 'Jewel of the Distant Mountain.

Because one contemplates that body and mind are driven by the power of the winds, and through the perfection of this contemplation attains its function, such that body and mind become transparently clear like vaidūrya glass, he is named accordingly."
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I recall that in the past, after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Immeasurable Sound (*Amitaghoṣa*).

He revealed the wondrous clarity of the Bodhisattvas’ fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), observing that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all turned by the power of the winds of delusive conditions. At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the realms.”
When observing the movement of the world, I observed the movement and stillness of the body and the movement and thoughts of the mind; all movements were non-dual, equal and without distinction.
At that time, I realized the nature of these manifold movements: they come from nowhere and go nowhere.

The deluded sentient beings, as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, are of one identical falsity. Thus it extends even to within a single world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds.
All sentient beings are like a hundred mosquitoes contained within a single vessel, chirping and clamoring in disorder, creating a frantic noise within a mere fraction of space.

Because there is no fixed direction to their boundaries, it is called "establishment" (*an-ling*). Because the world is subject to constant flux, it is called "moving time. This refers to the past and the present.
"Not yet. 'Movement and stillness' refers to the four modes of deportment; 'movement of thought' refers to arising and ceasing.

To reveal and demonstrate original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*), one then instructs the contemplation of the world and its sentient beings, so that the person may directly realize that this present body, faculties, and the external environment are all illusory conditions, fundamentally non-existent.
When this is so, original enlightenment naturally manifests; therefore, through this awakening, one comprehends the multitude."

The nature of movement neither goes nor comes; it is empty and false in its very place. The sentient beings of the sands of worlds are like mosquitoes inside a vessel, needlessly and wildly clamoring.
This may be called a profound penetration of the non-arising of all phenomena, yet one must simply realize this through direct personal experience;
then, one will naturally be of one identical, perfectly湛 (zhan) stillness with the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Not long after meeting the Buddha, he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). At that time, his mind opened and he beheld the land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the east.

He became a Dharma Prince, serving the Buddhas of the ten directions. His body and mind emitted light, penetrating all things without obstruction. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the faculties], [he spoke thus].
Observing that the power of the wind has no basis, I awakened to the bodhicitta and entered samādhi;
thus, I merged with the single wondrous mind transmitted by the Buddhas of the ten directions—this is the first.
At that moment, the mind opens and one directly realizes original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), no longer being turned by the power of the wind.

Delusion and ignorance have no master and drift haphazardly according to conditions; this is termed the "power of the wind. It is of the same substance as the external element of wind—a single delusion.

When the wind ceases and the waves subside, the ocean of awakening becomes clear and still; thus, above, one accords with all Buddhas, and below, one awakens the multitudes of living beings. This is the non-dual wondrous mind.
It is merely a matter of delusion versus awakening. △ Twenty-four: The Great Perfect Penetration of Emptiness.
Regarding Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva, Qingliang says:
"Dwelling in unimpeded giving, his practice of *dāna* is equal to space. This refers to Vajraratna Bodhisattva, who is likewise empty.
The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states that when the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja appeared within the Great Assembly, he manifested solely the appearance of empty space and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I have personally realized this through my own body; therefore, according to what I have realized, I am able to speak thus.
Why is this? My very body is empty space, for it is by means of empty space that I have realized it."
"All dharmas are sealed by the seal of empty space. At that time, five hundred great śrāvakas each offered their own upper robes (*uttarāsaṅga*) to Gaganagañja.
Having presented these upper garments, they spoke these words with one voice:
"Those sentient beings who have deeply resolved to attain bodhicitta have swiftly obtained excellent benefit. Regarding the Tathāgata..."
Within this treasury of great wisdom, nothing falls outside; thus, the robes offered there immediately disappear.
When the śrāvakas ask where the robes have gone, Gaganagañja replies, "They have entered my treasury.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja takes empty space as his storehouse and rains down [requisites] throughout the ten directions for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds.
Because all the treasures, clothing, food, and drink within the realms [are inexhaustible], the verse says:
"Since space has no height, its lowliness is likewise unattainable. All phenomena are likewise thus; their nature has neither high nor low.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha attains the treasury of space, which suffices for all sentient beings; this consciousness is without end or exhaustion.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I and the Tathāgata, under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, attained the Body of Boundless Dimensions.
At that time, I held four great precious jewels in my hands, which illuminated the Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions."
It transformed into empty space. Furthermore, within his own mind, he manifested a great circular mirror, from which ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-lights were emitted.

These lights flowed and permeated all the realms of the various banner-kings throughout the ten directions, reaching to the very limits of empty space; they then entered back into the mirror and merged into his body.

The body is identical to empty space; there is no mutual obstruction. The body is able to skillfully enter lands as small as motes of dust and extensively perform Buddha-works, attaining great accordance (*anuloma*).
"Dingguang" refers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha. Gushan says: "The Dharma-body is like space, pervading all places; this is what is meant by..."
It is boundless. This arises from a profound realization that the Dharma-body is identical to form and mind, interpenetrating one another like the jewels in Indra’s net.
The jewel represents form, yet it can illuminate the Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space;
this is what is meant by "entirely form is mind," where there is no distinction between the principal and its associates. The mirror represents mind, and it can cause its radiance to flow forth.
The various banner-king lands of the ten directions enter into the mirror and penetrate my body;
that is to say, the entire mind is form, not departing from the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). This uses spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) to manifest the Dharma;

thereafter, it truly demonstrates how the body can skillfully enter lands as numerous as atoms, extensively perform Buddha-works, and attain great accordance. As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka* says: "The Buddha-body is all-pervading..."

Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, he appears universally before all living beings; responding to conditions and fulfilling their needs without exception, yet he remains eternally upon this seat of enlightenment.
This seat of enlightenment constantly faces the ten directions, yet it never moves.

"This great supernatural power arose because I contemplated that the four elements have no basis, that the arising and ceasing of false thoughts and empty space are non-dual, and that the Buddha-lands are fundamentally identical.
By illuminating this identity, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied:
'By contemplating the boundlessness of empty space, I entered samādhi; its wondrous power is perfectly luminous—this is the foremost.'"
The four great elements arise from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Deluded conceptualization has no intrinsic nature; it is manifested solely by the mind.
Once one awakens to "mind-only," the four great elements and form are empty, fundamentally not being other things. Therefore, it is said: "To bring forth illumination within sameness.
This is precisely entering *samādhi*, attaining the Great Dharani, and achieving pervasive inclusion through perfect luminosity. △ Twenty-fifth: The Great Perfect Penetration of Consciousness.
Maitreya Bodhisattva. In full, he is called Maitreyīna; here it is translated as "The Kindly One" (Cishi). The "Chapter on the Enumeration of the Dharma" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa all took Miaoguang as their teacher. The last among them to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara. (8)
Among his hundred disciples, there was one named *Yaśaskāma* (Seeker of Fame). He was greedily attached to gain and offerings;
although he recited many scriptures, he did not master them and forgot much of what he had learned. Thus he was called Yaśaskāma. A verse says:
"At that time, this Dharma Master *Prabhāketu* had a disciple whose mind was constantly filled with indolence and who was greedily attached to fame and profit. This was Yaśaskāma."
He was insatiable in seeking gain and frequented the households of the noble clans. He abandoned what he had studied and recited, neglecting them until they were lost and no longer mastered.
For these reasons, he was called "Seeker of Fame. Nevertheless, he also performed various wholesome deeds and succeeded in seeing countless Buddhas.
Having made offerings to all Buddhas and practicing the Great Way in accordance with it, he has perfected the six pāramitās.
Now that he beholds the Lion of the Śākyas, he shall become a Buddha hereafter, named Maitreya, who will extensively deliver sentient beings in numbers beyond measure.

He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I recall that in the past, after the passage of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa.
From that Buddha, I went forth into homelessness; yet my mind placed great weight on worldly fame, and I delighted in frequenting the families of the nobility.
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to cultivate the samādhi of consciousness-only and enter into samāpatti.”
Śāriputra, throughout kalpas past, you have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with this samādhi; yet the mind seeking worldly fame has been extinguished and no longer exists.
All phenomena arise from the internal consciousness manifesting as external appearances; that consciousness, too, is illusory—it is but a single [reality].
The mind—this very *tathāgatagarbha* mind—is the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*.

It is the great *dhāraṇī* that can encompass all samādhis and destroy all delusions, just as boiling water melts ice. Therefore, it is said that when the mind seeking worldly fame ceases and is extinguished, it becomes non-existent;
this constitutes the fundamental great wisdom, while all subsequent states are its differentiated accomplishments.
When Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world, I then attained the supreme, wondrous, perfect Samādhi of the cognitive mind;
even unto the entirety of the Tathāgatas’ lands throughout space—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—all are manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind.

This is by means of discerning wisdom, which perfectly integrates the defiled and the pure, existence and non-existence, thereby extinguishing all conceptual discrimination and attaining great conformity—namely, the unsurpassed, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the cognitive mind (*vijñāna-citta*). This cognitive mind refers precisely to true *vijñapti-mātratā*.
Entering the true nature of consciousness-only, I spontaneously attained samādhi.
World-Honored One, because I have realized this mind-only consciousness, immeasurable Tathāgatas have flowed forth from the nature of consciousness;
I have now received the prediction that I shall succeed to the Buddha’s position.
Previously, we discussed the presence or absence of purity and impurity; both are equally wondrous and perfect.

From this wondrous perfection flow forth all Tathāgatas, just as a single instance of awakened clarity gives rise to worlds and sentient beings. These establish one another, such that delusion and awakening are each distinct.
Awakening and delusion are not distinct.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I observed with clarity that the ten directions are nothing but consciousness; that the mind of consciousness is perfectly luminous, thereby entering the stage of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

To remain far removed from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the grasping of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and thereby attain the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), is the foremost [practice].
Contemplating the ten directions as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), one realizes that all phenomena in the ten directions are transformations appearing from internal consciousness;

by means of these appearances, one penetrates the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). This nature is inherently perfect and luminous. Entering this perfectly luminous nature, one thoroughly understands that all names, marks, causes, and conditions are utterly non-existent.

This is attained by departing from the *paratantra* (dependent nature) and entering the perfectly luminous nature (*pariniṣpanna*). All notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," along with their underlying mental afflictions, are simultaneously extinguished;

this is departing from the *parikalpita* (imagined nature). When both [the dependent and imagined natures] are distanced, there remains only the precious awakening of the *pariniṣpanna*. This is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
△ Twenty-sixth: Seeing the Great Perfect Penetration.
Regarding Mahāsthāmaprāpta Dharma Prince, the *Fahua wenju* states:
"As for 'Attaining Great Power' (Mahāsthāmaprāpta), the *Siyi jing* says:
'Wherever I set foot, the trichiliocosm and the palaces of Māra are shaken. For this reason, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. The *Guanjing* further states that...
The light of his wisdom universally illumines all, causing them to leave the three miserable realms and attain supreme power;
for this reason, this Bodhisattva is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Together with fifty-two Bodhisattvas of his same rank, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha as follows:
He said: "I recall that in the past, as many kalpas ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*).

Twelve Tathāgatas followed one after another for the duration of a single kalpa. The last of these Buddhas was named Surpassing the Sun and Moon (*Sūryacandraprabhābhibhū*). That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha (*Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). It is like this:
suppose there is one person who is single-mindedly intent on remembering, and another person who is single-mindedly intent on forgetting; if these two people should meet..."

"Not meeting," or "seeing yet not seeing," refers to being exclusively mindful [of the Buddha] as an analogy for the Buddha's mindfulness of sentient beings, and being exclusively forgetful as an analogy for sentient beings' failure to mindfully recollect the Buddha.
As for "meeting yet not meeting" or "seeing yet not seeing," this means that although one person will certainly not meet the Buddha, it is still said "perhaps."
This is because the Buddha keeps sentient beings in mind.
Thus, these two people remember one another; their mutual mindfulness is profound. In this way, it continues from birth to birth, until they are like a form and its shadow.
They do not conflict or diverge;
they are like a form and its shadow, which do not conflict or diverge. Through this one sees that the Buddha and sentient beings share the same source.
Although memory and thought may be separated by distance, what is communicated through mindfulness ensures that their vital essence naturally harmonizes.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish and pity sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child flees and wanders away, what can the mother’s remembrance accomplish?
But if the child remembers the mother just as the mother remembers the child, then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall not be separated by distance. If the mind of a sentient being...

If one recollects the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future; not far from the Buddha, without relying on expedient means, one will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind.
The awakening and delusion of the mind are like a mother and her child. Original awakening is like the mother; unawakened consciousness is like the child.

When original awakening perfumes the mind, every thought-moment reveals awareness, like a mother longing for her child. When one turns one's back on awakening to unite with sensory dust, every thought-moment shifts toward emotion, like a child running away.
If emotions do not arise and one turns inward to observe and attain self-realization, it is like the child longing for its mother; immediately, there is a profound merging.
To see the Buddha face-to-face now—who can truly take this up? To see the Buddha in the future—how much will be missed!
What is called "not being far from the Buddha" requires no expedient means; it is a direct pointing to those who maintain mindfulness. The words and intent are profound and piercing.
Just as a person who has been perfumed with incense has a fragrance upon their body, this is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light.
This is a metaphor for mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). Being not far from the Buddha means that by means of the power of mindfulness, that which is remembered is adorned;
because the original fragrance is thereby incited and manifested, it is called "Fragrant Light."

In my original stage of practice, by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, I entered the patience of non-arising; now, within this world-realm, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.
By means of the mind that recollects the Buddha, one recollects the Buddha within one’s own mind. When both mind and Buddha are forgotten, they are equal to the nature of the Dharma-realm;

this is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). When it is so for one person, it is so for the entire world; all share the same Dharmakāya and mutually embrace one another.
By discerning the cause, one knows the fruit; such is the natural law.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I made no selection; I simply gathered the six sense-faculties together and maintained a succession of pure mindfulness, thereby attaining samādhi.
This is the foremost:
to gather the six sense faculties within a single thought-moment, and to bring those gathered six faculties back to converge in that single thought-moment.

With each thought following the next in succession, free from all other thoughts, one immediately enters samādhi. This is for the person themselves to know and realize; it is the model established by the Buddhas of antiquity.
To grasp this principle is not far off.
If one observes universally those sages who are said to have entered *samādhi*, is it not the case that the three—sense organs, sense objects, and consciousness—are precisely this?
Thus, exhausting the eighteen realms, all are *samādhi*. Among these twenty-five sages, there is no distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, nor between the provisional and the real.
Since realization is one and the same, those of the Great and Small Vehicles, the provisional and the real, are all entirely persons who have entered samādhi.

Thus we know that when deluded, the eighteen realms are in chaotic confusion, and the Great and Small, the provisional and the real, are utterly distinct; yet when awakened, every dharma is perfectly penetrating, and every person is perfectly penetrating.
Although the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* was taught to initiate instruction for the śrāvakas, people know it leads the provisional into the real and guides the distinct toward the ultimate.

It is perfectly round, yet it does not realize that the ultimate (the real) is enshrined within the provisional, nor does it point toward the Perfect [Vehicle] as being distinct. Its purport is even more profound and mysterious, as when it says:
"The seeing and the objects of seeing, along with the perceived characteristics, are like flowers in the sky; fundamentally they do not exist. This seeing and its objects..."
The original nature is the wondrously pure and luminous essence of bodhi; how could there be "is" or "is not" within it?
This is what is meant by "drawing the provisional into the real" and "guiding the distinct toward the perfect.

As for the selection of faculties, [the text] clearly abandons the circular and fusing (yuanrong) to speak solely of the sequential and distributed (xingbu), thereby manifesting both the ultimate and the conventional while revealing their respective identities and differences. I am surprised that the various commentaries of past and present still...

To be preoccupied with the various sages while insisting on examining their origins, and to fixate on spiritual cultivation while necessarily delimiting its stages, is like setting out for Qin while first heading toward Yue.
I await your refined insight; what words will you surely offer?

△ Twenty-seventh: The Perfect Penetration of the Ear Faculty. Divided into two parts. First, describing the causes for his cultivation, which is further divided into two. First, meeting the Buddha and receiving his teaching.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara...
In the Sanskrit language, *Avalokiteśvara* means "One Who Observes the Sounds of the World. As the Tathāgata explains in the *Lotus Sūtra*:
when sentient beings beset by suffering and affliction single-mindedly invoke his name, the Bodhisattva observes their voices and they immediately attain liberation.
This demonstrates that because the Bodhisattva is accomplished through great compassion, one who single-mindedly invokes his name will be perceived by the Bodhisattva;
such perception leads immediately to liberation. This resonance occurs spontaneously, without depending on deliberate mental effort. As the Bodhisattva himself explains in the original sutra:

"Because my observation and hearing of the ten directions are perfectly luminous, the name 'Avalokiteśvara' pervades the worlds of the ten directions. Furthermore, this is due to his causal practices.
The stage [of the ear] exists within the nature of hearing; it gives rise to its original wondrous clarity, universally illuminating the ten directions.

To speak of "contemplation" (guan) while referring to listening means that by following the act of hearing, one detaches from the sense organ and concentrates within the mind and eyes; thus, even at the gateway of fruition, one is able to contemplate the sounds of sentient beings.
The sense-faculties function interchangeably.
He then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Avalokiteśvara. Under that Buddha, I..."
I resolved to attain Bodhicitta. That Buddha taught me to enter samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.

Hearing corresponds to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) in the *Avataṃsaka*; contemplation corresponds to the ten abodes (*vihāra*); and cultivation corresponds to the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) and the stages of practice (*caryābhūmi*).

This is because the ten stages of faith are fundamentally established through understanding derived from hearing; once faith is fully perfected, one then enters the abodes. Abiding refers to dwelling securely within one’s own mind.
One gives rise to fundamental wisdom, and subsequently proceeds through the stages of practice until reaching the Vajra-samādhi; this constitutes samādhi.
△ Second, the fulfillment of realization through following the teachings.

At the outset, within the faculty of hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object of hearing. Once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise.
"At the outset, within the hearing" refers directly to the nature of hearing. To first contemplate the nature of hearing is precisely what constitutes "entering the stream.

This is because the six sense faculties usually flow outward in distraction, rushing toward external objects; here, instead of following that flow, one turns back to contemplate the nature of the sense-faculties themselves, and thus it is called "entering the stream. At this time—

When entering the stream, one immediately distances oneself from the realm of dust; hence it is said that there is "nothing to lose. Movement is the realm of dust, while stillness is the time of entering the stream.

Fearing that one might fall into the mark of stillness, this precisely demonstrates a profound penetration of the nature of the faculties: the two marks of movement and stillness are fundamentally not intermingled.
Thus it gradually increases until that which is heard and the hearing itself are exhausted.

The above constitutes the elimination of objects, for the two characteristics of movement and stillness belong to the objective realm; when movement and stillness are not involved, there remains only the true nature of the faculty.
This is the dispatching of the faculties so that they return to the Tathāgatagarbha mind; thus, both subject and object are exhausted.
When hearing is exhausted, one does not dwell [in it]; the perceived and the perceiver are both empty.
Since the faculty of hearing is exhausted, there is a danger of dwelling in the wisdom of awakening; therefore, it is said, "when hearing is exhausted, do not dwell. This does not mean non-dwelling.
This concerns the exhaustion of hearing. Where there is awareness, there is that which is aware.

Since the functioning of this nature of awareness cannot remain eternally subtle, the Bodhisattva here personally realizes the shifting of positions; therefore it is said: "The awareness and that which is aware are empty."
The awakening to emptiness reaches ultimate perfection; that which is emptied by emptiness is extinguished.

The preceding wisdom of the awakening to emptiness serves to manifest the mechanism of the transformative stage, thereby revealing that fundamental awakening’s true emptiness is supremely perfect and wondrous.
This subsequent statement that "that which is emptied by emptiness is extinguished" precisely clarifies this principle; it does not imply that there is yet another emptiness to be emptied.
And thus they are extinguished. When both arising and ceasing have been extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one.

Now, when movement and stillness are understood and the faculty of hearing is exhausted, awakened wisdom becomes empty, and the mark of emptiness itself ceases. This is what is meant by "arising and ceasing having been extinguished. Then—
The Tathāgatagarbha is the nature of true quiescence; it is clearly and eternally abiding. Therefore, it is said that "quiescence is manifest before one.
This is what is called the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa. Bodhisattvas enter samādhi herein, and the Tathāgatas of the ten directions realize Great Nirvāṇa herein;
herein there shall be no divergent paths.

From the very beginning during the stage of hearing, up until the manifestation of quiescence (*śamatha*), both Changshui and Gushan have assigned these stages to the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-mayī*, *cintā-mayī*, and *bhāvanā-mayī* prajñā).

This is unassailable from the perspective of principle; for it can be verified by the text that the Bodhisattva’s general heading speaks of entering samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Nevertheless, I, being ignorant, believe there is no necessity to divide them in this way, because [the practice] proceeds according to one's innate capacity (*indriya*).
This is the revelation: first, one must eliminate all objects of cognition in order to manifest the clarity and penetration of the nature of seeing;

next, one must exhaustively awaken to and dispel emptiness in order to reach the ultimate, wondrous perfection of the awakened nature. This is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, in which the cause encompasses the fruit, and the beginning must penetrate through to the end.
If one advances in practice, there will be periods of both acceleration and extension; the Dharma is fundamentally perfect and all-pervading, and the faculties of beings are not fixed.
Whether gradual or sudden, whether appearing sequentially or simultaneously, or whether perceived all at once—it is certainly impossible to treat every case as identical.

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas recount their own experiences, they describe what they traversed at that specific time; or perhaps they speak of what was appropriate for a particular audience on that day, necessarily referring to those who were first to attain realization.

Emptiness. This subsequently dispels attachment to dharmas; it is intended to cause one to discern the preceding text, though it may seem not to be the "discrimination of dharmas" (*dharmapravicaya*).
I have briefly set this forth for those who understand.
The first section, describing the causes through cultivation, is concluded. II. Exposition of the Resultant Virtues. Divided into three parts: 1. Attaining the Resultant Virtues.
Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains universal clarity throughout the ten directions and achieves two kinds of excellence:
first, above, one merges with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as the Tathāgatas;
second, below, one merges with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful longing as all those beings.

The above constitutes the perfection of enlightened nature (*prakṛti*). This is the manifestation of function arising from that nature. To speak again of the "fundamentally wondrous enlightened mind":

it does not mean that it is joined [to something] at this time; rather, one should understand that this fundamentally wondrous enlightened mind is of the same substance as both sentient beings and Buddhas.

Because it is now of the same substance as all Buddhas, it is able to share in the same power of compassion; because it is of the same substance as sentient beings, it is able to share in the same [compassion].
"Piteous yearning" (*biyǎng*) refers to the piteous yearning of sentient beings. It arises spontaneously through being permeated by the awakened mind;
it is also summoned forth by the power of compassion (*maitrī*), causing piteous yearning to arise. That they share this same piteous yearning only serves to further manifest the power of compassion.
△ Second, manifesting the wondrous function. This is divided into three parts. The first part, the thirty-two manifestations, is divided into seven sections. First, the general heading:
"World-Honored One, because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I received from that Tathāgata the Vajra Samādhi of Hearing-Perfuming and Hearing-Cultivation, which is like an illusion;
and because I share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgatas, my body has become [endowed with] thirty..."
Second, the stage of "Correspondence" (*anuloma*).
Entering all lands and realizing that all phenomena are like illusions, one is able to cease objective conditions and return to the root.

Through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one achieves the Vajra-samādhi, also called the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*). This Illusion-like Vajra-samādhi [is attained] from the tenth stage onward.
That which is subsequently realized does not transcend the wisdom of perfect, true enlightenment. It is like a diamond (*vajra*), indestructible, yet capable of destroying all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Adorning both self and others, it gives rise to illusory functions, manifesting transformed lands while remaining unmoved from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Responding according to conditions, the thirty-two manifestations are all elicited by the responses of sentient beings. From oneself...
However, this response does not mean that there is truly a physical body entering [the realm]. △ Second, the Holy Bodies, divided into four parts. First, the Buddha Body:

"World-Honored One, if various Bodhisattvas enter samādhi and advance in the cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava), such that their resolute understanding (adhimukti) becomes fully manifest, I manifest the Buddha-body to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation."
Having already entered samādhi, they still rely on further cultivation and remain hindered by their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
This is due to an extremely subtle ignorance regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). Therefore, the Bodhisattva manifests in the form of a Buddha to bring them liberation.

Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva was an ancient Buddha of the past who, out of great compassion, withdrew from his sovereign position to abide in a provisional status. Although this recounts his past causes, how can one know [the full extent of it]?
It is not that [the Buddha] was at that time a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood;

rather, Changshui claimed that he had long since attained the *bhūmi* stages and was able to manifest the higher ranks, which has led to the various commentaries being mired in confused debate—a truly lamentable state of affairs. △ Second, the body of a Pratyekabuddha.
If there are those in training who possess tranquil, wondrous clarity, and for whom the supreme and subtle manifests as perfect,
I appear before them in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
The Pratyekabuddhas loathe clamor and delight in stillness, seeking spontaneous wisdom; hence they are called "tranquil, wondrous, and luminous.

This manifestation as a Pratyekabuddha is for the purpose of demonstrating sameness of purpose (*samānārthatā*); in reality, however, they bring about liberation through the Buddha-vehicle by remaining silent.
It is from this that Bodhisattvas mostly conceal their inner [intentions]. △ Third, the body of the Pratyekabuddha.
If there are those in training who sever the twelve links of dependent origination, and through the excellence of that severance, the supreme and wondrous state manifests in full perfection,
I appear before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

*Pratyekabuddha* (辟支迦羅) is translated here as "Solitary Realizer" (*dokaku*) and also as "Conditionally Awakened One" (*engaku*). Changshui says: "The former [the *pratyekabuddha*] awakens by himself alone, whereas this one awakens based on the teachings.
He contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, performing two types of contemplation: that of the forward flow of transmigration and that of the reverse cessation.
'The excellence of the nature through the severance of conditions' means that the superior nature is manifested when the causal conditions are severed. 4. The Body of the Śrāvaka.
If there are those in training who have realized the emptiness of the Four Truths and enter cessation through the path of cultivation, such that their supreme nature manifests in perfection—
I appear before them in the form of a śrāvaka and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
"Knowing suffering, severing its origin, cultivating the path, and realizing cessation—this is the Dharma of the Śrāvakas. These are present in all Mahāyāna teachings as well.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, the Four Truths on the stages (*bhūmi*) belong to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Four Truths are taught for the sake of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), while simultaneously revealing the ultimate reality;

this leads them to liberation. Furthermore, based on what they have previously practiced, it provisionally accommodates the Perfect understanding, rather than being intended for their final accomplishment."

This is the fundamental vehicle. The above manifestations of perfection are all according to what was originally expected. This is because, at the moment of about to realize [the fruit], one refers to that which is not yet realized;
therefore, it is called "with-learning" (śaikṣa).
The above concludes the section on the two types of noble bodies (āryakāya). △ Third, the celestial bodies (*devakāya*), divided into seven parts. First, the body of Brahmā:

If there are sentient beings whose desire-minds are clear and awakened, who do not transgress against the dust of desire, and whose desire-bodies are pure, I manifest before them in the body of a Brahmā King and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
The Great Brahmā resides in the third heaven of the First Dhyāna. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra* states: "The Great Brahmā Heavenly King expounds the Discourse on Transcending Desire.

This refers to the manifested Brahmā King who displays a land of expedient means; it is because his mind of desire has attained clear awakening that he is used to entice others forward and lead them back to the Truth.
If one were the Brahmā King of actual retribution, then transcending desire would merely result in pure dharmas. 2. The Body of Śakra.
If there are sentient beings who wish to become lords of the heavens and exercise sovereignty over the devas,
I manifest before them in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.

This refers to those sentient beings who cultivate the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). [The Buddha] manifests in the form of Śakra to preach the supreme and wondrous ten wholesome actions for them, so that they may accomplish the true cause;
it is not merely for the sake of accomplishing rebirth as a celestial being. Śakra is the second heaven within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Śakra" is translated here as "Capable" (*neng*), because he is capable of subduing the asuras. "Śakra" (the Lord) is the sovereign of the thirty-two [gods]; thus he is called Śakra-devānām-indra.
This expresses both the Indian (Sanskrit) and Chinese designations. △ Third, the body of the Lord of the Gods (Īśvara):

If there are sentient beings who desire mastery over their bodies to travel throughout the ten directions, I appear before them in the form of the Lord of the Gods and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.
The Sovereign of the Peak Heaven of the Desire Realm. In Sanskrit, it is called Devavati; here it is translated as the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven (Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations).
Because they accomplish their own pleasures by means of what others have created, this is the King Māra.
Alternatively, it is said that above the six heavens there is a separate palace of Māra, which is also subsumed under the Sovereign Heavens. △ The body of the Mahābhūta-vaśavartin Heaven.
If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery and the ability to fly through the void,
I manifest before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal.
Regarding the separate explanation: Maheśvara is the same as Mahesvara at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* refers to this as Akaniṣṭha.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that beyond the Śuddhāvāsa heavens there are Daśabhūmika Bodhisattvas called Maheśvara.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says that the radiance of the Maheśvara devas surpasses that of all sentient beings. In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, offerings are presented to him. Great...
Īśvara is the most supreme. In the "Cloud of Coolness" (Śītalamegha), this is established as a Pure Land among the Three Vehicles;
it is the abode of the Saṃbhogakāya. In reality, it is the fruit of the retributive reward received by Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages, who mostly act as its lords.
△ [He manifests in] the body of a Great General of the Five Heavens.
If there are sentient beings who love to preside over spirits and deities to protect their lands,
I manifest before them in the body of a Great Heavenly General and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.
The "Celestial Great General" refers to the divine general Śakra-devendra. Furthermore, each of the Four Heavenly Kings has eight generals, with Vajrapāṇi as their chief.
"Territories" refers specifically to the territories of the four continents. △ Sixth, the bodies of the Four Heavenly Kings.
If there are sentient beings who love to govern the world and protect its inhabitants,
I manifest before them in the form of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goals.
The Four Heavenly Kings are the highest deities of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). They reside on Mount Sumeru, each occupying one of its four sides.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "The Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:

'We, the Four Kings, together with our twenty-eight divisions and hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities, constantly observe and protect this Jambudvīpa with our pure divine eyes. For this reason, we are called "Protectors".'"
Lord of the World. △ Seventh, the body of the princes of the Four Heavenly Kings:
If there are sentient beings who desire to be born in the celestial palaces and to command spirits and deities, I manifest as the Four Heavenly Kings before them.
He manifested in the form of a crown prince and preached the Dharma for him, causing him to attain accomplishment.
The *Mahā-maṅgala-artha-sūtra* states: "Each of the four world-protecting Heavenly Kings has ninety-one sons who are handsome in appearance and possess great power;
all are named 'Emperor' (*Ti*). Together, the four Heavenly Kings have three hundred and sixty-four [sons]."
"Son, you are able to protect the ten directions.
This concludes the bodies of the three heavens above. △ Fourth, the human body, divided into nine parts. First, the body of a human king:
If there are sentient beings who delight in being human kings, I manifest before them in the form of a human king and preach the Dharma for them."
May they achieve [this].

There are five kinds of kings of men: four are wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), and one is a "scattered-rice" king (*tandula-vikiraṇa*), so called because he is scattered about like grains of rice.
The gold-wheel-turning king rules over the four continents; the silver-wheel-turning king, over three continents; and the copper-wheel-turning king, over two continents.
The Iron-Wheel-Turning King rules over one world-system; the "scattered grain" kings likewise divide the lands among the four continents to educate and govern the people.
Regarding the five types of kings, there are varying depths and weights in the retribution for practicing the ten wholesome paths.

Furthermore, there are Bodhisattvas who manifest themselves to protect and uphold the True Dharma, guiding and encouraging all under heaven. These matters can be verified through their administration of government, as recorded in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*.
The Sūtra says: "When a king protects the Dharma, he increases three kinds of vital essence (*ojas*): first, the vital essence of the earth, which means the five grains ripen in abundance;
second, the vital essence of sentient beings, which means their physical forms are upright and dignified, and they are free from all epidemics;
third, the vital essence of wholesome energy, which means the cultivation of giving, precepts, faith, and so forth. △ Second, the body of a householder.
If there are sentient beings who cherish their clan and lineage and are esteemed by the world,
I manifest before them in the body of an elder and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.
An elder possesses ten virtues. The *Fahua wenju* (Textual Exegesis of the Lotus Sutra) states:

First, noble lineage—being a descendant of the Three August Ones and Five Emperors, from a family where the left [side] wears the sable fur (*zidiao*) and the right side has the hairpin (*youcha*). Second, high rank—holding positions as a counselor, regent, prime minister, salt-and-vinegar minister (*yanmei*), or chief steward (*eheng*).
Third, great wealth—possessing wealth like a mountain of copper and a valley of gold, with abundant abundance and luxury. Fourth, majesty and prowess—as for majesty... [text continues].

1. Solemnity and Dignity: He achieves gravity without the need for formal discipline. 2. Fivefold Wisdom: His wisdom is profound; his mind is like an armory, extraordinary and transcendent. 3. Sixfold Seniority:
His appearance is weathered and imposing, such that all things submit to his dignified bearing. 4. Sevenfold Purity of Conduct: His conduct is as flawless as white jade;
his actions accord perfectly with his words. 5. Eightfold Perfection of Rites: His etiquette is characterized by measured decorum and orderly progression, as esteemed by the world.

"Universally Regarded": nine times he was praised from above; "above" means he was revered by one person. Ten times he was returned to from below; "below" means he was the refuge for all within the four seas.
Internally, these correspond to the ten kinds of merit of the Tathāgata. △ Third, the body of a layperson (*gṛhapati*).
If there are sentient beings who delight in discussing names and phrases and dwell in self-purification, I manifest before them in the body of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve accomplishment.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "If he is among householders, he is the most honored among householders, severing their greedy attachments. Kumārajīva said:
"In foreign lands, those laypeople who possess great wealth and enjoy prosperity are called 'householders' (*gṛhapati*).
According to this, both Sudatta and Vimalakīrti were elders and householders of the Western regions, similar to Pang Yun here in this land. 4. The Body of a Government Official.
If there are sentient beings who love to govern territories and adjudicate the affairs of states and districts,
I manifest before them in the body of a high official and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.

Regarding the term "zhai" (宰): it carries the meaning of governance (*adhipati*). Regarding the term "guan" (官): it carries the meaning of functional capacity (*vṛtti*). The Three Dukes (*santai*) assist the sovereign in administration through their functional capacities;
therefore, they are called "zhiguan" (宰官). Districts and counties are also referred to as "zhiguan," for they govern the people below them. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"If one is among great ministers, one is the most honored among the great ministers, instructing them with the True Dharma. 5. The Body of a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*).
If there are sentient beings who delight in various arts and sciences and seek to protect and sustain themselves,
I manifest before them in the body of a brāhmaṇa and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.
"Brahman" is translated here as "Pure Conduct. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "If among Brahmans, he is the most honored among the Brahmans, having eliminated their arrogance.
Kumārajīva says: "They study extensively and seek heterodox paths; relying on their own wisdom, they are haughty and self-important, and are thus called Brahmans.
Sengzhao says: "In the Qin language, it means 'external intent. This caste has its own distinct scriptures."

From generation to generation, they have inherited the practice of taking the study of the Way as their vocation. Their "arts and calculations" (*shushu*) do not merely consist of divination and astronomical推算;
all discourse on the profound and explanations of principle that do not enter the Right Path are likewise termed "arts and calculations.

Thus, whenever they cite collateral evidence or establish firm proofs to complete their arguments, they invariably claim these are methods for "governing and protecting" (*shewei*). Furthermore, these are not limited to methods for regulating and nourishing the body. △ Six: Leaving Home (Renunciation)
The bodies of the two assemblies are divided into two parts. First, regarding the body of a bhikṣu:

if there is a man who delights in study and leaves the household life, upholding all the precepts and regulations, I will manifest before him in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for him, causing him to achieve fulfillment.
The Sanskrit term *śīla* is translated here as "precepts" (*jie*). The Sanskrit term *vinaya* is translated here as "discipline" (*lü*).
There are two hundred and fifty rules for the bhikṣu precepts. △ Second, the body of the bhikṣuṇī.
If there are women who delight in learning and leave the household life, upholding the various prohibitive precepts,
I shall manifest before them in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
The Bhikṣuṇī precepts consist of five hundred articles in total. *Ni* here translates as "woman," referring to female bhikṣus.
This concludes the section on the two monastic communities. △ Seventh, the section on the two lay communities, divided into two parts.
First, the section on the Upāsaka (layman).
If there is a man who delights in upholding the five precepts, I will manifest before him in the body of an *upāsaka* (lay follower) and preach the Dharma for him, causing him to achieve success.
The five precepts refer to abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking intoxicants. *Upāsaka* is translated here as "male lay practitioner. 2.
If there is a woman who abides by the five precepts, I will manifest before her in the form of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for her,
causing her to achieve accomplishment.

*Upāsikā* is translated here as "female lay follower" (*jinshi nü*). Taken together with the aforementioned males, they are called the two assemblies of the laity (*jiazai erzhong*), meaning those who are capable of serving the Great Sangha.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "This is translated as 'pure man' (*qingjing shi*) and 'pure woman' (*qingjing nü*)."
The above concludes the section on the bodies of the two groups of householders. △ Eighth, the body of the female ruler:
If there are women who establish themselves through internal governance and cultivate their families and states, I manifest before them in the form of a female ruler.
He also preached the Dharma for the ladies of the state (*guó fūrén*), the titled wives (*mìngfù*), and the great matrons (*dàjiā*), causing them to achieve spiritual accomplishment.

Their internal governance was like the virtuous transformation brought about by King Wen’s consorts and queens. Here, "female ruler" (*nǚzhǔ*) refers specifically to the empresses and queens of the Son of Heaven;

the wives of feudal lords are called "ladies of the state"; the wives of high ministers and great officers who have received their titles from the state are called "titled wives"; and "great matrons" refers to those of noble lineage.
For instance, Cao Shituo’s wife, the Empress Dowager, and the Imperial Consorts all served her as their teacher and addressed her as "Dajia" (Great Lady).
△ Ninth, the Child Body, divided into two parts. First, the Child Male Body.
If there are sentient beings whose male organ remains intact, I manifest before them in the form of a young boy and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.

"Remaining intact" means that from childhood until adulthood, they do not violate the precept against sexual misconduct; this is the cultivation of the Brahma-faring life through the arousal of the resolve for enlightenment.
Regarding those who dedicate [their merit] toward transcendence: △ Second, regarding the body of a maiden.
If there is a virgin who delights in remaining in her state and does not seek to be violated, I will manifest before her in the form of a maiden.
I then preached the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve realization.
"Maidens" (*chǔnǚ*) refers to unmarried girls. They took delight in remaining chaste, vowing never to marry and refusing to submit to violence or seduction.
All of these were those with the resolve to pursue the Way; they are what I call "Entering the Way as a Childlike Virgin" (*tóngzhēn rùdào*) within my Dharma.
The above concludes the bodies of the four classes of humans. △ Regarding the bodies of the devas and asuras:
if there are devas who wish to leave their celestial rank, I manifest in a deva body to preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.

Regarding those who grow weary of celestial pleasures and are unable to advance in their cultivation, the *Fayuan zhulin* states: "In discussing the retributions of the heavens, consciousness is further enriched and flourishing;
garments and ornaments are radiant and new; the physical form is light and subtle. Yet, within the Heaven of Sovereignty (*Īśvara*), one becomes a Māra-king;

the meditative state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is instead regarded as a heterodox path; and at the pinnacle of the four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*), deluded attachments are not slight. As for the six heavens of desire..."

For a long time, my delusions have been particularly grave; I have been unable to uphold the Prajñāpāramitā or make offerings to Nirvāṇa. My arrogance has increased further, and my attachment to self and personhood has grown ever greater.

Consequently, the flowers on my head have withered, my topknot has become disheveled, sweat flows from my armpits onto my collar, the radiance of the jeweled palace has faded, and the fine silks of my robes have gathered grime.
Relying upon this pure mind, I repent for all these transgressions. As a sūtra says: "A person possesses three things that are superior..."
Regarding the devas, there are three: first, valor; second, mindfulness; and third, the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If there are nāgas who wish to leave the class of nāgas, I manifest in the form of a nāga and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.
The *Pṛthak-caryā* states: "There are four kinds of nāgas: first, those who guard the celestial palaces, maintaining them so they do not fall;
second, those who raise clouds and bring rain to benefit the human realm; third, terrestrial nāgas, who channel rivers and open canals;

fourth, treasure-store nāgas, who guard the treasuries of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and those of great merit. The *Dīrgha-āgama* states: "The nāgas of Jambudvīpa have three afflictions: first, heat..."
First, wind, heat, and sand strike their bodies, burning their skin, flesh, and bones, causing them great suffering.
Second, two violent winds suddenly arise and blow their palaces, stripping away their precious ornaments, garments, and the like; the nāgas’ own bodies then manifest, causing them great suffering.
Third, when the nāgas are enjoying themselves, a garuḍa enters the palace, seizes the newly born nāga offspring, and devours them, causing them intense fear.
Regarding "Heat and Torment": the Lake Anavatapta is free from these three afflictions; therefore, it is named "Without Heat and Torment.
If there are yakṣas who wish to deliver their own kind, I manifest before them in the form of a yakṣa and preach the Dharma for them.
May they achieve [this]. *Yakṣa* is translated here as "light and swift"; it was formerly erroneously transliterated as *yecha*. There are three types: first, those on the earth;
second, those in the void; and third, those in the heavens. Earth *yakṣas* can only bestow material gifts and thus cannot fly through the air. Heavenly *yakṣas*...
Furthermore, because he gave away chariots and horses as offerings, he was able to fly through the air. When the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma, the earth-dwelling yakṣas proclaimed it;
the sky-dwelling yakṣas heard it. The sky-dwelling yakṣas proclaimed it; the Four Great Kings heard it. In this manner, it continued up to the Brahma Heaven.
If there are gandharvas who desire to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the body of a gandharva and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
"Gandharva" is translated here as "Seeker of Fragrance. They are the pleasure-spirits of Śakra, dwelling on the southern side of Mount Sumeru at Vajraparvata.
When Śakra, Lord of the Gods, intends to perform music and burns aloeswood incense, this deity immediately follows the fragrance and departs;
therefore, he is named Gandharva (Fragrance-Seeker).
If an asura desires to leave his own kind, I manifest before him in the form of an asura and preach the Dharma for him.
The Dharma causes them to achieve [this].
Asuras are here translated as "Non-Gods" (*asura*), because they engage in non-celestial conduct through flattery and deceit. The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states:
"Because they cannot endure what is good, cannot humble their minds, and despite being clearly instructed through various forms of teaching, act out of arrogance."
They are not virtuous heroes, nor are they gods; therefore, they are called asuras.
If there are kinnaras who delight in liberation from their own kind, I manifest before them in the body of a kinnara and preach the Dharma to them, causing them to achieve perfection.
The *kiṃnara*—translated here as "non-human"—has horns upon its head and is also a celestial musician deity (*devakinnara*). It is slightly inferior to the *gandharva*.
The *Bodhisattvagatyutpatti-sūtra* states: "The *kiṃnaras* dwell among the Ten Jewel Mountains to the north of Mount Sumeru.
By virtue of their past practice of giving, they reside in palaces made of the seven precious gems; their lifespan is exceedingly long, yet they are possessed by anger."
Because he had been angry with a śramaṇa, for eighty-four kalpas he constantly lacked hands and feet. When the devas held assemblies, he shared the upper and lower ranks with the gandharvas;
whenever the devas wished to perform music, sweat would flow from his armpits as he ascended to heaven.
There was a kiṃnara named Tūṇava who played the lute and sang of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena to praise the World-Honored One.
If there are mahoragas who desire to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the body of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for them,
enabling them to achieve accomplishment.

*Mahoraga* is translated here as "Great-Bellied. Master Kumārajīva says they are "earth-dragons" (*bhūmi-nāga*). Master Sengzhao says they are "great pythons that move on their bellies. The *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* states:
"These are the temple deities of the world who receive people's wine and meat; all of this enters the belly of the python.

Those who violate the precepts, are deceitful and sycophantic, harbor much anger and give little in alms, and are greedily addicted to wine and meat—whose discipline has slackened—fall among the ghosts and spirits [as these]."

Anger-demons enter their bodies and devour them. In the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, it is recorded that a fellow student of An Shigao fell into the body of a giant python due to his excessive anger;
he was subsequently delivered by the deity of Qingtang Lake. This is precisely an instance of such a case. △ Sixth:
Those who are not human yet take human form.
