If there are sentient beings who delight in being human or in cultivating themselves as humans, I manifest in a human form to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
For those who seek not to lose their human bodies so as to advance in their cultivation, Minister Pei said: "This can serve to rectify the mind and its deliberations."
To hasten toward Bodhi, only the human path is capable of it.
As for those who are non-humans— whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception— if they desire to deliver their own kind,
I manifest my body before them all and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
Changshui says: "Those with form possess the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), such as those described as 'auspicious or calamitous spiritual intelligences' (*jīngmíng*) below.

Those without form lack the aggregate of form, such as those described as 'empty, dispersed, dissolving, or sinking' below. Those with perception possess four aggregates, such as 'gods, ghosts, and spirits' below.
Those without perception lack the four aggregates, such as when 'the spirit is transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone' below. All of these..."

"They are not human beings. Wēnlíng says: "The reason the six classes of ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) do not include those in the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*) is that these types are submerged in obscurity and have not yet been able to hear the Dharma;
therefore, [the Buddha] uses the power of fearlessness to pull them out. △ Seventh, the summary.

This is called "wondrous purity. The thirty-two types of responsive bodies that enter various lands are all accomplished with sovereign mastery through the effortless, wondrous power of cultivation based on hearing and the permeation of hearing by means of samādhi.
The above thirty-two manifestations are all accomplished through the sovereign power of the wondrous, effortless samādhi.
This Bodhisattva’s illusory Vajra-samādhi is like a mani jewel that reflects the five colors;
while the essence of the jewel is pure and lustrous, this Dharma-body is likewise pure, perfected by great compassion, and able to respond inevitably whenever sentient beings invoke it.
It is like a bead that contains the five colors; though the two do not reach one another, the transformative activity is complete and perfect. Therefore, it is called "spontaneous accomplishment.
This concludes the first part, the thirty-two marks of response. △ Twenty-four Fearlessnesses, divided into fifteen sections; first, the general heading.
World-Honored One, by means of this power of the effortless, wondrous Vajra Samādhi— perfumed by hearing and cultivated through hearing—
and because I share in the same compassion and yearning as all sentient beings of the ten directions and three periods of time throughout the six realms,
I cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of meritorious qualities of fearlessness within my body and mind.
The awakened mind is fundamentally the same; it is only because emotions arise that wisdom becomes obstructed, and one is consequently moved by the winds of external objects.

When a Bodhisattva regains their original wondrous state, they constantly perceive sentient beings dwelling within their own body and mind. By the power of compassion, they cause those beings to give rise to a sense of longing and devotion.
This causes them to attain fearlessness. Just as that frightened pigeon, upon entering the shadow of the Tathāgata, has nothing further to fear—this may serve as one verification.
△ Second, the interpretation through observing sound.
First, because I do not observe myself by means of an observing subject, I cause those suffering sentient beings throughout the ten directions to observe my voice,
whereby they immediately attain liberation.
Because of this, the observer is fundamentally of one substance with all sentient beings. One substance necessarily permeates many substances, and many substances necessarily permeate one substance.

Upon hearing my voice, they immediately attain liberation; the principle is indeed thus. Therefore, know that when observation and listening are not perfected, it is merely because of obstructions caused by sounds and forms.
Once one sheds these defilements and turns back toward awakening, the response and stimulus are manifested without fixed direction, residing only in—
One should keep this in mind. △ Third, entering fire without being burned:
Second, through the revolving and returning of knowledge and vision, one causes all sentient beings such that even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them.
Fire arises from the mind; it originates in cognition and perception. Once cognition and perception have receded, there is no fire outside the mind.
As it is with me, so it is with all sentient beings. Simply understand that by reciting the name, phenomenon and principle are non-dual. △ Fourth: Entering water without drowning.
Third is the contemplation on the revolving of hearing. This causes all sentient beings who are adrift upon great waters not to be drowned by the water.
Hearing is carried away by sound; thus, externally, the water responds to it. When one turns hearing back toward the True, the waves of the mind naturally subside.
Sentient beings do not perceive this; they only understand the practice of invoking the name. Whether this is through the power of others or one's own power, only a Buddha can know. △ Five: Entering.

Fourth, by severing and extinguishing deluded thoughts so that the mind is free from killing and harming, one causes all sentient beings to enter the realms of ghosts where the ghosts cannot harm them.

Deluded thoughts are like thieves; they can destroy nirvāṇa. When one knows that the perceptions of the mind have ceased and the mechanism of killing is instantly halted, sentient beings’ illusory vision of ghostly realms will vanish as soon as they utter the name [of the Buddha].
It is like returning to one’s own homeland: once the ghosts of the mind have departed, who is there to cause harm?
△ Sixth, being harmed by weapons that shatter them.
Fifth, the cultivation of hearing through perfuming results in the restoration of the six sense organs; they become identical to the hearing of sound.

This can cause sentient beings who are about to be harmed by weapons to have their bodies shattered piece by piece, yet make their weapons as if cutting through water or blowing across light, for their nature is non-existent.

"Shaking. Regarding "perfuming the hearing so as to become the hearer": this means that externally one detaches from the faculty of hearing, while internally one turns back toward the nature of hearing. When one faculty is thus, all six faculties are likewise;
therefore it is said they are identical to the hearing of sound. When the six faculties have all ceased, the light of the nature is spontaneously tranquil. Directly...
The body and mind below are like the great void; the void has never received all touches. When sentient beings call upon the Name, it is also like this:
like a lost traveler who hears his mother’s voice from afar, he already knows in his heart that he will certainly not wander astray.

When the root delusion turns back once, one immediately becomes identical with true stillness. It is like a drop falling into the sea—how could its minuteness or magnitude ever be distinguished? △ Seven.
The ghosts cannot see it.
Sixth, when the clarity cultivated through hearing permeates the entire Dharma-realm, then the nature of all dark obscurities cannot remain intact;
this enables yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍa ghosts, piśācas, pūtanas, and others to [be seen] even though they are nearby.
Beside it, the eyes cannot see;

yet when the faculty of hearing is stimulated and reaches the pinnacle of clarity and brilliance, then all dark phenomena can never again obscure it. It is like the sun rising in the sky, where the gloomy mists vanish of their own accord.
Sentient beings, in their seeing and hearing, are deluded by sounds and forms; yet if they hold the name of Avalokiteśvara, they shall hear [the voice of liberation].
The faculty immediately turns; it naturally merges with the original wondrous clarity, like light penetrating a crack that illuminates the entire dark room.
*Rākṣasa* here translates as "the fearsome. *Kumbhāṇḍa* here translates as "papaya. This deity has a body shaped like a papaya;
when walking, it rests on the shoulders, and when sitting, it crouches upon them. *Piśāca* here translates as "eater of vital essence. It devours... [text fragment ends]
This is because they are the essence of emotions and the five grains. Pūtana is translated here as the "ghost of feverish disease. △ Eighth, the shackles and fetters do not adhere.

Seventh, when the nature of sound is perfectly dissolved, the faculties of seeing and hearing turn back inward; departing from all sensory dusts and delusions, it can cause sentient beings to be released from their imprisonment.
It cannot be bound by shackles.

Having departed from the dust of the world and returned to the hearing of the self-nature, its essence is inherently complete and liberated. Once the conceptual bonds have dissolved, how could phenomenal things possibly constrain it?

The substance of sentient beings is wondrous; though they may briefly wander onto divergent paths, their names remain as they were, no different from the original state. △ Nine: Not Robbed by Thieves.

Eighth, when sounds cease and hearing becomes perfect, one universally generates the power of compassion. This enables sentient beings to pass through perilous paths without being plundered by bandits.

When sound injures the faculty of hearing, it is like a bandit robbing a virtuous person; by reversing the hearing so that it is free from sensory dust, both sound and resonance become still. Thus, those who call upon [the name] shall be turned back.
The mind, like a thief, has no inherent nature. Through the pervasive application of the power of compassion, self and others are mutually embraced. △ Tenth, the departure from lustful desire.
Ninth: by permeating the hearing and departing from sensory dust, one is not plundered by forms; this can cause all beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greedy desire.
Forms can plunder the eyes; the mind races along with the eyes. Once hearing has departed from sensory dust, observation follows the sound back to its source.
You are called a "sentient being" because you respond to conditions in such a way, receiving the compassionate vows above. △ Eleven: Departing from Anger and Hatred.
Tenth, the Sound of Purity Free from Defilement: the faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused, such that there is neither subject nor object.
This can cause all sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment to be free from all hatred.
One who perceives pure sound attains the self-characteristic of sound; there is neither conformity nor opposition. Hence it is called "dustless.

When the faculty of returning-hearing confronts an object that is free from conformity or opposition, there is neither subject nor object. Therefore, it is said that the faculty and its objects are perfectly interfused.

Following the sense organs and their objects, one falsely perceives them as favorable or adverse, thereby giving rise to anger. By holding the Name and reflecting upon oneself, such dualistic opposition dissolves.
The Bodhisattva and sentient beings share the same loom. △ Twelve: Departing from the Darkness of Ignorance.
Eleventh is "Dissolving Dust and Revolving Radiance. The body and mind of the dharma-realm are like lapis lazuli, brilliantly penetrating and unobstructed.
This enables all those with dull natures and karmic obstructions, including the icchantikas, to forever leave behind the darkness of ignorance.

*Ātyantika* (translated here as "extreme forgetfulness") is termed "ultimate" (*atyanta*). Because they ultimately lack the nature of *nirvāṇa*, they are the *icchantikas* who lack the [Buddha-]nature;

thus, they are called those whose natures are hindered by dullness and ignorance. When Bodhisattvas reverse the sense-faculties and dissolve sensory objects, the luminous subtlety of original enlightenment flows through their bodies and minds;
internal and external clarity becomes transparent, and naturally there is no obstruction. Furthermore, regarding the *icchantika* and the Buddha...
The nature [of enlightenment] has already been granted through nirvana; it is only due to the darkness of ignorance that one exists therein yet remains unaware.

As soon as one utters the name of Avalokiteśvara and the faculty of faith is established, the obstacles to this nature are instantly dissolved. There is no question of long or short duration. △ Thirteen: Obtaining a Son.
Twelfth, while their physical forms are dissolved and they hear again, they do not move from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) yet enter into the mundane world without destroying it.
They are able to travel throughout the ten directions to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, serving as Dharma princes at the side of each Buddha.
For those sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu* who have no sons and desire a male child, they cause the birth of a son endowed with merit and wisdom.
The fusion of form and the fusion of the faculties constitute "form. Furthermore, hearing and the nature of hearing constitute "nature.

By allowing the nature to function spontaneously, one encompasses and enters all worlds, yet there is no person who enters them; therefore, it is called the "Immovable Site of Enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

All worlds are contained within the ocean of the Bodhisattva’s nature, neither falling into existence nor non-existence, yet each functions in accordance with its own conditions; therefore, it is called the "Unbreakable World."
The Realm: Universally making offerings to all Buddhas and succeeding to the Dharma-King of Emptiness, one accords with the non-duality of the mundane and supramundane worlds;
thus, by reciting the name once, each accord is fully satisfied. △ Fourteen: Seeking a daughter, one obtains a daughter.
Thirteenth: The six sense faculties are perfectly penetrating; their luminous illumination is non-dual and encompasses the worlds of the ten directions.

This establishes the Great Perfect Mirror, the Empty Tathāgata-garbha, which receives and upholds the secret Dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions without fail.
It can cause those beings within the Dharma-realm who have no children and desire daughters to give birth to daughters who are upright, virtuous, gentle, and compliant.
People love and revere women who possess auspicious marks.

When the six sense faculties return to their source, there is only the single precious awakening that naturally manifests throughout the ten directions. When mindfulness is present without interruption, it is called the Great Perfect Mirror.
By means of this, one clearly receives and upholds all the secret dharma-gates of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Through this one...
The jewel is luminous; its perfect mirror reflects without end. Like a woman’s virtue of constancy and compliance, it nurtures all classes of beings.
Possessing such auspicious gentleness, it responds to wishes according to their aspirations. △ Fifteen: The multitude of those who hold the name are without distinction; this concludes the section.

Fourteenth: Within this trichiliocosm, among the hundreds of millions of suns and moons, there are currently sixty-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Dharma Princes dwelling in the world.
They cultivate the Dharma and establish models to teach and transform sentient beings;
their skillful means and wisdom, which accord with the capacities of sentient beings, are each distinct.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "The sun and moon traverse the four continents, constituting one world-system (*lokadhātu*).
A thousand such suns and moons, a thousand Sumeru mountains, a thousand kings of the Yama heaven, a thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, and a thousand Brahmā heavens are termed a 'small chiliocosm'."

Counting one thousand of these small thousand-fold worlds makes what is called a medium thousand-fold world system. Counting one thousand of these medium thousand-fold world systems makes what is called a great thousand-fold world system.
Within it, there are ten billion Mount Sumerus, kings of mountains, as well as ten billion sets of four continents, suns, and moons.
All these are the transformation realms of a single Buddha, collectively called the Sahā World.

Within this Sahā World, there are Bodhisattvas—sons of the Dharma—as numerous as the sands of sixty-two Ganges Rivers. In all that they cultivate and establish as models for practice, they adapt their teachings to transform sentient beings;
each possesses distinct skillful means and differing wisdom, thereby manifesting the fundamental perfection [of the teaching] below.

This penetration constitutes true universal penetration (*samantamukha*). Cultivating the Dharma refers to one's own practice (*svārtha*), while establishing a model refers to transforming others (*parārtha*). One takes one's own practice as a model to effect transformation in others.
Expedient means (*upāya*) refers to the provisional, while wisdom (*prajñā*) refers to the real; these are the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real.
All these are matters of transforming others.

Because I have attained the fundamental root of perfect penetration and developed the wondrous gate of the ear, my body and mind have since become subtle and refined, encompassing and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
This enables sentient beings to hold my name, and together with them, to maintain it for sixty-two Ganges-sands of eons.
"World-Honored One, the merit of these two individuals is equal and without distinction, like the sands of the Ganges.
My single name is no different from their many names; it is because I have cultivated this practice that I have attained true and perfect penetration."

The Bodhisattva Ben-gen (Fundamental Root) speaks of the fundamental root of his own practice of perfect penetration; he refers here to the gateway of the ear. From this gateway of the ear, the subtle excellence arises:
it means that the hearing of sound is fundamentally empty, merging with the essence of wondrous enlightenment. It is like water containing the sky; the water and the sky are of one color.
Through this harmonious fusion, body and mind are integrated, encompassing and nourishing the Dharma-realm without limit. Therefore, he is able to realize it.
Many are subsumed within one; by means of one, the many are encompassed. The merit of upholding the name may be understood by analogy with this.
Attaining true and perfect penetration is a statement intended for those of specific capacities; it is precisely the principle of subduing and selecting the faculties.
This is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness. It provides beings with complete merit.
Although it is termed "bestowing fearlessness," it primarily resides in the realm of uprooting suffering.

The phrase "complete merit" is used here to manifest that there is nothing throughout the ten directions that does not rely upon the Bodhisattva’s wondrous virtues, which are universally pervasive; all who possess a mind without exception revere and look up to them.
How could there be anyone who does not believe in the World-Honored One Śākyamuni? Yet, none would dare to slight the Bodhisattva. The sentient beings of this land truly receive vast protection:
through the thirty-two manifestations, he aligns himself upward with the power of compassion; through the fourteen fearlessnesses, he accords himself downward with the yearning for mercy. This—
The Bodhisattva’s unconditional compassion makes no distinctions; yet, even though it is not directed toward a specific recipient, it cannot fail to respond.

This is just as when one person is exclusively focused on remembering while another is exclusively prone to forgetting: whether they meet or do not meet, whether they see or do not see, remains undetermined.
According to the thirty-two manifestations, these apply only to Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles who are on the verge of realization but have not yet attained it.
He manifests his own body and acts as an uninvited friend. This power of the Bodhisattva’s compassion, together with the person’s own roots of goodness, is sufficient to be remembered in two ways.

Among all sentient beings, there are none who do not receive a response without having first sought it; yet when it comes to seeking refuge through sorrowful longing, one relies entirely upon the invocation of the name.
In Changshui’s commentary, he speaks only of the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of causes, failing to address the compassion of sentient beings.

I look up and observe that although various commentaries mention these names, they merely attribute [the response] to the power of others (*tāraśakti*), yet fail to explain in detail how it is elicited by the self-power (*svaśakti*) of sentient beings.
Judging by the intent of the sutras, this too remains a deficiency. Now, that which obscures the minds of the multitude is nothing other than sound and form;
thus, hearing and seeing cause them to run outward, giving rise to false discrimination. Even when they reach a state of extreme terror, they still do not...
To know how to turn back is one interpretation of "calling upon the Name. When the mind has something to look up to, the ears and eyes will not be distracted;
this is precisely a moment of turning away from objects and returning to the sense-faculties. Thus, we know that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and deluded attachments can be transformed.

The power of self and the power of others manifest in mutual resonance. If one relies solely on the power of others, then throughout the lands of the Ganges River, all shall see themselves being saved and healed.
There still remains rising and sinking; what has compassion’s power to do with it?
The twenty-four fearlessnesses are concluded. △ Third and Fourth: The Four Inconceivables. This is divided into five parts. First, the general heading.

World-Honored One, because I have further attained this perfect penetration for the cultivation and realization of the unsurpassed Way, and because I am also able to skillfully attain the four inconceivable,
unconditioned, and wondrous virtues—
these four inconceivabilities being obtained from the ultimate fruit— it is said that I have cultivated and realized the unsurpassed Way. This is based on...
After the perfection of compassion and wisdom, that which is manifested through great compassion occurs simultaneously with the stimulus of the sentient being's capacity;
it does not arise from deliberate thought but is spontaneous, and is thus termed "inconceivable. △ Second, the manifestation of heads, arms, and eyes.
First, because I initially attained the most wondrous and sublime mind of hearing, my mental essence left behind all sensory perceptions;

seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing could no longer be partitioned, becoming a single, perfectly fused, pure, and precious awakening. Therefore, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and can proclaim boundless secret divine mantras.

The initial subtlety is the disappearance of the object; the subsequent subtlety is the departure from the faculties. When the faculties depart and merge with awareness, one attains the true nature of the faculties;

hence it is called the "hearing-mind. Once this has merged and returned to original awareness (*mūla-bodhi*), speaking from the perspective of this original awareness, it is said that "the essence of the mind leaves behind hearing.
When this essence of the original awareness-mind has already shed the nature of hearing, the six faculties become perfectly interfused—being both one and [many].

Six is precisely one; they are identical within the single precious awakening. According to the responses of sentient beings, wondrous forms appear individually and wondrous voices proclaim [the truth] individually;
there is no duality in this accordance with them.
Among them, some manifest with one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, nine heads,
eleven heads, and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, ten thousand heads, or eighty-four thousand śakara heads; likewise with two arms,
four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, up to twenty-two.
Fourteen. In this manner, up to one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms, and eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms;
two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, nine eyes, and so on, up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes.
Ten thousand eyes— eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes— whether manifesting as compassion or majesty, or as meditative concentration or wisdom,
they rescue and protect sentient beings, attaining great sovereign mastery.
*Śakara* is translated here as "complete" (*jùzú*); *mudrā* is translated as "seal" (*yìn*). Each possesses its own wondrous seal.
Changshui says: "The head emerges above all sages; this is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The arms are able to lift and receive; this is the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The eyes lead with clarity; this is the Wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*). This also symbolizes the Dharma. However, taken collectively, these represent the perfect penetration of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), whether they be few or many.
Responding in accordance with what is perceived—reaching the ultimate number of eighty-four thousand—is because sentient beings possess eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Bodhisattva transforms the coarse into the subtle and the limited into the perfect; such is the natural law (*dharmatā*), not something resulting from deliberate remedial application.
It is likewise with compassion, majesty, concentration, and wisdom: when sentient beings are suited to receive compassion, they immediately behold a compassionate countenance. When sentient beings...
If sentient beings are suited for awe, he immediately manifests a majestic appearance; if they are suited for concentration, he immediately manifests a concentrated appearance;
if they are suited for wisdom, he immediately manifests a wise appearance. These are accomplished through great compassion, yet fundamentally there is no intentional mind at work.
Nevertheless, various spiritual transformations manifest according to the capacities of beings—this is inconceivable. △ Third, Manifesting Forms and Reciting Mantras.

Second, because I have been liberated from the six sense objects through hearing and reflection, just as sound passes through a wall without being obstructed, I am able to manifest every single form and recite every single mantra with marvelous skill. These forms and mantras can bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings;
therefore, throughout the dust-mote worlds of the ten directions, I am known as the One Who Bestows Fearlessness.
Upon hearing it, one enters into contemplation; utterly detached from the six sense-objects, it resonates back like a sound, its response being sovereign and free.

This is what is meant by "not being a thing among things," and thus being able to accord with things. Whether manifesting form or reciting mantras, it follows sentient beings entirely, responding without a mind of its own.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata is one who bestows fearlessness upon sentient beings.
Whether he emits one ray of light, two, three, or more, he causes all to remain far removed from every kind of evil.
The Tathāgata now possesses such immeasurable power; if there is a bodhisattva who abides in such fearlessness..."
On this ground, one no longer fears the arising of greed, anger, and delusion, nor birth, old age, sickness, and death.
One also no longer fears the evil realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. Furthermore, one no longer fears śramaṇas, brahmins, non-Buddhist heretics with false views, or Māra Pāpīyān.
Nor does one fear the twenty-five states of existence. For this reason, this ground is named "Fearlessness."
Ground. When a bodhisattva dwells in the Ground of Fearlessness, they attain twenty-five samādhis and destroy the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).

Just as by attaining the Stainless Samādhi (*vimala-samādhi*), one can destroy [the suffering of] sentient beings in the hells and so forth. △ Fourth, seeking compassion through the relinquishment of the body.
Third, by virtue of my cultivation of the fundamental, wondrous, perfect, and penetrating root of purity,
all worlds where I travel cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion.
Because they have entered the stream through the fundamental faculties, their six sense-faculties are completely liberated and free from dwelling or attachment;

thus, the sentient beings they influence are able to relinquish both body and wealth, seeking compassionate acceptance. Summoned by the power of compassion, this is the natural state of the ground of practice.
△ Fifth, all that is sought is obtained.

Fourth, I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized ultimate fruition; I am able to provide various precious offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm.
If they seek a wife, they shall obtain a wife; if they seek a son, they shall obtain a son;
if they seek samādhi, they shall obtain samādhi; if they seek long life, they shall obtain long life—and so on, even unto seeking great nirvāṇa, they shall obtain great nirvāṇa.

Nirvana. This realization of the ultimate fruit is non-dual with that of the Buddha; therefore, one is able to see through to the equality of the nature and characteristics of sentient beings within the six realms.
Consequently, what is offered is also equal. One seeks nothing and fails to obtain nothing. Having manifested the power of compassion, [one regards] even wife and children...
Life-span and Great Nirvana likewise manifest that both the mundane and supramundane are equal.
Sentient beings perceive two, whereas Bodhisattvas see them as a single characteristic; they possess no dualistic contemplation.
The preceding two sections have concluded the demonstration of the wondrous function. △ Third, the conclusion regarding the fundamental perfect penetration.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration; I [attained it] through the ear-gate via the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination.
With mastery over the conditioned mind, I entered the phase of the "flowing-in" and thereby attained Samādhi, achieving Bodhi. This is the foremost.

Initially, one attains the true faculty-nature from within hearing. This true faculty-nature exhausts all objects of hearing. Subsequently, one enters the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination of the Awakened Mind.
In this Samādhi of Perfect Illumination, whatever the mind takes as its object, one realizes the true mark of all dharmas;
therefore, it is called "sovereignty. Regarding the phrase "attaining samādhi through the phase of entering the flow," it is because of the cause of entering the flow that—
He attained it. This clarity arises from the illumination within hearing; it is not that there is nothing illuminated.

When the Bodhisattva reaches this point, he speaks again of the cause, just as Sudhana, in the *Avataṃsaka*, traveled through one hundred and ten cities to study the Bodhisattva path, yet upon finally reaching Maitreya, was sent back to see Mañjuśrī. He said, "The various virtues you have seen..."
Knowledge, hearing the bodhisattva practices, entering the gates of liberation, and fulfilling great vows—all these are due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī attains ultimate perfection in all places. This is because the youth attained fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) from Mañjuśrī;
thus, although he exhausts all distinctions, ultimately there is no distinction. One may take this as an analogy.

It can be seen, World-Honored One, that that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well attained the dharma-gate of perfect penetration; amidst the great assembly, he bestowed upon me the prediction of my name as Avalokiteśvara.
Because I contemplate and listen to the ten directions with perfect clarity, the name "Avalokiteśvara" pervades the ten directions.

This demarcates the boundaries and connects [the practice] to that Buddha, thereby clarifying past causes and manifesting skillful means. As for the "observer and listener," this refers to observing and listening to this very state;

it signifies that as hearing revolves, one is liberated from the sense organs. When the mind and eyes are concentrated, the six gates are no longer bound, and one enters the far-reaching, perfect luminosity.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, the myriad responses accord with the capacities of beings.

This concludes the four preceding sections on the universal investigation of perfect penetration. △ Fifth, the section on the correct demonstration of perfect cultivation, which has five parts. First, the manifestation of auspicious signs through the emission of light.

At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One simultaneously emitted precious light, which reached far to drench the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, as well as the Bodhisattvas who are Dharma Princes. Those Tathāgatas likewise simultaneously emitted precious light from their five limbs;
from those directions as numerous as motes of dust, it came to drench the crown of the Buddha’s head, as well as the crowns of the great Bodhisattvas within the assembly.
And as for the Arhats, the forests, trees, ponds, and marshes all resound with the sounds of the Dharma; their interlacing lights entwine like a net of precious threads.
When a single faculty returns to its source, the six faculties become pure; there is but the single jewel-like awakening, whose essence and function are non-dual.
Therefore, light is emitted equally from the five faculties, so that one Tathāgata and the Tathāgatas of the ten directions mutually interlace their lights and pour them one upon another.

Furthermore, the crowns of the heads of all Bodhisattvas and Arhats, as well as the forests, trees, ponds, and marshes, all emit the sounds of the Dharma. This reveals that self and others are not separated;
the great and the small are manifested together; the one and the many are mutually fused; and the environment and its inhabitants are in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

This faculty-nature is that which has been universally realized by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas from their initial resolve to their ultimate fruition. Yet, through a single turning of the ear-faculty, the six functions [of consciousness]—
The radiance flowed forth; both internally and externally, all was empty and luminous.
As their mindfulness became perfectly penetrating, this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before, and all universally obtained the Vajra Samādhi.
The Vajra-samādhi is identical to the Śūraṅgama. All sentient beings inherently possess it; it is pure by its very nature.
By attaining it all at once and universally, they recover their original mind.
Immediately, a rain of hundred-treasure lotus flowers fell, with blue, yellow, red, and white intermingling and blending in profusion.

The voids of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures, adorned by the myriad practices like precious blossoms; the differentiated functions of wisdom were like the blue, yellow, red, and white, as the void itself was thus formed.
Form and the emptiness of form are non-dual; they are neither existent nor non-existent. Principle is manifested through phenomena, such that phenomena and principle are without obstruction.
At this moment, the great earth, mountains, and rivers of this Sahā world all disappear simultaneously, and one sees only the lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions.
They merge into a single realm where *brahman* chants and hymns are spontaneously performed.

This signifies that the precious clarity of empty awareness is perfectly blended and harmoniously fused; the distinction between the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*) completely dissolves, and even space itself perishes, leaving only the Land of Quiescent Light where all beings can see one another.
*Brahman* (or *bhāṣya*) refers to the eulogistic chanting of the Western [Land]; "eulogy" (*zàn*) follows the text...
Concluding Chapter. Regarding the chanting, it refers to the flowing verses of short stanzas. As the Sūtra says: "With subtle and wondrous sounds, one sings the praises of the Buddha’s virtues.
△ Second, the instruction for Mañjuśrī to select those with the proper faculties.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince: "Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training and Arhats, each of whom has spoken of the skillful means by which they first attained the Way.
They all claim to have cultivated true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). In their respective practices, there is truly no superiority or inferiority, nor any distinction of before or after."

That which is realized through these words alone is uniformly the single reality; therefore, there is no superiority or inferiority among them. As for the entryway, each follows its own skillful means;
therefore, there is a sequence of before and after.
I now wish to cause Ānanda to attain awakening through twenty-five practices. Which of these is suited to his faculties?

Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, for those sentient beings in this world who enter the Bodhisattva vehicle and seek the unsurpassed path, by what gate of skillful means can they achieve success with ease?
Because of Ānanda, this cause has been made universal for the future of this realm. Thus, the subsequent text says:

"The true essence of the teaching in this direction / Is pure within hearing and sound. △ Third, the exclusion of those who do not possess the perfect faculties, divided into three parts. First, praising the wondrous nature of the source of awakening.
To demonstrate that delusion is fundamentally empty,
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate command, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and,
sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha:
Mañjuśrī is the sublime wisdom of the Dharmakāya. Having first realized the Dharmakāya of fundamental gnosis (mūla-jñāna), he is able to give birth to the Buddha-family.

Once fundamental gnosis is perfected, one subsequently gives rise to practice based upon that gnosis. At this stage, as one specifically selects the faculties for cultivation and realization, one must sever the subtle delusions at their root.
Furthermore, there is no distinction in essence or function between fundamental gnosis and discriminative gnosis (prajñā); it is necessary to manifest them both from the fundamental source.
The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect; this perfect limpidity makes the awakening fundamentally subtle and wondrous.

First, the nature of awakening is clarified; subsequently, its distinctions are examined. "The ocean of awakening" refers to the primordial limit of the essence of awakening; it is vast, tranquil, and profound.

It is like the ocean. That the ocean of awakening is unstained and unmixed is called "clarity" (*ting*). That its true and false aspects are difficult to name and that neither enlightenment nor delusion can reach it is called "perfection" (*yuan*).

Furthermore, it is said: "The perfect, clear, and fundamental wondrousness of awakening. This means that the essence of awakening is fundamentally wondrous; it is eternally illuminating yet quiescent.
Right view cannot be considered awakening by means of luminosity alone. Yet luminosity must arise from an object; this is likewise always the case with the subtle.
One should know it thus:
when primordial luminosity shines forth and an object arises, the nature of that illumination perishes as the object is established.

"Enlightening-nature" refers to the essence of awakening; it means the nature of enlightenment. The nature of awakening is fundamentally luminous. When this luminosity "enlightens," it necessarily gives rise to an object.

This is because luminosity does not maintain its wondrous stillness, but follows the function of enlightenment and gives rise to delusion. Delusion does not depart from the True; yet, confronting form and emptiness, one fails to awaken.
Because one fails to awaken, the nature is lost—not a loss in the sense of absolute non-existence.
From delusion arises empty space; upon space, the world is established. When thought becomes clarified, it forms the land; when awareness awakens, it becomes sentient beings.
When illumination turns its back on enlightenment and gives rise to delusion, one necessarily perceives stubborn emptiness—what is called "obscure darkness becoming space."
Regarding the establishment of the world based on emptiness: the preceding text states, "Awakened clarity and empty dullness interact to produce agitation;
thus there is a wind-circle that sustains the world. This is how this world comes into being.

As for "the clarification of thought forms the land, while cognition constitutes sentient beings," this traces back to the original single nature of awakening, which, by relying on deluded cognition, gives rise to confusion. Confusion...
Delusive thoughts coalesce and congeal, becoming identical with the insentient; thus they form the physical world.

Yet, since the entirety of the delusive is fundamentally true, sentient beings continue their transmigratory flow, and their cognitive awareness still persists. This can be verified through one's daily activities.
Emptiness arises within Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. The minute dust-motes of worlds with outflows all depend upon emptiness for their birth.
This original enlightened nature, when viewed in contrast to delusion, results solely from a single thought of luminous awareness suddenly becoming empty and obscure;
yet the ocean of enlightenment remains clear and still, its tranquil illumination ever-present. The manifest emptiness of space and lands is truly like a single speck within the Great Clarity. One.
Recalling the return of the light, one transcends in utter detachment.
When the bubble has vanished, emptiness itself is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three existences?
The worlds and sentient beings possess the marks of the conditioned; the birth and death of sentient beings vanish in the blink of an eye. The kalpa-fire blazes forth...

Indeed, even the great trichiliocosm perishes; only empty space is boundless and seems immutable. Yet one does not realize that this depends entirely upon whether the person turns toward or away from it.
If in a single thought-moment one returns to the source, the ten directions vanish and dissolve, ultimately leaving nothing at all—this can only be personally realized.
△ Second, indicating the speed or slowness of the expedient means.
The nature of returning to the source is non-dual; yet there are many gates of expedient means. The holy nature is all-pervasive; whether following or reversing, all are expedient means.
For those of initial resolve entering samādhi, the speed of progress differs and cannot be compared.
The nature that returns to the source is one; the gates through which one first returns are many. If there is one, then every gate may serve as a point of entry for realization.

If there are many, then the distinctions between following or reversing, and between rapidity or slowness, will naturally arise. Therefore, those with a beginner's mind should seek out that which is direct, swift, and perfectly penetrating.
Both following and reversing are skillful means (*upāya*). Thus, we know that following is also a skillful means. The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states:
"Except for those who have attained sudden awakening, who do not follow along with phenomena. The Bodhisattvas constantly reveal this principle within every gateway of skillful means.
△ Third, the correct exclusion of what is not perfect.

The conceptualization of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) binds it into dust; its subtle discernment cannot penetrate through. How can one fail to achieve clear penetration? It is by this means that one attains perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna*).

Because the binding of darkness constitutes form, it is said that "the conceptualization of form binds it into dust. By contemplating form as empty, after a long time, one finally achieves thorough penetration.
This is like Upānanda, who contemplated the subtle dust of white bones, analyzing form to clarify emptiness until the dust of form was entirely exhausted.

The subtle form is dense and perfect; it is likewise spontaneously pervasive and unobstructed. However, for a beginner to wash away and awaken their refined clarity, it is appropriate to focus on the vast and open void;
therefore, this is not the chosen path.
"Sounds and voices are mixed with language; they consist merely of phonemes (*it*), phrases (*pada*), and flavors (*rasa*).

One does not contain all; how then can one attain perfect penetration? "Mixed" means "combined. This is because sounds and voices do not stop at mere language, and furthermore, language itself transcends phonemes and phrases.
That "one contains many" is what was realized by Kauṇḍinya; because it is easy to rely upon speech, it is [the primary] locus.

Selection: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the speakers; speech is the characteristic of the speaker; and the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*) are the characteristics of what is spoken.

A "name" (*nāma*) is like the word "pot. The written characters for the word "pot" constitute the body of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*). The pot, as a physical entity produced from clay, constitutes the body of phrases (*pada-kāya*).
The fact that names and phrases express meaning is called "flavor" (*rasa*). Therefore, names and phrases depend upon phonemes, and flavor depends upon names and phrases.
Fragrance is known through its combination; when separated, it fundamentally does not exist. Since that which is perceived is not constant, how can one attain perfect penetration?

The youth Fragrance-Veneration smelled fragrance entering his nose and realized that the scent of fragrance neither comes nor goes. Once the sensory dust of fragrance was extinguished, he attained awakening.

The nature of hearing remains distinct and clear. This refers to the fact that if one does not maintain constant awareness—meaning an awareness that is without dependence—it will not easily remain uniform and steady;
this also serves to distinguish it from what is difficult for a beginner to achieve.
The nature of taste is not inherently so; it exists only when there is tasting. Since its perception is not constant or uniform, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Medicine King and Superior Medicine understood that the nature of taste is neither existent nor non-existent, neither identical to the body and mind, nor separate from the body and mind.
By investigating the discrimination of taste, they revealed their fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). Because the nature of taste is not inherently or eternally so, they were liberated [from it].
Discrimination lacks the nature of the taste of gnosis; it also excludes the beginner who has departed from the taste of discrimination, for the nature of awakened awareness is difficult to abide in.
Contact is clarified by that which is contacted; there is nothing it does not clearly contact. Since the nature of union and separation is not fixed, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Bhadrapāla, suddenly he realized the cause of water: it neither washes away dust nor washes the body; in the interval between these, there is tranquility, and one attains non-existence.
From this, illumination is manifested, and the wondrous touch is proclaimed and made clear. This term "touch" (sparśa) clarifies that which is touched;

by seeing the wondrous touch apart from what is touched, both union and separation are discarded. Its nature is difficult to grasp as permanent, and it also distinguishes itself from the initial [state].

It is the mind. Phenomena are termed "internal objects. Since one must rely on objects, there is necessarily that which perceives them; thus, subject and object do not pervade all things. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Mahākāśyapa contemplated the decay and disintegration of phenomena, thereby awakening to their emptiness and stillness. With a mind of empty stillness, he cultivated cessation.
Exhausted, one suddenly empties the attachment to dharmas and perceives the wondrous nature of reality (*dharmatā*). This is indeed the simultaneous relinquishing of both subject and object.

This selection of what excludes the non-pervasive subject and object is because, for those at the initial stage, it is difficult for the nature of reality to pervade when they are separated from their objects of focus.
Although the seeing-nature is thus luminous, it illuminates what is before one but not what is behind; the four quarters are deficient by half. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Aniruddha, through cultivating the Samādhi of the Illumination of Delightful Vision, manifested the essence of seeing. Without using the eyes to look, he saw clearly throughout the ten directions.
This [account] excludes the case where one illuminates what is before but not what is behind, and where the four quarters are deficient by half; this too is based on...

What is seen by the eye-faculty cannot be grasped in its entirety; for one perceives only the initial moment of sight, which is difficult to penetrate thoroughly as it is detached from the faculty and shines alone.
The breath of the nose flows in and out, yet there is no actual meeting of these gases before one. Being fragmented and failing to interpenetrate, how can this attain perfect penetration?
The exhalation cannot join with the inhalation; the inhalation cannot join with the exhalation. Exhalation and inhalation proceed separately;

therefore, it is called "non-intermingling breath. This refers to the absence of the central junction (*madhyama-saṃdhi*). Regarding the "limbs" (*aṅga*) of the body: "separation" means that when there is inhalation, one enters the body;
when there is separation, one leaves the body. The two do not intersect; this is also what is meant by non-intermingling breath. Cūḍapanthaka contemplated the subtlety of the breath.
Subtle. To exhaustively investigate arising and ceasing, one awakens to the knowledge that this mind has no ground of arising or ceasing, thereby attaining great non-obstruction.

This is because the inhalation and exhalation of the breath do not intersect with one another; it is difficult to rely upon and maintain the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing by using the initial mind to exhaustively investigate the arising and ceasing of the breath.
The tongue is not an entrance without a cause; it gives rise to cognition because of flavor. When flavor ceases, cognition no longer exists.
How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Since the knowledge of flavor cannot exist spontaneously without a cause, it is said that "cognition arises because of flavor."

Since it arises because of flavor, it ceases when flavor vanishes. Kauṇḍinya, by contemplating the cognition of flavor as being neither the substance nor the object, you shall, upon such reflection, transcend all worldly outflows (*āsrava*).
Internally, you will be liberated from body and mind; externally, you will cast off the world.

The Dharma-eye is clear and bright; yet, I fear that because the mind of awakening is detached from flavors, it is difficult for it to abide. Thus, I select [this] because for a beginner, it is not easily penetrated.
When the body and its objects of touch are each distinct from the contemplation of Perfect Awakening, their boundaries do not merge in silent accord. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
The body that perceives touch and the objects touched, when compared to the perceiving mind, differ in their boundaries and natures—being conscious and unconscious respectively—and cannot be merged.
Because Pilindavatsa perceived pain through perception, he then perceived his pure mind;

being without pain and without perception, he focused his mindfulness for no long time, and suddenly both body and mind became empty. Pure perception remained as a residual body, and he attained enlightenment.
It is untainted (*anāsrava*). Yet, this involves bodily contact and sensation; its limits cannot be fathomed.

This is likely because, were one to separate from this bodily contact, the nature of sensation would have no basis and could not spontaneously merge with it. This also serves to distinguish those of the initial stage (*ādikarmika*).

If you know that the faculty of cognition is confused by discursive thoughts, then even with profound clarity, there will ultimately be no vision. As long as one cannot escape from these mental conceptions, how can one attain perfect penetration?
This faculty of cognition is none other than the mental faculty (*manas*). It means that the mind cognizes various thoughts; when thoughts become still and profound, cognition ceases.

As soon as there is something being observed, it is difficult to escape from mental conceptions. Subhūti has, since remote kalpas, already realized emptiness and quiescence; subsequently, he received the instruction of the Tathāgata.

One attains the awakening to the nature of fundamental consciousness as true emptiness; this emptiness is perfectly luminous, allowing for an immediate entry into the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of emptiness, thereby sealing the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

This is specifically distinguished because, when the fundamental consciousness is first revealed as the true emptiness of the nature of awareness, it is difficult to manifest due to the presence of conceptual thought.
Therefore, it is singled out.

"Consciousness and vision are intermingled with the three harmonies; when their root is examined, they are called 'without characteristics. Since their own substance has no fixed existence from the outset, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Vision, consciousness, and the faculties and objects are intermingled; hence it is said that 'consciousness and vision are intermingled with the three harmonies.

If the faculties and objects do not encounter one another, then consciousness has nothing to which it may attach. Since there is neither its own characteristic nor its own substance, Śāriputra first realized the principle of dependent origination."
Following the Buddha’s illumination, one realizes that the seeing-faculty is perfectly luminous and the mind’s vision emits light; this light reaches the ultimate limit of knowing and seeing.

Now, we distinguish that this seeing-consciousness is devoid of a dual nature and lacks substantiality. That is to say, this initial mind of seeing and awareness is separate from the threefold combination [of sense organ, object, and consciousness]; the light of the mind is perfectly luminous.
It is difficult to manifest alone.
The mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions; this arises from the power of the great cause. If the initial mind cannot enter it, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Samantabhadra hears with his mind and discerns all the knowledge and views possessed by sentient beings.
Whenever there is a sentient being who illuminates the practice of Samantabhadra, he immediately bestows a touch upon their crown. This is evoked by the power of Great Practice;
it is not something accomplished by those at the initial stage of the path. Therefore, it is said that they cannot enter.
Contemplating the nose is fundamentally a provisional means, intended only to cause the mind to settle and abide. Once the mind has settled and abides, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Sūndara-nanda contemplated the whiteness at the tip of his nose; through intense and tranquil observation, internal luminosity arose and external emptiness was perfected.

This light penetrated the ten directions. This selection of a provisional means is for the purpose of settling the mind; once the mind settles, it becomes an object of perception. It is not [the ultimate].
It is truly eternal and abiding. Yet, when one first suspects that while the body and mind are within and the world is empty without, this awakening mind is difficult to liberate completely;

and when one preaches the Dharma, playing with sounds and texts to awaken those who have already attained success—since names and phrases are not themselves untainted (*anāsrava*), how can one thereby obtain perfect penetration?
Pūrṇa, by virtue of his unimpeded eloquence, proclaimed suffering and emptiness and profoundly penetrated the true mark (*dharmatā*).

This constitutes the ripening of the faculties and the skillful transcendence of verbal expression; it is a secret attainment that, were it to involve even a single name or phrase, would result only in outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore, it is excluded from [the category of] discourse.

Observing precepts and violating them merely bind the body; if there were no body, there would be nothing to bind. Since this [binding] does not originally pervade all things, how could one attain perfect penetration?
"Body" here refers to body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*), not merely the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*); therefore, it encompasses both body and mind.

This is because Upāli’s observance of the precepts was pure, and his body and mind were in a state of quiescence; by realizing the truth through this, everything became universally penetrating and unimpeded. Now, however, we are selecting that which is not the body.
He then said: "If one were to separate from this body-consciousness, there would be nothing to restrain it; yet how could this 'mind of intimate sealing' (qīnyìn zhī xīn) possibly reach everywhere?
I fear it would sink into mere quiescent extinction."

"Supernormal powers originate from past causes; how could they be related to the discrimination of dharmas? If mindfulness relies on conditions rather than being detached from objects, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Supernormal powers originate from past causes—this refers to the supernormal powers of Maudgalyāyana, which cannot be produced by the consciousness that discriminates dharmas.
Because discrimination relies on sensory objects, it cannot produce such powers; this reveals that their cause lies in the revolving of the tranquil essence, the radiance of the mind."

It is proclaimed: this is not a matter for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). As for the discrimination of dharmas (*dharmavikalpa*), dharmas belong to the domain of the mind; therefore it is called the discrimination of dharmas.

If one contemplates them according to their nature as earth, they are solid and obstructive, not penetrable; being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not of a noble nature (*ārya-dharmatā*), how can one attain perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-prativedha*) through them?

The Bodhisattva Earth-Holder, by means of the level mind-ground, perceived that the subtle particles of his own body and all the subtle particles constituting the world were entirely devoid of self-nature and did not touch one another.
Upon hearing the wondrous Lotus Sutra, he awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

This selection of the nature of earth as being solid and obstructive belongs to conditioned phenomena; this is stated from the perspective of his state prior to realizing perfect penetration. Even so, regarding...
The beginner, although having already manifested fundamental wisdom, finds that a void awareness detached from objects is likewise not the chosen path.

If one contemplates through the nature of water, thoughts and perceptions are not real; if it is suchness itself, it is beyond both awareness and contemplation. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
The youth Candraprabha, by means of the contemplation of water, perceived the water within his own body as being equal and indistinguishable from the external fragrant water.
Suddenly, he lost the sense of self and merged with the nature of true emptiness; it flowed as a single flavor, and he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

Regarding the perfect penetration realized by Candraprabha, when compared to the initial arousal of the bodhicitta, there is the danger that one might involve themselves in mental observation and deliberation (*vitarka-vicāra*) while attempting to detach from the faculties and reverse habitual tendencies.
This is still not the ultimate reality; therefore, it is said that suchness is neither vitarka (applied thought) nor vicāra (sustained thought).

This means that the nature of suchness is not realized through vitarka and vicāra. Vitarka and vicāra are characteristics of the first dhyāna, which possesses both applied and sustained thought and does not transcend conceptualization.

If one contemplates through the nature of fire, one becomes weary of existence as non-real and seeks detachment; this is not a skillful means for a beginner. How, then, could one attain perfect penetration?
Avalokiteśvara, the Fire-Eater (Ucchuṣma), contemplated the warmth of his body. As the divine light coalesced within, he transformed his many lustful thoughts into the fire of wisdom.
This unimpeded flow gave rise to great jewel-flames. This [method] selects those who use a mind of weary detachment; it does not involve attaining the fundamental nature.
To become detached from this at the initial stage of awakening results, conversely, in obstruction.

If one contemplates it through its nature as wind, then movement and stillness are not without their opposites; yet such opposition is not the supreme awakening. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?

The Bodhisattva Lapis Lazuli Light, by contemplating that the body, mind, and world are all moved by the power of illusory conditions and winds, immediately realized immovability within that which moves and awakened to all true marks (*dharmatā*). Now, this contemplation of wind involves the mutual dependence of movement and stillness;
it is not a skillful means for initial practice, as it obstructs perfect interfusion, and is therefore excluded from the selection.
If one contemplates through emptiness, that which is dull and dark was originally not awakening; since non-awakening differs from Bodhi, how could one attain perfect penetration?
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, by contemplating that the four great elements have no basis and that the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts and empty space are non-dual, [attained liberation].
The Buddha-lands are identical; by illuminating this identity, one enters samādhi, wherein wondrous power is perfectly clear and bright.
This distinguishes [the state of] dull emptiness and昏钝 (obscure insentience) from the nature of bodhi, which are utterly different. This refers specifically to the contemplation of emptiness alone.

If, with the initial mind, one has illuminated the true emptiness of the awakened nature, the habitual tendencies that were previously whirled about should no longer give rise to such a contemplation.

Because emptiness turns its back on enlightenment, it becomes obscured and darkened. Thus it is said: "Obscure and dull, it was not originally awakening. That which is not awakening differs from Bodhi.
If one observes with the nature of consciousness, observing that consciousness is not permanent, yet maintaining such a mind is itself a delusion. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Maitreya Bodhisattva, by practicing the concentration on consciousness-only, attained the unsurpassed, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the conscious mind.

He realized that throughout all the lands of the Tathāgatas in the entirety of space—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—all are manifestations produced by the transformations of his own mind.
Because one has thus realized that this is merely mind-consciousness (*cittavijñapti-mātra*), the nature of consciousness flows forth as immeasurable Tathāgatas.

By remaining far removed from the two attachments, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Now, to distinguish that consciousness is not permanent: even if one were to discard the object while maintaining the mind, it would still be subject to arising and ceasing.
Although this has not yet explicitly revealed that what is manifested is merely the manifestation of mind, nor that what is manifested is merely mind, nevertheless, it is consistent with...
At the initial stage of awakening the mind, one merely conforms to the principle of discerning and revolving away from delusion; yet this is not yet perfect or subtle.

All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and the nature of thought is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. Cause and effect now manifest as distinct experiences; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Thought has arising and ceasing; the nature of thought is fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

If pure thoughts succeed one another, this is to unite the thought of arising and ceasing with the nature that is without arising or ceasing—just as a child remembers its mother, or as a mother remembers [her child]. Thus, one should remember the Buddha and mindfully recite his name.
One will certainly see the Buddha; this is the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, through the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, completely gathers the six sense faculties and maintains a succession of pure mindfulness.

What is meant by "completely gathering the six sense faculties" is to unify the six faculties into a single thought-moment, and to gather that single thought-moment back into the nature of mindfulness. This is truly attaining *samādhi*. Now...

Discerning that the nature of mindfulness is impermanent and guarding against pure mindfulness being difficult to sustain in succession merely serves as an obstacle for those who have newly entered the awakening mind.
This discernment of the faculties and the non-manifestation of the initial mind is intended for the purpose of turning practice toward realization; it does not, however, exclude the holy ones.
The twenty-four sages each attained perfect penetration through their respective skillful means, whether by following the forward order or the reverse order.

Before they had reached that state of perfect penetration, they relied solely on what they emphasized as an antidote to their specific afflictions; thus, there were cases where one method was to be discarded in this context and selected in that.

This was by no means fixed. To know the faculty to be discarded according to the practitioner's capacity is to understand the intent behind selecting the appropriate application for that capacity. To know the application...

Having understood the intent of this selection, one then realizes the application of the mind of discernment. This is done collectively to bring the initial resolve to fruition, transforming practice into realization.

Therefore, as long as the fundamental wisdom cannot be manifested through its ultimate distinctions to reach the pinnacle of radiant brilliance and glorious manifestation, the mind remains subject to selection.
Now, according to Mañjuśrī’s section on selection, he first cites the sense-object of form (*rūpa*) as the primary example.
Bound by delusive thoughts, the nature of the mind that is initially refined and understood is not easily cleansed;
thus, what is called "inability to penetrate" must be examined in light of the specific occasion. Ānanda has already attained clarity and swiftly achieved unimpeded understanding;

therefore, the selection of faculties for cultivation and realization is solely intended to eliminate habitual obstructions. If one were merely discriminating between persons and dharmas, would he not have already awakened? This...
If one remains obstructed by the dust of form (*rūpa*), then even the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) will find it difficult to achieve realization.
Regarding this point, the various commentaries rely solely on the wording of the verse; out of ignorance, they claim there must be a reconciliation [of these views].

In the *Avataṃsaka*, at the initial stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), the self-nature (*svabhāva*) is revealed, whereby one already becomes equal to a Buddha. Thereafter, one initiates practice and progresses through the stages until reaching the ultimate ground, where one reaches the final consummation.

Distinction. Although there is no difference from the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one must nevertheless undergo a single turning. Thus, we know that the cultivation and realization of the Mahāyāna certainly cannot rely on substantial dharmas.

The above three sections have concluded the exclusion of those who are not of the perfect faculty. △ Fourth, the formal selection of those with the perfect faculty, divided into six parts. First, relying on skillful means.
Instruction:
I now address the World-Honored One. Since the Buddha has appeared in this Sahā world-system, the true essence of the teaching in this region lies in purity within hearing.
If one wishes to attain samādhi, it must truly be entered through the faculty of hearing.

I now address the World-Honored One in six points. Having received the Buddha’s command, I shall select the faculties according to the regions and distinguish twenty-four types of noble ones who are not suitable for the faculties and capacities of this land.

For instance, in other Buddha-lands, there are those who perform the Buddha-work by means of the Buddha’s radiance, or by means of the Buddha’s Bodhi tree, or by means of gardens, groves, pavilions, and terraces, or by means of various fragrances.
Unlike this [other] method, the essence of the teaching must necessarily be proclaimed through words. For sentient beings to comprehend and understand, they must enter by means of hearing.
By taking the principle heard and confronting it with the faculty that hears, one attains the true nature of hearing. Entering the stream, the object of hearing perishes;
as hearing is exhausted, awareness becomes empty, and one achieves true stillness. This samādhi truly enters through the midst of hearing. It is explained through words.
The teaching distinguishes clearly between the provisional and the ultimate, remaining unmixed with worldly discourse; this is purity of sound.

To hear, listen to, and receive it, thereby forgetting the trap once the fish is caught and returning to one's own nature—this is purity of hearing. Thus, there may be sound without hearing, and there may be hearing without sound.
In all cases, the teaching is not established; yet sound and hearing manifest in mutual dependence, and purity is attained individually. This is the true essence of the teaching.
The essence of the teaching must accord with what is appropriate for the occasion; the selection of hearing is established based upon the faculty. Therefore it is said:
"If one wishes to attain samādhi, one truly enters through hearing. 2. Praising the Dominant Faculty (the Ear).

Free from suffering, they attain liberation. How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters buddha-lands as many as motes of dust, attaining the power of great mastery and bestowing fearlessness upon sentient beings.
O Wondrous Sound, Avalokiteśvara! Your Brahma-sound is like the tide of the ocean.
The Savior brings all to peace; by transcending the world, one attains eternal abiding.
The first two lines praise the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the true nature of hearing, reaching the point where quiescent extinction manifests and suddenly transcends [all obstacles].
This refers to the thorough exhaustion of the five abodes and the eternal disappearance of the two deaths; that is to say, the departure from suffering and the attainment of liberation.
Furthermore, two phrases praise the thirty-two manifestations, another two phrases praise the fourteen fearlessnesses, and another two phrases praise the mutual appearance of the virtues and titles.
Wisdom and principle are fused as "Miao" (Wondrous); pure and stainless as "Fan" (Brahman). As for Avalokiteśvara:
Pure compassion responds to things; there is nowhere it does not reach. Wherever there is a stimulus, there is a response, never missing its proper time, like the regular rhythm of the tides.
One enters the subtle through hearing, yet this is not called "subtle hearing," but rather "subtle sound. For hearing involves the duality of self and other.
Sound has neither self nor other; every particle is the truth, and every phenomenon is thus. The final two lines reach the ultimate goal of benefiting sentient beings:
uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness, equalizing the mundane and the supramundane—what is called seeking great nirvana and attaining great nirvana.
△ Third, praising the faculty of hearing.
I now address the Tathāgata as Avalokiteśvara has taught: "Suppose a person is dwelling in stillness, and drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions;
they hear them from all ten locations at once. This is the perfect reality."
This is spoken with respect to sentient beings: there are sounds that are all heard, and there is hearing that pervades them all.

There is no distance or proximity, no before or after, thereby manifesting that the nature of hearing is all-pervasive. Because sound reflects upon hearing and hearing engages with sound, both are devoid of form or segments, and likewise lack boundaries or limits.
Their nature and characteristics, self and other, are simultaneously harmonized; this does not depend on cultivation or realization, and it is without end.
Wait. The subtlety of the gateway of the ear can be fully realized here.
The eye does not perceive what lies beyond its range; the mouth and nose are likewise. The body knows only through contact; the mind’s thoughts are chaotic and without order.
Hearing sounds through a wall, both the distant and the near can be heard. That which is not limited by the five sense organs is what is called "penetrating reality.
This demonstrates that the faculty of hearing transcends the obstructions inherent in the other five organs; this is what is meant by "penetrating reality.
"Distant and near" refers to the range of the sentient beings' auditory faculties—whether far or near, there is no obstruction whatsoever, unlike the case with the other five organs.

This is indeed due to the limitations of the senses. It is only when the mouth, nose, and body all come together that one knows; it is likewise merely a matter of the phrasing of the subsequent verse.

Regarding the nature of sound as movement or stillness, its existence or non-existence is determined within hearing. When there is no sound, it is called "no-hearing," yet this is not truly the absence of the nature of hearing.
When sound is absent, there is no cessation; when sound is present, there is no arising. Being perfectly free from both arising and cessation, this is the true permanence.

The presence of sound is the characteristic of movement; the absence of sound is the characteristic of stillness. Although movement and stillness reside within sound, within the faculty of hearing itself, these two characteristics are fundamentally non-existent.
Since these two characteristics do not exist, then at the time when there is no sound, one says that there is "no-hearing"; yet this is not a case of the absence of hearing.
Therefore, one knows that the nature of hearing is ever-present; it does not arise or perish along with sounds. Thus it is said: "When sound is absent, there is no cessation;
when sound is present, there is no arising. That which is called "perfectly detached" refers to the nature of hearing, which is profoundly still and has been so from the very beginning.
Standing far beyond movement and stillness, existence and non-existence, this is what is called the eternally real.

Even when one is in a state of dreaming, it does not become non-existent through lack of thought; yet when awakening and contemplation transcend discursive thinking, body and mind can no longer reach it.

Now, when dreams and thoughts have already ceased, yet one still hears the sound of the pestle as if it were right before them, this further demonstrates that the nature of hearing transcends the realm of thought.
How could this possibly be accessible to body or mind? Awareness is, in fact, the very substance of the nature of hearing.
Contemplation is the function of the nature of hearing. The body encompasses the three faculties of eye, nose, and tongue; "mind" refers to the faculty of intellect (*manas*).
This also conveys the sense that the five faculties are not uniform. △ Fourth, reproaching mere learning and exhorting to practice.

Now, in this Sahā world, the science of phonetics may be proclaimed and clarified. Yet sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; because they follow sounds, they wander through saṃsāra.

Even though Ānanda possesses powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts. Is this not because he follows that which he has sunk into? By reversing the flow, one attains freedom from delusion.

The treatise on sound was originally intended to clarify the nature of hearing; yet sentient beings have been deluded regarding hearing for so long that they merely follow the teachings of sound and give rise to vain discrimination.

Even if the ultimate void is profoundly subtle and mysterious, they find no way to resolve or return to it, and it instead becomes an obstacle to the principle—this is precisely what constitutes saṃsāra.
This is because [the Buddha] rebuked Ānanda for his prodigious memory, which only served to increase his erudition, while his distorted thoughts toward objects remained nearly as they were.
As you follow the downward plunge, the revolving flow immediately causes the object to vanish. Once the object of hearing has vanished, the nature of awareness is brilliantly clear;
it requires nothing more than this brief turning back.
Ānanda, listen attentively! By receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall proclaim the Vajra King—illusory, inconceivable, and wondrous.
This is the true samādhi of the Buddha-mother. You have heard from as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust regarding all the gates of secrecy;
