yet, if you do not first eliminate the outflows of desire, your accumulation of learning will become a source of error. Since you intend to maintain the Buddhas through hearing, why do you not hear that which hears itself?

The World-Honored One again proclaimed in verse: "This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra King’s Jewel-Awakening, the Illusion-like Samādhi, by which one transcends the stage of No-More-Learning in the snap of a finger.
Thus we know that the Vajra-like Illusionary Buddha-Mother Samādhi is precisely this nature of hearing.
Although Ānanda has engaged in extensive learning throughout kalpas, there are no secret gates of all the Tathāgatas that he has not [mastered].

Though you possess a powerful memory, you alone have been unable to completely eliminate the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*). This is the error of being burdened by what you have heard; this has been so throughout all ages.

How could you know what matters are revealed by the proclamation of the teachings? If you can turn back and contemplate the nature of hearing itself, you will finally realize that the secret is right before your eyes.
When hearing is exhausted and no longer dwells, empty awareness becomes perfectly complete. This is the samādhi of one’s own nature, which is like—
Vajra! All phenomena are arrayed like an inconceivable illusion; all Buddhas and Tathāgatas emerge from this very source, which is called the Mother of Buddhas.
Hearing is not born of itself; it exists because of sound. When hearing turns back and detaches from sound, that which is able to detach—whom can one name?
Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation.
This directly points to the nature of hearing, which is the true awakened mind. When abiding in the state of delusion, it chases after sounds and runs wild; this is called "hearing.
If, within this hearing, one enters the stream and causes the objects to vanish, then both sound and hearing are exhausted. When sound is exhausted, movement and stillness do not arise;
when hearing is exhausted, empty awareness shines forth of itself. Who then could further name this as the "nature of hearing"? This is the single faculty.
Since this is true for all six sense faculties, when one is able to liberate them, hearing ceases entirely and does not abide. Is this not the ultimate perfection of empty awareness?

Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the faculties are removed, the dust of sensory objects vanishes and awareness becomes perfectly pure.

Flowers in the sky exist because of cataracts in the eyes; likewise, the three realms appear because of seeing and hearing. In truth, space originally has no flowers, and the eye originally has no cataracts.
To speak of "cataracts in the eye" refers to the single delusion within the self-awakened clarity. From this delusion, the six sense faculties arise.
Consciousness rushes forth uncontrollably and cannot return to its source, causing the perfectly pure essence to flow through the gates of the senses. There is no one [to stop it].

To perceive this and yet let it slip away in an instant is a grievous error. If you understand "entering the stream within hearing so that the objects of perception vanish," then sensory dust will dissolve and awareness will become pure;
why wait for it to subside?
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere; in silent illumination, it encompasses all of space. Returning then to observe the world, it is like a dream.
"Maudgalyāyana was in a dream; who could have retained your form?

This consciousness, when the dust of the eaves has dissolved, is pure and clear. When purity reaches its limit, that which was lost—the hearing—is exhausted. Therefore, the essence of awakening is luminously fused:

internally it is tranquil and still, yet illuminating; externally it encompasses empty space. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says, 'because its nature is empty space,' it is utterly devoid of anything at all."
Thus, with this mind of empty luminosity and tranquil illumination, one contemplates all worlds; are they not indeed dream-like affairs?

Therefore, know that the three realms are like dreams and illusions within the perfectly湛 (zhan) and profound essence, like a mirage or flowers in the sky—neither falling into existence nor non-existence.

Body and mind transcend them, like a wild goose passing through the vast sky, leaving no trace of its shadow or path. As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* says: "It is like the resonance within a vessel."
Sound issues forth from without; form follows the movement of the mind. Since the mind has already transcended, why should its form and shadow remain?
Thus, how could the Gaṅgā seen in a dream possibly detain you, Ānanda, who have already awakened?
Just as a skilled worldly illusionist conjures various men and women, and although one sees their faculties move, it is all drawn by a single mechanism;
when that mechanism ceases and returns to stillness, all illusions become devoid of inherent nature.
Changshui uses the illusionist as a metaphor for true nature (*tathatā*), and further uses the illusionist as a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*).
I, the fool, say that these two are neither partial nor exclusive; they should be combined as a single metaphor. For ignorance is itself true nature; through non-awakening, it manifests as illusion.

Thus there exist the six sense organs, men, and women, yet in reality, all arise from the movement of a single mechanism of deluded vision. If that vision ceases and the mechanism becomes still, then the six...
By means of revolving, they are originally without self-nature.
The six sense faculties are also like this: originally relying on one brilliant spirit, they are divided into six harmonious combinations. When one place attains stillness and returns, [all return].
The six faculties are all rendered non-existent; defilements dissolve as soon as they are perceived. Thus, the perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous state is achieved.

The preceding serves as the analogy, while this passage sets forth the dharma being illustrated: namely, the meaning of a single faculty returning to its source and the purification of all six faculties.
Defilements dissolve as soon as they are perceived, illustrating the swiftness with which the mechanism of delusion is overturned upon awakening.
This means that when one is deluded, the entirety of the true is immediately the false; when one awakens, the entirety of the false is immediately the true.
It is originally luminous and wondrous, ever-present within the six gates; once awakened, it is perfectly manifest.
When remaining dust still pertains to those in training, the ultimate clarity is the Tathāgata.

As stated above, "dust and defilements dissolve upon a single thought," resulting in perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrousness; this means that dust and defilements fundamentally lack inherent nature.
The luminous and wondrous source is primordially perfected. Originally there was no delusion; now there is likewise no awakening.
At the initial moment of resolve, one penetrates all at once, with no further meaning remaining. What the beginner of the Ten Abodes accomplishes is equal to that of a Buddha.

When it says "remaining dust still exists for those who study," this specifically refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two attachments, which are exhausted after the Tenth Ground. This is what is meant by "perfect interfusion without obstruction."

This refers to the culmination of practice. "The culmination of clarity" refers to the Tathāgata. One does not speak of the "culmination of practice" because one must know that while the wisdom of differentiation reaches its limit, it is merely the fundamental perfect wisdom;
it is not a separate entity in itself.

O Great Assembly and Ānanda: Turn back the mechanism of your inverted hearing; by hearing inwardly, you shall hear your own true nature. When this nature is perfected, the Unsurpassed Way is realized.
Such indeed is the reality of perfect penetration.
This exhortation to turn back upon hearing and return to the nature points definitively to the auditory faculty as the Tathāgata’s true suchness and wondrous awakening;

there is nothing else besides it. This is the truly perfect penetration. "Inverted hearing" refers to the fact that while the auditory faculty is fundamentally wondrous, one becomes deluded and follows after sensory objects.
Therefore, it is called "inversion. This demonstrates that if one listens in reverse, the nature of hearing is inherently wondrous; it is no different from that of a Buddha.
△ Fifth: Unifying the Three Times and the Universal Gate, Re-examining the Expedient Means.
These are the subtle dust-like Buddhas; this is the single path to the gate of nirvana. All Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate;
all Bodhisattvas of the present now each enter its perfect clarity; and those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this very Dharma.
I, too, have realized it from within this; it is not only Avalokiteśvara.
This praise establishes that "listening inwardly" is the sole path to Nirvana, citing the Buddhas of the past and the Bodhisattvas of the present.
This is intended to serve as a mirror for the future, leading one back to oneself; it reveals that the entire path is Nirvana, and there can certainly be no diverging roads.
It is truly as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said: "I shall inquire into various skillful means to rescue those in the final kalpa and seek those who transcend the world."
The mind that accomplishes nirvana—Avalokiteśvara is supreme therein. All other skillful means are the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.

By engaging with phenomena as they are, one abandons worldly toil; this is not achieved through long-term cultivation alone. Whether at a shallow or deep level, the teaching of the Dharma is the same.

The first four lines express the original intent of the Buddha’s command. Furthermore, the next two lines conclude the selection of the ear-faculty as the foremost among the various gateways to perfect penetration.

Finally, the last three lines clarify that each of the twenty-four sages, according to what they found most burdensome within the afflictions of worldly existence, attained liberation by renouncing those specific conditions.
"Phenomena" refers to the seven elements and eighteen realms. That "all arise through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas" is stated in the *Awakening of Faith*:
"If practitioners lack the manifest protection and hidden empowerment of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they will certainly not achieve success.

Furthermore, these two lines conversely clarify that the ear-door encompasses all three faculties, such that both shallow and deep levels are simultaneously realized; this can be cultivated for a long time, as it is identical to the teaching of the Dharma.
6. Seeking Augmentation from the Ritual Treasury (*Vinaya-piṭaka*).
Prostrating to the Tathāgata-garbha, which is untainted and inconceivable: may you bestow your grace upon those of the future, so that they may have no delusions regarding this gate.
This expedient means is easily accomplished and is fit to be taught to Ānanda, as well as to those submerged in the final age of dharma decline.
By cultivating through this faculty alone, one attains perfect penetration that surpasses all others; such is the nature of the true mind.

All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and three periods of time, as well as all beings within the twenty-five realms of the triple world, are all manifestations flowing forth from the Tathāgatagarbha mind.
They encompass both the true and the delusive while remaining eternally perfect; they appear according to delusion and enlightenment, yet do not establish themselves as independent entities.
This inconceivable realm has been profoundly and clearly elucidated by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.

Out of deep concern for those of the future, he prays for empowerment so that they may not stray from this root and achieve success with ease. Regarding the "true mind," Mañjuśrī speaks of it as being firmly rooted in his own fundamental mind;
it is known and seen with reality, and is not merely a concession to the capacities of others.
Delusion has no original cause; awakening is not something newly acquired now. The *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states: "All sentient beings have already attained the Buddha-way.

This refers to the fact that these Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, from the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith up to the two levels of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment, subsequently realize and know that [all beings] have already attained the Buddha-way;
this is not merely a statement of abstract principle. If so, then what is meant by "sentient beings"? It is said:

This is because they lack self-confidence. Why do they lack self-confidence? It is said: "Because one has already become a Buddha. Now, a Buddha does not become a Buddha by himself; he is a true Buddha.
Sentient beings likewise do not become sentient beings by themselves; they are true sentient beings. This is what the Buddha does:

he reaches the ultimate state of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and only then realizes that he did not become a Buddha by himself. As for sentient beings, they continue their flow through the three miserable realms.
Thereafter, one knows that [the Buddha-nature] does not arise from sentient beings; knowing it does not arise from the Buddha, one is then able to have deep faith in sentient beings.
Knowing it does not arise from sentient beings, one is then able to have deep faith in the Buddha.

Thus, for sentient beings, faith in the Buddha is the initial stage; for the Buddha, faith in sentient beings is the ultimate goal. Now, if faith in sentient beings is taken as the ultimate goal, then...
It is certainly not the case that he would allow those of initial resolve to lack self-confidence;
rather, it is clear that he repeatedly speaks of the path of cultivation and realization in order to delude himself and others.

Alas, since people do not believe in themselves, he first guides them toward knowing their destination, then speaks of the road, and finally speaks of arriving home—yet they fail to realize that this is swift without walking.

Regarding those who arrive swiftly, they know for themselves the time of their return; though they have known it for a long time, they must wait until they reach home before they begin to have deep faith.
If this is so, then what indeed should the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do in such a case? Mañjuśrī, selecting the faculties [of the audience], said:
For example, suppose a person is dwelling in stillness, and drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions; they hear them from all ten locations at once.

This is what is meant by "perfect reality. This refers to the nature of hearing realized by a beginner, which is already fully present as perfect listening within the current experience of sentient beings;
it does not involve some separate path or route. Furthermore, it says: "Hearing sounds through a wall, both near and far..."
It can be heard. That which is not uniform across the five sense faculties is precisely what penetrates reality. Who does not hear sound? Who limits it to being far or near?
This can also be realized through daily experience. Furthermore, it is said: "To call the absence of sound 'not hearing' is not truly hearing its naturelessness.
Since sound is absent, there is no cessation; since sound is present, there is no arising. Arising and ceasing are both perfectly transcended."
This is the eternal reality. How could this be something that must wait for cultivation before its permanence is attained?
As for hearing the sound of a pestle in a dream—transcending the realm of thought—the nature of hearing itself remains steadfast within samādhi.
Defilements dissolve at the very moment of realization, and clarity, wondrousness, and perfection are fully accomplished. These are all the practices demonstrated by Great Wisdom.
Regarding the gateway of realization, it is through the faculty of hearing that the direct and expedient path is most clearly revealed.

Therefore, what follows all says: The final answer to the question of the "one vehicle" (ekayāna) is found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, specifically in the "Expedient Means" (*Upāyakauśalya*) chapter. This teaching is presented as the Buddha’s definitive revelation of his ultimate intent, resolving the apparent contradictions between the various vehicles previously taught. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Buddha explains that while he has indeed taught three distinct vehicles—the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva vehicles—these were merely skillful means (*upāya*) employed to guide beings of varying capacities. He asserts that there is, in truth, only one vehicle. The Buddha states: > "There is only one vehicle, and no second, nor a third. Except for the case where, through skillful means, I manifest three vehicles. He further clarifies that all Buddhas of the past, present, and future have taught this same single vehicle. The distinction between the vehicles was a pedagogical strategy to lead sentient beings toward the ultimate goal of Buddhahood. By teaching the Śrāvaka vehicle to those who fear suffering, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle to those seeking solitude, and the Bodhisattva vehicle to those with great compassion, the Buddhas lead all beings to the same destination: the realization of the Buddha-way. Thus, the "one vehicle" is not a denial of the diversity of spiritual paths, but rather an affirmation that these paths converge in the singular realization of Buddhahood. It represents the Buddha's final word on the nature of his teaching, emphasizing that all his previous discourses were provisional, whereas the doctrine of the one vehicle is his definitive and ultimate truth. This teaching serves to unify the Mahāyāna tradition by providing a comprehensive framework that validates the various soteriological approaches while maintaining the supremacy of the Bodhisattva path. By establishing the one vehicle as the definitive teaching, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* resolves the tension between the diverse scriptural traditions and provides a coherent vision of the Buddhist path, wherein all practitioners are destined for the same supreme enlightenment. This doctrinal shift marks a significant development in Buddhist thought, moving from a pluralistic understanding of spiritual goals to a monistic vision centered on the attainment of Buddhahood by all. The Buddha concludes that because all phenomena are ultimately empty and devoid of inherent self-nature, there can be no real distinction between the vehicles. The diversity of teachings is thus seen as a reflection of the diverse dispositions and needs of sentient beings, rather than a fundamental difference in the nature of the path itself. Through this teaching, the Buddha invites all followers to recognize their shared destiny and to embrace the universal potential for awakening. In summary, the "one vehicle" doctrine of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* represents the culmination of the Buddha’s pedagogical art, revealing that the multiplicity of vehicles was a temporary expedient, while the one vehicle is the true and ultimate truth. This teaching underscores the unity of the Buddhist path and the common goal of all practitioners, thereby fostering a sense of inclusivity and universality within the Mahāyāna tradition. The final answer to the question of the "one vehicle" is thus established as the definitive revelation of the Buddha’s intent, providing a comprehensive resolution to the apparent inconsistencies in the Buddhist scriptures and affirming the ultimate unity of all spiritual paths. This teaching remains a cornerstone of Mahāyāna philosophy, emphasizing the inherent potential for Buddhahood in all beings and the essential harmony of the diverse teachings of the Buddha. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people of the末法 (mofa) era wish to establish a site for the Way, they should first take a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains."
They feed on the fatty, fragrant herbs of that mountain. These oxen drink only the pure water of the Snow Mountains;
their dung is fine and subtle, and can be mixed with sandalwood to smear upon the ground. Were it not for the Snow Mountains, these oxen would be foul-smelling and filthy.
It was not fit for smearing upon the ground. Therefore, he separately excavated the surface soil from a level plain to a depth of five chi or more, taking the yellow earth from beneath.
He then blended this with sandalwood, aloeswood, *suhaka*, *kunduruka*, saffron, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *sāla* resin, *candana*, *jātī* grass, and clove;
these ten ingredients were finely ground into powder and mixed with the earth to form a paste, which was used to smear the site of the ritual arena.
A square and circle of sixteen feet form an eight-cornered altar;
this indicates the method for establishing the *maṇḍala*. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called 'Fatty' (*medas*);
if a cow eats it, it produces only *ghṛta* (clarified butter). It further says: 'If it is a female cow, she does not eat wine.'"
It is fermented with malted barley flour and is smooth and unctuous. The calf is well-trained; the place where it grazes is neither on high ground nor in low-lying damp areas.
It is given clear water to drink and is not allowed to run about. It is not kept in the same herd as bulls.
Its drinking and feeding are moderate and appropriate, and its movement and rest are well-regulated. Milk such as this can eliminate all diseases; this is what is called [the milk of a cow].
The ambrosial and wondrous medicine combines these two sections; both use the metaphor of clarified butter (*sarpirmaṇḍa*) and ambrosia (*amṛta*) to represent the Buddha-nature of sentient beings.

If one relies upon the pure and wondrous water and grass of wisdom and principle, one will not be driven about by the winds of high and low objects, nor will one be deluded and disturbed by the herds of evil friends.
Thus, one shall immediately achieve the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of *tathāgata*.

It is the supreme, wondrous medicine; there are no diverging paths. When this sutra is established within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one first takes the white ox from the Snowy Mountains—one that has been nourished with rich, fatty food and watered with clear streams—and uses its remains to blend with various fragrances for the purpose of anointing and adorning the ground.
According to this analogy, one should understand that the "water and grass" of wisdom and principle can nourish the white ox of the Dharma-body.
The wisdom of the remaining distinctions pierces the ground of the five aggregates and emerges from the true land of original enlightenment.

Blending with the wondrous fragrance of the ten perfections, it together forms a single great, quiescent, and boundless square altar. This exists fundamentally within principle and is unimpeded in phenomena.
Wénlǐng remarked that regarding the Dharma-gate of a single word in the *Avataṃsaka*, even if one were to write with ink as vast as the ocean, it could never be exhausted. Five...

Regarding the ritual procedures for the stages of practice: these are elucidated according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The symbolic representations of the dharmas are further provided in full detail, each with its own specific elaboration or brevity; as the text would become too voluminous, they are not recorded here.
At the center of the altar, place a lotus flower fashioned from gold, silver, copper, or wood. Upon the flower, set a bowl. Within the bowl, first place [the following].

In the eighth month, collect dewdrops and place whatever lotus flowers and leaves are available within the water. Take eight round mirrors and place them in each of the cardinal directions, surrounding the flower bowl.
Outside the mirrors, erect sixteen lotuses and sixteen incense burners, arranging them in an alternating pattern as a solemn adornment.
In the incense burners, burn only aloeswood so that the flames are not visible. Take milk from a white cow and place it in sixteen vessels.
Milk cakes, along with various sugar-coated oil cakes, milk porridge, *sugandhaka* (stacte), honey, ginger, pure ghee, and pure honey—
sixteen of each kind surrounding the exterior of the lotus— to be offered to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
The lotus flower and its fruit appearing simultaneously symbolize the simultaneity of the cause and effect of Buddha-nature and *nirvāṇa*. The mirror represents the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*;

its light penetrates both within and without, forming the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Encompassing and reflecting all eight directions, essence and function are fused as one, such that the Dharma and its transformation are non-dual.
Outside the flower is the mirror; outside the mirror is the flower; they mutually encompass and enter one another.
It is layered and inexhaustible. Incense, flowers, and milk cakes are enjoyed by both self and others; principal and attendant deities intermingle, and bodies and lands mutually contain one another.
At every mealtime, or if it be at midnight, take half a *sheng* of honey and three *he* of clarified butter, and set them apart before the altar.
Prepare a small brazier and extract scented water by boiling *turuṣka* incense. Use this to bathe the charcoal, then ignite it until it blazes fiercely.
Cast this ghee and honey into the flaming brazier and burn them until the smoke has vanished, offering it to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Whether at every mealtime or in the middle of the night—meaning once during the day and once during the night—one should maintain mindfulness as if it were ten lifetimes, without distinction between the two times.
Adorned with fragrant light, its enjoyment is inexhaustible; this takes the fundamental skillful means as its basis to achieve perfect fulfillment and ultimate return.
It is not something known by wisdom, nor is it something cognized by consciousness. To offer this is the supreme among all offerings.
Cause banners and flowers to be hung everywhere on the four outer sides. Within the ritual chamber, arrange images of all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions upon the four walls.
One should hang images of Vairocana, Śākyamuni, Maitreya, Akṣobhya, and Amitābha facing the front;
furthermore, place images of the Great Transformation Avalokiteśvara along with Vajragarbha to their left and right.
Śakra, Brahmā, Ucchuṣma, and Lambodara, along with the various Cāmuṇḍīs, Bhṛkuṭī, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Pināyaka,
were stationed on the left and right sides at the entrance. Furthermore, eight mirrors were taken and suspended in the air,
facing the mirrors installed within the maṇḍala courtyard, so that their forms and reflections [would correspond].
Layer upon layer they interpenetrate;

banners are suspended and images are arrayed, each perfectly complete. Furthermore, eight mirrors are taken and suspended in the void, so that the Lords of Reward and Transformation throughout the ten directions and three periods, together with their retinues, may have wisdom and compassion mutually perfected, and through internal and external protection, behold one another all at once. Together...

The light of the single mind pervades the infinite oceans of lands and the inexhaustible realms of phenomena and principle; it resides solely within this, unmoving from the fundamental limit, its sound universally pervasive and perfectly interfused.

Vairocana—here translated as "Illumination"—is the Reward Buddha (*vipāka-buddha*) and the Lord of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), with the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Bodhisattvas as his retinue.
Śākyamuni is the Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) and the Lord of the present age; Maitreya is the Lord of the future; and Akṣobhya is [the Lord of the east].
The Buddha of the East represents wisdom (*prajñā*). Amitābha, the Buddha of the West, represents compassion (*karuṇā*).

Avalokiteśvara, who "ascends with and descends into harmony," also represents the companion of compassion; he further embodies the power of internal sustenance through perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
All others provide external protection. Ucchuṣma, the Fire-Head Vajra; Nīladaṇḍa, the Blue-Faced Vajra; and the Kūṭāgāra Dhāraṇī.
The *Saṃyuktāgama* refers to him as the Bodhisattva Kuṇḍalī; the *Ekākṣarabuddhoṣṇīṣacakravartin-tantra* refers to him as the Bodhisattva Bhṛkuṭī.
Both are Vajra deities. Piṇḍa has a pig’s head, and Nāga has an elephant’s trunk;
these are the names of the two messengers. △ Third, the actual instruction on practice and the attainment of realization.
During the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and those bearing the title of Arhat.

Constantly throughout the six periods of the day and night, one should recite the mantra while surrounding the altar, practicing the Way with a sincere heart, performing one hundred and eight recitations during each period.
During the second seven-day period, focus your mind single-mindedly on making bodhisattva vows without interruption. Within my Vinaya, there is a prior teaching regarding such vows.
During the third seven-day period, at all twelve times of the day and night, single-mindedly maintain the Buddha’s *pañcara* mantra.

Upon reaching the seventh day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions simultaneously appear at the place where the mirrors reflect one another’s light. There, they receive the Buddhas’ empowerment by stroking the crown of his head.
During the first week, he performs prostrations and repentance; during the second week, he makes vows and dedicates his merit;

and during the third week, he single-mindedly recites the mantra until it is heard by himself. He hears with his own mind as he recites with his own mind; hearing and recitation enter into one another, such that sound and listening are both present.
Dissolved. At the place where the mirrors reflect one another's light, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions behold one another all at once;
they stroke their heads and bestow predictions of enlightenment, so that there is no longer any obstruction between oneself as a Buddha and others as Buddhas.

One immediately cultivates samādhi within the site of enlightenment, which can cause the body and mind of those practicing and studying in this degenerate age to become clear and pure, like lapis lazuli.

This refers to attaining a temporary, momentary clarity and purity of body and mind at the point where recitation and hearing mutually enter one another; it is not yet the state of absolute uniformity.
After one hundred days, his spiritual eye will naturally open wide; hence there is the passage stating that he shall not rise from his seat.
Ānanda, if among this bhikṣu’s original preceptor or the ten bhikṣus in the assembly there is even one who is impure, such a site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) will for the most part not achieve success.
With identical purity, identical mental conduct, and identical dedication, whatever place of practice they enter will be fully accomplished;
if even one is not so, the ninefold assembly is in vain.
After the three weeks had passed, he sat upright in meditative seclusion for one hundred days. Those of sharp faculties attained the stage of Srotāpanna without rising from their seats;
even if their physical bodies and minds had not yet fully realized the holy fruit, they were certain to know for themselves that their attainment of Buddhahood was unfailing.
Regarding your question on the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it is established as follows:

The *srotāpanna*, who has attained the first fruit of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), corresponds to the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching.

He knows with certainty that he will attain Buddhahood without error; this must refer to the final mind of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching, because neither the Shared nor the Separate Teachings can provide such certainty.
This is self-confidence. The final two lines conclude the response to the preceding question.

The above four sections complete the demonstration of the rules for establishing the *maṇḍala* and its practice. △ Fifth, the actual proclamation of the Heart Mantra and the extensive demonstration of its benefits, divided into nine parts.
First, the emission of light to reveal it universally.
Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: “Since I left the home life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s affectionate love and sought much learning;
yet, because I had not realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), I was obstructed by the malevolent arts of that Brahmā. Although my mind remained clear, my power was not free.
Fortunately, I encountered Mañjuśrī, who enabled me to attain liberation. Thus, although I have received the secret protection of the Tathāgata’s *Uṣṇīṣa* mantra...”

We have not yet personally heard the power of this [teaching]. We only pray that, out of great compassion, you will proclaim it once more, to piteously rescue all those practicing in this assembly, as well as those in saṃsāra in the future.
Having received the Buddha’s secret voice, may their bodies and minds be liberated.
At that time, the entire great assembly in the gathering prostrated themselves in unison, waiting expectantly to hear the Tathāgata’s secret verses.
The followers of the Hīnayāna regard the four fruits as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Although they previously received secret empowerment, they had not yet heard [this teaching] directly.
Since they are present in this assembly, he requests that it be proclaimed once more.
At that time, from within the uṣṇīṣa on the World-Honored One’s crown, a hundred jewel-lights surged forth.

From within these lights, thousand-petaled jewel lotuses emerged, upon which transformed Tathāgatas sat amidst the precious blossoms. From their crowns, ten streams of hundred-jewel radiance were emitted; from each and every stream of light...
Throughout the entire realm of empty space, ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* numbers of Vajrapāṇis appeared everywhere, bearing mountains and holding vajras;

the great assembly gazed upward at them with a mixture of awe and affection, seeking the Buddha’s compassionate protection as they listened with single-minded devotion to the divine mantra being proclaimed by the Tathāgata Emitting Light from the Unseen Crown of the Head.
The invisible crown-mark (*uṣṇīṣa*) symbolizes the Buddha’s Dharma-body, which cannot be seen with the eyes nor contemplated by the mind.

From his crown, he emits light, producing transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*). Furthermore, from the crowns of these transformation-buddhas, precious light is emitted, proclaiming divine mantras (*dhāraṇī*).

This signifies that from the essence (*tattva*) arises function (*vṛtti*); function is itself the essence. The Buddha of the essence does not speak, but speaks through function; each and every transformative act is thus manifested.
All these belong to the wondrous function; the essence remains unmoving.

It is understood that this is not something that other noble ones are able to penetrate.

Employing both the provisional and the ultimate, he manifests nirvana and transmits [the teachings] to future generations.
There is nothing that can be accomplished apart from the mantra-heart; it is thus vast and thus universally bestowed. To the practitioner of the mantra, there is truly no duality of mind.

If one does not awaken to it, one merely relies on its spiritual efficacy; there is nothing that will not be fulfilled.

If I were to speak this Buddha-Usnīṣa-Raśmi-Sañcaya Pañcarakṣā Dhāraṇī from morning until evening,
with the sounds linked together and the syllables and phrases never overlapping, even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I could never finish it. Furthermore,
this dhāraṇī is also called the Tathāgata’s Crown.

"You who are still in training, not yet having exhausted the cycle of saṃsāra, have resolved with utmost sincerity to attain arhatship;

This ritual site (*maṇḍala*) refers to the aforementioned instruction for establishing a ritual site and exclusively reciting [the mantra].

Ānanda, I shall now further explain this mantra for you, which protects and rescues the world, grants great fearlessness,
and brings about the supramundane wisdom of all beings.

This is taught for those who have resolved their minds upon seeking supramundane wisdom through the recitation of mantras and possess a firm resolve; it explains how they may be freed from all obstacles.
From this point until the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), all matters—whether performed according to the Dharma or not—are equally pure.

If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are sentient beings in the final age who can recite this themselves or teach others to recite it,
you should know that such beings who uphold and recite it cannot be burned by fire, cannot be drowned by water, and cannot be harmed by great or small poisons.
In this way, even the evil spells of devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, earth deities, and māras cannot take hold;
the mind attains right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). All curses, sorcery, and poisonous drugs—whether from gold, silver, plants, trees, insects, or snakes—[cannot affect them].
The poisonous vapors of the myriad things, upon entering the mouth of such a person, become the flavor of nectar.

All malevolent stars, as well as various ghosts and spirits and those who harbor cruel hearts and malice toward others, cannot give rise to evil thoughts against such a person. Even the Piṇāyakas and all the wicked kings of ghosts cannot do so.
Together with their retinues, they all acknowledge this profound kindness and constantly provide protection;
their minds attain right concentration (*samādhi*). This is what is inspired in those who seek the wisdom that transcends the world.

Regarding "exorcising *gū* (malevolent spirits)," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to *gū* as foxes; the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* likewise mentions demonic *gū*. "Gold, silver, and poison" arise from the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*.
Gold and silver are poisons. Piṇāka and Yakṣa—these two messengers with pig heads and elephant trunks—are actually Dharma-protecting Bodhisattvas;
upon receiving this grace, they immediately respond to the power of the mantra.

Even if one wears impure or tattered clothing, whether walking or staying still, one is entirely as pure as ever. Furthermore, even if one does not construct an altar, enter a ritual site (maṇḍala), nor...

All attained the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
This is the accomplishment resulting from the firm resolve to seek supramundane wisdom through the turning of karmic bonds, the arousal of the bodhicitta, and the upholding of mantras.

This is evoked by the power of pure and single-minded recitation; it is the actual realization of the initial resolve, meaning that one knows with certainty that one will attain Buddhahood without error.

Whether involving both lay and ordained practitioners, or whether one has already attained realization or has not yet attained it, these [rules] are specifically opened up for them; this can be understood through the underlying intent.

The four parājikas are sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying; for bhikṣuṇīs, four more are added: namely, physical contact, reaching the period of menstruation, concealing [a grave offense], and [the fifth].

Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is a woman who has not yet given birth to sons or daughters and desires to conceive, if she can recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or if she can wear this *Sītātapatrā* [Mantra] upon her body, she will immediately give rise to merit.

The "fruits of retribution and benefits" refer to the fruits of retribution for men and women who seek longevity and all other such rewards.
These are all maintained by the Tathāgata through skillful means (*upāya*) so that they may plant the distant causes for Bodhi; yet, they are also the aspirations of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Rebirth after death will likewise never fail to be achieved. With great compassion, he accords with beings and skillfully guides them; what is there that he cannot reach?
△ Seventh, it is shown that the power of the mantra can eliminate national calamities and disasters among the people.
Ānanda, if there are kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages— whether stricken by famine and pestilence, or beset by the calamities of weapons,
bandits, and strife, or any other land of misfortune— if this divine mantra is transcribed and placed at the four gates of the city,
as well as at various caityas or atop gate-towers, and if all sentient beings within that kingdom are made to welcome this mantra with reverence and prostration;
With reverence and single-minded devotion, they shall make offerings and cause each of their people to wear it upon their persons or place it within their respective dwellings.
All calamities and misfortunes will be entirely extinguished. Ānanda, wherever there are sentient beings in any land, [this shall apply].
Wherever this mantra exists, devas and nāgas will rejoice; wind and rain will follow their proper seasons; the five grains will be abundant; and the myriad people will be peaceful and happy.
Furthermore, it can suppress all malevolent stars and regional portents; calamities and obstacles shall not arise, and no one shall suffer untimely death.
Manacles, fetters, cangues, and shackles shall not touch their bodies; they shall sleep peacefully day and night, and never experience evil dreams.

Ānanda, in this Sahā world there are eighty-four thousand calamitous and malevolent stars, with twenty-eight great malevolent stars as their leaders, and eight further great malevolent stars acting as their sovereigns.
When these appear in the world, manifesting in various forms, they are able to—
The various calamities and anomalies that arise among sentient beings will all be completely extinguished where this dhāraṇī-ground exists.
For twelve yojanas, it shall become a consecrated boundary (sīmābandha) within which no evil portents or disasters can ever enter.

From the moment various nations arise, until all evil calamities and portents can never enter, the power of the incantation is said to be supreme in its ability to dissolve and pacify them everywhere, such that the land becomes tranquil and the people enjoy health and happiness. *Cetiya* is here translated as "a place worthy of offerings.
Furthermore, where there are *śarīra* (relics), it is called a *stūpa*; where there are no *śarīra*, it is called a *cetiya*. *Dvāra* is here...

"Cloud Banner" (Yúndāng) is also called the "High and Prominent Place of the City Terrace. The eighty-four thousand malevolent stars correspond to the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings.
Generally, the auspiciousness or calamity of the constellations corresponds to human affairs, such as the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).

It serves as the governing principle for the four quarters. By inferring from the lunar mansion Mūla, one finds that Mūla is the foremost; it constantly traverses empty space, passing through the four continents, and always performs virtuous deeds.
Thus we know that these are all the result of the profound karmic seeds of sentient beings, where their responses and inducements have become disordered.
In this age of evil calamities and turbulent fortune, phenomena arise in opposition to one another; indeed, good and evil are inherently indeterminate.

According to the *Tianguan shu* (Book of Celestial Officials), all the stellar mansions take the five planets as their primary rulers, which constitute the fundamental principles of the Five Elements (*wuxing*).

When the Rāhu, Ketu, and Śani are added, they form the eight celestial bodies. Wherever this mantra prevails, it first reaches all sentient beings; once the obstructions of sentient beings are eliminated, disasters and anomalies will accordingly perish.

In ancient times, when the omens of comets and meteors appeared, the rulers and ministers could rectify their virtue to dispel and pacify them; how much more so should this apply to the Buddha-dharma?
*Yojana* is the correct transliteration of *yojana*; it has no direct equivalent in Chinese. It refers to a lodging where a Wheel-Turning King halts during his circuit of inspection.
The measurements vary in size; they may be forty *li* or twenty *li*. Among the various sutras and treatises, the smaller measurement is most frequently used.
△ Eighth, showing how to protect the initial mind so that it is freed from obstacles and the mind opens.

For this reason, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra. In future ages, it shall protect all beginner practitioners as they enter samādhi, so that their bodies and minds may be at ease and attain great peace and security.
Furthermore, no demons, ghosts, spirits, or the karmic debts and calamities of beginningless enmity and resentment shall come to afflict or harm them. You and those within this assembly...

All those who are still in training, as well as all practitioners of future ages, who rely upon my maṇḍala and maintain the precepts according to the Dharma, and whose precept masters they encounter are pure monks, shall not give rise to doubt or regret regarding this mantra-heart. Such good sons—
If, with this body born of one's parents, one does not attain mental penetration (*cittābhijñā*), then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods.

The Buddha taught this mantra specifically to bestow grace upon beginners at the onset of the final age; therefore, he now binds it again and again with earnest exhortation so that there may be no doubt or regret.
"Mental penetration" refers to sitting upright in meditation for a period of one hundred days; if one is diligent, [the result will be attained].
As for the "roots": without rising from one's seat, one attains the stage of Srotāpanna; this is the realization of the first dwelling-stage within the physical body.
This is the Buddha’s true word and his word of reality, which should be faithfully believed.
The Tathāgatagarbha resides within the eight consciousnesses of sentient beings, serving as the aperture for seeing and hearing.

Deluded by discrimination, it follows the false constructs of discrimination, thereby undergoing ascent and descent through the six realms and entering and exiting the four modes of birth; thus, when sound vibrates, hearing follows.
The forms appear before my eyes as clearly as if they were from yesterday. The compassionate power of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions extends only to this;
the sorrowful longing of all sentient beings summons only this. Yet, how earnest and urgent are the words of the Sages!
It is merely a matter of seeing and hearing; yet, when the disciple receives the instruction, they immediately resort to conceptual discrimination.

This doubt regarding the naturalness of causes and conditions is thoroughly cleansed and exhausted through the Sūtra’s treatment of the aggregates, bases, elements, and up to the seven great elements.

Finally, upon hearing the sound of the pestle in a dream, one only then glimpses [the truth]. To investigate it to its ultimate conclusion, it too is nothing more than seeing and hearing. Furthermore...

There is no separate finger to point toward it. When one investigates and exhaustively analyzes through discernment, it is found to be right before one’s eyes; when brought to the ultimate point of realization and cultivation, it is ultimately nothing other than this.

The Tathāgata said: “The faculties and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. The nature of consciousness is false and illusory, like flowers in the sky. He further said:
“To establish a knowing-perception within knowing-perception is the very root of ignorance; to have no perception within knowing-perception is itself Nirvāṇa.”
This mind of awakening on the causal ground likewise cannot abandon pure seeing and hearing while separately positing what is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
As for his own description of the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), he also said: "First, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object."
Is this not what is called the nature of hearing? Furthermore, it says: "Because I did not contemplate my own auditory faculty, I used contemplation to contemplate the contemplator.
It also says: "The faculties of seeing and hearing revolve back [to their source]. And:

"Severing and extinguishing deluded thoughts"—is this not externally cutting off the sensory object of sound and internally subduing discriminative thought, thereby leaving the nature of hearing exposed in its solitude? Mañjuśrī said: "Sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing."
"One wanders through transmigration because one follows sounds. Furthermore, it says: "If you are about to hear and maintain the Buddha-nature, why do you not hear the hearing itself?
And again: "By reversing the hearing, one hears the self-nature; this nature accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way.

Thus, is it not the case that the awakened mind of the causal stage cannot possibly abandon this pure faculty of hearing (*śruti*) and instead seek some other so-called *tathāgatagarbha* nature? This is the beginning.
From the initial illumination to the final realization through cultivation, there is nothing that does not sever all conceptual discrimination and uniquely manifest seeing and hearing.
The nature of hearing that enters the stream is externally detached from the sensory object of sound; the awakened mind that exhausts all hearing does not internally dwell in the wisdom of emptiness.

This is precisely the destination reached by the initial resolve, where one attains ultimate perfection through the consummation of practice. Thus, it reaches the point where the four admonitions hang high and resplendent.
To protect against Māra in the final age, this heart-mantra further awakens the mind and points toward the secret for the person concerned.
If one were to receive the great empowerment of the Tathāgata, it would already be a present-day missed opportunity. The Tathāgata said: "This is the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa-Teja-rāśi."
The *Siddhārthapāṇḍarā*, this secret gāthā and its subtle phrases, give birth to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Viewed in this light, that which is called "elucidating the nature of hearing" is precisely the elucidation of this very ear.

That which is called "externally severing the dust of sound and internally subduing discrimination, so as to reveal the nature of hearing alone," is precisely the solitary manifestation of this very ear.
That which the beginner reaches is reached here; that which the ultimate perfects is perfected here.

Within this subtle and wondrous gāthā, one is not aware that the entire body is encompassed by it, nor does one clearly perceive from dawn to dusk that light pervades as many worlds as there are grains of sand.
How could this be a mere leisurely pastime for a beginner? It is, in truth, the silent realization of Bodhi. To know it thoroughly and universally is not dependent on another.

[He] sets forth [the resolve] to definitely attain Buddhahood, without depending on a ritual site (maṇḍala). Only then does one come to know that while the Exoteric [teaching] points out the tracks, the Esoteric must be personally realized.
Out of ignorance, I have thus sequentially recounted the constant path from the initial aspiration to its ultimate consummation, returning it all to the silent realization of the mantra-mind.
This is because I perceive the Tathāgata’s repeated and earnest exhortations. △ Nine: The Vajra-holders in the Assembly.
"O virtuous deity, we vow to extensively protect [this teaching].
Having spoken these words, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *vajras* within the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha and prostrated themselves.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the Buddha has taught, I shall protect with sincere heart those who thus cultivate bodhicitta.
May my vow be fulfilled in sincerely protecting those who cultivate bodhicitta. By this, I include all the gods and the eight classes of benevolent spirits;
therefore, know that the mind of bodhicitta is most honored and unsurpassed. All devas and humans shall reverently uphold the Buddha’s command."
"I, a practitioner, ought to exert myself.
At that time, the Brahma King, together with Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Four Great Kings, also simultaneously prostrated themselves before the Buddha.

He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "If there are indeed such virtuous persons who practice and study in this way, I shall protect them with all my heart and utmost sincerity, ensuring that everything they do throughout their lives shall be fulfilled according to their wishes."
Among the gods of the desire realm, Śakra is the sovereign; among the Brahmā heavens, the Brahmā King is the sovereign. This is the established model for protecting the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, pūtana kings, and kumbhāṇḍa kings.
The King of the Piśācas, the great kingly spirits of Vināyakas, and all the generals of ghosts likewise joined their palms in prostration before the Buddha.
I, too, vow to protect and sustain these persons, causing their bodhicitta to swiftly reach full perfection.
These leaders of the eight classes are for the most part bodhisattvas manifesting in these forms; in various sutras they are referred to as bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable sun and moon devas, as well as masters of wind, rain, clouds, and thunder, along with the Lord of Lightning and others.
The Annual Cycle Officials and the retinues of all the stars likewise prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We, too, shall protect these practitioners of the path, establishing their sites of practice so that they may attain fearlessness.”
These belong to the category of the celestial hosts; "Master" refers to the leader who raises his head. "Fearing" refers to all the aforementioned demons, ghosts, and spirits.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable mountain deities and ocean deities, as well as all the numinous essences of the myriad things that move on land, in water, and through the air across all territories.
Together with the Wind Deity King and the gods of the Formless Realm, they simultaneously prostrated before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain bodhi, forever free from the works of Māra."

From those that travel by mountain, sea, land, and air, including all things such as trees, plants, and crops, as well as all spirits—encompassing every deity within the three realms—the Wind King is not the aforementioned Wind Master, but rather the Lord of Space.
His form is like the wind itself; together with the deities of the Formless Heavens, he has manifested for a brief moment through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.

At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Ganges-sands of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, within the great assembly, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, as for the meritorious deeds we have cultivated, we have long since attained bodhi; yet we do not enter nirvana, but constantly follow this mantra to provide protection and deliverance.”
"World-Honored One, regarding those who practice samādhi as correct cultivation during the final age— those who thus cultivate the mind seeking right concentration,
whether they are in the place of practice (maṇḍala), or elsewhere walking for meditation, or even when their minds are distracted as they roam through villages— we, your followers,"
We shall always follow and attend upon this person; even if Māra the King or Maheśvara seek an opportunity, they will ultimately find none.
As for the various minor spirits, they shall remain ten *yojanas* away from this virtuous person, except for those who have resolved their minds to joyfully cultivate *dhyāna*.
World-Honored One, if such evil Māras or the Māra’s retinue should wish to come and harass this virtuous person...
As for such persons, I shall shatter their heads with my precious vajra until they are like fine dust, so that this person’s endeavors may always be fulfilled as wished.
Having long attained the state of Bodhi and reached the ultimate fruit, they shall not enter nirvana, for their great compassion has become even more exalted. Or, in some cases...
Whether at the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), or while walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), or even when the mind is distracted in play, these are all times for cultivating *samāpatti*.
This Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattva is one who deeply understands right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) and thus provides true protection;
he is not comparable to other external protectors. The Māra King dwells atop the summit of Maheśvara Heaven; he does not rejoice when practitioners seek liberation.
Worldly wisdom constantly creates obstacles because it possesses great power;
the assembly of Bodhisattvas always follows [the Buddha], preventing it from finding an opportunity, unlike other māras.
The above five sections have fully proclaimed the Heart Mantra and concluded the extensive demonstration of its benefits.
△ Sixth, demonstrating the positions of the beginning, middle, and end of cultivation and realization, divided into six parts. First, Ānanda requests instruction on the sequential stages of practice.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We are dull-witted and fond of mere erudition;

regarding our minds still subject to outflows (*āsrava*), we had not yet sought liberation. Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, we have attained correct cultivation. Our bodies and minds are refreshed, and we have gained great benefit.
World-Honored One, such is the cultivation and realization of the Buddha’s *samādhi*; it has not yet reached *nirvāṇa*."
"What is meant by the stage of 'dry wisdom'? From what point among the forty-four minds does one gradually attain the vision of cultivation?
To what destination must one go to be said to have entered the stages? And what is meant by an Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva? Having spoken these words, [he asked].
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, the great assembly waited with single-minded devotion for the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him with fixed, unblinking eyes.
The two types of grasping and the seeds of habitual tendencies are all termed "outflows" (āsrava); this does not refer to the "outflow-free" (anāsrava) state of the Two Vehicles.

What is called "right cultivation" refers to the awareness of emptiness that arises from turning back the hearing; this is the initial entry into samādhi, yet it has not yet reached nirvāṇa, and thus proceeds from the stage of "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā).
He raises a question regarding the sequence of practice: by how many stages of awakening does one exhaust the causal state?
This is intended as a mirror held aloft for the final age. Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) is the initial cause, and Nirvāṇa is the ultimate fruit.
Passing through the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*), there are forty-four minds in total; this constitutes the practice.
Gradually and successively, he then enters the stages (*bhūmi*) until reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), thereby exhausting the ultimate limit of the causal stage.
Ānanda already knew its name, yet wishing to investigate its actual substance in detail, he therefore requested further instruction. △ Second, the praise, consent, and preliminary indication.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

You have been able to universally provide for the great assembly and all sentient beings of the future ages who cultivate samādhi and seek the Mahāyāna—leading them from the stage of ordinary beings to the ultimate Great Nirvāṇa—and to point out in advance the unsurpassed path of correct practice. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you."
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms and hollowed their hearts, silently receiving the instruction.
Since Ānanda had first selected his faculties, he has already clearly understood the path of correct cultivation; this is the initial stage of the Mahāyāna.
One thereby knows the matters within the ultimate stage; this is not like the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles (Zàngtōng), where one stage does not know another.
By observing the words of the Tathāgata’s inquiry—extending from ordinary beings to Nirvāṇa—it is evident that this is for the sake of the great assembly and all those in the final age.
"To hollow out" means to empty the mind. △ Third, showing the two perversions.
The causes of inversion are divided into three parts. First, the general indication of the causes of inversion:
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, transcending all names and characteristics; fundamentally, there have been no worlds or sentient beings."
Question: Regarding the stages of cultivation, there is a beginning, a middle, and an end; this is how names and characteristics are established.
There is currently a world, and there are beings therein at this very moment; this is how the distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas arises.

Thus, it first states that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and characteristics, and that fundamentally there have been no worlds or sentient beings. Although [this is so]...
In this final age, those of initial capacity do not depart from the principle of direct pointing. There is but one reality; the other two are not true.
It is revealed everywhere, yet people remain deluded and distressed—how truly pitiable!
Due to delusion there is birth; due to birth there is cessation. Birth and cessation are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called truth.
This is termed the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed bodhi and great nirvāṇa—the two designations for the transformation of the basis.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Not understanding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
What was previously described as the wondrous nature being perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks is this very ultimate truth. Not understanding it is termed "non-awakening" (*abodhi*).
This non-awakening gives rise to deluded movement, which constitutes thought. Thought is the phase of arising; as soon as it arises, it ceases. Having ceased, it arises again.
Because one cannot realize [the nature of mind] in the present moment, and because thoughts continue in an uninterrupted succession, they are called "delusion.

To realize delusion is itself the truth; there is no longer any duality of essence. Thus, Caoxi said: "The non-arising of the preceding thought is the mind; the non-extinction of the succeeding thought is the Buddha.
This means that if one realizes [this], one does not follow the continuity of the preceding thought; the present thought is perfectly manifest, and one never again falls into delusion.
This is what is meant by "transformation. It is the transformation of deluded awareness into bodhi, and the transformation of birth-and-death into nirvana.

Fundamentally, they are of one and the same substance; "delusion" and "awakening" are merely different names. Thus, Caoxi further said: "It is simply a change of name; there is no real nature [to it].
As for "relying," the *tathāgatagarbha* relies upon non-awakening to give rise to deluded movement; relying upon deluded movement, there arises...

Arising and ceasing—now, through awakening, one realizes they are without delusion, and thus there is nothing upon which to rely. The nature of the storehouse (ālaya) is inherently so; therefore, it is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate the true *samādhi* and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you must first recognize these two causes of inversion regarding sentient beings and the world. When inversion does not arise, this is the true *samādhi* of the Tathāgata.

Samādhi. Regarding the three types of continuity mentioned in the preceding text—wherein the world is presented first and sentient beings second—it is because the clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness interact to produce agitation.
Thus, there arises a wind-circle that sustains the world. Once the false has been established, sound and form...

It was suddenly silent. Thus, their understanding of principle did not transcend it; their hearing did not go beyond sound; their vision did not exceed form. This is what sentient beings do after the world has come into being.
Now, regarding the two kinds of inversion: fundamentally, the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and originally possesses neither world nor sentient beings.
It is due to the cause of inversion that there arise birth-and-death and nirvana.
Because they are distinct, sentient beings are mentioned first and the world second. This world is precisely what is perceived before one's eyes by sentient beings;
through false grasping, karma is formed, and all various categories of existence arise in succession. This does not mean that the world itself originates [from nothing].
By knowing the cause of these two inversions and no longer following discursive discrimination, one enters the perfect and luminous true samādhi.
Samādhi. △ Second, the delusions of sentient beings. This is divided into three parts. First, the cause of the delusions of sentient beings:
"Ānanda, what is meant by the delusions of sentient beings? Ānanda, it is because the nature of the mind is luminous, and the nature of the mind is perfectly full and bright."
Because of this, the nature gives rise to manifestation. This nature gives birth to deluded vision; from ultimate non-existence, it becomes ultimate existence.

The nature of awareness is fundamentally luminous and fundamentally quiescent. This luminosity does not maintain itself; failing to realize this, it moves delusively. Thus, this nature is fundamentally without delusion.

It arises based on conditions; thus, the false perception of inherent nature (*svabhāva*) comes into being. Nature itself is ultimately non-existent, while the false [perception] is ultimately existent.
This nature that lacks inherent nature is invariably responsive to conditions; this existence that is fundamentally non-existent remains unchanging despite its responsiveness to conditions.
All that follows should be understood in this light.
"This existence and its objects" refers to that which is not caused by a cause, nor does it abide in an abiding characteristic; it is utterly devoid of a fundamental basis.
This "existence" follows from the preceding discussion and ultimately refers to deluded vision.

Since there is the deluded vision that is the subject who sees, there must be the deluded appearances that are the objects seen; hence it is said, "this existence and its objects. These objects seen take deluded vision as their cause.
This is taking what is not a cause to be a cause. The deluded views by which one abides are fundamentally void; how could the deluded appearances upon which one abides be real?
Therefore, it is said that they have no root at all.
Based on this non-abiding, the worlds and all sentient beings are established.

This "based on this non-abiding" refers to the fact that, fundamentally, there was originally no abiding characterized by a root; yet, through delusion, the vessel-world and the sense-faculties and body were falsely posited.
Since both the vessel-world and the sense-faculties and body are subsumed under the "objective portion" (nimittabhāga), the term "worlds" is used here inclusively. △
Second is the characteristic of the delusion of sentient beings.
Being confused regarding the fundamental perfect luminosity, this gives rise to false imagination. The nature of this falsity has no substance and has nothing upon which it depends.

This originates from the false perceptions before the eyes of sentient beings; being without substance and without dependence, they arise through confusion regarding fundamental luminosity. Thus, this false imagination is produced.
It is delusion. Awakening is primordial truth. The world before one’s eyes is neither existent nor empty; how could the seeing and hearing directly present here be either confused or awakened?
If one does not understand this, one follows the power of various delusions; how can afflictions and karma ever come to an end?
If one intends to return to the true, that which is intended as true is already not the true nature of *tathatā*. Seeking to restore what is not true results in nothing but non-characteristics.
It is neither arising nor abiding; it is neither mind nor dharmas.
One who wishes to return to the truth is said to realize that delusion has no substance and exists as nothing other than this.

If one wishes to return to the truth, then within this very single thought, one perfectly manifests non-appearance upon the nature of *tathatā* (suchness); that is, while not being the appearance of truth, it appears as such.

Therefore, it is said that they are not characteristics. Consequently, what is fundamentally non-arising is called "arising"; what is fundamentally non-abiding is called "abiding"; what is fundamentally not mind is called "mind";

and what is fundamentally not dharmas is called "dharmas. From the perspective of the deluded perceptions before the eyes of sentient beings, all these are fundamentally non-existent yet falsely appear to exist.
This failure to realize the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is what is termed ignorance (avidyā). From...
This delusive power of ignorance arises through successive transformation, corresponding to the measure of what is known, and manifests according to karma.
Therefore, the subsequent text further states: △ Third, the karmic fruits of sentient beings.

They arise in succession; the power of arising brings forth illumination, which perfumes the mind to form karma. Through the mutual resonance of shared karma, there is the interaction of causes where karmic conditions are extinguished and produced.
It is for this reason that sentient beings undergo perversion.
The karma of sentient beings is the same; thus, love and hatred resonate with one another. Since there is resonant karma, there is a resonant fruit.
Because of hatred, they destroy one another; because of love, they give rise to one another. This is called perversion.
The two preceding sections on the inversions of sentient beings are concluded. △ Third, the inversions of the world, divided into three parts.

First, the cause of the world’s inversion: Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of the world? It is that which exists as having something to exist; it is the false arising of fragmented segments. Because of this, the realm is established;
it is not caused by a cause, nor does it abide in an abode. It flows and migrates without staying still; because of this, the world is formed.
"This is that which possesses existence" refers back to the preceding "this possessing existence. Since there is that which is characterized (*lakṣya*), there is immediately a separation;
thus, boundaries are established through segmentation. It is not the cause of causes, nor is it the abode of abodes. This also refers back to the preceding "not the cause of causes."

Regarding the characteristic of abiding: since there is already a delusive cause, there is likewise a delusive effect. Once delusive abiding is established, delusive cessation is likewise established.
Through this causal process of arising and ceasing, the flux of change constitutes the world.
The three periods of time and the four directions intermingle and harmonize with one another, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories.
Through the intersection of time and direction, and through the intersection of direction and time, twelve types are formed in each case.

Due to the deluded perceptions of sentient beings, they are restricted by boundaries and shifted by thoughts; thus, the categories they evoke also become twelve. II. The Characteristics of Worldly Inversion.
Therefore, in the world, sound arises from movement; form arises from sound; fragrance arises from form; touch arises from fragrance; flavor arises from touch;
and mental objects (*dharma*) are known through flavor. Because these six types of deluded conceptualization constitute the nature of karma, there arise the twelve divisions [of the sense bases].
By means of this, the cycle revolves; therefore, the world’s sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles exhaust twelve transformations to form a single rotation.
Since the nature of sound is motion and stillness, motion constitutes the characteristic of sound. However, sound is not the cause of form, nor is form the cause of smell.
Fragrance is not the cause of touch; touch is not the cause of taste; taste is not the cause of dharmas. Yet, one cause gives rise to one existence.
All of these arise from the sentient beings' recollection, cognition, chanting, and study, where deluded thoughts interpenetrate and manifest instantaneously all at once.

Thus, through the six types of disordered deluded thoughts, the faculties and their objects interact to form the causal nature of karma. Consequently, there are the twelve categories of living beings with their respective divisions.

"Result" (*phala*) refers to the revolving of its own characteristics. Exhausting the twelve transformations constitutes the twelve divisions. First the six perceptions are mentioned, followed by the six objects;
this collectively shows how the faculties and their objects interact to produce these transformations. This revolving back and forth is what is meant by "revolving.
△ Third, the distinctions among the classes of beings, divided into two parts. First, a general enumeration of the twelve classes.
Because they ride upon this wheel of inverted characteristics, there are beings in this world born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;
those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; and those who are neither with form nor without form, and neither with perception nor without perception.

If it were not for the state of non-conception, then by mounting this cycle of rebirth, one would immediately mount upon the mutual interpenetration of the superior faculties and objects; these would revolve and revert into one another.
Due to such inversion, the various classes of beings come into existence, as will be detailed below. △ Second: An analysis of the twelve classes, divided into twelve parts. First:
O Ānanda, as for birth from eggs:
due to the causes of the world’s false saṃsāra and its fluctuating inversions, the combination of vital energies produces eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.
Because of this, there is the flow and circulation of the oviparous kalala within the realms, such as fish and birds.
Tortoises and snakes—these species abound. Their eggs are produced solely through thought;

they belong to the realm of false conceptualization. Because thought is light, it moves; it stirs the vital energies until they harmonize and coalesce, resulting in the formation of creatures that fly or sink.
Thus they transmigrate through various realms. *Kalala*—translated here as "coagulated slime"—is the first stage of entry into the womb. (*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*)
It is said: There are five stages within the womb. The initial stage of entering the womb, when the embryo and the eggshell have not yet differentiated, is the same for all.
Among the various classes of beings that fly or sink, their number is immeasurable; fish, birds, tortoises, and snakes are cited as examples to represent the whole. △ Second, birth from a womb.

Due to the causes of the world’s defiled saṃsāra and because of the inversion of desire, eighty-four thousand horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts are formed through their conjunction and growth.
Thus, there is the transmigration through realms such as the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and *peśī* stages of the womb, as well as among humans, animals, nāgas, and ṛṣis.
Their kinds fill the world. The womb-conception arises due to emotion;
defilement belongs to emotion. Emotion gives rise to desire, which induces the harmony of union, resulting in horizontal or vertical birth.
One transmigrates through various lands. *Aṭa-puṭa* (translated here as "blister") is the second stage; at this point, the embryo and the egg have already differentiated.

Furthermore, the upright [orientation] constitutes human immortals and belongs to the orthodox; the horizontal constitutes dragons and beasts and belongs to the heterodox. △ Third, moisture-born beings:
due to the causes of attachment to the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) and following inverted paths, they combine with warmth to form eighty-four thousand types of chaotic and inverted thoughts.
For this reason, there exist moisture-born entities (*piśāca*) that conceal their forms, circulating through various lands as wriggling and crawling insects.
Their kind fills [the world].
Through moistness, there is mutual response; through attachment, they pursue different destinies. Due to the combination of warmth, they undergo reversals and transmigrate through various lands.
*Bhita* (here translated as "soft flesh") is the initial sign of receiving moisture; because one has not entered the womb, the first two stages do not exist.

Including crawling insects and flying creatures that move about without fixed direction, they approach and cling to it upon smelling its fragrance. △ Fourth, those born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Due to the world’s cycle of shifting and revolving, and because of false inversions, eighty-four thousand new and old disordered thoughts are formed through the conjunction of contact.
For this reason, there exist transformed *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands, shedding their skins and flying.
Their species fill [the realms].

They are transformed according to their individual responses; because they are motivated by aversion, they pursue craving and grasp at new forms. Through the conjunction of contact and perception, they form provisional aggregates.
