The path of the three realms. This is the manifestation of the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Arising wisdom from Suchness, one possesses the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and acts as a great Dharma teacher.
As the Sūtra says: "By means of immeasurable skillful wisdom, one gives rise to the four unimpeded eloquences. What are these four?

These are what are called the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
Because of these knowledges, one is named "One of Excellent Wisdom" (*Suvijñāna*).
Ānanda, from this point onward, these bodhisattvas complete their cultivation and bring their merit to full perfection;
thus, this stage is also called the Stage of Cultivation. When the wondrous clouds of the shade of compassion cover the ocean of nirvāṇa, it is named the Dharma Cloud Stage (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).
From this point onward refers to the period after the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*) and before this stage. All efforts regarding severance and realization are only completed here;
for it is because these efforts are concluded that one attains the name of "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). "Kindness-shade" (*maitrī-chāyā*) is compassion, and "wondrous cloud" (*vimala-megha*) is wisdom.
When compassion and wisdom are perfectly complete, one is able to provide protective shade for sentient beings. This represents the ultimate limit of the causal stage.
It is about to merge with the ocean of the fruit of Nirvana, like clouds pervading the void, encompassing all without exception;

it now awaits the downpour of rain to universally moisten the entire Dharma-realm. "Dharma" refers to the Dharmakāya, and "clouds" signify the shade of compassion. This title is established to accord with this stage.
△ Eighth, the conclusion of the two awakenings—Equal and Subtle—to manifest the perfection of Dry Wisdom, from the end of the gradual stages.
Regarding Bodhi:

the Tathāgata flows against the current; likewise, the Bodhisattva proceeds with the current until reaching the point where awakening and the limit intersect, which is called Equal Awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
To enter from cause into fruit is called "proceeding with the current"; to enter from fruit into cause is called "flowing against the current. The Tathāgata has already reached the stage of fruition.

To the utmost, one contemplates the cyclic wandering of sentient beings and manifests through retribution and transformation bodies. Emerging from the realm of true stillness and entering the ocean of birth and death—this is called "flowing against the current.
The Bodhisattva, relying on the Tathāgata’s teaching, emerges from the ocean of birth and death to give rise to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Progressing through the five stages of practice until reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)—this is called "flowing with the current. Since both following and reversing lead to the boundary of awakening, it is said:
Entering into interaction, wondrous enlightenment is itself Buddhahood. The Buddha proceeds from this [enlightenment] in reverse, while the Bodhisattva proceeds from this in forward order;

therefore, it is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Ānanda, from the mind of Dry Wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment, this awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Diamond Mind.
This awakening refers specifically to Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), meaning that one attains it only upon reaching this stage of awakening. The *Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses* states:
"After the Vajra Path, the maturation-consciousness is empty; the forty grades of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of ignorance arise from its cessation."
Only after reaching the stage of the Vajra Path does one finally sever the arising-phase of ignorance; therefore, this "Vajra" also refers to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).
It means that from the initial Dry Wisdom up to the mind of Equal Enlightenment, [the realization] first attains perfection.

What was previously stated—that one has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s flow of Dharma—refers to the period from the initial awakening of the mind onward, during which one still possesses the Buddha-nature of a sentient being as one progresses through the five stages.
Thus proceeding until one reaches Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one then realizes that there is nothing further beyond it.
In this manner, through these successive layers of single and double stages—twelve in total—one finally exhausts the Wondrous Enlightenment and accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way.
The Samyaksambuddha (Equal Awakened One) has reached the ultimate exhaustion of subtle ignorance; because there is something to be abandoned, he is called a "Superior Being" (Sottara-purusa).

The Pratyekabuddha (Subtle Awakened One) has attained ultimate liberation through the unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom; because there is nothing further to be abandoned, he is called the "Unsurpassed Being" (Anuttara-purusa).

Thus, these twelve stages—single and combined, repeated and layered—summarize the preceding text. From the attainment of "Dry Wisdom" (śuṣka-vipaśyanā), one traces back through all that has been traversed:
the stages of faith, abiding, practice, direction, application, and the grounds. It is like a person who, having reached home, looks back upon the road and only then realizes the toil endured;
yet it seems as though remaining at the starting point was even more direct and swift. This is what is meant by "the single and the combined."
Qiyun: A single position constitutes a "single" (dan) stage; a single position encompassing twelve positions constitutes a "repeated" (fu) stage.

By repeating the single through the repeated, and by repeating the repeated through the single, each reaches the full extent of the twelve. In the perfect stages of the Mahāyāna, a single position encompasses all positions.
This differs from the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings, wherein one stage does not know another. Therefore, the initial mind is identical to the ultimate;
even upon reaching wondrous enlightenment (*miaojue*), there is nothing that exceeds the initial mind. The unsurpassed fruit of the Way is present within the daily activities of sentient beings;
it is simply not easily believed with clarity.
These various stages are all observed with the diamond-like gaze and through the ten profound metaphors of illusion;
within *śamatha*, one realizes them through the pure cultivation of the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas, gradually entering deeper and deeper.

The "various stages" refers precisely to the twelve preceding positions. The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is not found only at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);
it is present in every stage, enabling one to sever afflictions and realize the truth according to each respective position. It is also the initial mind of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).
This diamond-like illusory samādhi observes all phenomena, as well as the practices and wisdom of what is to be severed and realized; both subject and object are...
[One realizes] emptiness. Thereafter, within the state of perfect concentration (*pariniṣpanna-samādhi*), one employs the Tathāgata’s perfect wisdom to gradually penetrate deeper.
*Śamatha* is translated as "quiescence," and *vipaśyanā* is translated as "illumination.

This *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* take pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the correct view established through pure hearing and reflection as their causes, and they rely upon a well-purified mind and a well-purified...

Pure wisdom is the fruit. From the initial resolve until the ultimate realization of emptiness, it counteracts the two subtle obstacles and ultimately realizes the omniscient vision that is unattached and unimpeded, establishing the most supremely pure *dharmakāya*.
There are ten profound metaphors: namely, a magical person, a mirage, the moon in water, flowers in the sky, an echo in a valley, a city of the *gandharvas*, a dream, and a reflected image.
It is a transformation,
Ānanda. Thus, by means of these three progressive advancements, one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi.

From the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) through the stages of Faith, Abiding, Practice, and Penetration—the four preparatory practices—and the ten *bhūmis*, there are fifty-five positions in total.
Equality (*samatā*) and Subtlety (*prakarṣa*) are the fruits; these constitute the path to Bodhi.
All are characterized by "threefold advancement," because the initial mind of Dry Wisdom is generated through these three advancements. This concludes the summary.
One who practices this contemplation is said to practice correctly; one who contemplates otherwise is said to practice erroneously.

This signifies the perfect contemplation as the true cultivation of the Tathāgata. If things were truly existent, they would become hierarchical stages; if they were truly non-existent, they would become annihilation. Both are erroneous views.
Ultimately, there is the perfect fusion of the sequential and the perfect fusion within the sequential—this is the truth.
This is the Dharma-eye.
Contemplate the Dharma-realm with clarity: from the ordinary person to the sage, it is nothing but a single state of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

To be deluded regarding this dry wisdom is to wander through the four modes of birth and exhaust the twelve categories of beings; these various disordered thoughts are not other than this very state. They exist within disordered thought.

From the perspective of the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), [the state of] the middle [stage] is as far removed as Dry Wisdom is from the ultimate fruit; it is entirely beyond one's capacity.

Yet, unaware that one must abandon deluded conceptions to attain Dry Wisdom—just as one must abandon Dry Wisdom to attain the ultimate fruit—one takes these deluded conceptions to be Dry Wisdom itself.
Thus, there appears to be both awakening and delusion; but when one reaches the stage of Dry Wisdom and looks back upon those deluded conceptions, one feels regret.
Not abiding [in the truth], one may still appear to concede what they have not yet attained; only then does one realize that delusion is not easily overcome.
Awakening within delusion is like encountering a wooden tortoise; delusion within awakening is like laboring to avoid one's own shadow.
The ultimate fruit is likewise so. Before reaching the ultimate fruit, dry wisdom serves as the cause; by showing the cause through the fruit, it is right before one's eyes.

Yet, if one looks toward the fruit from the standpoint of the cause, one merely wanders aimlessly outside the mind. Sharpen the blade of the sword of illusion to slay the six thieves of the *gandharva*-city;
cast the reflection of the moon in the water to merge with the empty clarity within the mirror. How could one know that the moon is originally...?
While in the heavens, the void was not a mirror for contemplation; one merely stared with unblinking eyes until, finally turning the head, one regretted it was too late.

Though one clearly knows the reason for this, there are times when one cannot avoid it. This is what is meant by "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*); it is only upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) that one realizes there is no other deceptive artifice.

Taking discursive thoughts to be dry wisdom is merely a matter of valuing self-knowledge; taking dry wisdom as [the ultimate]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

Awakening the mind must also involve reaching it directly through three stages of progressive advancement; how could one rely on questioning others? And through the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), who is it that awakens to Buddhahood?
Ultimately, it is the internal permeation of innate wisdom; when its power is exhausted, one sees for oneself.

Although one may reach the "flowing with the current" stage of the *bhūmis*, it is only at the ultimate Diamond Stage (*vajra*) that Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) first becomes perfected. By tracing back to the ultimate within the initial mind, one realizes the Buddha-mind.
Within the midst of manifold delusions, sentient beings achieve Buddhahood; only a Buddha knows that the Buddha is none other than sentient beings.
Sentient beings fail to realize this, but once they recognize it, they may thereafter be free from erroneous views.
The sixth section concludes the delineation of the stages from beginning to end for cultivation and realization. △ Seventh, the conclusion of the title of the sutra:
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named? How should I and all sentient beings uphold it?"
In this original sutra, there are four appearances of Mañjuśrī: first, he goes to provide protection while holding mantras; second, he asks questions to clarify two kinds of phenomena;
third, he commands the selection of those with the proper faculties; and now, he concludes the title of the sutra. This sutra emphasizes fundamental great wisdom (*mūla-mahājñāna*).

All sentient beings follow their sense-faculties (*indriya*) to grasp sensory objects (*viṣaya*); because they are deluded regarding fundamental wisdom, they give rise to inversion. To transform consciousness (*vijñāna*) into wisdom (*jñāna*) is the most [important].
Direct and straightforward. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Where there are afflictions, there is no wisdom; where there is wisdom, there are no afflictions.
It is not that wisdom destroys afflictions; rather, afflictions are themselves wisdom. To demonstrate this profound meaning, one must ultimately return to Mañjuśrī from beginning to end.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "This sutra is named 'The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śītata-Pāṇḍarā, the Unsurpassed Jewel Seal.
It is the pure ocean-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions."
The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally invisible; since its essence and its characteristics are non-dual, it is called the Buddha’s Crown (Uṣṇīṣa).
*Siddhārthapratara*, from which all Buddhas of the ten directions are born—this is the supreme jewel-seal of the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions possess the Great Dharma Eye herein; it is pure and unconditioned, with both essence and function fully perfected.
This principle is set forth at the outset and is also called "Protecting and Delivering One’s Karmic Causes," by which Ānanda and the bhikṣuṇī of this assembly were delivered and attained Bodhi.
"Focus the mind and enter the ocean of universal knowledge.
This is a designation established in reference to the perfection of compassion (*karuṇā-pāramitā*). Regarding "protecting and rescuing one's kinsmen and causes," the preceding text states:

"When the Tathāgata practices this mantra-heart, he is able to gather and sustain his kinsmen and causes throughout the ten directions, causing those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) who hear the secret treasury not to give rise to [fear or doubt]."
This is what is meant by "trembling with awe. Bodhicitta refers to true wisdom (*jñāna*). The ocean of universal knowledge is the ultimate truth of nirvāṇa.
To enter into this truth by means of wisdom constitutes the final consummation.
It is also titled *The Definitive Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization*.
"Cause" refers to the ground of original cultivation. This ground of original cultivation is neither born nor extinguished;

it is the secret of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), which cannot be known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. Cultivating in accordance with the nature, without falling into stages or gradations—this is the definitive meaning.
It is definitive in meaning, not provisional. This is the title established according to the persons and the Dharma.
It is also called the Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King, the Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions.

The essence of nature contains and encompasses the Dharma-realm; this is called "Great. It definitively establishes the path for both ordinary beings and sages, leading them all to the single road of Nirvana;
this is what the *Lotus Sūtra* refers to as "there is only the One Vehicle, and no second or third"—this is called "Square. From its essence, its function is manifested;

the provisional and the real are perfectly integrated, and the Great and the Small are equalized—this is called "Broad. The lotus flower and fruit are possessed simultaneously, serving as a metaphor for Buddha-nature and Nirvana, which exist together from the very beginning.
Its fruit-phase is all-pervasive; being purely and uniformly brilliant white, like a flower in full bloom, it is called "Wondrous. Being honored wherever it appears, it is called "King.
Being the source from which all Tathāgatas of the ten directions arise, it is called "Mother. Because the Śūraṅgama is the great dhāraṇī, it is called the "Dhāraṇī Mantra.
These names are derived according to its essential nature and its functions.
It is also called the "Mantra of Empowerment" (Abhiṣeka-pada). It is the Śūraṅgama of the ten thousand practices of all Bodhisattvas;
you should uphold it. Regarding this as a secret mantra, it is called the "Mantra of Empowerment.

For those who receive and uphold it, the Tathāgata shall empower their hearts and crowns with the water of wisdom, just as a Wheel-Turning King receives his office. From this, the ten thousand practices of the Bodhisattvas arise and find their fulfillment.
Ultimately firm and solid, all Tathāgatas and all Bodhisattvas together enter the ocean of self-nature awakening of Vairocana;
they conjoin the cause with the fruit, and thus it is named after its fruit. This sutra uniquely emphasizes the fundamental great wisdom (*mahājñāna*).
Within the gates of cultivation and realization, all are encompassed by the Perfect [Teaching]. Therefore, the Tathāgata specifically enjoined its upholding;
it should be propagated and disseminated for the sake of Bodhisattvas, just as with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. This may also serve as one proof. △ Eighth: Advancement through Hearing the Dharma.
Having spoken these words, Ānanda and the great assembly immediately received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the meaning of the secret seal, the *Paṭṭhāra*.
Furthermore, hearing the definitive titles of this sutra, they suddenly awakened to the sublime principles for advancing through the stages of holy cultivation in *dhyāna*.
Their minds became tranquil and concentrated, severing the six grades of subtle afflictions within the three realms that had been cultivated in their hearts.
The "secret seal" (mudrā) refers to this *pāṇḍarā*; it is the secret seal of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

"Definitive meaning" (nītārtha) refers to the realization and cultivation demonstrated in the preceding text; all of these are direct pointers to definitive meaning. Regarding the sublime wisdom of the Middle Way within *dhyāna*:
it means that by attaining this wisdom, one enters perfectly into ultimate truth, and all mental deliberations become stilled and tranquil. This is the sublime...
This is the verification of the abandonment and realization attained through wisdom; hence it is said that one abandons the six grades of subtle afflictions within the stage of cultivation.
Changqing said: "In accordance with the four fruits, each fruit is abandoned separately at its respective stage.

Therefore, within the body of the first fruit, one abandons the first six grades of the nine grades of afflictions belonging to the single stage of the desire realm, thereby realizing the second fruit. Within the body of the second fruit, one abandons the [remaining] lower three..."

[The practitioner] realizes the third fruit. Within the body of one who has attained the third fruit, having severed the seventy-two categories of afflictions belonging to the two upper realms, they immediately attain Arhatship.
Now, Ānanda has realized the second fruit; therefore, he has severed six categories. Although the principle is one of sudden awakening, the stages are realized gradually;
thus, the complete cultivation is also correlated with the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) accordingly.

The preceding three sections have concluded the broad exposition on the model of cultivation. △ Fourth, the detailed differentiation of karmic fruits and the precise elimination of demons and heterodoxies, divided into nine parts.
First, the inquiry into the fundamental nature of deluded habit-energies that give rise to the six realms of existence.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, your compassionate voice is all-encompassing; you have skillfully opened up the subtle, deep-seated delusions of sentient beings, causing my body and mind today to feel such joy and granting me great benefit.
World-Honored One, if this wondrously luminous, truly pure, and sublime mind is by nature universally pervasive and perfect, as..."

From the great earth, its grasses, trees, and wriggling insects, down to all sentient beings—these are fundamentally True Suchness (*tathatā*). This very True Suchness is the true essence of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood.
Since the Buddha-body is truly real, how can there further be such realms as hell, hungry ghosts, animals, *asuras*, humans, and devas?
World-Honored One, do these paths exist inherently from the beginning, or are they produced by the deluded habits of sentient beings?
"Arising.
"Opening up subtle delusions" refers precisely to the six grades of afflictions previously severed.

If this is the case, since one has first traced the wondrous mind as all-pervasive and perfect, and subsequently realized that the myriad dharmas are all true, there should not be a third [category] to arise.
Regarding the doubt as to whether the total emergence of the six paths of rebirth is due to what is originally inherent or due to the arising of delusive habituation:

one does not realize that these exist only when delusive vision exists and cease to exist when delusion is extinguished; thus, one cannot remain free from doubt regarding their existence simply because they appear to exist.

Furthermore, one must not allow that which is "existent" to obstruct that which is "non-existent. This constitutes the meaning of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*). Only thus can one begin to avoid erring in either awakening or cultivation.
△ Second, the question concerning the denial of existence, which leads eternally to a state of commonality and individual selfishness.
World-Honored One, it was like the bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā, who upheld the bodhisattva precepts yet privately engaged in sexual misconduct.
She falsely claimed that sexual conduct is neither killing nor stealing, and that there is no karmic retribution for it.

Having uttered these words, a great, fierce fire first broke out from her female organ, and subsequently, fierce fires burned through every joint of her body until she fell into the Avīci Hell. It was the same with King Virūḍhaka and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra.
"O Kṣatriya! Because Vimalacitra falsely preached that all phenomena are empty, he was executed by the Gautama clan and fell alive into the Avīci Hell.
As for these various hells, do they have fixed locations, or do they arise spontaneously? Each person generates their own karma and receives its retribution individually.
I pray that you will bestow great compassion and enlighten the ignorant, so that all those who uphold the precepts may understand."
Upon hearing the definitive meaning, they received it with joy and reverence, maintaining it with purity and without transgression.
The general intent of the question concerns whether there is a fixed location [for the reception of karma] or whether it occurs spontaneously;

for if each person generates karma and receives its retribution individually, one might suspect it is spontaneous and thus lack a fixed location. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Without severing the three types of karma, each..."
Each has its own private [cause]; because each has its own private [cause], the collective private [causes] share a common lot (*sabhāgatā*), and it is not that they lack a fixed location.
This is the meaning of the answer. It is unclear from what source the "Nun Ratnapadmagandhā" is derived. Jiaoguang says: "The offenses committed by the nun Ratnapadmagandhā were threefold:

first, committing sexual misconduct; second, slandering the precepts; and third, misleading others. These gradually reached the utmost gravity, and thus she fell into Avīci Hell. As for King Virūḍhaka:
The Sūtra says: "In the kingdom of Kāśī, there were five hundred elders of the noble Śākya clan who built a lecture hall for the World-Honored One.
They made a vow, saying: 'Neither śramaṇas nor brahmins, nor even the common people, shall ascend this hall before the Buddha.
Later, Prince Virūḍhaka of Śrāvastī, having become engaged to the daughter of a brahmin named Bhārgava, saw..."
The hall was high and spacious; [the Śākyas] took up residence upon it. A person of noble lineage scolded them, saying, "This offspring of a slave dares to sit within this place!
He drove them away, ordering them to leave. The Prince spoke to Bhadraka with great earnestness: "The Śākyas have brought such humiliation upon me. When I succeed to the throne, you must inform me.
Later, when he ascended the throne, Bhadraka came to inform him. He assembled his troops and attacked the country of Kāla, killing the Śākyas.
Three hundred million people. The Buddha said: "Seven days from now, you shall enter hell. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said, "The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, although he had studied the twelve divisions of the scriptures, destroyed the fetters of the desire realm, and attained the four dhyānas..."
They do not understand the meaning of even a single verse or a single phrase. They associate with evil friends and fall away from the four dhyānas.
Having fallen from meditative concentration, they give rise to evil and false views, speaking thus: "There is no Buddha, there is no Dharma, and there is no nirvāṇa."
Although the Tathāgata has indeed preached the Dharma for me, I truly maintain that there is no cause and no effect.
Now, while he was near the Nairañjanā River, the Tathāgata went with Kāśyapa to the place where Sunakṣatra was.
When Sunakṣatra saw the Buddha approaching from afar, he immediately conceived an evil and heterodox mind. Because of this evil mind, he fell alive into the Avīci Hell.
The Prison. △ Third, showing the internal and external divisions for sentient beings. This is divided into four parts. First, the general introduction:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "How excellent is this question! It will cause all sentient beings not to enter into false views. Listen attentively now."
I shall explain this for you.
The evil view of Śubhavyūha, who denied cause and effect by pointing to a jewel-lotus, was like that of Rāvaṇa, who saw the Buddha’s lecture hall and dared to enter it first.
Upon hearing these words, he did not repent, but instead gave rise to even greater anger; such a person is an icchantika and possesses an evil view as well.
Ānanda, all sentient beings are in truth originally true and pure. Due to that deluded vision, deluded habits arise;
because of this, they distinguish between the internal and the external.
The true nature is fundamentally pure. Through deluded perception, afflictions arise; due to afflictions, karma is created, thereby giving rise to deluded habits.

With afflictions and karma as causes, these constitute the "internal portion. Conversely, the opposite constitutes the "external portion," as will be explained in detail below. △ Second, the internal portion.
Ānanda, the internal constituent is the very essence of sentient beings. Due to various attachments and defilements, deluded sentiments are aroused;
as these sentiments accumulate without ceasing, they are able to produce the water of craving. Therefore, when sentient beings think of delicacies, water flows from their mouths;

when they think of others, whether with pity or resentment, tears fill their eyes; when they greedily seek wealth and treasures, saliva of craving issues forth from their hearts, and their entire bodies [tremble].

Glossy and moist, the mind becomes attached and engages in sexual conduct; from the two organs of male and female, fluids naturally flow. Ānanda, although various cravings differ, their outflowing fetters are the same.
Moistened and unable to rise, they naturally fall downward; this is called the "internal constituent."

Sentient beings, following the deluded vision of ignorance, bind themselves into the substance of a self. Thereupon, there arise opposition and compliance. Compliance with the self gives rise to attachment;
when that which harms the self harms the attachment, anger arises. This anger is also rooted in attachment; therefore, attachment is the foundation of emotion.

For this reason, it is called the "internal division," meaning that which exists within the domain of sentient beings. When the faculties of emotion become dense and heavy, principle must inevitably fall away, like water.

It also flows downward; this can be understood through the facts themselves. When emotional attachment is not severed, it is like a flowing stream; when one is dragged along and bound by oneself, it is like a knot. △ Third, the external factors.
Ānanda, the external factors are those beyond the sphere of sentient beings. Due to various forms of longing and thirst, they give rise to empty conceptions. These conceptions accumulate...
Without ceasing, one can generate a superior spirit. Therefore, when sentient beings maintain the prohibitive precepts in their minds, their entire bodies become light and pure;

when they maintain mantras and mudrās in their minds, their gaze becomes heroic and resolute; when they desire to be born in the heavens, they dream of soaring upward; when they fix their minds on the Buddha-lands, sacred realms manifest in the darkness;

and when they serve spiritual friends, they regard their own bodies and lives as insignificant. Ānanda, although these various thoughts differ, their shared quality of lightness and elevation is the same.
Soaring and moving without sinking, it naturally transcends; this is called the "external division" (bāhya-bhāga).

Sentient beings cling to a self, their thoughts stirring in accordance with their emotions; this [state] does not follow emotion, yet it gives rise to thirsty longing externally, hence it is called the "external division.

It must surely accord with principle (*li*); in contrast to emotion, which is substantial, it is termed "empty. Because the vital energy (*qi*) prevails through principle, it gives rise to "superiority" (*sheng*).
Qi. Lightness, clarity, vigor, resoluteness, soaring flight, and manifesting in the dark while lightening the body—all these are signs of the mind’s contemplation of superior empty qi.
△ Fourth, the specific transformation of emotional thoughts into heaviness, divided into eight parts. First, pure thought.
Ānanda, throughout all worlds, birth and death continue in succession. Birth proceeds from habitual tendencies; death proceeds from the flux of transformation.
At the moment of the end of life, before warmth and sensation have departed, the good and evil of one’s entire lifetime manifest simultaneously. Death is contrary while birth is conformable;
these two habits intersect.
Sentient beings cling to a self, regarding it as their mind and their essence. Because this is what they have practiced throughout their lives, birth is seen as conformity and death as change;

that is to say, death is called "change" because it reverses what has been habitually practiced. Before the warmth and tactile sensation are abandoned, one is at the end of the present *skandhas* and the beginning of the intermediate [state] and the subsequent *skandhas*.
Regarding these two types of practice: the preceding consciousness constitutes the former habit, while the subsequent consciousness constitutes...

At this very moment of new training, the good and evil deeds performed in this present life and the resulting states of elevation or decline experienced in future lives appear before one in an instant,
like seeing the events of a dream upon waking.

If one’s thoughts are purely focused on flight, one will certainly be reborn in the heavens. If, within the mind of flight, there is both merit and wisdom, as well as pure vows, the mind will spontaneously open to perceive the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the pure lands; one will then be reborn therein according to one's vows.
That those with purely conceptual thoughts are reborn in the heavens is the general rule.

Now, regarding those who possess purely conceptual thoughts combined with merit and wisdom and aspire to be born in a Buddha-land, one must know that although they combine merit and wisdom, if they lack the power of aspiration, they will not yet succeed in being born in a Buddha-land.
Sentient beings are born through karma; Bodhisattvas are born through aspiration. Thus, aspiration is indeed indispensable. △ Second, Sentimental Thought.
If their thoughts are few and their emotions are few, yet their thoughts are many, they will possess the power of light flight without traveling far;

they shall become flying immortals, powerful ghost-kings, flying yakṣas, or earth-walking rākṣasas, roaming through the four heavens with unimpeded movement wherever they go. Among them, if there are those with virtuous vows and virtuous minds, [they shall attain further progress].

They shall protect and uphold my Dharma; some shall protect the prohibitive precepts in accordance with those who observe them, some shall protect divine mantras in accordance with those who recite them, and some shall protect meditative concentration, preserving and sustaining the patience of the Dharma.
These individuals shall dwell intimately beneath the seat of the Tathāgata.

When emotion is slight and thought is predominant, one can fly upward but not for a great distance. This is stated in general terms; within it, there must be degrees of difference according to whether one possesses one, two, three, or four [elements].

If one separately opens up the gates of wholesome vows and a wholesome mind, then these are merely matters of comparing the relative abundance or scarcity of these qualities, and do not fall within this specific category.
△ Third: When emotion and thought are equal.

When emotion (*kleśa*) and thought (*saṃjñā*) are equal, one neither flies nor falls, but is born among human beings. When thought is clear, one is intelligent; when emotion is deep, one is dull-witted.

This clarity and intelligence, or depth and dullness, are each distinguished within the respective states of emotion and thought. Thus, even though the thought is the same, this [difference] arises from the predominance of the specific factor (*vastu*).

Since he excels through principle, his clarity in entering into principle must necessarily rely upon intelligence and wisdom. Though they share the same human nature, while this one indulges in affection and love, that one is devoted to the treacherous and dark;
thus, the profound depths of such guile and deceit must inevitably evoke dullness and obscurity. △ Fourth, those with much emotion and little thought.
When passion is excessive and reason is meager, one flows into the realm of horizontal birth. There, one becomes heavy as a member of the furred tribes or light as a member of the feathered clans.
Both the furred and the feathered possess the same six sense-faculties; what is referred to as "heavy" or "light" is merely a comparative assessment among these six.
Within the aforementioned state where feelings and thoughts are equal, there are likewise distinctions between the clear-witted and the dull-witted.
△ Five: Seven Feelings and Three Thoughts.
With seven feelings and three thoughts, one sinks down to the water-wheel and is born at the boundary of fire. Receiving the energy of fierce flames, one takes the body of a hungry ghost (*preta*).
They are constantly being burned. Water can harm them; for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they have neither food nor drink.
They sink down into the water-wheel and are born at the limit of fire—meaning, beneath the water-wheel, there is the limit of the fire-wheel, situated near the hells.
This class of beings belongs to those governed by Yama; they are born from the influence of fire, and their bodies depend upon the midst of fire. For...
It is ablaze with fire. Even if one obtains water to drink, it transforms into fire; thus, there is the calamity of water. △ Sixth: Nine feelings and one perception.

With nine feelings and one perception, one descends through the wheel of fire and enters the wind-fire. As these two intersect, one passes over the ground and is reborn lightly in the *Avīci* (Without Interval) hell.
They are reborn in two kinds of Avīci hells where wind and fire intersect;
this is the seventh hot hell. This "Avīci" is spoken of in contrast to the "Sāntara" (intermittent) hells, as the suffering experienced here is somewhat more severe than that of the lower Abhīci.
△ Seventh: those whose nature is purely emotional, combined with slander, and so forth.

Pure attachment leads directly to sinking into the Avīci Hell. If one sinks into the mind, there will be slandering of the Mahāyāna, violating the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, speaking deceptive and false teachings, vainly coveting offerings of faith, and unworthily receiving respect;
for these five heinous crimes and ten grave offenses, one is reborn in the Avīci Hells throughout the ten directions.

These [beings] reside perpetually within the path of Avīci. They are distinguished by four types: those who slander the Dharma, those who violate prohibitions, those who engage in false speech, and those who misappropriate offerings.

These are separately assigned to the ten directions rather than being restricted to a single direction; thus, the kalpas of their formation and destruction are each distinct, and they remain for an extremely long duration, making escape difficult.
△ Eighth: Concluding the commonality while distinguishing individual cases.

Following the commission of evil karma, although one invites retribution for oneself, within the *nikāya-sabhāga* (the commonality of sentient beings), there is also the "original ground" (*mūla-bhūmi*).

Each person creates their own selfish actions and receives a corresponding *sabhāga*. This answers the question regarding the fixed location of retribution; the original ground is precisely that fixed location.
Sentiment and thought are both of the mind; how can one speak of "internal" and "external"? If you consider sentiment to be within the realm of sentient beings, then thought must likewise be so.
If all worldly virtuous deeds do not arise from the fundamental mind, then since the cause is not true, how can the fruit be attained?
It is said: This arises because sentient beings delusively perceive a self. From this delusive perception of a self, they perceive a mind of self and perceive a body of self.
Following this delusive body and mind, every thought and every action is nothing other than for the sake of themselves; therefore, sentient beings create evil.

This is what constitutes true evil. When sentient beings perform good deeds, these are not yet true goodness. This is because evil necessarily pursues private interests and accords with the deluded self;
for this reason, it is considered "true. Goodness, however, follows the public good and has no concern for oneself; thus, it is easily mistaken for hypocrisy.

If the sages and worthies of the world do not, through the illumination of their original nature, attain the true mind of the source, and from that true mind of the source give rise to wholesome karma—then if one examines the origins of such things, they are not easily fathomed or scrutinized. Therefore, there is the exertion of diligent cultivation;

yet even if one slightly transcends [attachment to] body and reputation, it remains a manifestation of the skillful compliance with the deluded self. Why is this? Because the true nature is without...

If I were to clarify this point: when function arises based on the nature (*dharmatā*), all things and human affairs are seen through as a single essence, such that there is no further intention to pursue fame.
Thus one knows that the emotions of sentient beings are the true reality, arising from the deluded self (*ātman*).
Because they all follow the self, thoughts that aspire toward the good all serve to diminish the self. If one can take these thoughts that diminish the self and turn them [toward the Way]...
When one’s compliance with my nature increases by one part, the damage [to it] is reduced by that same one part;
as the perception of harm to me becomes ever clearer, the compliance with my nature becomes increasingly inferior. What begins through effort eventually proceeds to spontaneity.
By this means, when compared to the karma of those whose nature is compliant, although their origins differ, their efficacy is exactly equal. This is the state of the various heavens of pure thought.

This is for the sake of boundless radiance. When merit reaches its peak, wisdom arises; one may experience the opening of the mind and behold the Buddhas of the ten directions, or encounter virtuous friends through whose skillful means one attains awakening and clarity.
Thus, by following these reflections, one gives rise to the truth—who then could say it is false?

The above three sections have concluded the demonstration of the internal and external divisions for sentient beings. △ Fourth, the demonstration of the ten causes of habitual practice and the sixfold mutual retribution, divided into six parts.
First, the general heading:
"Ānanda, all these are what those sentient beings have experienced as the result of their own karma; they created the ten causes of habitual practice and received the six..."
"Mutual retribution.

These [categories] follow upon the preceding distinctions regarding the degree of emotional conceptualization (*saṃjñā*); they are all evoked by the individual karma of sentient beings and do not exist as actual realms of retribution external to the mind.
The "ten habitual practices" and "six mutual interactions" are presented in terms of evil karma to demonstrate both their general and specific aspects.
△ Second, the correct exposition of the ten causes of habituation (*daśa-vāsanā-hetu*). This is divided into ten parts. First, the habituation of lust. What are the ten causes?
Suffering and bondage give rise to delusion and karma; these are designated as "causes. These causes culminate in ten, which exhaust all evil fruits. Ten.
Among these causes, only sexual desire constitutes physical karma; the rest are all mental and verbal.
Ānanda, first, the habit of sexual desire involves mutual contact, arising from friction. This grinding continues without ceasing, and thus a great, fierce fire is ignited within.
It is like two people rubbing their hands together: the sensation of warmth immediately appears before them.

This refers to the mutual friction between the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) as the cause for the arousal of karma. "Interacting" specifically indicates the meeting of the organ and its object.

That this friction produces fire, which moves the mind and responds within the physical body, is illustrated by the analogy of one's own hand; this is merely to make the phenomenon of heat easily perceived.
The two habits mutually ignite one another; thus there arise such things as iron beds and copper pillars.
It is precisely because these two habits mutually ignite one another that the principle of the inevitable occurrence of action and its reception is established.

The body touched by the copper and iron serves as the faculty (*indriya*), while the copper and iron experienced as touch serve as the object (*viṣaya*). Faculty and object are non-dual, yet cause and effect remain distinct and clear.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate sexual misconduct by the same name: the Fire of Desire. When Bodhisattvas encounter desire, they avoid it as they would a pit of fire.

"Designating by color" (se-mu) means naming based on color and naming color based on the designation; thus it is said that sexual misconduct is designated by the term "color. They are given the same name.

Regarding the fire of desire: one should know that for the Tathāgata, the faculties and their objects lack the characteristics of faculties and objects. The following sections are all to be understood by this analogy.
The Bodhisattva deeply understands the causes of desire and further serves as a mirror for practitioners to observe and maintain detachment. △ Second, the habit-energy of greed.
Second, the habit-energy of greed intermingles with calculations, giving rise to mutual attraction. This attraction and grasping do not cease;
thus, there is accumulated cold and solid ice, freezing and chilling within. It is like a person drawing in wind through the mouth, whereby a sensation of cold arises.
As these two habits mutually oppress one another, there arise such phenomena as the *ṭa-ṭa*, *pa-pa*, and *ra-ra* hells, and the blue, red, and white lotus cold-hells. Therefore...
All Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate excessive seeking by the same name: "the water of greed. When Bodhisattvas perceive greed, they avoid it as they would a miasmic sea.

Within the category of greed, sexual desire is separately identified to demonstrate its extreme gravity; therefore, this specific instance of greed refers exclusively to material wealth. Thus it is reckoned.

This refers to calculation and the frantic pursuit resulting from such calculation, which carries the sense of grasping at and absorbing external objects. One clings firmly to this mind until it becomes like water turning to ice.
By discerning the causes, one knows the results; thus there are the eight cold hells. These two habits mutually oppress one another, and none of this is caused by anything else.
3. The Habit of Pride.
Third, the habit-energy of pride intermingles and overcomes one another, arising from mutual reliance; it flows and surges without ceasing.
Because of this, there is the leaping and rushing of waves, which accumulate to form water. It is like the mouth and tongue tasting each other’s flavors, whereby water is produced.

As these two habits strike against one another, there arise such phenomena as rivers of blood, rivers of ash, seas of hot sand and poison, and the pouring and swallowing of molten copper. Therefore...
All Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate pride as "drinking the water of delusion. When a Bodhisattva perceives pride, they avoid it as if fleeing from a great abyss.
Arrogance, contempt, and humiliation arise from a heart of self-reliance, such as relying on power or relying on fame; all of these involve galloping and leaping about.
Such is its appearance; this is precisely what is evoked by the River of Blood and the like.

In the original text, the analogy of "the flavor of cotton on the tongue" was intended to signify a state of lofty self-attainment, yet it has resulted in a flowery excess that must be cautioned against. △ Fourth, the habit-energy of anger.

Fourth, the habit-energy of anger clashes and conflicts. It arises from mutual opposition; this opposition knots together without ceasing, heating the mind until it emits fire and forging the vital breath into metal.

For this reason, there exist mountains of knives, iron spikes, sword-trees, wheels of swords, axes, halberds, spears, and saws. Like a person harboring a grievance, the murderous energy flies and stirs;
as these two habit-energies strike one another, there arise punishments such as castration, dismemberment, decapitation, hacking, mincing, piercing, and beating with mallets.
For all these reasons, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate anger as the "sharp sword.
When Bodhisattvas see anger, they avoid it as they would an execution.
Because of resentment and binding, the mind of binding becomes gold. The two habits of internal and external interact and stimulate one another;
what was originally created by oneself returns to be experienced by oneself. △ Fifth, the habit of deception.

Fifth is the habit of deceitful association and seduction, which arises from mutual flattery and incites incessant entanglement. Because of this, there are ropes, wooden stocks, strangulation, and cross-examination;

just as water soaking a field causes grass and trees to grow, so too do these two habits perpetuate one another, resulting in the various matters of cuffs, shackles, pillories, locks, whips, staves, clubs, and maces.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize such craftiness and falsehood with the same name: [the hell of] *Kālasūtra* (Black Rope).
Slanderers and malevolent thieves—when a Bodhisattva perceives such deceit, they fear them as if they were jackals and wolves.
Their mutual inducements possess the power of mockery and entrapment; therefore, all that [the Bodhisattva] receives is what they have bestowed.
It is like water soaking a field, causing grasses and trees to grow; this also describes how their practice of fraud and flattery involves the mind’s proliferation like creeping vines.
The sentiments of sentient beings reach their ultimate limit here. △ Sixth, the habit of deception.
Sixth, the habit of deception involves mutual cheating, arising from the intent to outwit one another. When such fraudulent delusion does not cease, the mind flies off to create villainy.
For this reason, there exist dust, excrement, urine, filth, and impurities, like dust carried by the wind, where each person sees nothing at all. These are the two habits.
These combine; therefore, there occur various events such as drowning, leaping, flying, falling, drifting, and sinking.

For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate deception with the same name as "killing by calamity" (*kalpa-vadha*). When a Bodhisattva sees deception, they regard it as treading upon a venomous snake or viper.

Deception belongs to the category of delusion (*moha*). A mind of falsehood and delusion is composed of many mixed elements; it shifts and transforms, floating and sinking like water tossed by the wind.
This is what brings about drowning or being cast down from flight. The soaring mind follows the wind; one must fully comprehend its various manifestations.
Each has nothing to see; thus, they delude others and delude themselves, remaining simply in a state of non-awakening. △ Seventh, the habit-energy of resentment.

Seventh, the habit-energy of resentment arises from mutual loathing, triggered by harbored hatred. For this reason, there are flying stones, thrown rocks, coffins, carriage enclosures, jars, and bags used for crushing.
It is like a person of hidden malice who harbors and nurtures evil within; as these two habits swallow one another, there are [such phenomena].
Because they engage in such acts as hurling, seizing, striking, shooting, tossing, and snatching, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate the enemy as a "hostile and harmful ghost" (*vighna*).
When a Bodhisattva sees an enemy, it is as if he were drinking poisoned wine.
When resentment turns into vengeance, every kind of treachery is prepared; its calamities will surely culminate in matters such as flying stones and caged carts.
Throwing, seizing, and capturing—these are all that one desires to inflict upon others, yet they now manifest before one's very eyes.
Should sentient beings not feel remorse for this? The "Violent Harm" spirits constantly lie in wait to seize people. [The poison] *zhèn*...
The name of a bird: its feathers and plumage, when dipped in wine, can all kill a person. △ Eighth, the habit-energy of views.

Eighth, the mutual illumination of the habit-energy of views: such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the grasping at precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and various karmas born of false awakening.

These arise from opposition and produce contrary results. For this reason, there are kings, messengers, officials, and clerks who testify to and seize upon written records, just as in the case of legal proceedings.

Passersby meet one another on their way; as these two habits intersect, there arise interrogation, deception, cross-examination, investigation, scrutiny, inquiry, and the illumination of good and evil.
The youth holds a ledger in his hand and eloquently distinguishes all that exists.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate this evil view with the same name: the Pit of Views. When Bodhisattvas perceive all such delusions...
Pervasive Clinging. It is like standing on the brink of a precipice filled with poison.

Regarding wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), there are five types: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which clings to "I" and "mine"; second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which clings to permanence or nihilism;
third, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which is a mistaken understanding that denies cause and effect; fourth, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which refers to all... [text continues].
Regarding various views: to regard what is not a cause as a cause, or what is not a result as a result, and to cling to these as supreme, thereby severing wisdom;

this is the clinging to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). To cling to one’s own precepts and meditative concentrations—or even to false precepts and concentrations—and to claim them to be supreme;

all such views hold that "this is correct and that is wrong," and are thus called "contradictory and opposed. Consequently, they give rise to all manner of interrogations, examinations, and karmic retributions.
△ Ninth, the habituation of injustice.

"Nine" refers to the intermingling of habits of injustice, which arise from slander and false accusations. Because of this, there are mountains joined together and stones joined together that crush, grind, plow, and rub [the beings].
Just as a slanderous thief coerces and wrongs the virtuous, these two habits push against one another; therefore, there is pressing down, crushing, beating, and squeezing.
In all matters of weighing and measuring, this is the case; therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate slander and calumny as the "Tiger of Slander.
When a Bodhisattva encounters such injustice, it is like being struck by a bolt of lightning.
"False accusation" (誣謗) means to wrongfully charge someone with what was not actually done; it refers to slandering and harassing the virtuous, like a malicious thief.
The various realms of mountains and stones are all manifestations produced by such wrongful harassment. When one is completely oppressed, then all these phenomena appear.
"Squeezing and straining" (蹙漉) refers to being pressed until blood flows out. "Measuring" (衡度) is like being measured while passing through a narrow opening.
As for the person themselves: slanderous tigers and slanderous beasts can harm others; they are even more cruel than tigers. △ Tenth, the habit of litigation:

this tenth refers to the habit of litigation within social relations, which arises from concealment and hypocrisy. Because of this, there is a mirror-like vision that illuminates and shines forth, as if in the midst of the sun where one cannot hide one's shadow.
As these two habits are laid bare before one another, there are evil companions, the karma-mirror, and the fire-pearl that reveal all.
Because past karma manifests in various ways as retributive experiences, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate concealment with the same name:
"the hidden thief. When a Bodhisattva contemplates concealment, it is as if they were carrying a mountain upon their head while treading upon a vast ocean.
The habit of litigation is rooted in concealment. Yet, one's own mind is not oblivious; it will inevitably give rise to doubt and regret.

Since the mind inherently possesses the function of discernment and illumination, there is the fruit of the "karmic mirror" for evil associates. Being unable to manifest this oneself is called a "hidden thief.
To carry mountains upon one's head and tread upon the sea is merely enough to crush oneself.
The above two sections conclude the formal presentation of the ten causes of habitual practice. △ Third, the general enumeration of the six retributions.
What are the six retributions? Ānanda, all sentient beings create karma through the six consciousnesses; the evil retributions they thereby attract emerge from the six sense organs.
Karma is fundamentally created by consciousness (*vijñāna*). It initially emerges from the six sense organs and returns to be experienced through the six sense organs;

hence it is called "retribution" (*vipāka*). What is created by one organ is experienced by all six; what is created by one is experienced by another, and what is created by another is experienced by this one;

hence it is called "interchange" (*saṃsarga*). Karma arises entirely from the mind, whereas retribution is mostly discussed in terms of form (*rūpa*). Yet, how could the mind not know that which is experienced by form? Furthermore, in the present life...
The color [of the former] differs from that of later births; since it must be a transformation of consciousness, one knows that all color is mind.
△ Fourth, the correct demonstration of the six retributions, divided into six parts. First, the retribution of seeing.
How is it that retribution for evil emerges from the six sense organs? First is the retribution of seeing, which invites and draws forth evil fruits.

When this karma of seeing intersects with other conditions, at the time of death, one first sees fierce fires filling the worlds of the ten directions; the departed consciousness flies and falls, riding upon the smoke.
They enter the Avīci Hell, where two aspects of perception arise. First is clear vision:
they see all manner of evil things everywhere, giving rise to immeasurable fear. Second is dark vision: in total silence nothing is seen, giving rise to immeasurable dread. Thus they perceive fire.
When it burns the ears, it becomes boiling cauldrons and molten copper; when it burns the nose, it becomes black smoke and purple flames;

when it burns the tongue, it becomes scorched pellets and iron gruel; when it burns the body, it becomes hot ashes, furnaces, and charcoal; when it burns the mind, it produces sparks that scatter and fly about.
The empty realm is stirred by the drum of karma;
all karma arises from consciousness. Being drawn forth by the eye, it becomes the karma of seeing; thus, one experiences the vision of fire at the moment of death.

Taking the apprehension of form by the eye as the cause, the sight of fierce flames by the eye constitutes the retribution. Since this retribution is summoned by the eye, it pervades the five [aggregates].

The faculties are likewise like a single root returning to its source, whereby the six faculties become pure. Whether awakening or delusion, truth or falsehood, they are ultimately not two separate paths.
Brightness and darkness both belong to the realm of seeing; once the karma of seeing is fully exhausted, all objects of sight are nothing but bonds of suffering.
Consequently, they burn their hearing, burn their smelling, burn their tasting, burn their touching, and burn their minds.

Initially, what was produced by a single faculty was experienced as false pleasure by all five faculties; now, what is retribution for a single faculty is experienced as false suffering by all five faculties.
Both suffering and pleasure are illusory; there is simply no way to escape them. 2. Hearing the Retribution.

Second is the retribution of hearing. This hearing of karma invites and draws forth evil fruits. When this karmic hearing intersects, at the moment of death, one first sees waves and surges that submerge heaven and earth.
The deceased’s consciousness descends and follows the current, entering the Avīci Hell. Thus two signs are manifested.

First is "listening with openness," wherein one hears various clamors and the spirit becomes confused and disordered. Second is "listening with closure," wherein there is silence and nothing is heard, and the dark soul sinks into oblivion.
Thus, when the waves of hearing pour forth, they can act as reprimands and interrogations;

when the waves of seeing pour forth, they can act as thunder and roars, serving as noxious vapors; when the waves of breathing pour forth, they can act as rain and mist, drenching all venomous insects.
When it permeates the entire body, if the flavor-element (*rasa-dhātu*) is infused, it can become pus and blood, as well as various kinds of filth;

if the touch-element (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*) is infused, it can become animals or ghosts, or excrement and urine; if the mind-element (*manas-dhātu*) is infused, it can become lightning and hail, crushing the heart and soul.
The sound of waves is the most vast and immense of all sounds; thus, what is summoned by one's karmic retribution first manifests as being submerged and drowned.

Wēnlíng says: "If hearing and seeing are reversed and restored, then water cannot drown one. Relying on this [perception] to create karma can evoke waves and surges—this too is a case of karmic coincidence.
The roar of thunder and poisonous vapors are not visible objects, yet they likewise cause the eyes to become terrified and frantic.

One must not be overly mired in literalism. Rain, mist, and venomous insects—upon hearing of them, they transform through the waves of vapor; all possess foul odors that correspond to the sense of smell.
Domestic animals, ghosts, and yin-natured beings, along with lightning, hail, rain, and thunder, are all manifestations of dark obscurity and turbulent surging.
What is experienced as a result of karmic actions through smelling does not fall outside this category. Third, the retribution of smelling:
this invites and draws forth evil fruits. When the karma of smelling intersects with these conditions, at the time of death, one first sees poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings.
The deceased’s consciousness surges up from the earth and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two distinct appearances.

First is "pervasive hearing": being permeated by various evil vapors, the mind becomes extremely agitated. Second is "obstructed hearing": the vapors block and do not pass through, causing one to faint upon the ground.
When such vapors strike the breath, they can become matter or footwear; when they strike the sight, they can become fire or torches;
when they strike the hearing, they can cause one to sink or drown, or to boil and bubble; when they strike the sense of taste, they can...
It causes hunger and exhaustion; upon being struck, it can cause tearing and rotting, becoming a great mountain of flesh with hundreds of thousands of eyes that insatiably devour.
Upon being struck by thought, it can become ash and miasma, or flying sand and gravel, shattering the body.
It wells up from the earth; because the vapor rises upward from below, it is "substantial" (obstructive), while "treading" (stepping) refers to penetration.

This corresponds to the two aspects of hearing being open and hearing being blocked. When vision belongs to fire, its surging forth becomes a torch; when hearing belongs to water, its surging forth becomes drowning.

As flavor changes according to the vapor, it becomes either putrid or fresh. As the body receives the熏 (xūn—pervasive influence) of the vapor, it becomes either cracked or... [the text is incomplete].
Decayed. When thought is obstructed by the breath, it becomes ash-like miasma or flying sand;
in sum, when the single faculty undergoes retribution, the five faculties become disturbed and manifest according to their respective types. △ Fourth, the retribution of taste.
Fourth is the retribution for [craving] flavors. This karma of flavors draws forth evil fruits;

when such karmic actions intersect, at the time of death, one first sees an iron net with fierce, blazing flames completely covering the world. The deceased’s consciousness passes through this iron net, and its head hangs upside down.
They enter the Avīci Hell, where two manifestations arise: first, their inhalation forms freezing ice that freezes and cracks their flesh;

second, their exhalation flies up as fierce fire that burns and rots their marrow and bones. Thus, when they taste flavors, through repeated tasting, these [manifestations] can become their support and their endurance;
when they see sights, through repeated seeing, they can become burning gold and stone; when they hear sounds, through repeated hearing, they can become sharp weapons.
When it passes through the breath, it can become a great iron cage that covers the entire land. When it passes through the touch, it can become bows and arrows, crossbows and projectiles.
When it passes through the thought, it can become flying red-hot iron raining down from the sky.
Craving flavors, one is caught in a net and burned; all those with feathers, scales, or shells receive their retribution exactly as they sowed the cause.
There is not the slightest discrepancy in what is received. To "receive" (承領) means to accept or endure. Whatever things have been endured by me, I now receive them all.
As one traverses through the various sense faculties, there is nothing that does not involve the grasping of objects out of craving for flavors. This is the retribution.
How skillful [is this]! △ Fifth, the retribution of contact.
Fifth is the retribution of contact, which draws forth evil fruits. When this karma of contact intersects, at the time of death, one first sees a great mountain.

The four directions close together, leaving no further way out. The deceased’s consciousness sees a great iron city, where fire-snakes, fire-dogs, tigers, wolves, and lions, along with ox-headed hell-wardens and horse-headed rākṣasas, brandishing spears and lances, drive them through the city gates.
Heading toward the Avīci Hell, two manifestations arise: first, contact through conjunction, where mountains press against the body, crushing bone, flesh, and blood;

second, contact through separation, where knives and swords strike the body, hacking and tearing the heart and liver. Such contact through conjunction, when experienced, can become the Way and contemplation, the hall and the desk;
such experience through seeing can become burning and scorching; and such experience through hearing can likewise [become...]
As for striking and hitting, thrusting and shooting—when experienced through the breath, they can become the act of encasing and the act of bagging, the act of examining and the act of binding.

As for tasting—when experienced through the breath, they can become the act of plowing and the act of tongs, the act of hacking and the act of severing. As for thinking—when experienced through the breath, they can become the act of falling and the act of flying.
They are roasted and grilled.
Touch has two characteristics: separation and union. When there is union, the touch joins and presses against the body; when there is separation, the touch parts from the body.
The paths one follows lead to the hells. One observes the gates and towers of the hell-king, as well as the halls and desks, all of which are places for the punishment of offenders.

The remainder can be understood from the text. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "This contact (*sparśa*) is the primary cause for the arising of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the root that binds the mind.
Why is this? While the other four sense-faculties each occupy their own respective domains, this [contact] pervades the consciousness of the entire body."
Because the place of birth is vast, many develop defiled attachments; because these are difficult to relinquish, they frequently commit grave offenses.
If they fall into hell, there are two divisions: first, the Cold Ice Hell, and second, the Blazing Fire Hell.
In both of these, one undergoes punishment through bodily contact, with myriad forms of bitter suffering. This contact is called the Great Dark Place, a perilous and treacherous path.
△ Sixth, the retribution of volition.

"Six" refers to the retribution of volition that draws forth evil fruits. When this karma of volition intersects with other conditions, at the time of death, one first sees an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land.
The deceased’s spirit-consciousness is blown upward into the air, then whirled down by the wind and falls into the Avīci Hell.
This elucidates two aspects. First is non-awakening: when delusion reaches its extreme, one becomes desolate, running about without ceasing.
Second is non-delusion: when awakening occurs, there is suffering; one is scorched by immeasurable heat, the pain so profound it is difficult to endure.
Such false thoughts and bound thoughts can act as the "direction" and the "object. Bound views can act as the "mirror" and the "witness. Bound hearing can act as the "great clapper-stone."
It becomes ice and frost; it becomes earth and mist. When the breath is bound, it can become great fire-carts, fire-boats, and fire-barriers.
When the taste is bound, it can become great wailing, regret, and weeping. When the touch is bound, it can become great or small.
Within a single day, one undergoes ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths; one is prone and supine as mental formations arise and perish.
Because the body disintegrates, one perceives the collapse of the realms. Furthermore, mental formations are as fleeting as the wind;
when the warmth and tactile sensation are abandoned, the winds of karma sweep them away. Mental formations perceive this first; were they not aware, there would be nothing but a desolate wilderness.
Accordingly, when one awakens, various sufferings assail one simultaneously. Sentient beings do not recognize their own minds and flow along with the currents of their thoughts;
their karmic consciousness is vast and茫然 (vast/uncertain), and while no retribution has yet arrived, they possess no autonomy—how much less so when the retribution actually arrives?

This is precisely the place where one undergoes punishment. Wēnlíng says: "To bind and listen constitutes the 'Great Convergence' and so forth; it is the mutual resonance of water and earth. The carriage...
The railing of the boat is merely the cessation of breath; it is what is transformed by turbulent thoughts. When one touches the tongue-root, it is there that sound originates.
All that follows regarding "large" and "small" refers to the body; these are but turbulent thoughts manifested through the karma of touch, appearing as nothing more than illusory projections.

The above four sections have completed the explicit demonstration of the six retributions. △ Fifth, the conclusion regarding the completeness or deficiency of causes and retributions, answering again the question of creating a commonality through individual actions:
"Ānanda, these are called the ten causes and six fruits of the hells; they are all created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings."

Contemplate this single phrase: "That which is created by delusion exhausts all causes and retributions, yet neither is truly existent. One is deluded regarding one's own fundamental mind and falsely perceives external objects;
thus, afflictions arise and karma is created, just as in a dream. One should realize this immediately, awakening from the dream.
All that appears before one is merely the residual vestige of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
If there are sentient beings who collectively commit evil karma and enter the Avīci Hell to undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas,

yet each of their six sense faculties has individually committed [evil], as well as those acts involving both objects and faculties, such persons shall enter the Eight Uninterrupted Hells (Aṣṭāvīcika).

Ten causes and six retributions, involving both faculties and objects, are termed "jointly created. Because the suffering of this Avīci hell and its duration in kalpas are both called "immeasurable," it differs from the [other] Uninterrupted (ānantarya) hells.
Those who create [karma] individually certainly differ in timing; their causes also have intervals.
Although they involve both faculties and objects, within the eight Uninterrupted hells, both the suffering and the kalpas are reduced.
If one commits killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the three [faculties] of body, speech, and mind, such a person enters the eighteen hells.
If the three karmas are not all committed together, but one commits either one instance of killing or one instance of stealing in between, such a person enters the thirty-six hells.
If one perceives each sense-base individually and violates only a single karma, such a person enters the one hundred and eight hells.
Body, speech, and mind constitute the three karmas in their entirety. Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the commission of two of the bodily karmas.

Entering the eighteen hells by means of these [three] demonstrates that the three karmas are not exhaustive; since the bodily karma consists of only two [of these offenses], one should enter thirty-six hells.
If one currently observes a single faculty, this constitutes one of the body, speech, or mind; thus, it is the solitary commission of a single karma. This is...
For those who commit one of the three—killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct—they shall enter one hundred and eight hells.
Thus, as sentient beings act and create individually, they enter the common ground within the world, and false conceptualization arises.
It does not exist inherently from the beginning;
those who act and create separately each have their own private [nature]. Those who enter the stage of the homogeneous share in a commonality of these various privates.
This is the formal conclusion answering whether it is spontaneous or whether there is a fixed location—namely, what was previously called the "homogeneity of the multitude."
Within this division, there is also the inclusion of the original ground. It is further said: "Delusive thoughts arise; they do not exist from the beginning.
Thus we know that if various private [karmic] conditions exist, the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneous class) remains manifest. It is like being in a dream—once awakened, what remains?

This is certain, most certain; it is like blinking one's eyes from the very start. △ Six: Showing the Remaining Retributions. This section has eleven parts. First: A General Indication of Ghostly Retribution.

Furthermore, Ānanda, these sentient beings—having violated the codes of discipline, transgressed the bodhisattva precepts, and subverted the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, as well as through various other miscellaneous karmas—shall burn for many kalpas.
After their retribution is eventually exhausted, they will receive the forms of various hungry ghosts.

This refers to "remaining karma. By citing these three most grave offenses, all others are illustrated by analogy. Once the punishment for these has been fully endured in hell, one further receives the body of a hungry ghost (*preta*) to exhaust the remaining retribution.
It is not that those who have violated the *vinaya* discipline are neither [violators] nor [non-violators]; rather, it means they lack the discipline.
The *prajñā* of a Bodhisattva and the *nirvāṇa* of a Tathāgata are both the life-force of wisdom for sentient beings; to violate even one of these—
First is "Destruction. Because it is extremely grave, [it is listed first]. △ Regarding the twenty kinds of ghostly classes:

if, in their original cause, one committed the offense of coveting objects, then when that person's retribution is exhausted, they encounter an object and take form; these are called *guàiguǐ* (strange ghosts).

Lusting after physical beauty is a transgression. When this person’s retribution for that sin is exhausted, they encounter the wind and take form; such a being is called a *pātra* ghost. Being deluded by greed is a transgression.

When this person’s retribution for that sin is exhausted, they encounter a beast and take form; such a being is called a *mèi* ghost. Harboring resentment through greed is a transgression. When this person’s retribution for that sin is exhausted...

When they encounter insects and take form, they are called *gudu* ghosts; their transgression was greed and obsessive thought. When these people’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter decay and take form, being called *lei* ghosts;
their transgression was greed and arrogance. When these people’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter vapors and take form, being called hungry ghosts (*preta*).

To covet and deceive is a sin. When this person’s retribution for the sin is exhausted, they encounter the essence of darkness (*yōu*) and take on a form; this is called a *yan-ghost* (a ghost of sleep paralysis). To covet brightness is a sin.

When this person’s retribution for the sin is exhausted, they encounter the essence of spirit (*seishin*) and take on a form; this is called a *mōryō-ghost* (a wood-demon). To covet success is a sin. When this person’s retribution for the sin is exhausted...

When encountering light, it takes on form; this is called the "ghost that employs others. When driven by greed and factionalism, one commits offenses; when these offenses are exhausted, the person encounters human beings and takes on form;
this is called the "transmitting ghost."
Because they gave rise to greed for material objects, they received the retribution of the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). They still depend upon material things;
generally, all those who rely on grass or water to become demons and monsters are of this species. When males and females entice one another, it is called "wind" (*vāyu*);

as a remnant of their habitual lust, they take form upon encountering the wind. The *pó* female ghost is also called a "female monster" (*yāo*); she receives this retribution due to her indulgence in lewdness.
Delusion is the cause of deception; relying on the void to confuse what is correct, it is like a fox that can manifest as a beautiful man or woman—this seductive ghost is therefore called a *mei*.
Hatred is the cause of resentment; the residue of resentment becomes poisonous *gu* charms.
Therefore, all toxic *gū* poisons are manifestations entrusted by ghosts. When one harbors resentment without ceasing, it accumulates and becomes a persistent memory (*smṛti*).
