Taking advantage of a person’s declining fortune, it enters their body as a disease; this is called a "pestilential ghost" (*rākṣasa*). Haughty and overbearing toward others, it takes on the quality of breath as its substance, yet within it is nothing at all;
it is constantly hungry. This is the residual retribution for arrogance. Deceptive and false in pretension, it uses these to deceive those without discernment.
Because the mind is obscure and hidden, it encounters the obscure and becomes a nightmare; a nightmare is that which deludes one while asleep.

When one clings to views and claims clear awakening, such heterodox interpretations conflict with the truth. Other retributions can borrow the brilliance of the sun and moon, or the numinous qi of mountains and rivers, to manifest forms for themselves;
these are called *wangliang* (sprites). They create causes of injustice and press upon others to forge evidence of injustice; these are further retributions.
They must rely on manifest spirits to provide their services; these are called "servant ghosts," such as the attendants of spirit temples.
They lead their own kind and conceal themselves, like a ghost possessing a person. Today, shamans and invocators are possessed by ghosts, who transmit matters of good and ill fortune.
This is the residual retribution for litigation. △ Third, concluding on the retribution of ghosts:
"Ānanda, these people all fall because of their pure passions. Once the fires of karma have burned them dry, they emerge above as ghosts.

All such beings are summoned and led by the karma of their own deluded thoughts. If they were to awaken to Bodhi, then it would be wondrous, perfect, and luminous; fundamentally, there is no [ghosthood]."
All these fetters are the remaining retribution of ten causes. Yet it is said that if one awakens to Bodhi, then it is wondrous, perfect, and luminous, fundamentally having nothing at all.
One must know that this wondrous nature is perfect and luminous, ever-present even within the three miserable realms of hell, without interruption. That is to say:
The Buddha-nature transmigrates through the five paths. It is for this reason that Bodhisattvas manifest bodies according to their kind.

How then could one know that there are sentient beings without roots of goodness who, while in the midst of extreme suffering, might suddenly manifest enlightenment? How much more so for a human being—how could one abandon oneself?
Since the retribution of past deeds has been exhausted, it is said that "the fires of karma have burned them dry. △ Fourth, a general indication of animal retribution.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the karma of the hungry ghost has been exhausted, both emotion and thought become empty.
Only then does one encounter the person originally owed a debt in the world, taking birth as an animal to repay that past debt.
These perceptions are all comprised within the realm of emotional attachment (*qing*); they are not the perceptions of those in higher realms who fall, nor the perceptions of those ascending.

Since it is said that both emotion and perception are empty, animals exist solely to repay their debts; nevertheless, due to the predominance of residual habits (*vāsanā*), they each follow their respective categories, as will be detailed below.
△ Fifty kinds of animal species.
The ghosts of material anomalies, when their retribution for their existence is exhausted, are born into the world mostly as species of owls.

The ghosts of wind-demons, when their retribution for their existence is exhausted, are born into the world mostly as all manner of ominous portents and strange creatures. The ghosts of animal-spirits...
When the retribution for being born as a domestic animal ends and they are reborn into the human world, they mostly become foxes or spirits of worms and vermin.

When the retribution for being a spirit of worms and vermin ends and they are reborn into the human world, they mostly become venomous creatures or spirits of pestilence. When the retribution for being a spirit of pestilence ends and they are reborn into the human world, they mostly become those who are impoverished and destitute.

Those who were mostly *kṛmi*-type ghosts receive their retribution through vital energy (*prāṇa*); when that energy is exhausted and their retribution ends, they are born into the human world, mostly as types of food.

Those who were *mianyou*-type ghosts receive their retribution through the exhaustion of the subtle; when that subtlety is exhausted and their retribution ends, they are born into the human world, mostly as types of clothing. Those who were *hejing*-type ghosts...
When their harmonious retribution is exhausted, they are born into the world, mostly as responsive spirits or intelligent ghosts.

When their intelligence is extinguished and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the world, mostly as auspicious omens among all classes of beings or as ghosts that depend upon humans. When a person dies and their retribution is exhausted—
Born into this world, they mostly follow their kind;

they cling to material things as strange spirits or, clutching clods of earth, become owls. This is the residual habit of greed for objects. Their baleful omens are like swarms of rats and flocks of sparrows, portending famine and scarcity.
They bring about floods when merchants trade in water, and respond to drought with the dancing of cranes. They practice deception to act as seductive demons.
In another life they take birth as foxes; previously they were ghosts inhabiting animals, and now they have become animals themselves. The venomous class includes vipers, snakes, and scorpions;
the parasite class refers to roundworms and pinworms—previously the malevolent ghosts took advantage of physical decay, while these parasites now inhabit the abdomen.

The edible class consists of all living beings that may serve as food and drink; formerly they were hungry ghosts, whereas now they provide sustenance for human satiety. The domesticated class refers to silkworms.
Silk and animal furs are all fit for clothing and use; they arrive according to their seasons, much like the swallow that visits in spring and the wild goose that arrives as a guest in autumn.

This is what is moved by the refined brilliance of cultivated practice. For ghosts, it is a matter of entrusting themselves to clarity; for animals, it is a sign of auspicious rest. Thus, creatures such as the qilin and the phoenix serve as omens of good fortune for humans;

it is not that these beings can cause such things on their own. Ghosts depend upon humans, and animals likewise remain dependent upon humans. As it is said: [The text continues with a citation from the *Lunyu*].
The cats and dogs of the world—indeed, all such classes of animals—even when they are repaying past debts, do so entirely due to residual habits; thus, each is moved by its own kind.
△ Sixth, the conclusion on the retribution of animal births.
Ānanda, these beings are all withered by the fire of karma as they repay their past debts; thus they become animals as collateral for their obligations.
These states, too, are all summoned and drawn forth by one's own false and delusive karma. If one awakens to Bodhi, then these false conditions will be seen to have never existed at all.
In the previous section on the realm of ghosts, it was said: "Thus, wondrous, perfect, and luminous clarity is fundamentally non-existent.

In this section on the retribution of animals, it is further said: "Thus, these delusive conditions are fundamentally non-existent. One should know that the wondrous nature is untainted and that all that is false and illusory is originally nothing at all.
These points have been raised and emphasized again and again; one ought to reflect upon them for oneself. △ Seventh: Reiterating the previous inquiry to provide further instruction.
It is as you have said. The evil karma of those such as Ratnapadmagandha, King Vaidūrya, and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was originally produced from within themselves;
it did not descend from heaven, nor did it emerge from the earth, nor was it bestowed by others. It was summoned by their own delusions.
They return to be received within the bodhicitta itself; within the bodhicitta, all are merely the solidification of floating, empty, and deluded thoughts.
Within the bodhicitta, there is fundamentally no such thing as karmic fruit; therefore, one observes these karmic bonds from the perspective of the bodhicitta.

This is empty and lacks substantial reality; yet, because the delusive thoughts of sentient beings have coagulated and they remain in the midst of present confusion, it cannot be said that they do not exist.
What is called "no-self, no-doer, and no-experiencer" does not mean that the karma one has created perishes. When the mind awakens to the emptiness of karma, its realm becomes distinct;
these two states cannot be spoken of as being on the same level. △ Eighth: Replying to the remaining points and returning to the original inquiry.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when these beings emerge from the animal realm to repay their prior debts, if the debtor pays more than what was owed, these beings will again become human and demand back that surplus.
This occurs if the debtor possesses both power and merit.
Thus, among humans, one does not relinquish the human body to repay that power. If one lacks merit, one returns to the state of an animal to compensate for the remaining balance.
"Exceeding what was repaid" refers to the debt already repaid; "remaining of what was owed" refers to the portion still outstanding. This may refer to the person who received the debt.
If one’s exploitation and demands are excessive, these animals will return to being human once their remaining karmic debt has been exacted.
This is like a sheep dying to become a human, or a human dying to become a sheep. To possess strength means to have the capacity not to lose the power of the human body;
this includes such things as having protected the Dharma in past lives or receiving the precept against killing, all of which serve as causes for longevity. Merit likewise stems from previous lives.
All the merit from serving the Triple Gem performed throughout one's life has not yet been exhausted; therefore, it is repaid in the present life, without waiting for a future rebirth.

By this analogy, one should understand that when a wealthy or noble person happens to owe a debt to another, they should conceive of it in this way, and thus will have no further obligation to repay the creditor beyond the current debt.
△ Ninth: The Mutual Succession of Repayment.
Ānanda, you should know that if one uses money or goods, or exerts their labor, the debt is settled once fully repaid and then ceases.
However, if in the interim one takes another's life or eats their flesh, then even after passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, they will continue to devour and slaughter one another.
It is like a turning wheel, rising and falling alternately without rest; it cannot be halted except through *śamatha* or the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
This refers to the use of wealth and power as a means of requital; once the debt is satisfied, one rests. However, if one kills another’s life, the resentment will be endless.

The animal requited in this life is precisely the person who comes to collect the debt in a future birth. Debt turns back into a debt to be collected, and collection turns back into a debt to be repaid;
there will be no end to it. Only when this person awakens to their own fundamental nature and attains true samādhi will karma [be extinguished].
Deluded regarding the two kinds of emptiness, they do not encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world; thus, each must attain liberation before they can find rest.

The precept against killing should be strictly observed, equal in gravity to that against sexual misconduct; one must not fail to engrave this in mind. △ Tenth: The remaining karmic retributions of human beings.
You should now know this: those of the owl class, once their retribution is fulfilled and they restore their physical form, will be born among human beings as members of the dull-witted classes.

Those of the ill-omened class, once their retribution is fulfilled and they restore their physical form, will be born among human beings as members of the eccentric classes. As for those of the fox class...
When their retribution is exhausted and they restore their physical forms, they are born among human beings, joining the ranks of the mediocre.

Those of the poisonous class, when their retribution is exhausted and they restore their physical forms, are born among human beings, joining the ranks of the violent. Those of the worm-like class, when their retribution is exhausted and they restore their physical forms, are born among human beings.
Those who combined with the subtle class, having their retribution fulfilled and their forms restored, were born among the human realm, combining with the gentle class.

Those who combined with the submissive class, having their retribution fulfilled and their forms restored, were born among the human realm, combining with the laboring class. Those who combined with the responsive class...

Having fully repaid their debts and regained their physical forms, they are born into the human realm and join the ranks of the literate. Those who possessed auspicious signs, having fully repaid their debts and regained their physical forms, are born into the human realm and harmonize with the class of the enlightened.
Those who followed the various social norms, having fully repaid their debts and regained their physical forms, are born into the human realm.
They participate in the realm of Da-lei (the "reaching categories").
Human existence is the primary cause for the Five Precepts; now, because they have resumed the form of an animal, they are said to be "participating and merging" with it.

Those who fall due to greed for material things become ghosts that possess objects to act as monsters; among animals, they embrace clods of earth to become owls; and when they return to the human state, they become stubborn and dull-witted.
Thus we know that when the mind clings to external objects, it loses its spiritual clarity. Bewildered by greed and desire, one becomes a source of calamity and misfortune;
though one may regain a human body, one becomes a creature of a different species, incapable of meaningful discourse. Such is the power of lust to corrode the human spirit.
Like the fox, one becomes seductive and alluring, losing all sense of integrity and shame, approaching the state of the ignorant and dull-witted; though still nominally human, one is utterly deluded.

It is even more so. Among beasts, the primal ghosts become *gǔ* (poisonous vermin); in humans, they become stubbornness. Whether their dispositions are difficult or easy to change persists across lifetimes.
Just as intestinal worms dwell within a person’s belly while their will is weak and inferior, so too do humans of cold status and low birth possess true causes from past lives.

Beasts of prey survive on the remnants of knives and blockades; their supple nature is not robust. This remains true for humans as well. Furthermore, clothing and gear are mostly derived from fur and hide.

The residual habits of oxen and horses manifest as toil and exhaustion in human form; the capacity for knowledge in animals corresponds to the consciousness of knowing the proper time, while clarity in birds corresponds to the intelligence of worldly discernment.
Following these categories, one understands the causes of misfortune and fortune. Worldly wisdom and clever discernment are among the eight difficulties.
When a person possesses talent and sagacity, it does not arise from innate wisdom; rather, it serves to obstruct the Path, for such qualities are surely the result of past karmic conditions.
There is a reason for this. △ Eleven: Concluding the remaining retributions.

Ānanda, these beings have all settled their past debts and returned to human form. Yet, due to the inverted karmic calculations from time immemorial, they have been born to one another and killed one another.
Had they not encountered the Tathāgata and heard the True Dharma, they would have remained within the midst of worldly afflictions by the very nature of things.
They revolve in saṃsāra; such people are called those who are to be pitied.

Again, the ten causes and six retributions are all due to the delusions of sentient beings. Although past debts may be temporarily repaid, they continue to give birth to one another and kill one another, never coming to an end.
Only by encountering the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and realizing the nature as the Way can one transcend this cycle. [In the heavens...]
In the world, there is nothing further that can bring an end to the cycle of saṃsāra. Sentient beings are bewildered; they are truly to be pitied.

The above four sections have concluded the demonstration of the ten causes of habitual practice and the sixfold mutual retribution. △ Fifth, the separate cultivation that results in delusion, divided into three parts.
First, the general heading.

Ānanda, furthermore, there are followers who do not rely on perfect enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead cultivate deluded thoughts and fixate their mental images to preserve the physical form.
They roam in mountain forests and remote places inaccessible to ordinary people; these are the ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*).
"Perfect Enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*) refers to the primordial self-nature of true awakening; "samādhi" refers to the samādhi of self-nature.
To depart from this is to practice erroneously as a separate discipline based on false views. "Deluded thought" refers to the essence of a self within the body of the five aggregates.

Taking this as one's nature, one maintains mental focus to restrain the body and dwells in mountain forests where humans do not reach, hoping that upon completing these efforts, one will become an immortal (*ṛṣi*). Briefly stated...
There are ten types. Each will be detailed below. II. Specifically establishing the ten kinds of *ṛṣis*:
"Ānanda, those sentient beings who take medicinal elixirs with steadfast persistence without ceasing, until the path of food is perfected, are called earth-walking *ṛṣis*."
By pounding and combining various medicinal ingredients, one produces a medicinal paste (*gao*). This paste is characterized by solidity and stagnation;
it can only maintain the physical form and prolong life, but it cannot facilitate lightness of movement. Therefore, its practitioners remain earth-bound.
One perseveres with herbs and plants without ceasing until the Way of Medicine is perfected; such a person is called a Flying Immortal (*khecarī-siddha*).

Herbs and plants possess many powers for prolonging life, yet one must take them for a long time before success is achieved. Because this method is lighter than ingesting [metals], one attains the ability to fly.
Remaining as firm as metal and stone without ceasing, they bring the path of transformation to full completion; these are called the Wandering Immortals (*cāraṇa-ṛṣi*).

Like the refining of cinnabar through the "nine transformations" (*navakṛtvaḥ paryāvartana*) and the "great return" (*mahāpunaḥpratyāgama*), all stages above this rely entirely upon the power of external medicinal substances.
Maintaining firmness in movement and stillness without ceasing, one brings the vital energy (*prāṇa*) and essence (*bindu*) to perfect completion;
this is called the *khecarī-siddha*. "Movement and stillness" refers to the guidance of the vital energies, such as the methods of "bear-stretching" and "bird-extension.
From this point downward, all practices are fulfilled within the body.
One consolidates the vital fluids (*rasa*) without ceasing; when the virtue of moisture is perfected, one is called a *devayāna-ṛṣi*.
"Vital fluids" refers to the method of ingesting the *rasa*. Through this transformation, perspiration naturally subsides, and the skin becomes firm and dense.
This uses internal moisture to dissolve and melt away the fires of depravity, so that the true fire becomes self-sufficient; hence it is called the "virtue of moisture."
Maintaining firm vigor and radiance without ceasing, one inhales the essence until it is perfectly realized; this is called the "Transcendent of Penetrating Practice.
This vigor and radiance consists of inhaling and gathering the solar essence and lunar flowers, as well as clouds, mists, dew, and frost.
Although these rely on external elements, there are also internal methods of resonance; otherwise, one will contract the ailment of wind-evil. "Penetration" refers to [harmonizing] with Yin and Yang.
Their vital energies are thus interconnected.
By maintaining firm and unceasing incantations and prohibitions, one brings the methods of the arts to perfection; such a person is called a "Daoxing-xian" (Immortal of Daoist Practice).

This involves using talismans and incantations to cure illnesses and relieve misfortunes. The Daoist tradition also places great importance on the accumulation of merit through acts of broad salvation and assistance. Furthermore—
Gathering stillness and maintaining it is also the principle of collecting the spirit and concentrating the essence; therefore, it is called the "Method for Accomplishing Reverence.
Yet, because it actually relies on internal power, it is termed an "Art" (*shu*). Because it reaches out to affect others, it is also named the "Way" (*dao*).
To maintain firm mindfulness without ceasing until its recollection is perfected is called the "Illuminating Practice Immortal.
This involves a mind of serene stillness, unmixed with divergent thoughts; it is the constant practice of embracing the One and guarding stillness.
Even Daoists call this "seeing one's nature," likening it to the bright sun in a clear sky, yet they do not realize that this is identical to the act of mindful recollection.
When the union is firm and uninterrupted, the resonance is perfectly accomplished; this is called the "Immortal of Refinement.
"Union" refers to the union of water and fire. Among the four great elements produced therein, when water and fire assist one another, earth and wind follow suit.
This begins with fire arising from the *kan* position, penetrating directly through the upper barrier (*shàngguān*), transforming into water to meet [the essence] at...
To say that one merely follows this cycle of resonance and circulation, whereby blood is naturally transformed into essence and essence into qi—
claiming even that it refers to the union of male and female essences— is nothing more than the demonic discourse of the Daoists.
Firmly established in transformation without ceasing, one awakens to perfect realization and is called a transcendent immortality (vidyādhara).
When a human body has a master, it transforms; when it lacks a master, it changes. If there is transformation without change, one is mired in the physical form.
If there is change without transformation, one gradually moves toward dissolution and extinction. To awaken to this is to transcend the earth.
When the time arrives, they can naturally manifest or conceal themselves at will; whether far or near, they leave no trace.

Only this one category, together with the eighth mentioned previously, constitutes the orthodox transmission of the Daoist school; all others are merely byways. △ Third, the conclusion on the Way of the Immortals.
Ānanda, these individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate true awakening.

Instead, they attain a distinct mode of existence and live for ten million years, dwelling in deep mountains or on remote ocean islands far from the realm of men. This, too, is saṃsāra; it is the wandering of deluded thoughts.
Failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more and are scattered into the various realms of existence.

In summary, these paths of the immortals are criticized because they are not the correct cultivation. All ten of these types do not transcend deluded thought and turn their backs on right knowledge and vision.
To employ the mind in this way until the end of one’s life, one will not achieve success even once in ten attempts. Even if success is attained, it merely extends one’s years;
and even if one gains supernormal powers, they are sustained by deluded force. When that force is exhausted, one falls back into ruin. It would be better to spend a single day [in true practice].
One cultivates untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), which, though not yet perfected, has already planted the true cause that shall never be in vain.

Furthermore, through the five precepts and ten wholesome paths, one directly attains a celestial body. To view the celestial beings as compared to the immortals (*ṛṣi*) is like comparing a king to his subjects;

even the celestial realm is easily exhausted, let alone the state of an immortal. The mind is fundamentally unborn; it is only when one first turns away from the awakened mind that one rushes toward the gateway of birth. Within this process, there naturally exists...
This is the inevitable principle; having grasped its vital essence, one exerts no effort. Yet, that which arises must necessarily perish; where there is no arising, there is no perishing.
To distinguish this is to exclude what is not the primary cultivation.

The five higher realms, having been completed as distinct meditative attainments through delusion. △ Sixth, the distinctions among the various devas. This is divided into four parts. First, the Desire Realm. This is divided into seven.
First, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Ānanda, there are people in the world who do not seek permanence and have not yet been able to relinquish their affection for wives and concubines;
yet, regarding sexual misconduct, their minds do not wander astray, and they polish themselves until clarity arises. After their lives end, they dwell in proximity to the sun and moon.
Such a class of beings is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

The six desires are all differentiated according to the completeness or deficiency, and the coarseness or subtlety, of the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala*). This sutra does not mention the ten wholesome actions;

it merely cites the cessation of sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*) as a standard for the remaining wholesome actions. It is not that this refers to only a single wholesome action. Anything outside of one’s own wife and concubines is termed sexual misconduct.
When the mind has its limits, it does not flow into dissipation. Because it does not flow into dissipation, it is said to be "clarified and polished" (*caṅxing*).
This also clarifies that those who possess few desires and are clear-minded are like the sun and moon; thus they are born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
Their nature is awakened and eternally abiding, yet because they do not seek eternal abiding, they do not cultivate correct awakening. △ Second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Regarding their own wives, their lustful desire is slight; yet when dwelling in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), they do not attain full flavor.
After the end of their lives, they transcend the brilliance of the sun and moon and dwell at the summit of the human realm. This class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Sensual desire is slight, and thus there is no complete flavor of craving. This state is far superior to the worldly mind; therefore, one is born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
"Trāyastriṃśa" translates as "Thirty-three. This heaven is situated on the summit of Mount Sumeru, surrounded by thirty-two heavens at its four corners, with Śakra as their ruler.
These two aforementioned heavens both rely upon Mount Sumeru and are thus called "earth-dwelling" (bhūmi-vāsin).
The Heaven [of the Thirty-three] is eighty-four thousand *yojana* above the earth. △ Third, the Suyāma Heaven (Heaven of the Yama Gods).

When encountering desire, they unite briefly; afterwards, there is no further thought or recollection. In the human world, movement is slight and stillness is predominant. After the end of their lives—
Abiding serenely in the midst of empty space, the radiance of the sun and moon cannot reach them from above.
These beings possess their own natural light; such a class of beings is named Suyāma Heaven.
If one encounters [an object] only briefly and departs, it is evident that the thought of desire will certainly not arise; this applies to other such cases as well.

When both emotion and conceptualization are thin, movement is slight and stillness is abundant, whereby there is the realization of dwelling in emptiness. Since sentient beings possess a thick and heavy mind of desire, they consequently encounter many obstructions;
conversely, when this is reversed, one dwells in a state of vast openness and clarity. This can indeed be known through inference.
Yama is translated here as "Time" (kāla). Day and night are determined by the opening and closing of lotus flowers. △ Fourth is the Tuṣita Heaven.
It is tranquil at all times; though sensory objects may arise, one is unable to transgress [the meditative state]. After the end of life, one ascends to a subtle and refined realm.
It does not reach down to the realms of humans or the lower devas; even until the destruction of the kalpa, it is not affected by the three calamities.
Such a class [of beings] is called the Tuṣita Heaven.
Tuṣita is translated here as "Contentment with Joy. Bodhisattvas in their final birth teach there, cultivating many practices of contentment.
To find joy in obtaining a small measure of what one desires is "joy" (tuṣi); to not seek anything further is "contentment" (tuṣṭa). One should encounter [objects] without conflict.
This is merely a matter of conformity; therefore, it is known that [the Pure Land] is tranquil at all times. "Subtle and refined" refers to the heavens.
This heaven is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Having made great vows, they attain rebirth there;

because of the Bodhisattvas' power of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*), the three calamities do not reach them. This refers to the Inner Court. The present sutra speaks of the most excellent [heaven]. △ Five: Pleasures.
As for the Nirmāṇarati Heaven:
I have no desire in my heart; I engage in your activities only as a matter of formality. At the time of union, the flavor is like chewing wax.
After the end of life, one is born in the Realm Beyond Transformation. This class of beings is called the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
Being free from desire, they respond to those [beings] just as in Tuṣita; they find no flavor in sensory objects, yet they surpass even that [Tuṣita].

This refers to the occasion when they respond to the objects of desire by lying across them. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Because those devas, for their own sake, transform themselves into the objects of desire."
It is not for the sake of others; it is solely one's own transformation (*nirmāṇa*). "Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to the process of transmutation, such as changing the coarse into the subtle.
"Manifestation" (*nirmita*) refers to the sudden appearance of what was previously non-existent. 6. The Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
They possess no worldly mind, yet they engage in worldly affairs; amidst such interactions, they remain clearly transcendent.

After their lives end, they are universally able to transcend and manifest in realms both with and without transformation. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations.
Regarding the objects of various desires, one does not exert effort to transform them oneself, but enjoys them as they appear; hence it is called "Paranirmita" (Other-Transformation).

The former [Heaven] merely lacks flavor, whereas this has already transcended it, distinguishing between the mind that abides in itself and the mind that does not abide. "Transformation" refers to the transformation of pleasure.
The "untransformed" refers to the preceding four heavens. △ Seventh, the conclusion on the Desire Realm:
Ānanda, these six heavens, although their forms have transcended movement, the traces of their minds still intermingle. From this point downward, it is called the Desire Realm.

In the human realm, regarding desires—whether they have not yet been encountered or have already been encountered—the body and mind waver and stir. In the heavens, the mind follows as objects arrive and comes to rest within those objects;
thus it is said that movement has emerged. Although the traces of the mind still intersect with objects, it is nonetheless not entirely non-existent.
Direct Pointing to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Eight:
Phonetic Transliteration and Explanations.

*Xiè* (pronounced *xiè*): garlic. *Yíng* (pronounced *yíng*, departing tone): to polish or grind. *Lì* (pronounced *lì*): the trigger of a mechanism. *Cùì* (pronounced *cuì*): to harden the edge of a blade. *Jiū* (same as *zhē*, *zhē*: a horse-whip). *Huǐ* (pronounced *huǐ*): a species of snake. *Lè* (pronounced *lì*):

the sound of stones. *Dèn* (pronounced *dèn*, departing tone): a poisonous bird. *Jù* (pronounced *jú*): to interrogate. *Niǎn* and *Āi* (*niǎn* is the same as *zhàn*; *ài* is pronounced *kāi*, departing tone): a device for crushing or grinding things.

*Cu*: (pronounced *cù*, meaning to contract). *Zha*: (pronounced *zhà*, a tool for pressing objects). *Mao*: (pronounced *mào*, an appearance of stupidity). *Za*: (the rhyme of *jiù* in the entering tone;

to bite). *Shao*: (pronounced *shuò*, a type of spear). *Zi*: (pronounced *zì*, to thrust a blade). *Zhan*: (pronounced *zhǎ*, to move). *Bie*: (pronounced *bá*). *Yè*: (pronounced *yè*). *Qi*: (pronounced *qì*, to rest).

The Direct Pointing to the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, the Cultivation and Realization of the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Nine.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Huṅshì Tiānrán of the Thirty-Fourth Generation of the Dòng Lineage.
Dharma-heir of the Succession, the present-day monk Dan-gui, having read the current exposition on the Joyful Discourse, completes the comparison with the first section concerning the Desire Realm.
△ Second, the Form Realm. Divided into six parts: First, the Heavens of the First Dhyāna.
Ānanda, among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, there are none who, without relying on *dhyāna*, possess wisdom.
The *Qīngliáng sāndì shū* (Commentary on the Three Stages of Purity and Coolness) states: "The term *dhyāna* is a Western [Sanskrit] sound; here it is translated as 'calm contemplation' (*jìnglù*).

'Calm' (*jìng*) means tranquility; 'contemplation' (*lù*) means discernment. Calm can sever the fetters, while contemplation can effect correct observation. Although the various formless realms possess calm, they lack contemplation. Even so...

It can sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) but cannot correctly contemplate; it maintains the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), yet lacks tranquility (*śamatha*).

Although it can correctly contemplate, it cannot sever the fetters; therefore, only the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) alone receives this designation. The first of the four dhyānas is the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) with directed thought and sustained thought;

the second is the meditative absorption without directed thought and without sustained thought; the third is the meditative absorption free from joy (*prīti*); the fourth is the meditative absorption free from pleasure (*sukha*).
Consider this: it is said here that without relying on *dhyāna*, there is no wisdom;

this implies that for the cultivation of the mind in the mundane realm, one must rely on *dhyāna* in order to give rise to wisdom. This is precisely the time when one relies on *dhyāna* within the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Therefore, those from the first fruit up to the third fruit all take their station therein. As for those who are nearly Arhats (*aśaikṣa*), the text below states: "Although this is not true cultivation..."
Regarding samādhi: although this indeed exists within dhyāna, because true wisdom has not yet arisen, it cannot be compared to the samādhi in which concentration and wisdom are in equilibrium.

If one can restrain the body and refrain from sexual desire, whether walking or sitting, such that neither thoughts nor mental images arise and no defilement of craving is produced, one will not remain in the realm of desire.
Such a person, by virtue of this mindfulness, becomes a companion to Brahmā. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārṣadya).

Devoid of both conceptualization and discursive thought, and with the non-arising of passionate attachment, this distinguishes them from the Desire Realm and reveals that body and mind have attained seclusion as they first enter dhyāna;
therefore, they are called the Brahmakāyika (Assembly of Brahmā).
Once the habitual tendencies of desire have been eliminated, the mind free from desire manifests; such a person delights in and accords with all forms of discipline (vinaya).
Being able to practice the virtues of Brahma at the appropriate time, this class of beings is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahma (Brahmapurohita).
The mind manifests free from desire; it is characterized by love, joy, and compliance. This is the "joy and bliss born of seclusion.
Because they are able to practice brahmic virtue and furthermore assist in promoting virtuous transformation, they are called the Brahmapurohitas (Ministers of Brahmā).

With body and mind wondrously perfect, their majestic deportment unimpaired, and their pure prohibitive precepts augmented by clear awakening, such persons are able, at that time, to preside over the Brahma hosts as Great Brahma Kings.
This class of beings is called the Mahābrahmā Heaven.
"The marvelous perfection of body and mind" refers to the complete liberation of the precepts and the mind, manifested in every movement and stillness and arising from superior resolve;

hence it is said that "one's dignified deportment is never deficient. Furthermore, this is augmented by clear awakening, which is precisely the assertion of the Brahma-Teaching (Brahmanism), as its understanding surpasses that of the preceding [non-Buddhist] schools.
Ānanda, these three superior classes cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction.
Although they have not yet attained the true, authentic Samādhi, within their pure minds, the various outflows (āsravas) remain unmoved; this is called the First Dhyāna.
Suffering arises from the various desires. The first dhyāna is tranquil, being free from desire; its power of vitarka and vicāra is supreme, such that it is not moved by coarse outflows (āsrava).
This is attained through the concentration of the *anāgamya* stage. Once this concentration has itself become free from desire, body and mind merge into stillness;
whether sitting or reclining, one is vast and open, as if like empty space. Because it can give rise to the first dhyāna, it is called the "pure mind."
[The Second Dhyāna Heavens]. △ Second, the heavens of the second dhyāna.
Ānanda, next is the Brahmā Heaven, which governs the Brahmā-puruṣas. Having perfected the Brahma-conduct, their minds are limpid and unmoving; from this profound stillness, light is produced.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha).
These devas are superior to those of the first dhyāna. Light arises from internal tranquility; because this is their initial manifestation, they are called the "Limited Light" (Parīttābha).
There is a distinction between the light of the first and second dhyānas: the light of the first is like a mani-jewel, which has radiance on the outside but lacks radiance within;
the light of the second is like a bright lamp, which emits radiance externally and illuminates itself internally. Thus, both internally and externally, [the second dhyāna] is...
There is radiance;
light upon light blazes forth, shining without end and reflecting throughout the worlds of the ten directions, everywhere becoming like lapis lazuli.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Amitābha).
Compared to the previous day, this radiance was even more intense, like pure lapis lazuli; its light shone even further.
This refers to the ten directions within one's own realm, not to all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Inhaling and sustaining the circular radiance, they accomplish the essence of the teaching; their transformative activity is pure and its application inexhaustible.
Such a class is called the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven).

This means that the body of the teaching (*śāsana*) is sustained by its own radiance, and it employs light to proclaim the transformation [of beings]. Its application is directed toward the capacities of sentient beings, inexhaustibly elucidating and manifesting [the truth].
Changshui (Changlu Zongze) stated that the second dhyāna stage lacks the first five consciousnesses; this must refer to being in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This is because ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles are all unable to give rise to the first five consciousnesses for the purpose of cognizing objects while they are in meditative concentration. — *Jiushi* (Record of the World).
It is said: Since the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven use light as their speech, the dignified deportment and every movement of the higher celestial beings is nothing other than verbal instruction.
Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be assailed by any anxiety or apprehension; although they do not constitute the true cultivation of the Threefold Training, [they are nonetheless...]
In the *samādhi* of the pure mind, the coarse outflows (*āsrava*) have already been subdued; this is called the Second Dhyāna.
Because the joy and bliss born of the Second Dhyāna concentration is named the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), there is no longer any anxiety or sorrow.

In the First Dhyāna, the coarse outflows were not yet stilled, but these have now been subdued by this deity. The *Sanzhu* (Third Ground) Commentary states: "Regarding 'joy and bliss born of concentration,' the First Dhyāna celebrates its departure from desire."
Because it is free from evil, it is called "born of seclusion. Now, rejoicing that the mind of applied and sustained thought has ceased, it is called "born of concentration.

It is like a clear mirror or still water; thus, body and mind are at ease and joyful. Desire and evil are like mud; the concentration of the first dhyāna is like water that was moving but is now still.

Now, being free from desire and evil, and having further extinguished applied and sustained thought, it is like pure, still water. This is how one rejoices in what has been abandoned in the first dhyāna.
This is their celebration of what they have attained, for they have attained the extinction of illumination. △ Third, the Heaven of the Three Dhyānas.

Ānanda, such celestial beings possess perfected radiance that forms sound; they unveil the sublime by unfolding this sound, and they give rise to refined practice that penetrates the bliss of tranquil extinction.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha).

Following the aforementioned Ābhāsvara Heaven, one uses light to explicate principle; as principle accords with practice, the joy of tranquility arises, extinguishing the preceding mind of rapture and manifesting pure serenity.
Because the initial speech is pervasive, it is also called Parīttaśubha (Limited Purity).
Pure emptiness manifests before them, giving rise to boundlessness; body and mind become light and tranquil, achieving the bliss of cessation.
This class of beings is called the gods of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha).
Purity is devoid of the mark of purity; therefore, it is concentration (*samādhi*). Concentration is itself boundless, accomplishing the bliss of cessation (*nirvāṇa*).
Because body and mind are in a state of cessation, it is called "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*). How could such bliss have any limit?
The body and mind of this world are entirely perfect and pure; having accomplished pure virtues, they manifest a supreme reliance and return to the bliss of quiescent extinction.
This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven (the Heaven of Universal Purity).

The immeasurable bliss previously experienced was confined to body and mind; now it pervades the entire world, leaving nothing empty or silent. With both internal and external states extinguished, one achieves a state of abiding reliance.
Therefore, it is said that "the supreme refuge manifests before one," and "returning" means returning to this very state.
Ānanda, these three superior classes of beings possess great conformity; their bodies and minds are tranquil and secure, and they attain immeasurable bliss.
Although they have not yet truly attained genuine *samādhi*, within their tranquil minds, joy is fully present; this is called the third dhyāna.

In the third dhyāna, there is sublime bliss free from joy (*prīti*). Joy is the opposite of sorrow; this stage is free from joy, yet the body is completely suffused with bliss that is beyond reproach.

Therefore, it is said to be "endowed with great conformity. Although bliss reaches its peak by transcending joy, the description "fully endowed with rapture" refers to the state within a mind of tranquility, which differs from the agitation of joy;
it is simply that bliss has reached its ultimate fulfillment. — *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom)
It is said: Pleasure is of three grades—lower, middle, and upper. The lower is the first dhyāna; the middle is the second dhyāna; the upper is the third dhyāna.

In the first dhyāna, there are the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*). The faculty of pleasure is associated with the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), while the faculty of joy is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

In the second dhyāna, there is only the faculty of joy associated with the mental consciousness. In the third dhyāna, there is only the faculty of pleasure associated with the mental consciousness. These belong to the five consciousnesses...
They are unable to discern; they do not know the characteristics of names. Eye-consciousness arises for the duration of a finger-snap, by which time mental consciousness has already arisen.
Therefore, the faculty of pleasure associated with the five consciousnesses cannot fulfill pleasure, whereas the faculty of pleasure associated with mental consciousness can fulfill pleasure.
△ Fourth, the heavens of the four dhyānas.

Ānanda, furthermore, there are gods and humans whose bodies and minds are no longer oppressed; the causes of suffering have been exhausted, yet pleasure is not permanent and will inevitably give rise to decay after a long time.

They simultaneously and instantaneously relinquish both the mind of suffering and the mind of pleasure. The characteristics of coarseness and heaviness are extinguished, and the nature of pure merit arises.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Birth of Merit (Puṇyaprasava).

It does not afflict the body or mind. If the causes [of suffering] have already been exhausted, one attains the first two dhyānas; however, their bliss is not permanent and will inevitably perish after a long time, leading to rebirth.
One then attains the third dhyāna. If one simultaneously and suddenly abandons the two types of mental pleasure, one then emerges from the fundamental dhyāna.

The previous three stages involve aversion to suffering and longing for pleasure, all of which are coarse and heavy. By neither accepting pleasure nor [suffering], and through the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, this constitutes pure merit.
Furthermore,
with a mind of equanimity that is perfectly integrated and a resolute understanding that is pure, they attain wondrous compliance within the unobstructed merit. Extending to the end of the future,
this class of beings is called the Heaven of Merit-Love (Puṇyaprasava).
The perfection of the mind of equanimity means that one does not abide in a state of mere equanimity, yet is still able to permeate and arouse the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state.

This is because all noble ones (*ārya*) on the path of cultivation rely upon this to practice the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇasamādhi*), and so forth; hence it is said that they attain "wondrous conformity.
To "reach the end of the future" means to reach the future limit of this stage. Furthermore, if one can permeate and arouse the outflow-free state, then it extends throughout [all time].
Throughout the three periods of time, it is without limit. This merit of relinquishing pleasure increases and becomes ever more excellent;
it is peerless in the world and is solely worthy of being cherished and delighted in.

Ānanda, from this heaven there are two diverging paths. If, based on the previous mind of immeasurable purity, one dwells having perfected and realized the full clarity of merit, such a class is called the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).

Regarding the bifurcation of paths within the realm of merit and love: because the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*) predominates in the four dhyānas, if one develops the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*) from the Light of Infinite Radiance (*Apramāṇābha*) and proceeds directly to the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*), one dwells in common with the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) and brings forth wisdom;
one may then become an Arhat or enter the stage of a Bodhisattva. However, if one dwells exclusively in equanimity...

To immediately enter the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*) is what is called being an outsider (*tīrthika*). As for the "Immeasurable Purity" (*Apramāṇaśubha*), it was previously [discussed as] the third dhyāna;

because one has not yet entered the stage of equanimity (*upekṣā*), this mind manifests fully. Therefore, this is specifically examined here. Regarding the "Vast Fruit" (*Bṛhatphala*), Qingliang says:
among the wholesome fruits of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), this is the most vast; furthermore, all its merits surpass those of the two lower [stages] and the second [dhyāna].

If, within the preceding state of mind, one simultaneously loathes both suffering and pleasure, refining the mind of equanimity until it flows in an uninterrupted succession and fully masters the path of equanimity, then body and mind both cease;
the mental faculties become ashen and congealed for five hundred kalpas. Because this person takes arising and ceasing as their cause, [they remain thus].
They are unable to manifest the nature that is neither arising nor ceasing. For the first half-eon they cease, and for the latter half-eon they arise;
such a class is called the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).

The fundamental awakening of the self-nature has neither arising nor ceasing, nor does it involve grasping or rejecting. This is truly because sentient beings are unable to proceed directly [to realization].

The following clarifies this point: [this state] must arise from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Having abandoned desire and attained purity, one relinquishes joy and delights in equanimity (*upekṣā*), reaching the point where both suffering and pleasure are discarded.
Although this equanimity is subtle, it can obstruct the eye of wisdom (*jñānacakṣus*) and lead to a state from which there is no return.

As for those who attain cessation during the first half-aeon, they extinguish what is maintained by the mind; this is not true quiescence (*śānti*). Once extinguished, they are born again; therefore, birth and extinction serve as its cause.
Ānanda, these four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly objects of suffering or pleasure.
Although they are not the unconditioned stage of true immovability, because their attainment of a goal and their application of effort have reached full maturity, they are called the Four Dhyānas.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: From the first dhyāna onward, all afflictions of the lower stages have been severed—namely, vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
Therefore, within this state, equanimity and mindfulness are pure and pristine. Consequently, the mind abides unmoved in this dhyāna;
that is to say, the attainment of a referential object has ceased and its application has become fully matured. This dhyāna possesses four factors (*aṅga*).
First is the factor of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. When abandoning the third dhyāna, one variously censures pleasure;
once pleasure has ceased and vanished, the immovable concentration arises together with equanimity (upekṣā). Therefore, the inner mind is serene, being free from both pain and pleasure.

Second is the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-aṅga*). Having attained the immovable true concentration of the fourth dhyāna, one relinquishes the difficult-to-relinquish pleasure of the third dhyāna and does not give rise to regret.
Third is the factor of pure mindfulness (*smṛti-pariśuddhi-aṅga*).

Having attained the true concentration of the fourth dhyāna, one should contemplate the faults of the lower stages and reflect upon one’s own merits, employing skillful means to nurture it so that it does not regress, thereby entering [the state].
This is the category of excellence. Fourth, the factor of one-pointedness of mind:

having attained the concentration of the four dhyānas, one uses the two preceding factors of equanimity and mindfulness to guard it, so that the mind remains single-pointedly in samādhi, like a bright mirror or still water, serene and constantly reflecting.
△ Fifth, the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Ānanda, herein there are further five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*). Within the lower realm, their nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are extinguished simultaneously;
both suffering and pleasure have vanished, and since they no longer dwell below, they establish their abode within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of equanimity.
The nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) refer to the nine grades each within the desire realm, the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, and the third dhyāna.
By severing the eighty-one grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) across the nine stages of the three realms—nine times nine—the two vehicles attain the fruits of Arhatship and Anāgāmin.
Having already severed the nine grades of afflictions for each of the three dhyānas and four stages of the desire realm, they have severed the afflictions of one stage of the desire realm.

The nine grades [of afflictions] are eliminated, and thus there is no longer a provisional dwelling in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). One eliminates the nine grades of each of the upper three stages;

pleasure is extinguished, and thus there is no longer a provisional dwelling in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). These five heavens are established separately from the fourth dhyāna and are collectively termed "purity of equanimity and mindfulness" (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi*);
hence it is said that their minds share the same category of equanimity (*upekṣā-sabhāgatā*). The *Nirvāṇa-kāśyapa-parivarta* states: "Within these four dhyānas, there are furthermore..."
There are two types: first, those who delight in samādhi; second, those who delight in wisdom. Those who delight in wisdom enter the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*).
Those who delight in samādhi enter the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). For these two types of persons, there are five progressive stages in the cultivation of the four dhyānas.

Second is non-cultivation. What are the five? They are: inferior, middling, superior; superior-middling; and superior-superior. Those who cultivate the superior-superior dwell in the Heaven of the Lesser Gods (Parīttābha).
Those who cultivate the superior-middling dwell in the Heaven of Good Sight (Sudṛśa). Those who cultivate the superior grade dwell in the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudarśana).
Those who cultivate the middling grade dwell in the Heaven Without Heat (Atapa). Those who cultivate the inferior grade dwell in the Heaven of Limited Radiance (Parīttaśubha). Furthermore...
There are two types. First, those who cultivate profound dhyāna and enter the five Pure Abodes.

Second, those who do not cultivate profound dhyāna but are born in the Formless Realm, where they attain parinirvāṇa at the end of their lifespan. These are called those who attain parinirvāṇa by going upstream (ūrdhvasrotas-parinirvāyin).
If one wishes to enter the Formless Realm, one cannot cultivate the four dhyānas with their five distinctions; yet if one does cultivate these five distinctions, [one enters the Form Realm].
Thus, they are able to censure the formless absorptions.
Ānanda, where both suffering and pleasure have ceased, and the turbulent mind does not engage, such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha).
When both suffering and pleasure are extinguished, the two minds of longing and aversion no longer stand in opposition; hence it is said that "struggling minds do not intersect.

Although the fourth dhyāna has already transcended suffering and pleasure, it is not called "free from affliction" (an-ūrdhva-saṃjñā), because for ordinary beings these are merely suppressed temporarily rather than being ultimately extinguished.
The trigger and the notch act alone; there is no ground for their meeting. Such a class [of beings] is called the Heaven of No-Heat (*Atapa*).

The trigger is the tip of the crossbar of a bow, and the notch is the end of the arrow—the place where the string is received. "Acting alone" means that once released from the hand, there is only the present moment of mindfulness, with no further ground for meeting.
This is because the ability to relinquish and that which is relinquished constitute what is called a "ground of meeting. Where there is no such meeting, it is the "ground of no-meeting."
Then the function of wisdom will be perfectly liberated. Subtle affliction is called "heat"; the absence of heat is more subtle.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, wondrous vision is perfectly clear and limpid; there are no further images of dust or any defilements whatsoever. Such is this class [of beings].
They are named the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa).
All five Pure Abodes delight in wisdom; this "Sublime Vision" arises from the relinquishment of extremes through the development of wisdom.
Within this state of wisdom, one perceives the ten directions sublimely: externally there are no sensory objects, and internally there is no defilement of the mind.
Refined vision manifests before them; they mold and fashion things without obstruction. This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna (Good Appearance) Heaven.

This is the same as the previously mentioned Sudarśana (Excellent Vision), but the term "refined" (*jing*) indicates that through the application of wisdom, they polish and refine until clarity is spontaneously revealed, reaching the ultimate limit of transformative power—just as one uses water and fire to smelt and cast all manner of vessels and implements.

They have reached the ultimate limit of the subtlest forms (*jī*) and exhausted the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*), entering the boundless. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*).
When form reaches its most minute state, it is called *jī*; when form is exhausted and its true nature manifests, this is what is meant by "exhausting the nature of form. This is the nature of form.
This nature is without limit; it is precisely the place where the noble ones of the three fruits develop the truth and return to the source.
Therefore, one should know that these five types of non-returners merely rely on the cultivation of similar classes [of beings].

It is at this very point that the meditative concentrations of the formless realm are criticized, for while one may sever the afflictions of the four upper stages, one cannot enter the boundless state by treating all cases as uniform.
The four emptinesses will be explained in detail below.
Ānanda, as for these heavens of the Non-returners (Anāgāmin), even the various Heavenly Kings of the four stages of the fourth dhyāna can only hear of them with admiration;
they cannot know or see them. It is like the vast wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the sacred path in this world today, which are all inhabited by Arhats.
Because it is maintained, it cannot be seen by the coarse people of the world.
The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage acts as the Great Pure Heaven King (*Mahāśuddhadeva*) of the fourth dhyāna heaven.

Having attained the Samādhi of the Exhaustion of Principle, he shares the sphere of activity of the Buddhas, reaches the source of the triple realm, and transforms sentient beings. This refers to the Bodhisattva acting as...

The various sages manifest and entrust their traces to the world to awaken people's wisdom; thus, they inspire those who hear with reverence and further guide those in the four dhyānas to transcend the mundane world.
△ Sixth, the conclusion on the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Ānanda, these eighteen heavens are solitary and without sexual union; yet they have not exhausted the burden of form. From this point downward, they are called the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*).
Taken collectively, these eighteen heavens are said to be "solitary and without sexual union" because they have transcended the realm of desire; thus they are called "the same in form."
Because they are obstructed, it is said that they have not yet exhausted the burden of form.

The above concludes the two realms of form (rūpadhātu). △ Third, the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), divided into six parts. First, the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana). First, the preliminary selection of those who turn their minds [from the lower realms].
Furthermore, Ānanda, from within this limit of form at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), there are again two divergent paths.
If one illuminates wisdom through a mind of equanimity (upekṣā-citta) such that wisdom is first perfected and pervasive, one then transcends the realm of dust and becomes an Arhat.
They enter the Bodhisattva vehicle. Such a class is called "Great Arhats who have turned their minds.
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the summit (*mūrdhan*), which is the ultimate. The "limit of form" (*rūpānta*) refers to that which is delimited by the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

There are two divergent paths within the four dhyānas: first, those who delight in cultivating samādhi and go directly to the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); second, those who delight in cultivating wisdom and... [proceeds].
One enters the five purities; this is the constant practice. Having entered the five purities, one naturally brings forth illumination, sheds all defilements and burdens, and becomes an Arhat.
Those who enter the Bodhisattva vehicle do so by means of the Arhat’s state entering the Bodhisattva vehicle; therefore, it is called "turning the mind.
For this reason, one enters [the Bodhisattva path] only after having already attained the fruit of the third stage and become an Arhat.
If one abides in a mind of equanimity, having accomplished the relinquishing of aversion, they perceive the body as an obstruction; by dissolving this obstruction, they enter into emptiness.
This class of practitioners is called the Sphere of Infinite Space.

This should generally be understood as referring to the four dhyānas. If one becomes an anāgāmin through the five pure abodes, then at the time of realizing the stage of srotāpanna, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has already been extinguished;
how could one then again perceive the body as an obstruction?

Nevertheless, there are also ordinary worldlings who, without passing through the stage of srotāpanna, realize the second or third fruits of the path; perhaps these are of that same category. 2. The Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Once all obstructions have been dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation; within this state, only the ālayavijñāna remains, together with a portion of the manas that is subtle in its activity.
This category is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).
All obstructions are precisely the obstruction of the body. If the obstruction of the body is not dissolved, then all obstructions will not be dissolved.
When it is said that "all obstructions are dissolved," it means the obstruction of the body is dissolved. When this obstruction is dissolved, the mind that perceives obstructions is also dissolved.
If one is unaware of this, then one relies solely upon the *ālayavijñāna*, which is entirely dependent on the *manas*. The delusion of the *ālaya* is a delusion regarding the *manas*.
Therefore, it is said that the manas is "complete" yet "half-fine. This refers to the half-fineness of the objects of the six consciousnesses as perceived by the manas.
The manas cannot perceive external objects; it can only take the discrimination of the six consciousnesses as its own object of discrimination.
This state of being half-fine is severed only when one becomes an Arhat. Thus, once this half has been severed—
When it becomes subtle, the six consciousnesses are entirely severed. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "I say that the cessation of the discriminating consciousness is called nirvāṇa.
Does this also grant that the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles is identical to that of the Tathāgata?

Now, regarding the statement that the cessation of the discriminating consciousness is called nirvāṇa, this is spoken from the perspective of one who clearly understands the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). The followers of the two vehicles do not know the eight consciousnesses; they merely [sever]...
Regarding the objects of the six consciousnesses, the sensory realms of the five consciousnesses cease to function as external objects;

furthermore, the internal half that serves as the object of the *manas* (seventh consciousness) also ceases. Through the cessation of this half, one realizes the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

However, the fundamental eighth consciousness, which remains the object of the *manas*, has not yet ceased; this constitutes the obstruction of the selfhood of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*). △ Third: Non-existence.
In this station,
as both emptiness and form have vanished and the conscious mind has utterly ceased, the ten directions are silent and there is nowhere to go.
This class of beings is called the Station of Nothingness.
Once both emptiness and form have vanished, the preceding consciousness of the heavenly realms is extinguished; this extinction refers to the subtle state of the half-portion.

Why is it that this half-portion’s extinction does not result in the nirvana of the Two Vehicles? It is because it is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), suppressed but not severed;
that is to say, they have never yet realized the true nature of non-self. "Nirvana" here refers to that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
One cannot even attain the true nature of non-self, let alone the true nature of self. What is meant by "cannot attain" is that this is spoken in contrast to the notion of a self;
it does not mean that there is no attainment of truth at all. Even "attainment" is merely that which is realized as being without a self.

It is utterly without destination, wherein the objective realms perceived by consciousness are extinguished of their own accord, becoming identical with the obscure principle (tattva). △ Four: Neither Non-Non.

In the sphere of perception, the nature of consciousness is unmoving. By exhausting one's inquiry through cessation, within the inexhaustible, one proclaims the nature of exhaustion. It is as if existing yet not existing;
as if exhausted yet not exhausted. This class of beings is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
This is precisely the nature of consciousness that was previously extinguished; yet, upon seeing its reality, one realizes it has never been extinguished.

Through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one investigates and exhaustively examines it, merely manifesting the nature of exhaustion within the inexhaustible. Therefore, it is said: "As if existing, it does not exist; as if exhausted, it is not exhausted.

Without this consciousness undergoing the illumination of the true nature (*tathatā*), one will ultimately be unable to realize it; to labor in exhaustive investigation in vain is entirely [in error].

Deluded thoughts cannot be self-awakened; therefore, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. △ Fifth, the summary of the four formless attainments and a detailed account of their divergent paths.

Those who exhaustively investigate emptiness in these realms do not fully realize the principle of emptiness. This class of beings consists of those who have reached the limit of the holy path from the Heaven of No-Return.
They are called "non-distinguished, dull-witted Arhats. If they depart from the realm of the non-conceptualizing externalist devas, they exhaust the state of emptiness without returning;
lost in their outflows and lacking hearing of the Dharma, they then enter the cycle of rebirth.
Except for those who have reached the ultimate through the noble path of the Pure Heavens (*śuddhāvāsa*), they are called "dull-witted arhats. They do not enter saṃsāra;

this refers to those who have already seen the truths (*satyadarśana*) and thus lack the portion of falling back into the wheel [of existence]. However, because they are attached to the savoring of samādhi, they obstruct the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and remain close to ordinary worldlings and outsiders.
How much more so for those who see nothing at all and merely relish nirvāṇa—such people are rarely not in error. This is what is meant by "exhausting emptiness" (*kūṣu*).
They do not return. If they were to return, there would simply be no fault. △ Sixth, the summary of all the heavens:
Ānanda, among these various heavens, each of the devas and humans is a common person receiving the retribution of their karma; when that retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth.
Those Heavenly Kings, however, are Bodhisattvas who, while traversing samādhi, gradually advance and turn their merit toward enlightenment.

The path practiced by the noble ones is that which all devas universally bind through the realms of desire, form, and formlessness. Since the *Avataṃsaka* is entrusted to the realm of retribution, it does not reach the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

Furthermore, the fact that the various devas are bound first and the four formless attainments are bound later serves as one further proof. The *Diaozhi* states: "The Bodhisattvas of the ten stages..."

It is reported that these correspond to the Ten Kings: the first stage is the King of Jambudvīpa; the second stage is the King of the Four Heavenly Kings; the third stage is the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

the fourth stage is the King of the Yāma Heaven; the fifth stage is the King of the Tuṣita Heaven; the sixth stage is the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; the seventh stage is the King of the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven;
the eighth stage is the King of the Second Dhyāna; the ninth stage is the King of the Third Dhyāna; and the tenth stage is the King of the Fourth Dhyāna. Thus it is.
Maheśvara. When Bodhisattvas advance in their cultivation, they do not abide in the first dhyāna because they still carry residual heterodox views.

All of this is by means of skillful means to lead toward the ultimate reality. While dwelling among the devas, they transform those devas who possess the retribution of real karma, causing them to be liberated from celestial karmic bonds;
thus, he is entitled to be called "King."
Ānanda, in these four heavens of the formless realm, body and mind are extinguished, and the nature of concentration manifests before them; there is no physical matter resulting from karma.
From this point until the end, it is called the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
"Manifestation of the nature of concentration" refers to the existence of matter that is the fruit of concentration; this indicates the absence of matter that is the fruit of karma.

Although the physical form of this celestial being is entirely exhausted, the mind does not perish. Because it is refined by the power of concentration, it is neither existent nor non-existent, and is therefore also said to be "extinguished."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The gods of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) move, turn, bend, and look up; these are not seen by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Thus, their bodies do not perish; it is simply that they are not perceived."
All of this arises from failing to understand the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind; through the accumulation of delusions, the three realms of existence are produced.
Within these realms, beings wander in delusion, sinking into the seven destinies according to their respective types. These are the *pudgalas*, each following its own kind.
From the six heavens of the desire realm up to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, all fail to realize the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind.
From this luminosity, objects arise; thus, the three realms of delusion are produced.

"In between" refers specifically to the various heavens, where they vainly expend effort, ultimately following their delusions to give rise to afflictions and karma within the seven destinies, each hastening toward its own kind. (The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of eight types of persons.)
The sixth is called the *pudgala* (person). This refers to that which repeatedly takes up various realms of existence—whether being born there or being born here.
That which truly brings about this process is the grasping at a person (*pudgalagrāha*). It is because of relying upon this that the six destinies and four modes of birth revolve without end.
The three formless realms have been concluded. △ Fourth, the specific attachment to the four types of asuras among the non-gods.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms, there are again four classes of asuras. If they belong to the realm of hungry ghosts...

By the power of protecting the Dharma, they ride upon their supernatural faculties and enter into space. These asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
The *Fahua wenju* states: "Those categorized within the realm of hungry ghosts dwell on the shores of the great ocean;

having taken refuge in the Buddha and protected the Dharma, by the majestic power of protecting the Dharma, they ride upon their own innate supernatural faculties to enter the void and go forth to protect the Buddha-dharma."
If they descend from the celestial realms due to a loss of merit, their dwelling place will be adjacent to the sun and moon;
these asuras are born from a womb and are categorized within the human realm.
The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states: One thousand *yojanas* to the east of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, lies the city-palace of Śambara.

It has sevenfold walls composed of the seven precious substances. On the southern, western, and northern sides, there are likewise palaces of the Asura kings, equally exquisite and similar in appearance, equal in rank to the gods who dwell upon the earth.

There are asura kings who uphold the world; their power penetrates all, and they are without fear. They are able to contend for authority with the Brahma King, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
These asuras arise through transformation and are categorized within the realm of the gods.
The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* states: The wife of the asura Citta was a goddess of the Mount Gandhamādana music deities.
She conceived and carried the child for eight thousand years before giving birth to a daughter named Śacī. Kauśika sought her hand in marriage; she was called Manoharā.
When Śakra arrived at the Nandana Grove and entered the pool with his various celestial maidens to sport therein, the woman became filled with jealousy.
He dispatched five yakṣas to inform his father-king, who immediately mobilized the fourfold army to attack Śakra.

He established himself upon the waters of the great ocean and sat atop the summit of Mount Sumeru. With nine hundred and ninety-nine heads, he acted simultaneously, shaking the city of Sudarśana and rocking Mount Sumeru;
the waters of the four great oceans surged and trembled all at once. Śakra was struck with terror as he sat upon the [Aśvattha] tree.
In the Dharma Hall, he burned various famous incenses and made great vows, reciting the Great Bright Mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Then, from the midst of the void, a wheel of blades descended spontaneously; it struck the asura, and his ears, nose, hands, and feet all fell off at once.
It turned the waters of the great ocean red like the pearls of oysters, and the asura fled in retreat.
Abiding there, he enters the hollow of a lotus fiber.
Ānanda, there is another class of inferior asuras who are born in the heart of the great ocean and dwell in the mouths of underwater caverns;
they roam through the void by day and return to their watery lodgings at night. These asuras exist due to moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: Vemacitra is translated here as "Resounding Height" (*xiǎnggāo*) and also as "Cave-Dweller" (*xuéjū*).
This refers to the fact that from the bottom of the great ocean, a great sound emerges that penetrates beyond the seas; hence he is called "Cave-Dweller. It further states:
there is an asura who dwells at the base of Mount Sumeru in the great ocean. Within the desire realm, he manifests transformations of body, both large and small, according to his will.

The *Manas* (Mind) is capable of such action. It dwells in the City of Radiance (*Prabhāpurī*). Encompassing all four of the aforementioned types, although their karmic retributions vary in quality, each attains mastery over its own power, influence, and enjoyments.
Generally, the cause for this lies in harboring a spirit of suspicion toward the Triple Gem and constantly desiring to surpass others, thereby increasing one’s anger;
thus, although they possess celestial merit, it does not equal that of the [genuine] devas, and although they possess human merit—
These obstruct progress on the Path. Although they exist among ghosts and animals, they can still leap lightly and travel great distances;
thus we know that practitioners should cultivate their causes with reverence and caution, lest they find themselves at a fork in the road.
