The distinctions among the various heavens have concluded. △ Seventh, showing the falsity of the seven realms of existence to encourage correct cultivation.
This is divided into five parts. First, showing their falsity:
Ānanda, in this way, the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and immortals; devas and asuras—examine these thoroughly.

The seven realms of existence are all states of delusion and the characteristics of conditioned phenomena; they arise from false conceptualization and follow from false conceptualization according to karma.

Within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind of non-action, they are all like flowers in the sky—originally having no point of attachment, being nothing but a single void delusion without any root or source.

This summarizes the falsity of the seven realms of existence. It involves a meticulous and thorough investigation: to examine the various conditioned phenomena of the seven realms with discernment, one finds they all arise from delusion.
The fruits of rebirth thus summoned are nothing other than the effects of their respective karmic causes.

Delusion, karma, and suffering—these three—fundamentally never touch the wondrously luminous mind; they are like flowers in the sky, having no root or source whatsoever. To measure them [is to see they are empty].
The cause leads to the fruit without failing by even a hair’s breadth; yet, when the false is mistaken for the true, everything becomes a mere dream or illusion. 2. Showing the Karmic Cause:
“Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and thus undergo this cycle of saṃsāra for immeasurable kalpas, without attaining [liberation].”

True purity arises from following the precepts against killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Conversely, by turning away from these three, one gives rise to the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

That which possesses these [transgressions] belongs to the realm of ghosts; that which lacks them belongs to the celestial realms. As existence and non-existence mutually oppose one another, the nature of saṃsāra arises.
The previous statement said that all realms of existence fundamentally do not exist within the wondrously luminous mind.

This present statement says that if one does not recognize the fundamental mind and follows the path of karma, then cause and effect will be clearly manifest: if [the mind) exists, there is killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; if it does not exist, there is no killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct.
Therefore, it is said that existence and non-existence mutually oppose one another, giving rise to the nature of saṃsāra. The fundamental, wondrously luminous mind is inherently...
Profoundly round, both existence and non-existence are abandoned; one should simply entrust oneself to this. △ Third, revealing the correct cultivation:
If one attains the wondrous arousal of *samādhi*, then there is wondrous and eternal stillness; both existence and non-existence are absent, and even the absence of duality is extinguished.
Since there is not even "non-killing," "non-stealing," or "non-lust," how could one further follow after the matters of killing, stealing, and lust?
To speak again for the purpose of illuminating the fundamental mind: the fundamental mind is itself wondrous; it does not even possess "non-killing," "non-stealing," or "non-lust."

How could there be anyone else who, at this very moment, can perfectly accomplish *samāpatti*? Furthermore, they are certainly not of the Two Vehicles; how could they be the same as ordinary worldlings or outsiders?
△ Fourth, the conclusion that rewards those of the same class.
Ānanda, the three karmas are not severed; each has its own private [cause]. Because of these respective privacies, there is a commonality among these privacies.
It is not that they have no fixed location; they arise from one's own delusions, and since their arising is delusory and without cause, they cannot be traced or investigated.
This answers the question regarding the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of various individual groups. It is not that there is no fixed location;

yet, to further claim that birth is delusory and without cause, such that it cannot be investigated, serves only to show that all faculties and capacities are formed by delusive vision. If one illuminates this in a single thought-moment, what form would appear before one?
To investigate its source, there is truly nothing to point to or designate. △ Five: Exhortation to Sever and Eliminate.

Exert yourself in practice. If you wish to attain Bodhi, you must eliminate the three delusions. If you do not exhaust these three delusions, even if you should acquire supernormal powers, they will all be merely worldly, conditioned functions;
with habitual tendencies unextinguished, you will fall into the path of Māra. Though you may desire to remove delusion, [you will fail].
Twofold falsehood is what the Tathāgata calls pitiable. You have fabricated it yourself through delusion;
it is not the fault of Bodhi. All things in the world are created by the mind; arising from the mind, there is nothing that does not manifest.

Therefore it is said that even if one attains supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), they are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Thus, know that the mind is fundamentally unborn, and that whatever is born must return to extinction. Whatever is created...
Delusion and karma can never be extinguished. The mind does not know karma, and karma does not know the mind;
yet from beginning to end, cause and effect naturally form a cycle of rebirth, which is merely experienced by the mind.
To speak thus is called the correct teaching; for any other to speak otherwise is the teaching of Māra.
This is stated with even greater earnestness for the sake of the final age, in order to prevent false teachings from conflating with this true cultivation. The Sage’s compassion is profound and deep;
practitioners must examine themselves.

The preceding seven sections have concluded the demonstration of the falsity of the seven destinies to encourage correct cultivation. △ Eighth, the elimination of the *skandha-māra*. This is divided into two parts.
First, the original cause for the arising of the deeds of Māra, which is further divided into seven. First, the self-exposition without being questioned.
At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his session on the lion throne, he took up the seven-jeweled desk,
turned toward the Purple-Jade Mountain, and leaned against it once more, addressing the great assembly and Ānanda, saying:
As the Dharma assembly concludes, this is suspended here to reveal the hidden māras, so that all who practice authentically may, according to their realization, observe and discern them.

This is that which is universally known by the All-Knowing Wisdom and that which is protected and mindful of through unconditional, profound compassion. Strive with all your might to cleanse the mind;
the kindness [bestowed] is so great it is difficult to repay. △ Second, pointing out that the activities of māras are difficult to recognize.
"You who are still in training—whether pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas—have today turned your minds toward great bodhi and supreme, wondrous enlightenment.
I have now taught you the method for true practice; yet you do not yet recognize the subtle demonic activities that arise during the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
When such demonic realms manifest before you, you fail to recognize them. Your purification of mind is not correct, and you fall into false views."
Perhaps it is your aggregate-demon (skandha-māra), or perhaps it is a celestial demon (deva-māra); perhaps you are possessed by a ghost or spirit, or perhaps you have encountered a malevolent ogress;
thus your mind is not clear, and you mistake a thief for your own son.
The wondrous contemplation of original enlightenment does not give rise to discrimination. If there is even the slightest thing seen, it is not the true cleansing of the mind.

To mistake a thief for one's own son—as described in the following passage—is to take what is not yet a realization of the holy as such. The "demon of the aggregates" refers to the immeasurable habitual tendencies of discrimination perfumed by the various aggregates;
these flash forth momentarily within the midst of tranquil illumination. If one fails to observe them with awareness, heterodox views will inevitably arise.
The celestial Māra is the son of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; all ghosts and spirits are his retinue.
However, when practitioners fail to purify their minds, Māra finds an opportunity to exploit them, as detailed in the following text. △ Third, the admonition against obtaining little.
I exhort you to listen to and receive my instructions.
Furthermore, do not consider a small attainment to be sufficient, like the bhikṣu who lacked learning in the fourth dhyāna. He falsely claimed to have realized the state of an arhat;
when his celestial retribution was exhausted, the signs of decline appeared before him. Having slandered the arhats, he underwent further existence and fell into the Avīci Hell.
"You should listen attentively. I shall now explain this to you in detail. Ānanda rose from his seat, as did the other students in the assembly;
with joy, they prostrated themselves and waited in reverence for the compassionate instruction.
This admonition serves to show that one should be content with what little has been attained. It cites the unlearned bhikṣu as a warning for those who follow.

Although great false speech is excluded from the category of *adhimāna* (conceit), it nevertheless begins with the attachment to one's own views and the desire for victory, culminating in self-deception;
thus, one does not realize until it is too late that one has already fallen into ruin. Therefore, this has been analyzed in detail out of the compassionate grace of the Sage.
This is merely what you should respectfully contemplate. △ Fourth, showing that the essence of awakening is non-dual and that the world arises through delusion.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly: "You all should know that within the worlds of outflows, there are twelve classes of living beings."
Fundamental enlightenment is wondrously luminous; this perfected essence of the mind is non-dual and indistinguishable from that of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

It is due to your deluded thoughts that you mistake the principle for error. From ignorance and craving, birth arises; this arising gives rise to pervasive delusion, whereby the nature of space appears. As this delusion continues without ceasing, transformations unfold.
When worlds arise, these lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are not free from outflows; they are all established through deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization.
This is because sentient beings and the Buddha’s fundamentally enlightened mind are originally one and the same in their perfect subtlety; yet both have turned away from it due to deluded clarity.
This true wisdom does not perceive a reality; therefore, it gives rise to emptiness. That which is called "delusion" is space.

Since there is already the realm of space, it is not without outflows (*anāsrava*); this distinguishes it from the provisional and real rewards of the Buddhas, for all else is established through deluded thought.
△ Fifth, showing that the world is fundamentally void: when truth arises, emptiness perishes.
You should know that empty space is born within your own mind, like a stray cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky; how much more so, then, are all worlds contained within empty space?
If even one person among you gives rise to the true path and returns to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions will all vanish and perish.
Why is it that the lands within space do not tremble or shatter?

They are established based upon the preceding false imaginings. These delusions reside in the mind like dust upon a mirror; therefore, as soon as one awakens to the truth, the great earth collapses and cracks.
This principle is inherently so: because of delusion, there is space; because of space, there are realms. Upon awakening, even space [vanishes].
When extinction is fully realized, how can the world continue to exist? This must be known by each person for themselves.
That the palace of Māra collapses and disintegrates is a matter that must necessarily occur. △ Sixth, demonstrating the penetration of mental mastery, the heavenly Māras were startled and disturbed.
"You all practice dhyāna and adorn yourselves with samādhi.

The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as well as the great Arhats free from outflows, possess minds of penetrating clarity and remain profoundly tranquil in their respective states. Yet even the Māras, ghosts, spirits, and all ordinary devas—"

They saw their palaces collapse and crack for no apparent reason; the great earth quaked and split open; and all creatures of water, land, and air were struck with such terror that they could not contain themselves.

Yet, ordinary beings remained mired in ignorance and failed to perceive these transformations. Those beings all attained the five supernormal powers, with the sole exception of the extinction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Attached to these worldly defilements, how could I cause you to shatter that place?
For this reason, when you are in samādhi, ghosts, spirits, celestial māras, and all manner of demons and fiends come together to harass you.
The practitioner, within samādhi, is identical in essence with all bodhisattvas and arhats;
this reveals the ground of returning to the source, which is profoundly still in its very place. Enlightenment results in perfect union; delusion manifests as separation.
All māras, yakṣas, and devas see their palaces collapse and crack—this too is a state of deluded self-differentiation arising from extreme darkness. Following this...

He passed away; having exhausted his outflows (*āsrava*), he felt no attachment. It was only because of this demonic desire that, due to his possession of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), he became naturally terrified.

Thus, within his samādhi, they all came to disturb and confuse him; these were merely the *piśācas* and *yakṣas* whom [the demon] had dispatched. △ Seventh: The Subtle Enlightenment is Difficult to Shake.
Because of violating prohibitions and failing to guard against them.
Yet those various māras, though they may be greatly enraged, within their own afflictions and within your wondrous awakening, are like wind blowing against light or a blade cutting through water;
they do not touch one another at all. You are like boiling water, while they are like solid ice; as the warmth gradually approaches, [the ice will surely melt].
Before long, they will perish and vanish; you merely rely on supernatural powers, acting only as their guest, thereby bringing about ruin and disorder.
This is because you are the master within the five aggregates (skandhas) of your own mind. If the master is deluded, the guest gains the advantage.
Within that state of worldly affliction (*kleśa*) lies your own wondrous enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*); this is the ultimate distinction between the demon and the Buddha.

Wondrous enlightenment is like light, like a boiling liquid, and like a host; worldly affliction is like the wind, like ice, and like a guest. The difference between awakening and delusion is vast and absolute; spiritual powers are but a vain labor.
Unless the practitioner’s own latent discriminative mind spontaneously awakens from its doubts and perils, one will ultimately never enter [the Way].
If you remain in *dhyāna* and awaken without delusion, then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you.

As the *skandhas* dissolve and enter into clarity, all those various evils will be compelled to receive their dark vapors; since clarity can destroy darkness, they will soon perish on their own. How would they dare remain to disturb your *dhyāna*?
If you do not attain clear awakening and are instead deluded by the *skandhas*, then you, Ānanda, will surely become a child of Māra.
The accomplished Māra-person, such as Matanga, was exceedingly insignificant and inferior. He merely used incantations to break your monastic discipline;
among the eighty thousand practices, he destroyed but a single precept. Because your mind remained pure, you had not yet fallen into ruin.

This [Māra], however, destroys your entire body of precious awakening, like a high minister’s family suddenly being subjected to confiscation of property—utterly dispersed and ruined, beyond all hope of rescue.

This demonstrates that in *dhyāna* one must always maintain vigilance; if deluded, one lacks awareness, but if aware, there is no fault. "Shadows" refers to the habitual tendencies of subtle discrimination.
Once these tendencies are dissolved, clarity arises in their very place, using light to dispel darkness—just like blowing dust with the wind;
what difficulty or danger could there be? If one harbors even slight doubt, one will immediately be obscured by it. This is comparable to a *brahma-mantra*.
The Māra is inferior; that [which you have received] was merely a spell cast upon you. Examining the power of that spell, it can destroy but a single precept of yours.

However, because those who have attained the first fruit (srotāpanna) have seen the Truths and thus their views obstruct their thoughts, it is said that "because the mind is pure," they have not yet sunk into ruin.
This refers back to the aforementioned destruction of precepts, up to the point where it ruins your entire body of precious awakening; it is not a matter of the mind being pure.
"Purity" is like the confiscation of a high minister's property; it becomes scattered and unrecoverable.
When a minister violates a grave state law, his official records are erased and he is reduced to the status of a commoner; this is what is meant by "scattered."
The first section, "The Original Source of the Arising of Māra’s Deeds," is concluded. △ Second, the main exposition of the Skandha-māras, divided into seven parts.
First, the Rūpa-skandha, divided into four parts. First, the domain of the Rūpa-skandha.
Ānanda, you should know that when you sit at the site of enlightenment, you must cause all thoughts to dissolve and fall away.

When those thoughts are exhausted, then all states of clarity and brilliance that are free from thought will remain unmoved by motion or stillness, and recollection and forgetfulness will be as one. You should abide in this state and enter samādhi.

It is like a person with clear vision who dwells in great darkness; though their essential nature is wondrously pure, the mind has not yet emitted light. This is what is called the domain of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

When all discursive thoughts dissolve, it is not that all thoughts do not arise; rather, one should contemplate while remaining free from contemplation, for there is no such thing as being "free from contemplation. Thus it is said.

It is said that all states of clarity and brilliance arising from the departure from discursive thought are described in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*: "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts;
yet, do not suppress or extinguish those deluded minds. Abiding within the realm of delusive perceptions, do not apply further cognitive scrutiny;

and in this absence of scrutiny, do not discriminate what is real. It is precisely at this point that it is said that movement and stillness do not shift one’s ground, and recollection and forgetfulness remain as one.
Only then would it be truly corresponding. However, to form such an understanding is not genuine samādhi.
It is like a person with clear vision who, having already attained a refined, essential, and wondrous purity upon entering samādhi, yet claims to be dwelling in great darkness.
This is a metaphor for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) not yet being shattered; that is to say, the mind has not yet emitted light, as if one were truly within a state of profound darkness.
Nevertheless, when the practitioner reaches this point, their essential nature is wondrously pure; they simply do not realize themselves that light has not yet been emitted.
△ Second, the sign of the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*):
If one’s vision becomes clear and bright, and the ten directions open up with total transparency, free from any further gloom or darkness, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Upon examining its origin, one finds that solidified false conceptualization (*dṛḍha-vikalpa*) constitutes its root.

The previous metaphor compared [the mind] to clear vision; now, "concentration intensely radiates light" is a metaphor for the eyes becoming bright and lucid, such that the ten directions open up completely and there is no longer any darkness—this is the state of the realm when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is shattered.
The turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) constitutes the primary substance of the four great elements;
it corresponds precisely to the point where space and seeing are not yet distinguished. If the aggregate of form is shattered, one can immediately transcend it. Observe its origin.
This is an observation of the origin of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). It arises from the firm grasping of awakened clarity and the obstructions left by deluded thoughts;

thus, one knows that for those who enter right concentration, there are indeed skillful means in the application of the mind. △ Third, the distinctions of the objective realm of form, divided into ten parts. First:
the body is able to transcend obstructions.

Ānanda, you should investigate this subtle luminosity within with diligent precision until the four great elements no longer interweave. In a brief moment, your body will be able to pass through obstructions.
This is called the overflowing of refined clarity into the external realm; it is merely a temporary attainment through spiritual effort and is not a realization of sainthood.
If you do not regard it as a sign of sainthood, it is called a "wholesome state"; if you interpret it as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately be possessed by various demons.
To investigate and refine the wondrous clarity is itself to accord with that wondrous clarity; one does not miss its proper timing.

When the mind is free from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it naturally ceases its weaving. There can be no separate act of refining. The internal and external four great elements are what obstruct the mind;

it is not that the four great elements themselves are the obstruction. When the essence of spirit flows forth in abundance, there is a sudden, seamless integration. Whether emerging or non-emerging, both are neither of the two dualistic realms.
By this he knows for himself that it is merely a lack of noble realization. 2. Picking out Worms from the Body.

"Ānanda, if one further uses this mind to investigate the subtle brilliance until it penetrates deep within the body, this person will suddenly pick out roundworms and pinworms from within their own body.
Their physical form remains intact, without any injury or damage. This is called the overflowing of refined spirit."

As for these physical forms, they are merely the temporary attainment of such states through refined practice; they do not constitute holy realization. If one does not conceive of them as holy, they are called "auspicious realms.
If one interprets them as holy, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
The wondrous clarity penetrates itself; there is no distinction between inner and outer body. Seeing the worm picked out was as if taking it from before one's eyes;
the physical form remained perfectly intact. How could this have begun only today? If one can be thus, from where would "sage-like understanding" arise? △ Third: Empty Hearing of the Secret Meaning.

Furthermore, as one investigates this mind with refined precision both internally and externally, at that time the *po*, *hun*, will, and spirit—excluding the body which they sustain—all enter into mutual interpenetration, with none acting as host or guest.
Suddenly, one hears the sound of the Dharma being preached in the void, or hears the secret meanings being expounded throughout the ten directions.
This is called the successive separation and union of the refined spirits; it accomplishes the seeds of goodness, and for a time, such experiences are attained.

This is not a realization of the holy; if you do not conceive of it as being holy, it is called a "wholesome state. If you interpret it as a holy attainment, you will immediately fall under the sway of various demons.
The soul, the spirit, the will, and the consciousness each have their own respective functions, just as the six sense organs each have their own perceptions.
That these—excluding the physical body they grasp—now interpenetrate and serve as both guest and host to one another, arises from the fusion of wondrous luminosity.
"Chè! This is also like the six sense organs functioning for one another, each acting as both host and guest. That he heard the Dharma and expounded its meaning is the very proof of this.
What is called the 'separation and union of essence and spirit' is nothing other than this. △ Fourth, the Buddha appears and the lotus emerges.

Furthermore, as this mind becomes clear, exposed, bright, and penetrating, an inner radiance shines forth, causing all ten directions to become the color of Jambūnada gold and all species of beings to transform into Tathāgatas.
At that moment, one suddenly beholds Vairocana seated upon the Terrace of Celestial Light.
Surrounded by a thousand Buddhas, a hundred billion lands, and lotus flowers all appear simultaneously. This is called the defilement of the awakening of the soul and spirit;
it is the heart-light becoming refined and bright, illuminating all worlds. To attain such a state for a moment is not yet a holy realization.
If one does not give rise to the thought of being a sage, it is called a "wholesome state. If one forms a conception of being a sage, one immediately succumbs to various delusions.
When the true nature is revealed, one thoroughly knows that both the internal and external, throughout the ten directions, are entirely filled by the great body of Vairocana.
Matter and mind are non-dual; essence and function are simultaneous. Judging by what is seen now, none of it constitutes a supernatural marvel. As it is said:
The mind is the awakening of the spirit. The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra says: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, appearing universally before all sentient beings;
responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi.
When the practitioner’s wondrous clarity coalesces, whatever is revealed is truly nothing other than this. An ancient master said: "All sounds are..."
The Buddha’s voice. All forms are the Buddha’s form; understand this deeply and do not entertain other views. △ Fifth:
Jewel-colored light fills the void.
Furthermore, with this mind, one minutely investigates the wondrous clarity, observing without ceasing, suppressing and subduing it, restraining and transcending it.

At that moment, suddenly the empty space of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures, or the color of a hundred treasures, simultaneously filling it all without obstructing one another.
Blue, yellow, red, and white each appeared in their pure forms. This is called the power of suppression surpassing its limits.
To attain such a state for a time is not yet a holy realization. If you do not conceive the thought that it is a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm.
If you interpret it as a holy realization, you will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.
This, too, is a manifestation of a single form. It arises simply because the practitioner’s knowledge and vision have not yet been liberated;
because the power of their effort at total cessation is insufficient, mind and object arise as distinct entities. If one can awaken to this, they will naturally return to their original state. △ Six:
Night is the same as Day.
Furthermore, by using this mind to investigate until it becomes clear and transparent, its refined radiance remains undisturbed.
Suddenly, in the middle of the night, within a dark room, one sees various objects no different from those seen in broad daylight, yet the objects in the dark room do not vanish.

This is called the mind becoming subtle and dense such that its vision clarifies the profound darkness; though one may temporarily attain such a state, it is not a realization of sainthood. Do not regard it as a state of sainthood.
This is called a "wholesome realm. If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
The wondrous clarity is concentrated and still; when stillness reaches its extreme, light is emitted. Nothing dark or obscured can darken it, yet objects in a dark room are not thereby annihilated.
Before one's eyes there is no dharma, yet the realm remains manifest. What the light of the mind penetrates is as clear as day.
What does "the night" mean? Within *samādhi*, it is inherently like this. △ Seven: The Body Is Not Perceived When Cut.
Furthermore, when this mind enters completely into the void and fusion, the four limbs suddenly become like grass and wood; even when burned by fire or cut with a blade, [one feels nothing].

One has never experienced such awakening. Furthermore, the firelight cannot burn or scorch; even if one cuts the flesh, it is as if carving wood. This is called the merging of the sensory objects (*viṣaya-saṃhāra*).
It pushes aside the natures of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and enters exclusively into purity. To attain this for a time does not constitute a realization of the holy state (*ārya-siddhi*).
Not giving rise to the mind of holiness is called a wholesome state; if one forms a conception of holiness, one immediately succumbs to various delusions.
The wondrous clarity transcends the body, for its essence is not cognition. Formerly, the four elements constituted the body, which caused awareness to arise;
now, the five sense-objects have all dissolved and the four elements no longer interweave. When function enters the state of purity, how could it be otherwise by the nature of things? △ Eight.
Universally accomplishing the Buddha-fields, and further, by means of this mind,
having perfected the function of the pure and purified mind to its ultimate limit, one suddenly sees that the great earth, the mountains,

and rivers of the ten directions have all become Buddha-lands, complete with the seven treasures and filled everywhere with radiance; furthermore, one sees the Buddhas and Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
They pervade the entire realm of space. The towers and palaces are magnificent; looking down, they see the hells, and looking up, they observe the celestial palaces, attaining unimpeded vision.

This is called the deepening of focused contemplation through the practice of longing for the higher realms and revulsion toward the lower ones. After long contemplation, these images become manifest; yet this is not a realization of sainthood. One must not mistake this for the state of a sage.
This is called a "wholesome realm. If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, one will immediately succumb to various deviant influences.

To harbor thoughts of longing for the sublime and loathing the mundane, and for these thoughts to persist until they solidify into a transformation—this is something that should not occur within *samādhi*.
However, if one spontaneously awakens to this and thoroughly understands it as such, then this very knowing-mind itself becomes the realm; it is just like ordinary sentient beings.
One performs actions and likewise knows them oneself; this very mind of knowing manifests the signs of the three miserable realms.
It begins with self-interest and ultimately enters into the common lot. The Dharma is also like this. △ Ninth: Seeing Afar at Night.

Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate what is profound and distant, suddenly in the middle of the night, one may see from afar the markets, streets, lanes, relatives, and kinsmen, or hear their voices.
This is called "oppressing the mind. Because it is so intensely pressured, the consciousness flies out; therefore, one frequently sees things beyond physical barriers.

This is not for the purpose of realizing sainthood; if one does not give rise to the mind of sainthood, it is called a "wholesome state. If one interprets it as the realization of sainthood, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
Whether distant or near, whether of the present or the past, all objects and persons within one's own mind are fundamentally not separated; in a single thought-moment, they are thus.

It is because of being obstructed by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) that there appear the ten directions and the three periods of time. When the practitioner brings forth illumination, they verify this through principle.

[The Master] replied: "I know. Now, driven by the exertion of effort, such phenomena manifest; it is not to be considered extraordinary. △ Ten: The Meaning of the Transformation and Pervasion of the Body.

Furthermore, when one investigates this mind to the ultimate degree of refinement, one may see the physical form of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) undergo transformation and shift, appearing for a brief moment without apparent cause.

These various shifts and changes are called the "deviant mind. One thereby harbors demons and spirits, or encounters celestial Māras who enter one's heart and belly, causing one to preach the Dharma without cause or reason and claim to have mastered subtle meanings;
yet this is not a sign of saintly realization. If you do not give rise to the thought of being a saint, the demonic activities will subside.
If one forms a holy understanding, one will immediately succumb to various deviant influences.
When the initial mind first gives rise to illumination, one follows *samādhi* in the hope of gradual realization. At first, one perceives the transformation of physical form;

subsequently, one penetrates the subtle meaning. All of this results from deep observation and the culmination of merit. Yet, were one to stir even a single thought, one would immediately be disturbed by demons.

The preceding nine [levels] still belong to the realm of dhyāna; this, however, is what is summoned by actual realization. One simply knows for oneself that it is not [the ultimate], yet there is nothing lost.
This concludes the distinctions among the three types of colored objects. △ Fourth, the conclusion and instruction to transmit [this teaching].
Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states that appear during *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a conflicted manner toward the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Thus, these phenomena manifest. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering such conditions, they remain lost and fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming instead that they have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, you should rely upon [the teachings] in the final age...
Within the Dharma, I proclaim this meaning so that the celestial Māras may find no opportunity to interfere; I shall maintain and protect you, enabling you to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

When the mind of dhyāna is concentrated and stabilized, the delusions of the aggregates become firm obstructions. As these fluctuations differ from one another, many manifestations appear. Thus it is for the practitioner.
Clearly perceive the awakened mind. When the awakened mind accords with all objective realms, there is no longer any seeking.
It is like curd within milk; through the ripening of practice, one realizes it for oneself. Only when the sentiments of both the holy and the ordinary are exhausted can one attain such a state.

The Tathāgata has repeatedly and earnestly exhorted us, his protective concern being most profound. If one speaks of great falsehoods, or if the meditative mind is coarse and restless, one will only become further stubborn and deluded.
How profound!

The first section, the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), is concluded. II. The Aggregate of Feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). This is divided into four parts. First, the domain of the aggregate of feeling:
"Ānanda, when that virtuous man, practicing *samādhi* within *śamatha*, has exhausted the aggregate of form, he perceives all..."
The Buddha-mind is like an image appearing within a clear mirror. If there is something perceived that one has not yet been able to employ, it is like a person under a spell:

though their hands and feet are perfectly present and they are not confused regarding what they see or hear, because their mind has been contacted by an external malevolent spirit, they are unable to move.
This is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

It was stated previously: "If the eyes are clear and bright, the ten directions open up completely, and there is no longer any darkness; this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Regarding this statement that the aggregate of form is exhausted: when one perceives the minds of all Buddhas as images appearing within a bright mirror, while not yet realized it was merely called a "境" (*viṣaya*, objective realm), but now that it has been personally realized, one speaks only of the mind itself. When the original mind first illuminates, it is...

The Buddha is precisely the mind. As one gradually realizes and manifests this clarity, it is "the mind is the Buddha. Their essence is fundamentally identical; they appear different only through mutual observation.
If there is something attained that one has not yet been able to employ, it is because while the nature and substance are fully present, the wondrous function is not yet uniform.

It is like a person suffering from a nightmare whose hands and feet remain perfectly intact, and whose sight and hearing are unimpaired; this is just as if one were directly seeing the Buddha-mind, like an image within a mirror.
Furthermore, being unmoved by contact with the depraved, it is likened to having no further use for them; this constitutes the domain of the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation). 2.
The signs of the exhaustion of the *vedanā-skandha*:

If the affliction of being stifled by a nightmare ceases, the mind departs from the body and turns back to look at its own face; going and staying are then free and spontaneous, and there is no longer any obstruction or hindrance.

This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Observing its origin, one finds that empty, luminous false imagination constitutes its root.
One falsely perceives the substance of the self and clings to it as real; this is what is produced by the aggregate of sensation. If sensation is already destroyed, then—

However, it departs from the body and moves about without obstruction. Your current body is manifested as a mass composed of the four great elements—water, fire, wind, and earth—which you perceive through awareness.
This knowing mind that perceives is termed "empty clarity. Because of this clarity, you grasp at it with firm attachment, taking it to be the fundamental self.
III. The Differentiation of Experiencing Objects. This section is divided into ten parts; first, the arising of compassion upon seeing objects.

Ānanda, that good man, while in this state, shall attain a great radiance. His mind becomes luminous and clear, yet because he suppresses it excessively within, a boundless compassion suddenly arises from that state.
Thus, even upon seeing a mosquito or a gadfly, he regards them as his own infant;
a heart of pity arises, and he involuntarily sheds tears. This is called the overstepping of effort through excessive suppression. If he awakens to this...
There is no fault; this is not the realization of a sage. When one awakens to this and is no longer deluded, [the affliction] will naturally dissipate after a long time.

If you mistake this for the realization of a sage, then the demon of sorrow will enter your heart and viscera. You will feel pity upon seeing others and weep without limit, losing your correct meditative absorption and inevitably falling into ruin.
Once the aggregate of form has dissolved, the aggregate of sensation manifests before one. To "repress" means to suppress this very sensation.

When internal suppression is excessive, one perceives within this state that all sentient beings are fundamentally of one and the same body; it is only because they lack awakening that they undergo suffering and drowning in vain.

Therefore, sorrow and lamentation arise. Vasubandhu’s commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Being unable to enter deeply into the marks of meditative concentration (*samādhi-lakṣaṇa*), one perceives sentient beings and gives rise to attachment in the mind;
because of this, compassion arises, which is termed 'great compassion born of attachment and views' (*sneha-dṛṣṭi-mahākaruṇā*).

One who possesses compassion born of attachment and views will have a mind of weariness toward birth and death (*saṃsāra*). If one can depart from this, then in whatever place one is born, one will not be subject to attachment and views."
...that which covers it. △ Second, Resolute Will Equaling the Buddha.

Ānanda, furthermore, when those good sons within that samādhi perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear, and as superior signs manifest before them, they are moved by an excess of emotion.
Suddenly, within this state, they give rise to boundless courage; their minds become fierce and sharp, and their resolve becomes equal to that of a Buddha.
The Buddhas of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can, in a single thought-moment, transcend them all. This is called "surpassing and leaping over through effortful application.

If one awakens to this [nature], there is no fault; it is not a state of saintly realization. Once one has attained clear understanding and is no longer deluded, [the affliction] will naturally subside after a long time.

If one takes this to be a saintly attainment, then mad demons will enter one's heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, one will boast with incomparable arrogance, and one's mind will even—[not ascend].
Upon seeing the Buddha, they look down and do not see others; thus, they lose their right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) and are liable to fall away.

Those whose aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear and bright thoroughly understand the faults of sensation. Relying on the superior marks of meditative power, they are moved to a sudden surge of vigor;
yet, failing to measure themselves, they rashly claim to have transcended the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in a single leap, giving rise to great conceit (*māna*) which obstructs right concentration.
Therefore, know that the practitioner who exerts diligence merely follows the samādhi, naturally regulating their own state.
Possessing only a single mind, they harbor no further thoughts or expectations; this is called true samāpatti. From beginning to end, there shall be no divergent paths.
△ Third, the mind gives rise to dullness and forgetfulness.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear.

Having no new realization before them and having lost their former dwelling place, their power of wisdom declines and they fall into a state of desolation. Seeing nothing at all around them, a great parching thirst suddenly arises within their hearts;
at all times, they dwell in a state of deep, unceasing recollection, taking this to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called "cultivating the mind and losing oneself through a lack of wisdom. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a realization of the holy state.

If one takes this to be a holy realization, then the demon of recollection will enter one's heart and viscera. Morning and evening, he will seize the mind and suspend it in a single place, causing one to lose right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
One will then fall into ruin. Changshui said:

"The aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has not yet been emptied, yet there is no new realization before one; the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has already been exhausted, yet one loses the old dwelling place behind.
Having lost the standard of both before and after, one falls between the two pillars, with nothing to rely upon; this is called 'the ground of collapse in the middle. Since, at this point..."
The mind has no place to rest, and thus gives rise to deep brooding; taking this to be cultivation, one mistakes it for diligence.

Now, that the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is not yet empty means there is no new realization; that the *skandha* of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already been exhausted refers to what was previously realized.
How could one claim to have lost their former abode? I, the fool, say that those who cultivate *samādhi* should only follow along with original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), deeply...
Entering samādhi, one has no mind that grasps at realization; being neither conscious nor aware, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

If the mind that grasps at realization is superior, then internal power will inevitably decline; this is called "returning to lose one's original dwelling" and is also termed "entering the middle and destroying the ground.
To give rise to a mind of diligent effort merely accomplishes recollection; it is not the accordant functioning of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). △
Fourth is being satisfied with a small attainment.

Furthermore, within that state of concentration, those sons of good family see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear; the power of their wisdom surpasses the concentration.
They have lost their vigor; harboring various superior natures within their hearts, they already suspect their own minds to be Vairocana.
Content with a mere trifle, this is called losing constant discernment through the mind’s negligence and becoming mired in intellectual views. To realize this is to be without fault.
This is not true realization. If you mistake this for a state of sainthood, then the demon of inferiority and complacency will enter your heart and mind.
You will see others and claim for yourself that you have attained the unsurpassed ultimate truth; you will lose right concentration and fall into ruin.
If the power of wisdom exceeds that of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one then incurs the fault of being overly aggressive; hence it is said that one "loses [the quality of] fierce intensity.
Because they maintain this superior nature as the ultimate goal, although they possess wisdom, it merely results in cognitive discernment.

It is said that those of the Two Vehicles have an abundance of concentration and a deficiency of wisdom, and therefore do not perceive the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) have an abundance of wisdom and a deficiency of concentration; therefore...

They perceive the Buddha-nature only slightly. This refers to those who, amidst such slight perception, consider what they have attained to be sufficient. △ Fifth, the mind encounters perilous difficulties.

Furthermore, among those good sons within that state of concentration, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has become clear, yet they have not yet attained the new realization.
Thus, the mind has already perished. Surveying the two limits [of past and future], one encounters inherent hardships and perils;
suddenly, within the mind, inexhaustible sorrow arises, like sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison. The mind has no desire to live and constantly seeks someone to end its life.
They seek liberation prematurely; this is called failing in the skillful means of cultivation. If they awaken to this, there is no fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization.
If they mistake it for such a realization, a demon of constant anxiety will enter their heart and viscera to a certain extent, holding a sword and blade in its hand.

They cut their own flesh, yet rejoice in relinquishing their lives; or they are constantly filled with sorrow, fleeing into mountain forests, unable to bear the sight of people, and having lost right concentration, they are destined to fall into ruin.
The new realization has not yet been attained, yet the old mind has already perished; thus, between these two extremes, one naturally encounters hardship and peril.

This is precisely what is meant by losing the skillful means (*upāya*). When a practitioner cultivates *samādhi*, at the moment they illuminate their own mind, they should achieve steadfast endurance through the power of great *dhāraṇī*.
Both the realization and the one who realizes shall be without anything to be grasped, such that joy and sorrow arise spontaneously.
Both are lost; memory and forgetfulness are as one. To perceive two extremes is to lose right concentration (*samādhi*).

From the time of initial awakening until it is perfected, one may regress along the way and give rise to divergent thoughts; one must simply examine and reflect upon this. △ Six: When mental joy does not cease.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanāskandha) become clear and bright.
While abiding in this purity and their minds are subsequently at peace, suddenly an infinite joy arises within them; their hearts are filled with such rapture that they cannot restrain themselves.
This is called "lightness and ease without wisdom" or self-restraint; if one awakens to its true nature, there is no fault. It is not a realization of the holy state.
If one takes it to be such a realization, then a portion of the demon of "delightful joy" will enter one's heart and marrow. Upon seeing people, one laughs by the side of the road.

They sing and dance by themselves, claiming for themselves that they have already attained unimpeded liberation (*anāvaraṇa-vimokṣa*). Having lost their correct meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they shall fall into ruin.
Regarding profound dhyāna-concentration, they are close to liberation, peaceful, tranquil, and experience physical and mental pliancy and joy; yet such is the natural law.

Lacking wisdom, they maintain themselves by their own means and do not realize they are drifting into dissipation. Thus, Māra finds his opportunity. △ Seventh: the arising of great self-conceit (*māna*).
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Believing themselves to have reached sufficiency, they suddenly experience groundless great conceit (*māna*), extending even to pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*).

Whether it be through overweening pride or inferiority complex, these may arise simultaneously; such a person even holds the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt within their heart, let alone those of lower rank, such as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is called "seeing oneself as superior while lacking the wisdom to save oneself. Should they awaken to this, there will be no fault.
This is not a sign of saintly realization. If one mistakes this for such a realization, then a portion of the great demon of pride will enter their heart and viscera.
They will cease to pay homage to stupas and temples and will destroy scriptures and images, saying to their donors: "These are merely gold and copper, or perhaps clay and wood."

The scriptures are made of tree leaves or *karpāsa* (cotton) flowers; the physical body is truly eternal, yet you do not respect it yourself, instead venerating earth and wood—this is truly a perversion.
Those of deep faith should take these [scriptures], tear them to pieces, and bury them in the ground, lest they mislead and delude sentient beings.
They will enter the Avīci Hell and lose their right concentration, destined to fall into ruin;

this is called "seeing superiority without the wisdom to save oneself. It refers to suddenly attaining a superior understanding within meditative absorption—a realization that is, in fact, an excessive discourse even within the Buddha-dharma.
If one lacks true wisdom, one will not grasp its essential meaning and will inevitably give rise to [delusion].
Arrogance. Many of the "mad Chan" practitioners of recent times suffer from this ailment; they deceive themselves and others, so one should exercise careful discernment.
Zizhong said: "There are seven types of pride (*māna*). To rely on oneself and look down upon others, characterized by loftiness, is called 'pride of self' (*asmimāna*).
To weigh oneself against others and compare one's own virtues with theirs is simply called 'pride' (*māna*). To claim superiority over those who are equal to oneself is called..."

*Abhimāna* (excessive pride) is to claim superiority over those who are superior; this is called *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride). To claim attainment when one has not attained it is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride).
To look back with self-conceit despite knowing one’s own inferiority is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride). If one disparages the sutras and images, this is *mithyāmāna* (false pride);
the ignorant also call it *mahāmāna* (great pride). △ Eighth, the mind gives rise to *praśrabdhi* (lightness and ease).

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright.

Within this state of refined brilliance, they perfectly realize the principle of essence and attain great compliance. Suddenly, their minds give rise to immeasurable lightness and tranquility, and they declare themselves to have become sages.
One attains great mastery; this is called obtaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom. If one realizes this as such, there is no fault. It is not a holy realization.
If one takes it to be a holy realization, then a portion of the "demon of fondness for lightness and purity" will enter one's heart and viscera, leading one to claim self-satisfaction.

They will no longer seek progress; for the most part, these will become unlearned bhikṣus who mislead sentient beings, fall into the Avīci Hell, lose right concentration, and shall surely sink into ruin.
Yuanwu’s refinement of principle leads to great compliance and the arising of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); this is also a state that ought to occur within *samādhi*. Yet he says:
"This is called attaining various states of lightness and clarity through wisdom;

it should also rely upon resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), and one realizes for oneself that this is not true pliancy. Furthermore, he claims for himself that he has become a sage and considers himself fully satisfied. This—
As well as misleading oneself and others—this is no different from those who lack learning. △ Ninth, turning toward eternal cessation:

Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, these good sons see that the aggregate of form has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation becomes clear and bright. Within this luminous awakening, they...
One attains a nature of empty clarity. Within this state, one suddenly turns toward eternal extinction, repudiating cause and effect, and enters exclusively into emptiness.

When the mind of emptiness manifests before one, even to the point that a long-standing understanding of annihilation arises in the mind—if one awakens to this, there is no fault; yet it does not constitute a holy realization.
If one forms a sacred understanding [of this], then a "void-demon" (śūnyatā-māra) will enter their heart and inner organs;

they will then slander the observance of precepts, calling it the "Lesser Vehicle" (Hīnayāna), claiming that since a Bodhisattva has realized emptiness, what need is there for observing or violating precepts? Such a person will constantly drink alcohol and eat meat before faithful donors.
They engage extensively in lewd and impure acts; by means of demonic power, they captivate those before them so that no suspicion or slander arises.

Once the ghost’s mind has long since entered them, they may consume excrement and urine, as well as wine, meat, and the like—all of which are equally empty. Thus they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code and lead others into sin through error.
Having lost right concentration, one shall fall into ruin.

Within this state of apparent enlightenment, one attains a nature of empty clarity; while in meditative absorption, one perceives that the mind is empty and unimpeded both internally and externally, and thus regards all phenomena as empty.
Consequently, one gives rise to false views, failing to realize that phenomena themselves are fundamentally empty, and [failing to recognize] the person.
Holding fast to the notion of existence, the mind remains within existence, following along with and becoming attached to it. Since the cause of bondage already exists, how can one escape its fruit?

As for slandering the precepts and misrepresenting the sages, thereby misleading future generations—how can such a downward spiral ever end? Such is the state of the "Zen sickness" prevalent in recent times;
what is seen everywhere is exactly like this, and it is truly pitiable. 10. Love gives rise to frantic greed.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) becoming clear.

They savor its empty luminosity, which penetrates deep into the marrow of their hearts. Suddenly, infinite attachment arises within their minds; when this attachment reaches its peak, it triggers madness, which then becomes greed and desire.
This is called "the state of meditative concentration entering the mind with ease and compliance. Lacking wisdom to sustain oneself, one mistakenly enters into various desires;

though there is no fault in awakening from this, it does not constitute a realization of the holy. If one takes this to be a holy realization, then the demon of desire will enter one's heart and viscera, constantly claiming that desire is the path to Bodhi.
Such a person will convert laypeople to practice desire equally, asserting that those who engage in sexual intercourse are "sons of the Dharma who uphold the teaching."

By the power of divine spirits, they gather the common and ignorant during the final age, their number reaching as many as one hundred, or even two hundred, five, six, or seven hundred, until it fills many thousands or ten million; then the demons become weary and depart from their bodies.
Deprived of majestic virtue, they fall into royal calamity; misleading sentient beings, they enter the Avīci Hell;
losing right concentration, they shall surely descend into ruin.

This is called "the state of emptiness being peaceful and compliant as it enters the mind. Lacking wisdom, one maintains oneself [merely through concentration] and mistakenly enters into various desires.
To savor these words in detail is a profound admonition. Indeed, concentration is governed by wisdom; thus, wisdom does not lead to madness. Wisdom is maintained by concentration;
thus, concentration does not lead to intoxication. This, however, is concentration devoid of wisdom; savoring various states of peace and compliance can give rise to attachment, leading one astray.
Regarding the realm of desire: this arises because the afflictions of volition lie latent within the *ālayavijñāna*, skillfully flowing and staining until they reach such a state.
A practitioner of meditation must deeply examine this. Is it not merely a matter of self-deception? To deceive others and destroy the Dharma—how could one avoid falling into ruin?
If one awakens to this, there is no fault; for the Dharma has no fixed nature. One should simply not remain complacent in abandoning it.
The distinctions regarding the objects of the three types of sensation above are concluded. △ Fourth, the conclusion and instruction for transmission:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of present objects during *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a state of mutual interaction within the *vedanā-skandha*.

Thus, these phenomena appear. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering these conditions, they remain lost and fail to recognize them for what they are, saying:"
To claim sainthood is a great falsehood; one shall fall into the Avīci Hell.

You all should likewise take the Tathāgata’s words and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Final Dharma period, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any advantage;
maintain and protect [these teachings] so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

These are bound together within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). However, when the aggregate of form intermingles with others, one frequently manifests states of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) intermingles, one frequently enters into false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This is because form belongs to the sense organs and their objects, whereas sensation acts as the basis for grasping; thus, the afflictions of volition (*saṃskārakleśa*) are difficult to uproot.
Consequently, even while remaining in the stillness of meditation, the transformations and manifestations become increasingly intense.
The first two aggregates of sensation are concluded. △ Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). This is divided into five parts. First, the domain of the aggregate of perception:

"Ānanda, when that good man practices *samādhi* and the aggregate of sensation is exhausted, although his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet ended, his mind is detached from its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage.
He has already achieved this; from this ordinary body, he ascends through the stages of the Bodhisattvas' sixty..."
The stage of the Sages. Attaining the mind-born body (manomayakāya), one proceeds everywhere without obstruction. It is like a person who, while sleeping soundly, utters words in a dream;
although that person has no distinct awareness, the words he speaks possess phonetic rhythms and sequential order, causing those who are not asleep to fully understand their meaning.
This is what is called the realm of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).

Form constitutes an obstruction for the body; sensation constitutes an obstruction for the mind. Once these two aggregates (skandhas) are exhausted, one is naturally able to enter and exit at will according to the mind, no longer burdened by physical form.
Although the outflows have not yet been fully eliminated, one can, from this very ordinary body, traverse the sixty sacred stages of a Bodhisattva and attain the mind-made body (manomayakāya).
This occurs through the spontaneous illumination of the perfect faculties, entering samādhi and attaining mastery over the aggregate of sensation.

[This] refutes [the previous view]. It differs from those who have not yet attained illumination; for them, the lower aggregates are not yet exhausted, and demonic activities become even more numerous.

Deep sleep and talking in one's sleep serve as metaphors for being shrouded by the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Being awake during the day represents perception, while dreaming at night represents it as well.

Thus, even within this metaphor, there is something specifically indicated. This generally illustrates that the aggregate of perception has not yet been shattered, prior to the illumination of the perfect faculty.
As long as the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) has not been exhausted, it likewise cannot necessarily act as an obstruction.

Those who have personally realized the ultimate fruit—such as those referred to by the "sleepless person"—all understood these words and did not consider them erroneous. △ Second, the signs of the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception.

If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating perceptions are eliminated, it is like removing dust and grime from the awakened, luminous mind. When the beginning and end of a single cycle of birth and death are perfectly illuminated, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Observe its origin: *The Treatise on the Five Aggregates*, Fascicle One, Part One. Interfused delusive thoughts serve as its root.
These thoughts arise from the mind’s recollection of all objects across the past, present, and future, giving rise to mental activity.

When this mental activity does not cease, it becomes an obscuration to enlightened clarity, like grime upon a mirror. Once the grime is removed, the mirror reflects with perfect, luminous clarity. Thus it is born.
The beginning and end of death are as if before one's eyes. Although birth and death are not yet exhausted, one is not deluded by them; this is what is meant by "the same category.

"One category of birth and death" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Even though the aggregate of formations still exists, it cannot act as an obstruction. Afflictions arise from perception (*saṃjñā*), namely:
recollection, cognition, habitual study, and the nature that gives rise to knowledge and views. Therefore, when perception is exhausted, one can suddenly [attain liberation].
It transcends [the ordinary]. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to effect transformation, causing the mind to follow the faculties and objects, and causing the faculties and objects to follow the mind.

It is like imagining a sour plum, where water flows from the mouth; the faculty, the object, and consciousness—these three—are simultaneously and universally present. Therefore, it is called "pervasive delusive perception" (*yōutsū mōsō*).
△ Third, the distinctions among the objects of perception. This section has ten parts. First, the craving for skillful arts:

"Ānanda, when that son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes luminous.
Within this *samādhi*, his mind craves perfect clarity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and craves skillful arts. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity."
Taking advantage of the situation, a flying spirit possesses a person and speaks of the sutras and the Dharma with their mouth. The person does not realize they are possessed by a demon;
they claim for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed nirvana. They come to the dwelling of a seeker of skillful means, a son of good family, where they arrange seats and preach the Dharma.
For a brief moment, their form may appear as a bhikṣu so that the person may see them; or they may become Śakra, or a woman, or a [bhikṣuṇī].
A bhikṣuṇī may sleep in a dark room and possess a radiance upon her body; such a person is deluded and confused, claiming to be a Bodhisattva.

People believe their teachings, which agitate their minds and cause them to violate the Buddha’s Vinaya while secretly practicing lust. Such individuals delight in speaking of calamities, auspicious signs, and extraordinary portents;
they may claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in a certain place, or speak of the kalpa-ending fires, or of wars and weapons, thereby instilling terror.
Regarding humans, it causes their family wealth to dissipate without cause. This is called the "Strange Ghost," which becomes a demon in old age.
It harasses and disturbs such a person until its mind is satisfied; it then leaves the person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal peril.
You must be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
The aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has already dissolved, and the mind is now empty and subtle. Furthermore, within *samādhi*, the perfect luminosity becomes increasingly penetrating.
Becoming attached to this perfect luminosity, one further seeks skillful means (*kauśalya*). "Skillful means" refers here to all wondrous functions for accomplishing the benefit of others.
As soon as this thought arises, Māra finds his opportunity. Thus, one should know that if a practitioner of meditation is hasty regarding functional efficacy, they will give rise to a grasping mind.

When [the spirit] takes possession, there are no demonic activities; one has already lost right concentration (*samādhi*). An ancient master said: "If you only obtain the root, do not worry about the branches.

This does not mean the branches are useless; rather, the branches arrive of their own accord. When a flying essence (*fei-jing*) attaches to a person, it is said to attach to a specific individual, causing them to lose awareness.

They utter false words from their mouths and manifest transformations with their bodies. For those deluded regarding meditation, they are mistaken for Bodhisattvas, and people place their faith in them.
Regarding their transformation through teaching: those who practice desire all do so because practitioners of dhyāna cherish a mind of skillful means, which leads to agitation and confusion.
Upon awakening, they naturally recover, requiring no further expedient means. △ Second, the experience of greedy seeking.

Ānanda, furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within *samādhi*.
At that time, if his mind loves to wander and he casts his refined thoughts abroad, greedily seeking to experience various realms, the celestial Māra will watch for such an opportunity.
He will dispatch a refined spirit to possess a person, who will speak the sutras and the Dharma. That person, moreover, will not realize they are possessed by a demon, and will also say:
Having attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, he came to the place where that son of good family seeking liberation was, spread out his seat, and preached the Dharma.
His own form underwent no change, yet those listening to the Dharma suddenly saw themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers; their entire bodies were transformed into a mass of purple-gold light.
Every member of the assembly experienced this individually, attaining what they had never known before. These people, being foolish and deluded, were confused by it.
A bodhisattva whose mind is licentious and who violates the Buddha’s code of discipline secretly practices lustful desires.

Such a person delights in saying that various Buddhas have appeared in the world, claiming that a certain person in a certain place must be the emanation of a particular Buddha come here, or that a certain person is such-and-such a bodhisattva come to transform the human realm.
Because people see them, their hearts develop a longing for them; thus, false views secretly arise, and the seeds of wisdom [are destroyed].

It will be extinguished. This is called the *pūtana* ghost who, having grown old, becomes a demon. It harasses and disturbs this person until it feels satiated; then it departs from the person's body.
Both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth;
if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
The mind loves to wander; it also desires to ride upon this emptiness and subtlety to traverse various buddha-fields.

[The practitioner] transforms all listeners so that each becomes a Buddha, and further speaks of certain Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming from certain places—all of which skillfully incite the thought of wandering.
When this thought is self-awakened, demonic affairs suddenly vanish; ultimately, these are not the works of celestial Māras acting without a medium.
This is because they enter [the state] themselves. The *pó* ghosts take form when encountering wind; they also resonate with a wandering mind.
△ Third, seeking a harmonious fit through craving.

Furthermore, when the son of good family’s *shòuyīn* (receptive aggregate) is empty and subtle, and he does not encounter perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration (*yuándìng*) gives rise to illumination within *sānmódì* (samādhi).
The mind cherishes its attachments; it clarifies its refined thoughts and greedily seeks points of accord. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to exploit this.
A flying spirit takes possession of a person, who speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their mouth. That person is truly unaware that they are possessed by a demon;
they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana. They come to the place where the son of good family seeking union resides, spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma.

The form of the speaker and those listening to the Dharma undergo no outward change, yet they cause the listeners to experience spontaneous awakening in their minds even before they have heard the Dharma.

From moment to moment their states shifted; some attained the knowledge of past lives, some possessed the power of knowing others' minds, some beheld the hells, or knew all manner of good and evil affairs among humans;
some spoke verses aloud, while others recited sutras from memory, each rejoicing in these unprecedented attainments.

Seeing people who are deluded and confused, they falsely claim to be bodhisattvas. Their hearts are permeated with attachment, and they violate the Buddha’s precepts while secretly indulging in greed and desire.

They take pleasure in saying that there are great and small Buddhas—that such-and-such a Buddha is a former Buddha and such-and-such a Buddha is a later Buddha—and that among them there are both true and false Buddhas, as well as male and female Buddhas; they say the same for bodhisattvas. Because these people see such things, they wash away their original minds.
It is easy to fall into deviant understanding. This is called a *māyā-ghost* that has grown old and become a *māra*. It will harass and disturb this person until it becomes satiated;

once its desire is fulfilled, it will leave the person's body. Then both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal calamity. You must be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Those whose love is as dense as tangled silk desire to enter into secret accord with ultimate truth.

When a practitioner of Zen experiences a silent, intuitive resonance in their mind, demons may attach themselves to them, causing those who listen to them to suddenly awaken on their own, recognize their past lives, perceive the minds of others, and so forth.
All such matters correspond to a tacit understanding. This skillfulness in catering to the desires of others easily gives rise to delusion;
when practicing samādhi, if one mind-moment follows after what is heavy, one will immediately suffer subjugation and extinction.
To "wash away the original mind" means that the original initial mind is from this point onward completely swept away. △ Fourth, the pursuit of analytical discrimination.

Furthermore, when the son of good family’s *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, he is no longer beset by perverse thoughts; within the *samādhi* of the perfected concentration that illuminates clarity, his mind becomes attached to its own fundamental source.
He exhaustively examines the beginning and end of the nature of the transformation of things, refining his spirit and mind as he greedily seeks analytical discernment.
At that time, a celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to exploit it; he dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their own mouth.
That person does not initially realize they are possessed by a Māra, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed Nirvana. They come to the place of that good man who seeks the source.

He spread his seat and preached the Dharma. His body possessed majestic spiritual power that subdued those who sought instruction, causing them to submit their hearts spontaneously even before hearing the teaching.
These people came to understand that the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi-dharmakāya* are none other than this very physical body of mine before them;
that fathers and sons, succeeding one another in mutual generation, are themselves the eternally abiding and uninterrupted *dharmakāya*.
They all claim that the present world itself is the Buddha-land, asserting that there is no separate Pure Abode (*śuddhāvāsa*) nor the golden-hued marks [of a Buddha].

Such people accept this with faith, losing their former resolve; they surrender their very lives in devotion and experience what they have never had before. These deluded and confused ones mistake themselves for Bodhisattvas.
Investigating his mind, one finds that he has violated the Buddha’s code of discipline and secretly practices lustful desires.
He delights in saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all pure lands, and that the male and female organs are the true locus of bodhi and nirvana. Such is this ignorant man.
To believe such foul words is to invite calamity; these are known as the malevolent spirits of *gudu* and *yan-sheng*, who have become demons through old age.

They afflict and disturb this person until they are satiated, at which point they depart from the person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into royal punishment. You must be aware of this beforehand.
They do not enter the cycle of saṃsāra; deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
When a practitioner of dhyāna seeks to exhaustively investigate the root of the myriad transformations, a māra may possess a person and teach that the Dharma resides in the manifest physical body.
Furthermore, that father and son give birth to one another constitutes the eternally abiding and uninterrupted Dharmakāya.
