What appears to be a contradiction is in reality a dark convergence; what appears to be coarse speech is in reality a profound discourse on similarity.

This is because, fundamentally, there is no second person and no second dharma; purity and defilement are both empty, and essence and appearance are non-dual. This is what the practitioner of Chan [perceives].
This is for the purpose of deluding and confusing others. In recent times, there have been eccentric currents that have altered these words, yet their underlying intent cannot transcend this [error].
How lamentable it is! △ Five: Seeking a response from the unseen through covetousness.
Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of feeling is empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the samādhi.

At that time, his mind craves a distant response; he circulates through and minutely investigates [the state], greedily seeking a hidden resonance. Then, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity and seizes it.

A flying spirit attaches itself to a person, and that person speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. The person is originally unaware that they are possessed by a demon, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana.
They come to the place of the good man who seeks a response, spread out their seat, and preach the Dharma, being able to cause the audience—

Upon seeing his body for a brief moment, it was as if they had been together for hundreds of thousands of years; their hearts were filled with affection and attachment, such that they could not bear to part from him.
They served him as slaves, providing the four requisites of life without feeling weary, each causing those in his retinue to recognize him as their former teacher.

Originally a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he has separately given rise to attachment to dharmas that is as sticky as glue or lacquer. Having attained what he had never experienced before, this person is deluded and confused, taking himself to be a bodhisattva.
Those who draw near to his mind violate the Buddha’s precepts and secretly practice lustful desires. He is fond of saying in his own mouth:
"In a previous life, among such-and-such births, I first delivered such-and-such a person; at that time, they were my wife, concubine, brother, or sibling."
I have now come to receive you. I shall accompany you back to a certain world to make offerings to a certain Buddha.
Or it may be said that there is another world called the Land of Great Radiance, where a Buddha dwells; it is a place where all Tathāgatas take up residence, yet no one knows of its existence.
Belief is deceptive; it causes one to lose their original mind. This is called a fierce ghost that has become a demon through old age.

It harasses and disturbs this person until, having become satiated, it leaves the person's body. Then both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal calamity. You must be aware of this beforehand.
They do not enter the cycle of rebirth, yet they remain deluded and ignorant, falling into the Avīci Hell.
Malevolent spirits can enter the human heart, causing each person to briefly see [the deceased] and giving rise to attachment;

or they cause each person to recognize [the deceased], giving rise to a dharma-love for them—even toward former wives, concubines, brothers, and so forth. These are all matters of remote response and hidden resonance.

If this mind did not exist beforehand, there would be no basis for it to enter [the state of concentration]. Therefore, one should know that when practicing *samādhi*, one must always maintain vigilant awareness.
△ Sixth: Craving for Quiescence.

Furthermore, when a good son’s aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, he is no longer beset by deviant thoughts; his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within *samādhi*.
At this time, his mind desires to penetrate deeply, and through diligent self-discipline, he delights in dwelling in the stillness of the aggregates and craves profound tranquility.

Then, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity, dispatching a refined spirit to possess another person, who speaks the teachings of the sūtras. That person originally does not realize they have been possessed by a demon.
He also claims to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* and comes to the place where that seeker of the aggregates (*skandha*) dwells as a son of good family.
There he spreads his seat and preaches the Dharma, causing those who listen to each recognize their own past karma. Or, at that location, he says to one person: "You have not yet died."
Having already been reborn as an animal, he commanded one person to step on its tail from behind; this caused the person to be suddenly unable to rise.

Thereupon, the entire assembly bowed their hearts in humble submission. If someone conceived such a thought, the Buddha already knew its inception. This was beyond the scope of ordinary monastic discipline.
They further increase their ascetic rigor, slandering bhikṣus, reviling their followers, and exposing the private affairs of others without avoiding censure or suspicion.
They are fond of speaking of future calamities and blessings, which, when the time arrives, are not off by even a hair’s breadth.
This powerful ghost has grown old and become a demon; having exhausted its desire to disturb this person, it departs from the person's body, leaving both the disciple and the teacher.
Both shall fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this first; do not enter the cycle of rebirth. If you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

If you delight in dwelling in the darkness of stillness and greedily seek tranquility, this extreme desire for stillness will give rise to supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); thus, Māra will find his opportunity.
They attach themselves to various people; all these are matters yet to come, yet they perceive them without missing even a hair’s breadth. This is also a form of demonic penetration;
however, it is a deceptive and erroneous cause that ultimately leads to ruin. △ Seventh: Craving for past lives.

Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of sensation is empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination. Within this samādhi, his mind comes to cherish knowledge and vision;
he exerts himself with diligent effort to investigate and seek, greedily craving the knowledge of past lives. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity and seizes it.

A flying spirit takes possession of a person, who speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person is utterly unaware that they are possessed by a demon, and likewise claims to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place of a good man seeking the Way, spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma.
Without cause, this person obtains a great precious jewel at the site of their preaching. At times, the demon transforms into an animal, holding the jewel in its mouth.
He first bestowed upon those people various rare treasures, books, official documents, and all manner of extraordinary objects, which he later placed upon their bodies;
or, luring the listeners, he concealed them underground, where a bright moon-jewel illuminated the spot. All those listeners—
He attained what he had never experienced before: consuming many medicinal herbs instead of fine delicacies, and at times eating only one grain of hemp and one grain of wheat per day.
His form is plump and robust because he is sustained by demonic power. He slanders bhikṣus and reviles their assemblies, showing no regard for reproach or suspicion.
With his mouth, he delights in speaking of treasures in other regions and the hidden abodes of sages and worthies of the ten directions; those who follow after him [will likewise fall].

One often encounters individuals of strange and extraordinary appearance; these are known as the spirits of mountains, forests, lands, city walls, rivers, and peaks who have grown old and become demons.
Some may proclaim lustful desires and violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly indulging in the five desires with those who serve them.
There may be those who practice asceticism, subsisting solely on grasses and trees, yet lacking in disciplined conduct. These beings will harass such persons until they become weary and satisfied;
they will then leave the person's body. Both the disciple and the master will often fall into royal punishment. You should be aware of this beforehand so that you do not enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

Their minds crave knowledge and vision, desiring to know all and see all; they give rise to thoughts of attaining supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Thus, they are entered by Māra, who responds to them with such powers.
These reach from the past to the future and extend throughout the ten directions. Māra transforms himself into an animal and bestows hidden treasures upon them.
Beneath the earth, all [spirits] exist prior to their attachment; they first use seduction to cause others to become possessed.
△ Eight, Greedily Seizing Supernatural Powers:

Furthermore, son of good family, when the *skandha* of sensation is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts, the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes manifest within the state of *samādhi*.
Their hearts cherish supernormal powers and various transformations; they research the source of such manifestations and greedily seek spiritual might.

At that time, a celestial demon waits for an opportunity, flies its essence into a person, and speaks the sutras and Dharma with their mouth. That person truly does not realize they have been possessed by a demon.

He also declares that he has personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. He comes to the place where that son of good family seeking supernatural powers resides, spreads out his seat, and preaches the Dharma.
This person may then take fire in his hand, grasp that light with his hand, and distribute it over the heads of the fourfold assembly who are listening.
As for these listeners, flames several feet long issued from the crowns of their heads; yet they lacked the quality of heat and never burned them.
Some walked upon water as if treading on level ground; some sat unmoving in mid-air; and some entered into jars.
Sometimes he was inside a sack; sometimes he passed through windows and walls without ever encountering any obstruction. Only regarding weapons did he lack mastery.
He claimed to be a Buddha, wore white robes, and accepted the prostrations of bhikṣus. He slandered dhyāna and the Vinaya, and reviled his own followers.
They expose the private affairs of others without avoiding censure or suspicion; they constantly speak of supernatural powers and mastery while in their mouths;
or they cause people to see Buddha-lands from the side. Such are the delusions of demonic power, lacking any reality. They praise sexual misconduct and do not condemn coarse behavior.
They take all manner of vulgar and lewd things to be the transmission of the Dharma;

these are called the mountain spirits, sea spirits, wind spirits, river spirits, and earth spirits of great power within heaven and earth, as well as the accumulated karmic ghosts and enchantments of all plants and trees over many kalpas, or perhaps dragon spirits, or immortals whose lifespans have ended.
They are revived as *māra* spirits; or, when their celestial term ends and they ought to die according to their years, their forms do not dissolve but become possessed by other monsters.

As they grow old, they become demons who harass and disturb these people. Once they have become satiated and the thought of departure arises, they leave the person's body. Thus, both the disciple and the teacher [are affected].
They will often fall into royal calamities. You should perceive this beforehand; do not enter the cycle of saṃsāra. If you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
To investigate the source of transformation means that one desires to exhaustively understand the origin of transformations in order to master all phenomena within the state of samādhi.
A fondness for the extraordinary arises; failing to awaken to this oneself, one becomes deluded by it.

The practitioner loses their composure in meditation, reaching such a state that they lack mastery even over weapons. This reveals the influence of malevolent spirits, which ultimately leads to being overtaken by royal calamities.
△ Ninth, craving for profound emptiness.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes void and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within *samādhi*.
Their hearts delight in entering cessation; they investigate the nature of transformation and greedily seek profound emptiness.

At that time, a celestial Mara seizes his opportunity, dispatching a refined spirit to possess a person, who speaks the Dharma and the sutras with their own mouth. That person never realizes they are possessed by a Mara, and likewise claims to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana.
They come to the place of those good men who seek emptiness, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma within the great assembly.
His form suddenly became empty, and the assembly could see nothing; then he emerged abruptly from the void.

He exercised mastery over his appearance and disappearance, sometimes manifesting his body as transparent as lapis lazuli, sometimes extending his hands and feet so that they emitted the fragrance of sandalwood, and sometimes even discharging excrement and urine.
Like thick rock honey, they revile the precepts and hold those who have left the household life in contempt.

Constantly speaking of the absence of cause and effect, they claim that upon one death there is eternal extinction and no further rebirth, nor any distinction between ordinary beings and sages. Though they may attain a state of empty stillness, they secretly indulge in lustful desires.
Those who indulge in such desires likewise attain an empty mind and deny cause and effect. These are known as the vital essences of solar and lunar eclipses;
they are like gold, jade, *zhicao* fungi, qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes, which do not die for thousands of myriad years and become spirits, being born into this land.

When they grow old, they become demons who harass and disturb these people. Once their desires are satisfied, they leave the person's body. Both the disciples and the master will often fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
This is responding with emptiness to an invitation with emptiness; both involve grasping at phenomena outside the mind and losing the correct samādhi.
This is truly worthy of serving as a mirror for dhyāna. △ Ten: Seeking Eternal Years through Greed.

Furthermore, when the son of good family’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination.

Within this samādhi, his mind comes to cherish long life; he labors diligently to investigate the subtlest points, greedily seeking eternal years, and abandons the birth of segmented existence (kalala-ja) in favor of suddenly aspiring for the transformational birth (nirmāṇa-ja).

While these subtle signs remain constant, at that time a celestial Māra awaits his opportunity. He dispatches an essence to possess a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their own mouth.
That person does not realize at all that they are possessed by a Māra, and likewise claims to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

He comes to the place where those seeking the Way among good men reside, spreads out his seat, and preaches the Dharma. He delights in speaking of traveling to and from other regions without obstruction, even across ten thousand *li*.
In an instant they return, and from that very direction they recover their objects.

Or, within a single dwelling, over the span of a few paces, they cause a person to go from the eastern wall to the western wall; though this person runs with great haste, they would not reach the destination even after many years.
Therefore, with faith in his heart, he doubted that the Buddha was manifest before him. He constantly said: "The sentient beings of the ten directions are all my children;
I give birth to all Buddhas, I bring forth the worlds, and I am the primordial Buddha. My appearance in the world is spontaneous; it is not attained through cultivation."
This is called the Lord of the Heavenly Māras who dwells in the world.

He causes his retinue—such as Cāmuṇḍa, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Vaiśravaṇas who have not yet resolved their minds—to take advantage of its empty clarity and consume its vital essence; or else, they do so without relying on a teacher.
The practitioner personally witnesses [this being] appearing as Vajradhara, granting them long life; it manifests in the form of a beautiful woman and indulges extensively in lustful desires.
Before even a year has passed, their liver and brain are withered away, and they engage in solitary muttering that sounds like the speech of a malevolent spirit.

The details of those predecessors are not clear; many fell into royal peril. Before they could even face execution, they had already withered and died. They tormented and disturbed others until those others perished.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth. If you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

The two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) have only just departed from the *pariccheda* (segmented) existence and have attained the *pariṇāmanī* (transformative) existence. Because they have not yet reached the ultimate state of no-more-learning, they give rise to thoughts of seeking realization;

thus, there exist subtle signs of demonic delusion, which is precisely the "life-span self" (*jīvātman*) characteristic within the *Pariniṣpanna-jñāna*. In terms of principle, this is extremely subtle;

yet, regarding phenomena, they fail to understand and greedily desire to dwell long in the world—all of which constitutes the non-severance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment refer to these as "demons."
The emissary: "Once they have awakened the mind, they can protect the Dharma; when they have not yet awakened the mind, they can afflict others.

That which benefits their empty clarity refers to the empty clarity within the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of a practitioner of Chan; their vital energy (*ojas*) likewise becomes empty and clear.
This is what the demonic emissary benefits from. 'Not relying on a teacher' means not relying on a teacher possessed by a demon, yet the practitioner perceives it directly."

The Māra manifests; first by means of life-force and delusion, and subsequently through sexual acts, he withers and dries them to death—all of which results from the depletion of vital essence (*ojas*).
Cchamundā has no equivalent translation [in Chinese]. She is led by the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa. The *piśāca* child is the *piśāca* demon;
this is translated as "one who consumes vital essence."
The distinctions among the objects of the three aforementioned perceptions are concluded. △ Fourth, the subtle [perceptions] are transmitted for instruction:
"Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of māras will, during the final age, appear within my Dharma, having left the household life to cultivate the Way."

Some attach themselves to human bodies, while others manifest their own forms; all claim to have already attained the realization of Perfect Universal Wisdom (Samyaksaṃbodhi) and praise sexual desire, thereby violating the Vinaya rules of the Buddha.
These were originally evil demonic teachers and their disciples who transmitted their lustful practices from one to another. Thus, such perverse spirits bewitch the hearts and viscera of people;
for as few as nine lifetimes, or for many more than a hundred generations, they cause those who practice true cultivation to become entirely part of the demonic retinue.
After the end of your life, you will inevitably become a subject of Māra; you will lose right and universal knowledge and fall into the Avīci Hell. You need not first seek parinirvāṇa now.
Even if you attain the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), remain by your vow within that age of the final dharma and give rise to great compassion.

I rescue and deliver sentient beings who possess a correct mind and deep faith, ensuring they do not fall under the influence of Māra and that they attain right knowledge and vision. I now deliver you;
having emerged from birth and death, if you follow the Buddha’s words, it shall be called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
The Tathāgata gave this prophetic declaration: "In the final age of the world, these ten kinds of Māras will enter my Dharma and destroy right knowledge and vision;
therefore, those who are close to worldly false views are all followers of Māra. This is one clear proof.

If a student does not personally possess the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), even a slight error will be sufficient to cause regret that is as futile as trying to bite one's own navel once it is too late. Thus, the Sage’s entrustment remains, wishing for our rescue and deliverance.
I take pity on future generations; they will all fall into these same ranks, and one can do nothing but feel profound sorrow for them. △ Fifth, a summary of the causes of delusion:

Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifestations during *dhyāna* are all the result of the interaction between the mind and the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of mental formations). Therefore, they appear.

Regarding this matter: sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering these causes and conditions, they remain lost and fail to recognize their own state, claiming instead that they have attained the rank of a sage.
Thus, having committed a great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

You must take the words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Age of Dharma-Deterioration, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to gain the advantage over them.
Through skillful means, they maintain, protect, and bring to fulfillment the unsurpassed path.
Master Si of Mount Nanyue said: "These four foundations of mindfulness have thirty-seven distinct names."

This is called the Section on the Path (*mārga-varga*). One contemplates the impurity of the body and realizes that this impure body is the root of ignorance (*avidyā*), empty and without a place of arising.
The method of contemplating impurity can destroy the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). Men, women, those who feel hatred or love, and neutral persons—all return to emptiness and stillness;
this is called destroying the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*). One contemplates the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
Dharma: All things are suffering. Abandon them and do not cling to them. Contemplate this pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*): it can act as a cause for suffering; abandon it and do not accept it.
First, by abandoning both pain and pleasure, one attains neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*).

Furthermore, contemplate this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling: it has no basis of support. When contemplating in this manner, there is emptiness and nothing to be attained, nor is there anything [to be grasped].

One abandons [them], yet one cannot find any dharma that can be abandoned; both the true and the false are quiescent. At this time, one immediately destroys the demons of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas).
One contemplates that the mind is impermanent, arising and ceasing without staying. Observing this mind, from where does it originally arise?
When contemplating in this way, one sees no mind at all, nor is there any arising or ceasing; it is neither annihilated nor eternal, abiding in neither extreme but in the Middle Way.
Having contemplated in this way, there is immediately no Mara of Death.

Within the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one contemplates all phenomena—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—as being like space, incapable of being selected or differentiated. Amidst all phenomena, the mind ultimately remains unmoving.
Furthermore, there is no abiding mark. One attains the Immovable Samādhi (*acala-samādhi*), wherein there is no celestial Mara (*devaputra-māra*).
This Great Master’s compassionate skillful means intends for those who practice dhyāna to rely on these expedients to subdue their own delusions and thereby avoid the delusions of others.
In sum, it is all but this single mind. If one can bring this forth and illuminate it, within this single mind, one does not grasp at its own characteristics.
Apart from the single mind, do not grasp at other characteristics. All things are equal, yet there is even no view of equality.
Use this to discern delusion and exhaust all doctrinal meanings; these can be indicated through words, but as for profound awakening, it is that which each person must attain for themselves.

Direct Pointing to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Nine:
Phonetic Explanations.

*Xù* (pronounced like *xù*, meaning "to encourage" or "exert oneself"). *Mì* (pronounced like *mì*, interchangeable with *mù*, meaning "subtle" or "obscure"). *Chè* (pronounced like *cè*, meaning "to split" or "tear"). *Měn* (pronounced like *mén*, meaning "to fit together" or "seamless").
*Àn* (the second tone of *ān*, meaning "dull" or "obscure"). *Ráo* (pronounced like *ráo*, referring to short worms within the abdomen). *Nì* (pronounced like *yì*, meaning "to talk in one's sleep").

The Direct Pointing to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, the Cultivation and Realization of the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Ten.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Huanshu Tianran of the Danxia Lineage, the Thirty-Fourth Generation of the Dong School.

Dharma-heir of the Succession, the present-day monk Dan-gui, having read the present *Bianle-shuo*, completes the comparison with the preceding three [stages of] the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
△ Fourth, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Divided into five parts. First, the superior characteristics of the exhaustion of perception.
Ānanda, when that son of good family practices samādhi and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, his ordinary dreams and fantasies are extinguished;
whether awake or asleep, he remains constantly one. His awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky, no longer burdened by the coarse and heavy shadows of external objects.

When he contemplates the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers, they are like reflections in a clear mirror: as they come, there is nothing to which they adhere; as they pass, there is nothing...
Traces [of past experience] receive illumination and response in vain, for there is no longer any lingering habituation; there is only the single, pure reality.
Because one awakens from thoughts, one dreams while asleep. Now that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted, one is as if awake even while asleep;
because there are no thoughts, there are no dreams, and because there are no dreams, one is eternally one. "Coarseness and heaviness" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*). All afflictions...
It arises from perception. The nature of awakening is inherently empty and luminous, yet it is obscured by perception.
When perception is exhausted, the nature of awakening is revealed, like a clear sky in which all mirages and motes of dust come and go through the air, neither dwelling nor clinging.

The clarity of awakening is likewise so. When conceptualization is exhausted, awakening manifests; it responds to the encounter between the faculties and their objects like space receiving things, without further entanglement—it is solely the true nature.
"Clinging to old habits" refers to past deluded thoughts; "realizing they are non-existent" means understanding clearly that they are void.
II. The Realm of the Aggregate of Formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
The root-source of arising and ceasing is now revealed from this point. One beholds all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category.
Although one has not yet penetrated the specific origins of their respective destinies, one sees their common basis of birth, which is like a shimmering mirage—vibrant, clear, and turbulent.
It serves as the ultimate pivot for the floating sense organs and their objects; this is what is called the domain of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Birth and death constitute the root source of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. As long as the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) has not been exhausted, one is distracted within the entirety of these formations by that perception and is unable to see.
Now that perception is exhausted, one is able to observe the birth and death of the twelve classes of beings.

Regarding the "characteristics": that which has not yet exhausted its individual life-continuities refers to the initial characteristic of arising and ceasing. This characteristic must be recognized as empty before it can be suddenly understood.

For the object-condition of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). The "wild horses" refer to a mirage, serving as a metaphor for the subtlety of the aggregate of volitional formations.
Within the awakening to emptiness, if one has not yet exhausted the perception of ideation, one cannot see [this]. These are all the causes for birth within the three realms.
It is based on this. Therefore it is said that the sense organs and their objects are like pivots and sockets. When a pivot has a socket, the door can be closed.

This is the basis for the arising of the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) state. "Gleaming" refers to the appearance of shimmering light, like a mirage. It is called "clear" despite its turbulence because, through the exhaustion of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), there is no longer any agitation.
△ Third, the signs of the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

If this turbid and flickering fundamental nature enters its original clarity, and once clarified, its original habitual tendencies are extinguished—like waves subsiding and transforming into clear water—it is called the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings. One should observe the source from which this arises.
Deep-seated delusive thoughts serve as its foundation.

That which flickers and is turbidly agitated is called the "original nature"; yet because one is deluded regarding true consciousness, there arise birth and death. Thus, both birth and death are manifestations of the nature of consciousness.
When practice reaches its consummation, one returns to the source; when the source is clarified, habitual tendencies revolve back. Therefore, it is said to be like waves.

The waves subside and transform into clear water. Because the birth and death of sentient beings never ceases, when their karmic formations are exhausted, they transcend the turbidity of sentient beings.
This cycle of birth and death is subtle and extremely profound; therefore, it is said that "profound and hidden delusive thoughts constitute its root.
△ Fourth, the distinctions among the objects of practice, divided into ten parts. The first two concern theories of no-cause, divided into three sections. First:
General Summary:

Ānanda, you should know that among those sons of good family who have attained right awareness within *śamatha*, the ten classes of celestial Māras cannot find an opportunity, as they maintain a concentrated, luminous, and upright mind.
Only then are they able to investigate with refinement and exhaust the root of all living beings; and within that fundamental category...
Regarding the source of birth being exposed: when one contemplates that profound clarity, it is the circular source of agitation and movement.
If, within this circular source, one gives rise to conceptual calculations, such a person falls into the two theories of causelessness.
The practitioner of meditation has not yet emptied the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); thus, following the arising of thoughts, delusion arises, and they are struck by Māra.
Now that the aggregate of perception is exhausted, this awakened mind clearly distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox, remaining still and unmoving.

With this very mind, one investigates the fundamental thread of the arising and ceasing of the twelve classes of beings. At the moment the source of one's own class of birth is revealed, one contemplates its profound purity.
The fundamental source of circular agitation has no root. Because one does not know that it is shrouded by ignorance, one is deluded regarding the nature of true consciousness.
One erroneously considers the marks of arising and ceasing to be fully exhausted within this [circularity], such that nothing further exists; thus, it arises without cause.

Now, the Tathāgatagarbha, through non-awakening, moves delusively and gives rise to views. From these views, there arise marks, and the flow of arising and ceasing continues in an unceasing cycle of transmigration.

If one does not exhaustively penetrate the source of consciousness and return to the Tathāgatagarbha, then even if the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) becomes empty and still, and one understands the causes of the triple world to realize the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the Two Vehicles, the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) has not yet been eliminated.
This is a ruinous impairment; it still cannot be called the attainment of right knowledge and vision.
△ Second, the view that there is no cause for existence. First, this person perceives that there is no fundamental cause. Why is this?

Because this person has already completely shattered the mechanism of rebirth and, by means of the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty, sees all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas, their karmic currents winding and circling as they die.
They see beings being born there and circulating within that place; beyond eighty thousand kalpas, it is dark and nothing can be perceived.
They then form this interpretation: "These sentient beings of the ten directions in the world have existed spontaneously without cause for eighty thousand kalpas.
By such deliberation, they lose the correct universal knowledge and fall into the paths of externalists, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This view is fundamentally without cause. By investigating the root of sentient beings and tracing it back through eighty thousand kalpas, one finds no point of origin.

This is because one does not understand that the eight consciousnesses are the cause of delusion; even if one were to continue for another ten million kalpas, there would still be no root or thread to grasp.
It is not that the merit of the eye fails to reach it, nor is it that the power of meditative concentration cannot attain it.
To regard delusion as being without cause is to turn one's back on perfect enlightenment. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* asks: "What is 'perfectly and universally knowing' (*samyak-saṃbuddha*)?

'Perfect' (*samyak*) means non-erroneous. 'Universally knowing' (*saṃbuddha*) means being thoroughly penetrating regarding the four perversions. Furthermore, 'perfect' (*samyak*) refers to the world."
In the middle [of the path], the "thorough knower" (parijña) attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through ultimate knowledge of cultivation.

Now, by suddenly giving rise to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding this cultivation, it is said that one "loses the nature of bodhi. △ Third: The absence of cause at the end, together with the conclusion.
Second, these people perceive that the end has no cause. Why is this? Because these people, having already observed the roots of birth, know that humans produce humans and that birds produce birds;
they see that crows have always been black and cranes have always been white; that humans and devas are fundamentally upright while animals are fundamentally horizontal;
and that whiteness is not produced by washing nor blackness created by dyeing. From eighty thousand kalpas ago, nothing has ever changed or shifted. Now...
Even when this physical form perishes, it is likewise so. Since I have never from the beginning perceived bodhi, how could there be any further matter of attaining bodhi?
You should know that today all phenomena are fundamentally without cause.
This arises from seeing that the root has no cause; therefore, one sees that the branches likewise have no cause. This is because the nature of consciousness has not been thoroughly investigated;
one merely observes the activity-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) manifesting before one as all things being spontaneously formed, wherein there is neither delusion nor enlightenment.
Before eighty thousand kalpas, one does not see Bodhi; ultimately, after eighty thousand kalpas, there is likewise no matter of attaining Bodhi. It is like...
Śāriputra observed the body of the pigeon for eighty thousand kalpas past and future, yet its retribution did not change.

Now, having seen this sign within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), he applied it as a general principle: the transformation of karmic fruits during the intervening period is beyond the reach of intellectual power.
It is erroneously claimed that all things have been non-existent for eighty thousand kalpas. The treatise states:
"There are Arhats who know one lifetime, or two, three, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even eighty thousand kalpas;
yet beyond this, they cannot know. Nevertheless, because they do not give rise to conceptual calculations, they do not incur this fault."

By means of such conceptualization, they lose the correct universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha-jñāna*) and fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the first type of non-Buddhist doctrine: the theory of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).
The *Qingliang shu* states: "The eleventh is the teacher of the theory of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).

They reckon that all phenomena arise spontaneously and perish spontaneously, being without cause or condition. Therefore, this spontaneity is eternal; it is the cause of all phenomena and the cause of nirvāṇa.

This [view] reckons that there is no cause for either defilement or purity in anything whatsoever, just as the sharpness of a thorn is natural, or the black color of a crow is not a result of dyeing."

The color of a crane is naturally white. Both the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* state: "Because of this, one gives rise to the view of causelessness and establishes the doctrine of causelessness.
This concludes the first two types of the doctrine of causelessness. △ Second, the four doctrines of universal permanence, divided into five parts. First, the general heading.
Ānanda, when these good sons within this samādhi concentrate their luminosity and align their minds, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally quiescent source of movement. Yet, if they give rise to conceptual calculations within that which is perfect and eternal, such persons fall into the four theories of universal permanence.
In calculating the arising and ceasing within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one regards them as uninterrupted and pervasive-eternal, asserting that all phenomena are likewise so.
This takes arising and ceasing to be permanent; it is a case of misperceiving the impermanent as permanent, and thus belongs entirely to the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Qingliang says that the four types of pervasive-eternalists mean that the self and the entire world are all eternal, existing merely through alternation of concealment and manifestation.

Based on the superior and middling levels of dhyāna, they give rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Following this recollection, they give rise to four types of eternalist views. △ Second:
Eternalism for twenty thousand kalpas. First:

This person exhausts the nature of the two spheres—the mind and its objects—and finds them to be without cause. Through cultivation, he becomes able to know [the events] within twenty thousand kalpas.
All sentient beings of the ten directions, with all their births and deaths, circulate in an endless cycle without ever being lost; they reckon this to be permanent.
All phenomena are manifestations of the mind alone; yet both this mind and these objects are ungraspable and cannot be lost.
This state of thorough investigation persisted for twenty thousand kalpas, and they reckoned it to be permanent. △ For thirty-four thousand kalpas, it was considered permanent.
Second, this person investigates the source of the four great elements, concluding that their four natures are eternally abiding.

Through cultivation, they are able to know the births and deaths of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions within forty thousand kalpas; they perceive that all these phenomena are fundamentally constant and have never been lost or dispersed, and thus reckon them to be permanent.
The four great elements arise from false conceptualization; false conceptualization has no inherent nature and abides by depending on the Truth.

By practicing in this way for forty thousand kalpas, one perceives that there is neither increase nor decrease, and thus reckons it to be eternal. This is the fourth [stage]: eternity for eighty thousand kalpas.
Third, this person exhaustively investigates the fundamental source within the mind, intellect, and consciousness that is grasped by the manas through the six sense faculties;
because its nature is eternally constant, through cultivation they are able to know all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas, their cycles never being lost.
Originally and eternally abiding, it exhausts its limit without losing its nature; thus one reckons it as permanent.
All sense-faculties belong to the objective portion (*nimitta-bhāga*).

As long as the *manas* clings to them, if one does not bring forth illumination to transform this storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) into the Tathāgata-garbha, then this mind, thought, and mental consciousness will never cease. One should practice based upon this.

Exhausting eighty thousand kalpas, they perceive that which is fundamentally non-existent as being without loss, calculating it to be permanent. △ Fifth, the permanence of neither-arising-nor-ceasing, including the conclusion:

Fourth, since this person has exhausted the source of ideation, the principle of their nature no longer involves flowing, ceasing, or circulating; thus, the mind of arising and ceasing ideation [is stilled].

Now it has been eternally extinguished. Within the principle, non-arising and non-extinction are spontaneously established. Because one measures what is realized through the mind as being permanent, arising and extinction depend upon conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).

Since conceptualization is exhausted, the principle of arising and extinction has no basis; yet this is not a true, eternal severance, for it is considered "non-existent" simply because conceptualization has ceased.
That which is called "spontaneously established within the principle as non-arising and non-extinction" means that the nature of arising and extinction is without dispersion.
There is no error. One takes that which arises and ceases, yet does not cease, to be non-arising and non-ceasing, and reckons it to be permanent.
Because of this reckoning of permanence, one loses right universal knowledge and falls into the ranks of the heterodox, becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the second heterodox school’s doctrine of the "Perfectly Constant."

This interpretation is identical to the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuka*). The former view of causelessness led to the loss of the Perfectly All-Knowing One; this current view of being "perfect and eternal" likewise results in the loss of the Perfectly All-Knowing One.
"Eternal" is itself "causeless," meaning that this causeless arising and ceasing has been thus from the very beginning.
The first two sections on the four types of theories of eternalism are concluded. △ Third, the theories of partial impermanence and partial eternity, divided into five parts.
First, the general introduction:

Furthermore, O sons of good family within the state of *samādhi*, with minds firm, concentrated, and upright, Māras cannot find an opportunity; they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

Contemplating that profound stillness, one perceives the source of constant agitation. Those who give rise to conceptual calculations regarding self and others fall into the four inverted views, specifically the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.
"Self" refers to one's own person; "other" refers to sentient beings and the physical realm. Either the self can produce the other, or the other can produce the self.
That which produces is permanent; that which is produced is impermanent. This constitutes the doctrine of partial impermanence and partial permanence.
△ Second, the self is eternal while that [the world] is impermanent.
First, this person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions; they regard its profound stillness as the ultimate divine self (*ātman*).
From this, one then calculates that the self pervades the ten directions, remaining still and unmoving in its concentrated clarity.
All sentient beings are born and die within my own mind; thus, my mind-nature is called "permanent," while those who undergo birth and death truly possess an impermanent nature.
This calculation holds that the self (*ātman*) is eternal while sentient beings are impermanent. This "spiritual self" (*puruṣa*) is what is postulated by the Sāṃkhya masters of the Western Regions;
it is the same as the previously mentioned spiritual self that pervades the ten directions. △ Third, the destruction and non-destruction of the kalpas.
Second, this person does not contemplate their own mind, but instead surveys throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Seeing places where kalpas are destroyed, they designate them as having the nature of ultimate impermanence; seeing places where kalpas are not destroyed, they designate them as ultimately permanent.
This is the single contemplation of the land. One takes that which is presently perishing as impermanent, and that which is presently not perishing as ultimately permanent.
For example, from the third dhyāna downward, the three calamities can destroy it; from the fourth dhyāna upward, the calamities cannot destroy it.
This is the place of ultimate nirvāṇa. △ Fourth, the nature is permanent while birth-and-death is impermanent.
Third, this person separately contemplates the essence of his own mind as being subtle, fine, and secret, like a minute particle.

It transmigrates through the ten directions, its nature remaining unchanging, capable of causing this body to arise and perish in an instant. This indestructible nature is called the permanence of the self-nature (*ātman*).
All birth and death flow forth from this "self," which is termed the nature of impermanence.
This calculation that my mind possesses both permanence and impermanence is the most subtle;

it transmigrates through the ten directions, its nature unchanging, and is able to cause my body to undergo birth and extinction. That which does not extinguish is mostly regarded as the nature of permanence. From this...
It flows out and undergoes transformation according to conditions; this is called impermanence. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Non-Buddhists cling to a self-substance that is eternal and produces subtle [transformations], like a single atom secretly moving within the body to perform various activities; thus they claim its substance is eternal."
This is precisely the nature that is immutable. When the subtle arises, it flows forth from the self;
this is my mind calculating permanence and impermanence. △ The five aggregates are permanent; form, sensation, perception, and mental formations are impermanent. [This concludes the summary.]

Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and perceives the flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because the aggregate of formations flows constantly, they reckon it to have the nature of permanence.
They regard form, sensation, and perception—which have now been extinguished—as impermanent.
This takes arising as the nature of permanence and cessation as impermanence. While the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has not yet been emptied, its present flux is termed "permanent";
the cessation of form, sensation, and perception is termed "impermanent. Since this permanence is not true permanence, its cessation is likewise not true cessation.
As long as one has not exhausted the source of birth and perceived the awakening of the true nature, both suppression and severance are merely provisional, not ultimate.
Because they calculate that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the third non-Buddhist doctrine: the theory of partial permanence.
The analysis of the [terms] is the same as the previous explanation.
This concludes the section on the four theories that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent. △ Fourth, the four theories regarding whether existence has limits, divided into five parts.
First, the general statement.
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi who have stabilized their minds with correct concentration, such that Māra finds no opportunity,

they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. If, amidst these various states, they give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons fall into the four theories of finitude.
There are four states of being: namely, the state of the three time periods, the state of seeing and hearing, the state of "that" and "self," and the state of arising and ceasing.
By reckoning these states as infinite, one establishes the existence of finitude. △ Second, the three times.

First, these people calculate the source of birth; as their mental activity flows on without ceasing, they calculate the past and future, which they call "having limits," and they calculate the continuous mind, which they call "being limitless."
This takes the uninterrupted flow of the active mind manifesting before one as "boundless," which necessarily implies that the past and future are "finite.
Thus, it establishes the finite by means of the boundless. This is because one does not realize that the mind has no three temporal limits;
to stir a thought is immediately an error. This is not the vision of those who have not yet exhausted the functioning of consciousness. △ Third, regarding sentient beings.
Second, this person contemplates eighty thousand kalpas and perceives sentient beings; yet prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, there is a state of silence where nothing is heard or seen.
This state of no hearing or seeing is called "boundless," while the place where sentient beings exist is called "bounded."
Sentient beings are themselves arising and ceasing. This takes the arising and ceasing of the currently perceived *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) as having a limit;

that is to say, it is characterized by discrimination. One claims that eighty thousand kalpas ago there was neither hearing nor seeing, a vast expanse without boundary, and thus regards it as being without limit.

It is not, however, that there truly was silence and no hearing or seeing eighty thousand kalpas ago; rather, it is because the practitioner has not yet investigated the source of consciousness that their seeing and hearing [fail to reach it].
Furthermore, they falsely calculate that this [mind] possesses infinite characteristics. Fourth, regarding the nature of the mind:
thirdly, these people reckon that their "self" is all-pervasive and has attained an infinite nature; thus, all those people appear within the scope of their own knowing.
I previously did not know that their nature of knowing was such; thus I could not call them those with boundless minds, for they possessed only a limited nature.
That I am able to universally know all those people is because I have attained a boundless nature.
I previously did not know that their nature of knowing was such; therefore they could not manifest within my knowledge, and thus they were limited. This is certain.
This means that it is pervasive by way of the objects known, not by way of the knowing itself. What they call "boundless" is actually merely having a limit.
△ Fifth: Arising and Ceasing, including the conclusion.
Fourth, this person exhausts the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).

Using the mental pathways they perceive as a measure, they calculate all sentient beings within a single body to be half-born and half-extinguished, and they clarify that everything existing within the world is likewise so.
"Half has limits and half is limitless.
This refers to one who, while investigating the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), desires to exhaust it until it becomes empty;

yet, because they still remain within the cycle of arising and ceasing, they consequently reckon that within the bodies of all sentient beings there is likewise "half-arising and half-ceasing," and that the world is also thus.
However, they take birth to be finite and cessation to be infinite.
By such conceptualization of finitude and infinity, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the fourth non-Buddhist school that establishes the doctrine of finitude.
The explanation is the same as the preceding conclusion.
The above concludes the four sets of four propositions on the existence of limits. △ Fifth: The Fourfold Evasive Discourse on Immortality. This is divided into five parts;
first, the general introduction.
Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi*, if they stabilize their minds in right concentration so that Māras cannot find an opportunity,

yet they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source, they may give rise to conceptual calculations within their knowledge and views.
Such persons fall into four kinds of inverted, "undying" equivocation and pervasive false theorizing.
Regarding "knowledge and vision" (*jñānadarśana*): when investigating the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), one perceives and sees them as presently arising and ceasing;

yet, when [the aggregate of] perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) has already been exhausted, one perceives them as being without arising or ceasing. Thus, amidst this profound agitation and subtle clarity, one is unable to reach a definitive conclusion through such deliberation, and consequently falls into equivocation.
The four types of equivocation are detailed below. Regarding "equivocal evasion regarding immortality" (*amarāvikkhepa*), the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* provides the following explanation:
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain that the gods are eternal and call this "immortality. They further maintain that by answering questions without confusion, one will be reborn in those heavens.
[They think] if one truly does not know but nonetheless answers, it might be considered evasive or deceptive.

When questioned, they respond with cryptic terminology, saying that everything should not be disclosed, or that the answer is "indefinite" (avyākṛta). My Dharma rebukes them, saying: "This is truly evasive and deceptive. Therefore...
This is called the "Immortal's Evasive and Vacuous Discourse. △ Second, eight [types of such discourse].
First, this person contemplates the source of transformation. Seeing the place where things shift and flow, they call it "change"; seeing the place where things continue, [they call it "continuity"].
That which is called "constant" refers to the locus where seeing is perceived; that which is called "arising" refers to the locus where seeing is not perceived;

that which is called "cessation" refers to the cause of continuity, the state where its nature is uninterrupted; and that which is called "increase" refers to the state within the midst of correct continuity where it is separated from the middle.

That which is designated as "diminution" refers to the various places where things arise; that which is designated as "existence" refers to their mutual presence; and that which is designated as "non-existence" refers to their mutual disappearance.
When observing through principle, one perceives them distinctly with the mind. If there is a seeker of the Dharma who comes to inquire about this meaning, I answer:
"I am now both arising and ceasing, both existent and non-existent, both increasing and diminishing. At all times, my speech remains thus disordered.
This causes that person to lose the chapters and verses.
"The source of transformation" refers to the very source of arising and ceasing. Within the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), there are eight phases:
namely, change, constancy, arising, ceasing, increase, decrease, existence, and non-existence. To observe these through principle means to view them collectively by means of the principles of dhyāna.
First, regarding "observing with a distinct mind": this refers to the eight characteristics that arise when one discriminates with the mind.

The practitioner of dhyāna does not penetrate the fundamental cause of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) and fails to ascertain its true meaning regarding priority and sequence. In response to the question posed, these six phrases are set forth.
They deceive their interlocutors by losing the sequence of the chapters and verses, claiming that the chapters and verses lack coherence and cannot be explained in debate.
△ Third, the position of absolute non-existence:
Second, such a person observes their own mind and sees that it has no locus whatsoever; based on this non-existence, they attain realization. When someone comes to question them...
He answered with only a single word, saying merely that it is "non-existent. Beyond this non-existence, there is nothing further to be said.
It arises in its own place and perishes in that very place; all mental phenomena are thus. Observing this arising and perishing in succession, it is said that they are "mutually non-existent.
Regarding this mutual non-existence, one takes non-existence as the realization, answering only with "non-existence" because there is no cause [for existence].
To rely on conditions is not the meaning of true emptiness; therefore, it constitutes a deceptive and confused argument. △ Fourth, as for "only":
Thirdly, this person carefully observes that his mind has its own distinct locations, and because of these, he attains realization. When someone comes to question him...
He answered with only a single word, merely saying "it is so. Beyond this, he had nothing further to say.
Furthermore, because he regarded that which arises in every moment as being substantially real, he took this as proof and thus became attached to existence.
To answer in such a manner is to engage in evasive equivocation (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*). Fifth, the conjunction of both existence and non-existence:

these four views consist of the dualistic perspectives of existence and non-existence regarding persons. Because their objects are fragmented, the mind is likewise distracted. When someone comes to question them...
He replied, "To say 'it both exists and does not exist'—within that state of non-existence, it is not the case that it also exists. This is entirely evasive and confused;
there is no way to interrogate it to its conclusion.

This occurs within the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations); he was unable to penetrate deeply to its source and bottom, seeing only the superficial flow, and thus remained deluded.
Regarding existence and non-existence, they give rise to this evasive and confused discourse that cannot be scrutinized; branch by branch and twig by twig, they claim it is inexhaustible.

Through such conceptualization, they engage in deceptive, empty, and nihilistic talk, falling into the ranks of external paths and deluding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the fifth class of externalists:
those of the fourfold inverted nature who practice the "immortal evasion" and engage in pervasive false theorizing.
The explanation is the same as the previous conclusion.
The above four types of the "Evasive Discourse on Immortality" are finished. △ Sixty-six: The Discourse on the Existence of Characteristics. This is divided into three parts.
First, the heading.
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally quiescent source of constant movement. Yet, regarding this inexhaustible flow, they give rise to conceptual calculations;
such persons fall into the error of perceiving signs after death, and their resolve becomes inverted.
The characteristic of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is an endless flux. To perceive this characteristic as it appears is like seeing a mirage;
since it is not a real entity even now, how much less so after death? To give rise to such a mind is an inversion. △ Second, the explanation, divided into two parts.
First, the fundamental view.
Some solidify their own bodies, saying, "Form is the self. Some perceive the self as encompassing and pervading all lands, saying, "The self possesses form.
Some perceive that preceding objects revolve according to the self, saying, "Form belongs to the self. Or again, they perceive the self as persisting through the continuity of mental formations.
To say "I am in form" is to conceptualize that there is a sign [of self] after death; thus, in such cycles, there are sixteen signs.
"Form is I" is the reckoning of the self within the aggregates (*skandha*). "I possess form" is the reckoning that all external forms are pervaded by the self.
"Form belongs to me" is the reckoning that all phenomena of form revolve around the self. "I am in form" is...
One calculates that within all form (*rūpa*) there is a self (*ātman*). Having calculated form as the self, it possesses four characteristics;

when combined with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*), they together constitute sixteen [characteristics]. All of these are said to possess characteristics after death.

As for the mention of consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is not what is perceived [in this calculation], nor is it the case that consciousness throughout the entire body acts as the calculating subject. 2. Specific Calculations.
From this point, one may alternatively calculate that afflictions and enlightenment are two distinct natures that proceed side by side, never touching one another.

This calculation holds that afflictions and enlightenment are truly two separate natures that pose no obstruction to the self; thus, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) belongs to the category of afflictions.
These are the afflictions (*kleśa*) that exist from the very beginning. Through me, they are exhausted; once the afflictions are exhausted, Bodhi is near, and through me, it is realized.
Thus, it is said that we "drive side by side. If one does not know that there are afflictions, then there is no Bodhi;
where there is Bodhi, there are no afflictions. Their single nature is non-dual; it is merely a turning away from delusion, for there is no real characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) whatsoever.
The two preceding explanations are concluded. △ Third, the conclusion:
Because of these speculative calculations regarding existence after death, one falls into the ranks of external paths and becomes deluded concerning the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the sixth external path; it establishes a theory of inverted mind that posits the existence of signs after death within the five aggregates.
The commentary is the same as the previous conclusion.

The sixty-sixth section on the Discourse on Having Characteristics is finished. △ Seventh and Eighth: The Discourse on Being Without Characteristics. This is divided into three parts. First, the heading:

Furthermore, O good sons among the assembly in samādhi, with their minds firm, concentrated, and upright, Māras cannot find an opportunity; they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

Observing that profound clarity, one constantly disturbs the fundamental source. If, prior to this, one eliminates form, sensation, and perception and gives rise to conceptual calculations, such a person will fall into the state of signlessness after death; their initial resolve is inverted.
Although the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has not yet ceased, because the preceding three aggregates have already ceased, one infers that the aggregate of formations will also cease.
Based on this calculation regarding cessation, one says that after death there is no sign (*animitta*). △ Second, the explanation, which is divided into two parts. First, the fundamental view.

Seeing that form has ceased, the physical body has no basis. Contemplating that perception has ceased, the mind has nothing to which it is bound. Knowing that sensation has ceased, there is no further connection.
The nature of the aggregates has dissolved; even if the processes of life persist, they are devoid of sensation and perception, being the same as grass and trees.

If this physical body cannot be found even when present before one's eyes, how could there be any further characteristics after death? By investigating and examining this, one finds that no characteristics exist after death.
Thus, through such repeated cycles, there are eight instances of the absence of characteristics.

Form constitutes the physical shape; perception constitutes the mind. Feeling conditions both form and mind, binding them together in mutual succession. Now that these have all ceased, it is said that the nature of the aggregates has dissipated.
The "principle of arising" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Since there is no longer perception or feeling, formations have nothing to rely upon;

though they exist, they are as if non-existent. As the present cause is absent, the future fruit is likewise extinguished; thus the eight characteristics [of arising and ceasing] are established. △ Second.
A separate calculation:
from this point, one may calculate that the causes and effects of nirvana are all empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately subject to total annihilation.
This is because, since the characteristics of present birth and death no longer exist, how could the characteristics of future nirvana possibly exist?

This is truly because from the very beginning you have never clarified the nature of awakening; you have merely relied upon the profound concentration of *dhyāna* to break through the three *skandhas*.

Now that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is about to end, yet true consciousness has not yet appeared, you find yourself adrift with no place of refuge, and thus give rise to heterodox views.
The two preceding explanations are concluded. △ Third, the conclusion:

Because of this speculative reckoning that there is nothing after death, one falls into the ranks of the externalists. To be deluded regarding the nature of bodhi is what is called the seventh type of externalist.
They establish a theory of inverted mind within the five aggregates, asserting that there is no sign of existence after death.
The commentary is the same as the previous conclusion.

The above concludes the Seven Treatises on Signlessness (Asaṃjñika). △ Eighth: The Eight Treatises on Neither-Existence-nor-Non-existence (Ubhayānubhaya). Divided into three parts. First, the heading:

Furthermore, O good sons among the practitioners of samādhi, when their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, Māras cannot find an opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the fundamental nature of all living beings.

Observing that profound clarity, he perceives it as a source of constant agitation. While remaining within the state of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), he simultaneously suppresses sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).

By dualistically calculating existence and non-existence, his own essential nature and its characteristics cancel each other out. This person falls into the view that after death one neither exists nor does not exist, giving rise to a perverse doctrine.

This is not a doctrine of neither-existence-nor-non-existence. One calculates that [the self] exists while it is manifest in its activity; one calculates that it does not exist once the preceding three stages have ceased.

Thus, because it was previously existent and is now non-existent, and because it is currently existent and will later be non-existent, it is called the dual calculation of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, one uses the existence of the present activity to refute the non-existence of the preceding three, and uses the non-existence of the preceding three to refute the present.

Because these practices exist, it is said that their own essential natures and characteristics are mutually destructive. Since the four aggregates are all "neither," eight views are consequently formed;
these are detailed below. △ Second, the explanation, divided into two parts. First, the fundamental views.
Within form, sensation, and perception, they perceive both existence and non-existence; within the flux of mental formations, they contemplate neither non-existence nor non-non-existence.

Thus revolving, they exhaustively investigate the aggregates and elements. Regarding the eightfold "neither-nor" characteristics, whenever they encounter a single condition, they all claim that after death there is either a sign or no sign.
The first three aggregates existed previously but are now no more; the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is likewise. Thus, these four are both not existent and not non-existent.
After the aggregate of formations, there is necessarily nothing; yet we presently see that it exists. The same applies to the first three. Thus, these four are both not non-existent and not existent.
Exhausting this cycle means precisely to push this "neither-nor" to its limit, forming the eightfold characteristic of "neither-nor. Take any one of the aggregates as an example, and so on until—
After death, all are neither existent nor non-existent. △ Second, the specific reckonings:

Furthermore, because one reckons that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is subject to transformation and distortion, the mind gives rise to a penetrating realization that they are neither existent nor non-existent, and one loses the sense of whether things are empty or real.

"All formations" (*saṃskāra*) here still refers to their phenomenal characteristics (*ākāra*). Because these characteristics shift, change, and are indeterminate, the mind gives rise to penetrating realization:

namely, that by means of this, one realizes that all aggregates (*skandha*) and all phenomena (*dharma*) are without exception like this. Existence is not fixed existence; how could it ever have been real?
Non-existence is not fixed non-existence; how could it ever have been empty? One who loses their bearings becomes utterly bewildered and finds no foothold.
The two preceding explanations are concluded. △ Third, the conclusion:

Because this speculative reckoning that after death there is "neither [existence nor non-existence]" leaves one ignorant regarding the future limit (*aparānta*) and renders it impossible to speak of, one falls into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

This delusion regarding the nature of Bodhi is called the eighth heterodox path. It establishes the "theory of the post-mortem state being neither-existent-nor-non-existent" within the five aggregates—a deluded view of the mind.

Regarding the future limit (*paścima-koṭi*), it is shrouded in darkness such that nothing can be predicated; "dao" here means to follow or pursue. This refers to the state where both existence and non-existence are negated, which pertains to death.

Thereafter, there will be nothing left to follow. This arises from failing to recognize the fundamental limit (*koṭi*) of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, becoming deluded regarding existence and non-existence, being utterly bewildered and without a master, and losing the nature of bodhi—this is truly a matter for profound lamentation.
The eight sections on the "Neither-Is-Nor-Is-Not" doctrine are concluded. △ Ninth: The Seven Sections on the Doctrine of Annihilation. Divided into three parts. First, the introduction:

Furthermore, O sons of good family within the state of *samādhi*, when you stabilize and concentrate your correct mind, Māra shall find no opportunity; you will exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

Observing that profound stillness, one perceives it as being constantly agitated at its source. If, subsequently, one fails to conceive of a plan for non-arising, this person falls into the seven theories of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).

Observing that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) shifts and perishes from moment to moment, they reckon it to be an ultimate annihilation; therefore, it is called "the absence of what follows."
Seventh, the detailed explanation of annihilationism. △ Second, the interpretation:

some reckon that annihilation occurs through the destruction of the body; some through the exhaustion of desire; some through the exhaustion of suffering; some through extreme bliss; or some through extreme equanimity.
Thus it cycles through until the seven limits are exhausted, whereupon it is extinguished before one's eyes; once extinguished, it no longer exists.
"The extinction of the body" refers to the exhaustion of the present manifestation, namely the humans and devas of the desire realm. "The exhaustion of desire" refers to the first dhyāna.

"The exhaustion of suffering" refers to the second dhyāna. "Ultimate bliss" refers to the third dhyāna. "Ultimate equanimity" refers to the fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments. These seven locations taken together constitute this cycle.
All return to extinction. This is because when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) manifests, one perceives its extinction as each thought-moment dissolves;
having ultimately ceased, it no longer exists. The Āgamas state: "There may be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, during the final eon..."

They have not seen [the truth] and give rise to the doctrine of annihilationism. Altogether there are seven such views: some reckon that my body, having arisen from causes and conditions, must inevitably return to destruction;
some reckon that I am annihilated in the desire heavens; and some reckon that I am annihilated in the form-body realm.

Or they may calculate that the self is annihilated in the formless realm, in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
△ Third, the conclusion:
By such calculations, one falls into the view of annihilation after death, descends into the ranks of external paths, and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is what is called...
The ninth heterodox school establishes the inverted view that the mind is annihilated after death within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Regarding the arising and ceasing of the formations aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*), during the interval when it is about to cease but has not yet ceased, they do not first realize its nature; instead, they frequently give rise to the calculation of non-existence.
Yet, they regard this very state as ultimate annihilation and calculate it to be *nirvāṇa*, as well as the absence of further transition or resolution.

Thus ends the ninth section, the theory of annihilation through the severance of the seven [elements]. △ Fifteenth: The Theory of Manifesting Nirvāṇa. This is divided into three parts. First, the heading:

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within the state of samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright; thus Māras find no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the fundamental nature of all living beings.

Observing that profound stillness, one perceives it as a state of constant agitation at its source. If, subsequently, one gives rise to speculative calculations regarding "existence after existence," such a person falls into the five theories of nirvana.

This occurs within the skandha of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) at the point where thoughts arise moment by moment; because one claims that this is not ultimately non-existent, it is called "existence after existence," and from this, the notion of nirvana arises.
As for the calculation, it is said that "five are manifest" because one attains the bliss of nirvana in the very place where one is born, without waiting for the extinction of the body.
△ Second, the explanation:

Alternatively, the desire realm may be taken as the primary basis of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), because one perceives its perfect clarity and conceives a longing for it; or alternatively, the first dhyāna [may be so taken].
Because their nature is free from sorrow; or because in the second dhyāna the mind is without suffering; or because in the third dhyāna they follow extreme joy;
