or because in the fourth dhyāna both suffering and pleasure have perished, and they do not undergo the nature of birth and death within saṃsāra—yet they remain deluded regarding these tainted heavens.

One forms the understanding of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The five locations are secure and peaceful, serving as a supreme, pure basis. Thus circulating, one reaches the ultimate in these five locations.

Regarding the taking of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as the primary basis for transformation (*parāvṛtti*), this is Tiantai’s interpretation of dhyāna. Within the desire realm, there are two concentrations: first, the concentration of the desire realm;

second, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*). Within these two concentrations, the mind and eyes are perfectly clear and bright; one relies upon this perfectly clear and bright concentration.
The objective realm serves as a place of peace and security. For one who has correctly achieved the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), saṃsāra is transformed into nirvāṇa;

this [notion] is a false conceptualization of those practicing dhyāna. Because the first dhyāna possesses joy and bliss born of seclusion, there is no sorrow. Because the second dhyāna possesses joy and bliss born of concentration, there is no suffering.

Because the third dhyāna possesses the ultimate bliss and thus lacks joy, it is characterized by supreme rapture. In the fourth dhyāna, there is neither suffering nor bliss; the mind of equanimity is pure.
To claim that one who does not undergo the arising and ceasing of saṃsāra is also a practitioner of dhyāna is the false conceptualization of a dhyāna-practitioner.

A dhyāna-practitioner fundamentally cultivates right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), yet falsely regards abiding in the realms of tainted pleasure as secure, pure, and superior; they mistakenly take this to be the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
In truth, it is not ultimate; they merely falsely regard it as ultimate. △ Third, the conclusion.
Based on this speculative reckoning, they conceive of five forms of nirvana in the present life; thus they fall into the ranks of external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of bodhi.
This is called the tenth external path: the inverted doctrine of the mind that establishes five forms of nirvana within the five aggregates.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: Regarding those who propound theories of imagined purity, there are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who give rise to such views and establish such doctrines as follows:
"When my mind is liberated and attains mastery, and my contemplation attains mastery..."
That is to say, they are firmly attached to and grasp at the subtle fivefold sensual pleasures of the devas; they sport, enjoy themselves, and experience them as they please.
This is what they call attaining the first purity of *nirvāṇa* in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*).
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who give rise to such views and establish such doctrines: "If one is free from desires and unwholesome states, one attains the first dhyāna."
Abiding fully endowed [with these qualities], up to attaining full endowment with the fourth dhyāna—this is also called the first purity of nirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*).
The distinctions among the objects of the four superior practices are concluded. △ Fifth, the conclusion and instruction for transmission.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings arising from *dhyāna* are all the result of the interaction between the mind and the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Thus, these realizations appear. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. When these states manifest before them, they mistake their confusion for understanding and claim to have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You must take the words of the Tathāgata as your guide regarding me.
After my parinirvāṇa, transmit this teaching to the age of the final dharma, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning.

Do not allow the demons of the mind to give rise to deep afflictions within themselves. Maintain and protect them, so that false views may be extinguished. Teach their bodies and minds to realize the true meaning, so that they do not encounter divergent paths on the unsurpassed way.
Do not let their hearts pray for minor attainments and consider them sufficient; rather, become great awakened kings of purity.
The pointing finger:
the former statement refers to the celestial Māra waiting for an opportunity; this statement refers to the mind-māra arising of its own accord as a deep affliction.

This is because when thought is broken, practice manifests, yet birth-and-death remains without reliance and the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) has not been reached. With every single thought that arises, one inevitably enters into perverse reflection.
The Tathāgata has here issued this profound and earnest admonition, so that you may know how to rest yourselves upon reaching this point and transmit it to future generations.
This is the ultimate path to awakening, the unsurpassed guiding pointer; there are no further branches or divergent paths.

The above concludes the four aggregates of formative activity (saṃskāra-skandha). △ Fifth, the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), divided into five parts. First, the supreme characteristic of the exhaustion of formative activity:

"Ānanda, when that virtuous man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of formative activity is exhausted, the various natures of the world—those subtle, pure, and turbulent movements, the generative impulses of the common lot—all suddenly collapse and fracture. The fine, underlying cords and the *pudgala* that recompense karma [are likewise resolved]."
The profound channels of resonance are suspended and severed.

The natures of all worldly beings are precisely the aforementioned twelve types of sentient-being lineages. At the initial emergence of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), one perceives the generative potential of co-arising, which is like a mirage;
now, the generative potential of the homogeneous class suddenly collapses and fragments—this is the triple world.
The causes for rebirth have already been severed; this stage corresponds to that of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas of the Two Vehicles.

If one follows the Mahāyāna from the initial resolve, reaching this point would correspond to the seventh bhūmi. "Gang" refers to the main rope of a net; "niu" refers to the fastening at the collar of a garment.
This means that the subtle causal knots of the life-and-death cycle for the twelve categories of beings have already perished. As for *kalpa*, it refers to the retribution of karma.
The retribution also fades away. The deep channels and their responsive inducements all point to the place where cause and effect are interconnected;
reaching this point, the cause perishes and the fruit is lost, and both are utterly transcended. *Pudgala* means "one who repeatedly takes up a rebirth."
Regarding the "heaven of nirvana" about to break into great enlightenment, it is like the crowing of a rooster at dawn; looking toward the east, there is already a brilliant light.

This "heaven of nirvana about to break into great enlightenment" refers to the Great Parinirvāṇa. If measured against the Two Vehicles, it is when the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is being destroyed that one has already realized the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Previously, when the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) was exhausted, it was like the first crowing of the rooster; now, as for the *saṃskāra-skandha*...
It is exhausted. Since this rooster has already crowed, it is said that "looking toward the east, there is already a brilliant color. This serves as a general metaphor for the exhaustion of movement.
△ Second, the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
The six sense faculties become empty and still, no longer wandering or dissipated; internally and externally they are profoundly clear and bright, entering that which has nothing to enter.

One deeply penetrates the fundamental source of life for the twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions. By contemplating the source through its manifestations, one realizes that none of these classes can summon the spirit back; thus, within the realms of the ten directions, [the spirit remains free].
Having attained this sameness, the refined essence does not sink; the hidden and secret are revealed. This is what is called the domain of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Once the formation-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, birth and death cease within, and the sensory objects no longer summon [the senses]; thus, the six faculties attain empty stillness.
There is no further wandering or dissipation. Consequently, as the faculties and their objects do not intersect, the concentrated mind becomes naturally luminous.

Regarding "inner and outer clarity and stillness," Changshui (Zhiyuan) says it refers to a profound and deep tranquil illumination. Once this tranquil illumination is profound, one penetrates to the very source and bottom within; thus, one enters that which has nothing to enter.
All of these occur after the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has become empty, and consist purely of the realm of dhyāna; they do not arise from the awakened mind.

Yes. Because there is still the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), although one has profoundly penetrated the fundamental source of the life-force of the twelve classes of beings, it is said that "one contemplates the source through its attachments.
This remains the pivotal axis of the basis for birth.

Since this axis does not summon the various classes [of beings], one has already attained identity with them throughout the ten directions. This is also because both arising and ceasing have been extinguished, leaving only a single, profound stillness. This...
Deeply still and unmoving, like a rushing torrent that appears tranquil from afar—this is the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*). When practice breaks through this consciousness, it manifests;
thus it is said that its "refined color does not sink. Because it has not yet been fully dissolved, it is said that "the profound and secret is revealed.
This is what is called the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha*. △ Third, the signs of the exhaustion of the *vijñāna-skandha*.

If, within the collective invocation, one has attained sameness therein, the six sense-gates are dissolved and refined; opening and closing are perfected, seeing and hearing penetrate one another, and their mutual functions are pure.
The ten directions of the world, as well as one’s own body and mind, become like *vaiḍūrya* crystal, transparent and luminous both inside and out.
This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life-span (āyuṣkaṣāya).
Upon examining its origin, one finds that it is based upon the formless, the void, and inverted false imaginings.

Having followed the preceding [analysis], the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has already been dismantled. All categories no longer summon one another; their commonality has been attained.
This "commonality" refers precisely to the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Since arising and ceasing have vanished, the faculties and objects no longer meet.

Although there is nothing entering from without and nothing emerging from within, these six gates are purely and uniformly quiescent, yet they are unable to function for one another because of the presence of consciousness.

While one remains here, attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) still persists; therefore, it is necessary to polish away the six gates. This involves polishing away their common perceptions, rather than polishing away their divergent attachments.
Only when divergent attachments begin to perish can one unify the six and return to the one. When common perceptions are extinguished, one is then able to be both one and six.
This is what is called the accomplishment of unification and differentiation, where seeing and hearing interpenetrate; reaching this point—

The evolving consciousnesses are transformed into the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), fully manifesting the nature of awakening. The world, the body, and the mind are all transparently clear within and without. Seeing and hearing originally possess no different natures;

yet, due to the partitioning of the various sensory objects, they arise in an inexplicable diversity. They recognize one another within their essential nature, yet they turn away from one another in their functional operation.

This is what is called the turbidity of life-force (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). The turbidity of life-force is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Now that this consciousness is shattered, one is able to suddenly transcend the net of delusion.

The elephant is empty and non-existent. Tracing its delusion and awakening to the formation of consciousness, one finds that ignorance gives rise to the marks of phenomena; being without substance and illusory, it serves as the root.
△ Fourth, the differentiation of the objects of consciousness is divided into ten parts. First, the attachment to causes and their causes.
Ānanda, you should know that this good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and returned to the source within consciousness.

He has already extinguished arising and ceasing, yet his subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected. Consequently, he is able to cause the barriers between his own sense organs to merge or open, and likewise [to extend this] to the ten directions.

The universal cognition of all categories perceives the universal flow and is able to enter the perfect source. If one establishes the cause of true permanence regarding that which is taken as refuge, [one attains this].
Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the attachment to causes and their underlying conditions.

They become companions to Śābikāra and those who take refuge in the obscure principle (tattva), becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the first instance of establishing a mind that seeks to acquire something gained.
They achieve the fruit of their refuge, yet they remain far removed from perfect penetration; turning their backs on the city of Nirvana, they give rise to the lineage of externalists.

Those who have already extinguished birth and death, yet have not perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescence—referring to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is fundamentally quiescent and fundamentally perfect—have merely emerged from the initial cessation of birth and death through the manifestation of meditative power. They have not attained fundamental quiescence itself; therefore it is said:

It is not yet perfected. Nevertheless, it can cause the faculties and the body to merge and open, so that the various perceptions flow through one another and enter the fundamental source of perfection.

This is because the nature and consciousness are of the same substance; they are merely obscured by birth and death, causing the faculties and objects to appear as distinct entities. Now that birth and death have ceased, the fundamental source is revealed.
One may thus know with certainty that the gates of the faculties are non-dual and that the myriad classes of beings are identical. Yet, regarding this ignorance—

If the initial signs are not yet abandoned, the subtle aspects of what is known will ultimately constitute an obstruction; thus, there is a path toward which one turns, relying on transformation as the cause.
Within the state of true permanence, to falsely have something upon which to rely is to fall into the *tattva* (ultimate principle) of the *Sāṃkhya* heretics.

These outsiders recognize the obscure initial sign of the *ālayavijñāna* as the causal basis for their refuge. This is because they employ a mind that grasps at existence, thereby losing right knowledge.

Awakening. To turn one's back on that which is not to be turned away from, and to seek causes where there are no causes, is to needlessly create divergent paths. II. Grasping at Capability and Incapability.

Ānanda, furthermore, if a good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and has already extinguished birth and death, yet his subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected, he may take that to which he has returned as his own self-nature. Within the entirety of the empty realm, among all twelve categories of beings...
"All sentient beings flow forth as one kind from within my own body"—one who gives rise to such a resolute conviction falls into the dualistic grasping of "agent" and "non-agent.
Maheśvara manifests boundless bodies to become their companion; they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision.
This is called the second [stage]: establishing the mind as an agent, thereby accomplishing the fruit of agent-like activity. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on Nirvana.
In the city of Pāṭaliputra, there arose the Greatly Arrogant Heaven (Mahāmāna-deva), the lineage of the All-Pervasive and Perfect (Vibhu-pūrṇa).
Taking consciousness as its substance, it is able to produce all things. Previously, consciousness was taken as that to which one returns; now, the "Self" (ātman) is taken as that which produces.
This is precisely what the Great Īśvara-deva calculates. That which manifests as the boundless body is said to be "I" who am able to manifest and arise.
Boundless sentient beings falsely cling to the notion of "I" as being capable, yet in reality it is not capable; therefore, it is called "clinging to capability and incapability.

Since they establish this capability as the mind, they must necessarily produce the fruit of capable activity. Being born in the Heaven of Great Arrogance (*Mahāmāna*) is precisely the fruit of capable activity.
Because they cannot but claim to be capable, it is called "Great Arrogance" (*Mahāmāna*). The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Beyond purity..."
In the Heaven of Abiding (Vihāra), there are dwelling places for Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages, which are also called the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa).

They are known as the Great Maheśvara Heavenly King. The *Jinglü yixiang* states: "In the Realm of Form, there are twenty-two heavens, including the Akaniṣṭha Heaven as the twenty-third and the Maheśvara Heaven as the twenty-fourth.
Beyond the five Pure Abodes, there are eight locations. The *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of opening [the path] for the Maheśvara Heavenly Son. Great...
The Sovereign Deva (Īśvara-devaputra). Thus we know that Maheśvara is a distinct heaven beyond Akaniṣṭha;
therefore it is said he dwells at the summit of the Form Realm, yet is not Akaniṣṭha itself. Maheśvara has three eyes and eight arms;
he is Mahādeva, the object of veneration for non-Buddhists. △ Third, the attachment to permanence and impermanence.

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected,
may— regarding that to which he returns— have a sense of dependence upon it, and thus suspect that his own body and mind flow forth from that [source], as do the empty spaces of the ten directions.
They all give rise to this [delusion]. Within the very ground from which all arises and flows forth, they conceive the notion of a true, eternal body that is without birth or extinction.

Amidst birth and extinction, they prematurely calculate that there is permanence; thus, they are deluded regarding non-arising and likewise confused about birth and extinction, remaining settled in their deep-seated confusion.

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the dualistic attachments of permanence and impermanence. They take the Lord God (Īśvara) as their companion, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision.
This is called the third stage: establishing a cause based on the mind, thereby forming a falsely conceptualized result.
This deviates from and distances itself from perfect penetration; it turns its back on the city of Nirvana and gives rise to the seed of inverted perfection.
Previously, one reckoned that consciousness is the self, and that all myriad things flow forth from this self.

Now, one reckons that the self is born from consciousness, and that the empty space of the ten directions all issues from it. One takes that [consciousness] to be the true, eternal refuge to which the self returns. By means of this consciousness...
They take what is impermanent to be permanent; they reckon this present arising and ceasing to be eternally abiding.

Having become deluded regarding the nature of non-arising and further confused by the mind of arising and ceasing, they mistake the impermanent for the permanent, which is identical to their previous reckoning and merely forms its companion.

Since that which relies on consciousness is already incorrect, to reckon it as permanent remains a delusion. Therefore it is said: "The established cause relies on the mind, resulting in the formation of a falsely reckoned fruit. △ Fourth, Knowing.
This is the attachment of ignorance.

Furthermore, a good man may exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and have already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*śānti*), he has not yet perfected it.

If, with respect to what is known, because his knowledge is pervasive and complete, he establishes a view based on that knowledge, then he will claim that the grasses and trees of the ten directions are all sentient beings.
They are no different from others. Grasses and trees become humans; when humans die, they return to becoming the grasses and trees of the ten directions.

Those who lack discerning universal knowledge yet give rise to a superior conviction fall into the attachment of knowing what is unknowable. They are like the Pāṭhas and Sainikas, who cling to the notion that all things are consciousness.
They form their own companions, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fourth calculation: reckoning the mind as perfect.
It results in a false and erroneous fruit, straying far from perfect penetration, turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, and giving rise to the seeds of inverted cognition.

Observing that consciousness possesses cognition, one sees that all myriad phenomena are transformations of consciousness. Therefore, it is said that the grasses and trees of the ten directions are all sentient beings, no different from humans.
When grasses and trees become humans, and humans become grasses and trees, this is because, upon discerning the sentient and the insentient, they are all equally pervaded by a single cognition.
Because one clings to the idea that grasses and trees lack cognition when they actually possess it, it is said:
To know that there is no knowing and yet to cling to it, taking this absence of knowing to be knowing, is also called "inverted knowledge. The *Qingliang shu* states:

"The Sūtra says that Buddha-nature excludes tiles and stones; the Treatise says that when it is included among insentient things, it is called 'Dharma-nature,' and when it is included among sentient beings, it is called 'Buddha-nature.
It is clearly understood, therefore, that insentient things do not possess conscious awareness. Thus, one should explain it as follows:"
When nature follows conditions, then the sentient and the insentient differ, and their natures likewise differ. This refers to the two non-Buddhist practitioners, Pāṭha and Śreṇika.
Among the Brahmins in *Nirvāṇa*, there was a Brahmin of the Pāṭha clan, and another Brahmin named Śreṇika.
The Tathāgata extensively expounded for them the teachings on the permanent and the impermanent, and how Nirvāṇa is eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
They all attained the right Dharma-eye and realized arhatship. △ Fifth: Grasping at Birth and Non-birth.

Furthermore, a good son who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) has already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*śānti*), he has not yet perfected it.

If, within the mutual functioning of the perfectly interfused sense organs, he has already attained compliance, he will then bring about the manifestation of all things through perfect transformation.
Seeking the light of fire, delighting in the purity of water, craving the circulation of wind, and contemplating the accomplishment of dust—each venerates these as supreme.
Taking these various elements as the fundamental cause for their arising, they establish a view of eternal permanence. Such persons fall into the attachment to birth and non-birth.
All the Kāśyapas, together with the Brahmins, diligently applied their minds and exhausted their bodies, serving fire and venerating water in their quest to transcend birth and death;
thus they became companions in delusion regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fifth form of attachment: the devotion to external services.

The deluded mind follows external objects, establishing false causes for seeking and falsely hoping for results. Thus it becomes estranged from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of inverted transformation.

The previous statement said that if the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is destroyed, one can then achieve the mutual integration and opening of the six sense-gates, such that their functions are pure.
This present statement says that within the mutual functioning of the faculties, one has already attained compliance;

within this state of compliance, one beholds this realm of the perfect fusion and transformation of *vijñapti-mātra*, whereby all four great elements can be manifested and transformed. This, however, does not yet constitute a profound penetration of the source of awakening.
They do not realize that the four great elements arise from deluded conceptualization and are fundamentally impermanent; how then could they produce an eternal fruit?

Thus it is said: "Giving rise to attachment to the non-arising [of phenomena]. For those who cultivate the mind to instead seek efficacy from external objects is truly what is called "perverting the principle of transformation.
△ Six: Attachment to the Non-returning as Return.

Furthermore, a good man may have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation, he has not yet perfected it.

If, within this perfect luminosity, he reckons the voidness within the light to be the non-extinction of the manifold transformations, and takes this eternal extinction as his refuge, [he will fall into the error of the Ābhāsvara Heaven].

One who gives rise to such superior resolve falls into the attachment of taking refuge in that which offers no refuge. Among the Śūnyatās (void-beings) in the Heaven of No-Thought, they become their companions;
they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the sixth: the "perfectly void and heartless."
This results in the fruit of emptiness and non-existence. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seed of nihilism.
Within the perfectly luminous state of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*), one perceives that arising and ceasing have been exhausted;

seeing only a phantom-like void, one reckons this void as the place of refuge and thus seeks to destroy all manifestations. "All manifestations" refers to the body with its sense organs and the physical world.

These are the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought and the four heavens of the Formless Realm. They take refuge in that which cannot be taken as a refuge; hence it is said they "take refuge in non-refuge.
Śūnyatā (the void) is their dwelling place, yet they mistake this emptiness for Nirvana, thereby achieving only annihilation. 7. Grasping at non-craving as craving.

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected—should he form a resolute conviction that by making his body firm and permanent, it will be identical to that subtle perfection and never again decline or pass away; This is the first stage of the *samādhi* of the mind-ground. Because he has not yet attained the true essence of the mind-ground, he is unable to transcend the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). After his life ends, he will be reborn among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*). There, he will enjoy celestial pleasures for twelve great kalpas, after which he will fall back into the human world. This is called the "Stage of the Mind-ground. If he subsequently practices with diligence, he may eventually attain the fruit of Arhatship. However, because he has not yet severed the roots of affliction, he cannot escape the cycle of birth and death. This is known as the "Stage of the Mind-ground" within the *Śrāvaka-vehicle*. Such a person falls into the attachment of grasping at what is neither greed nor non-greed. They become companions to those Asitas who seek long life;

they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision. This is called the seventh attachment, which clings to the source of life and establishes a foundation for false delusion.
One pursues long-lasting toil as the fruit, straying far from perfect penetration and turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, thereby producing the seeds of delusive prolongation.

The essence of consciousness is perfectly constant, yet it is not truly eternal; it manifests when its activities are exhausted. When the profound stillness merges with the profound, one mistakenly takes this for permanence.

Having already failed to attain clear awakening, one further desires to solidify the body, treating it as if it were the same as the refined and perfect [consciousness], greedily clinging to what is illusory for a long time.
Abiding through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it is therefore said that greed is not the grasping of greed. This is certainly due to one's own delusion;

striving for its fruit is merely labor in vain, resulting in nothing but falsehood and causing one to lose right knowledge and vision. Asita—translated here as "Incomparable"—is the name of an ancient seer.
△ Eighth: Grasping at the non-true as true.

Furthermore, a good son who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected, contemplates that life-force is interpenetrating.
Fearing that his remaining traces of worldly toil might be completely consumed, he sits within a lotus-flower palace at this very juncture.

They extensively transform the seven treasures, greatly increasing their precious ornaments, and indulge their own minds. Those who give rise to such superior understanding fall into the attachment to "the real as unreal.
They become companions of the *Ṭakkirāja* demons, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision.

This is called the eighth cause for giving rise to perverse thoughts, which establishes the fruit of blazing afflictions. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving birth to the lineage of celestial demons.

Consciousness serves as the fundamental source of life; there is a mutual connection and a sense of maintenance between them. Fearing that consciousness might perish, they dread that both body and mind will perish together.

Therefore, at this juncture, he extensively indulges in the objects of desire for his own peace and security; yet, as he prepares to return to the state of truth, he instead remains within the mundane world.
Thus it is said: "In truth, there is no attachment to truth. From this erroneous cause, the affairs of worldly toil arise.
*Ṭakkirāja* refers to the deity Īśvara of the Desire Realm (*Kāmadhātu*). △ Ninth: The Śrāvakas of Fixed Nature.

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation is not yet perfected, distinguishes between the refined and the coarse within the clarity of life, and discerns the true from the false.
He regards cause and effect as mutually compensating and seeks only for a response through spiritual resonance.

They turn their backs on the path of purity—namely, seeing suffering and abandoning its origin, realizing cessation and cultivating the path—and having settled into cessation, they rest there, no longer advancing to produce superior resolve.
Such persons fall into the category of those with fixed nature as *śrāvakas*. They become companions to the unlearned monks and those of overweening pride;
they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the ninth stage of "perfect refinement."

This should be understood as the mind. It achieves the fruit of quiescence, yet it remains far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.
Consciousness is the source of life; its essence is inherently perfect and luminous, and thus it is called "life-luminosity.

Because this consciousness is perfect and luminous, it can naturally discern that suffering, its origin, and all outflows are coarse and false, while the Path and Cessation, being without outflows, are subtle and true. By knowing this...
The severance of causes leads to the realization of the fruit of cultivation. As the cause elicits its corresponding fruit, these śrāvakas of fixed nature do not advance further;
the Tathāgata designates them as "fools of the Dharma" and also calls them "those with overweening pride. Those who are entangled in emptiness are bound by emptiness itself;

they are deluded and turn away from the precious awakening, remaining as ignorant as those who have never heard the teaching—this is truly to be deeply lamented. △ Ten: Those of Fixed Nature as Pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, a good man may exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and have already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, he has not yet perfected it.
If, within this perfectly integrated, pure, and luminous awakening, he initiates an investigation into its profound subtlety and establishes it as *nirvāṇa*, he will cease to advance further.
Those who give rise to such resolute conviction will fall into the fixed nature of pratyekabuddhas, belonging to the class of those who dwell in solitude among conditions.

Those who do not turn their minds back [toward the Great Vehicle] become their companions; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the tenth delusion of mind regarding Perfect Enlightenment.

They achieve a fruit of stillness and clarity, yet they remain far removed from perfect penetration (*pariṣvaṅga*) and turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa. They give rise to a seed of "awakened, perfect clarity that does not transform.
When their karmic formations are exhausted and consciousness is exposed, there remains only a single pure, awakened clarity; it is at this very point that they establish what they call Nirvāṇa.

Unaware that the entry into stillness and the merging with stillness are not true Nirvāṇa, they take that which is called "the heart of the *huì* (subtlety)" in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* to refer to this.
Profound clarity is left behind as a wondrous function; thus it is said that they do not transform the perfect seed.

As for the various types of pratyekabuddhas—the solitary pratyekabuddhas, the fixed-nature pratyekabuddhas—they rely on the teachings to contemplate conditions. They merely distance themselves from the false arising of conditions and name this "liberation.
The fixed-nature solitary pratyekabuddhas do not follow the Buddha's teachings; dwelling alone in the mountains and wilds, they observe the flourishing and withering of the four seasons, and thereby—
Establishing ultimate *nirvāṇa*, the *Sūtra on the Definitive Karma Obstructions of the Sublime Dharma* states:

The Buddha said, "If, within the three realms, Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas all act as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) through their practice, they are so—with the sole exception of the *śrāvakas*, who are not spiritual friends.
Because *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* seek only their own benefit, they encourage and lead those who have newly begun their practice [toward their own limited goals]."

Even those who practice the Bodhisattva path but revert to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), or all those who break the precepts and engage in deviant conduct, cannot obstruct the Buddha-way of a Bodhisattva.

Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas perceive no-self according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and are free from afflictions (kleśa), they are able—by means of this wisdom—to lead beginning Bodhisattvas into the teaching-path of the Śrāvakas; yet this is not the skillful knowledge of a Bodhisattva.

This is consciousness. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra describes ten kinds of demonic activities (*māra-karman*). These are as follows: forgetting the bodhicitta while cultivating various roots of goodness is a demonic activity;
even to delight in seeking the two vehicles, not delighting in taking birth [in saṃsāra], and directing one’s aspirations toward nirvāṇa.
To seek purity through the renunciation of desire is the work of Māra; a bodhisattva should swiftly distance themselves from it and diligently seek the work of the Buddha.
For this reason, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also fall within the number of those who follow Māra.
The above concludes the distinctions among the objects of the four consciousnesses. △ Fifth, the conclusion urging transmission and instruction:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* lead to madness midway through the practice because they rely on delusion; while one has not yet attained fulfillment,"
The arising of the realization of satisfaction is entirely due to the interaction of the mind with the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); thus, this stage is produced.
Sentient beings, stubborn and deluded, do not reflect upon themselves; when this state manifests before them, each rests according to their own cherished, previously habitual, and deluded mind.
It will become the ultimate ground of refuge and peace, naturally fulfilling unsurpassed bodhi. [Otherwise,] one commits a great falsehood;
at the end of the karma induced by external paths and demonic influences, one falls into the Avīci Hell. For śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it prevents further progress.
The former eight erroneously enter the realms of Māra and externalists; the latter two settle in the Two Vehicles.

When their karmic momentum for meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is exhausted, one falls into the hells (*niraya*), while the other reaches the limit of further progress (*viśeṣa*). To examine the cause in detail:

in each case, because the objects previously habituated through their own attachments manifest before them, they suddenly give rise to demonic views. Sentient beings have limited merit and wisdom; thus, they go mad midway. The Tathāgata knows this.
The vision is boundless; the mind is difficult to fathom to its ultimate limit. We rely upon the secret empowerment of the Great Awakened One and the distant instruction of *dhyāna*.

When the initial mind first illuminates the unsurpassed awakened mind, it does not fall into objective realms. Observing according to conditions, one may encounter two or three divergent paths—how could these be confused with true cultivation?
Provided that attachment and views do not arise, one will know that the beginning and the end are non-dual.
Among the fifty *skandhas*, the application of the mind in *dhyāna* varies; naturally, it begins shallowly and deepens later.

In the sutras, when first entering *dhyāna* within the *rūpa-skandha*, there are only distinctions in the meditative states (*dhyāna-viṣaya*), and one has not yet encountered the disturbances of demons (*māra*).
Therefore, from the *vedanā-skandha* onward, as *dhyāna* gradually deepens, demonic affairs arise. This refers to the three types of agitation and distress caused by demons.

This is something one cannot avoid. However, upon close observation, the subsequent demonic realms of the *ābhāsvara* (after-shadow) become increasingly coarse, and the practitioner’s loss of mindfulness becomes even more inferior.

Furthermore, compared to the initial stage of the *rūpa-skandha*, the commentary on the scriptural text here explains the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) with meticulous precision in every detail.
Since the nature of seeing has been so precisely elucidated, one's *dhyāna* practice naturally deepens; thus, it is appropriate that one [focuses] on the nature.
When the body is stable and refined, even if demonic states arise, they should be subtle; one must not again encounter those that are wild and dissolute. It is said:
"The fifty *dhyānas* differ from one another; in truth, they comprise both the initial awakening of the mind and the state where the initial mind has not yet been awakened."
Therefore, the Sage’s intention varies between detail and brevity. Now, when one first awakens the mind and enters *dhyāna*, the fundamental wisdom ought to be clarified.
The Commentary takes this principle as its core and, regarding all that is intended to be elucidated in the scriptural text, treats it with exhaustive thoroughness.
This is done so that beginners may easily examine the meaning and achieve self-awareness; for this reason, such detail is appropriate. Regarding this detail:

For those at the initial stage, they gradually enter deep dhyāna, and demonic activities will not disturb them; this is appropriate for brief practice within the midst of detailed cultivation, remaining silent to allow for natural subsiding.

If one has not yet realized the initial mind but merely relies on concentration to break through the skandhas, one will become intoxicated by samādhi and inevitably give rise to heterodox views, becoming a demon to oneself and a demon to others, each gradually sinking deeper into dhyāna as their mental objects expand.
Therefore, the Sūtra alone, at the time of breaking down the aggregates (*skandha*), searches and investigates with redoubled effort.

This is intended for beginners who have not yet attained realization, so that they may know how to practice introspection in every situation. If one has already attained realization, then fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is luminous and its various manifestations are also thoroughly investigated;
thus, for those who have attained realization, this [investigation] should be brief. Consequently, it is appropriate to be detailed for those who have not yet attained realization.

People see only that he is meticulous regarding demonic realms and encounters such coarse and fierce phenomena repeatedly; they do not realize that the Sage’s intention actually has a specific destination.
As for those of the Two Vehicles who have not yet broken through the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), they merely block their own progress, while all others fall into ruin.
How could it be that those who have already attained illumination still face such crossroads? By observing this together, you should naturally have no doubts.

Thus ends the preceding section on the five aggregates of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha). △ Sixth, the summary of the exhaustion of the aggregates to achieve the adamantine state of dry wisdom (vajra-śuṣka-prajñā),
the perfection of the stage of fruition, as an exhortation to diligent cultivation.

"You all must keep this in mind. Upholding the Way of the Tathāgata, you shall transmit this Dharma-door after my parinirvāṇa to the final age, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning.
Do not allow them to encounter demons or bring about their own ruin; rather, protect, sustain, and compassionately rescue them."

To eliminate distracting conditions and cause their bodies and minds to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that from the very beginning of their accomplishment they do not encounter byways—this is the entrustment of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to the assembly present here, specifically for the sake of protecting and sustaining the bodies and minds of future generations so that they do not fall onto byways.
The Tathāgata’s compassionate intent is profound and earnest; all who bear responsibility for this Way ought to [heed it].
I reverently contemplate this Dharma gate:
in the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Tathāgatas as many as motes of dust have, by relying on this mind,
attained awakening and realized the Unsurpassed Way.
This refers to the binding of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), tracing them back through fifty-five stages to ultimately emphasize the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*).

Thus, it directly points to the Dharma-gate for shattering the aggregates. Among the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, there are none who have attained unexcelled Bodhi without first shattering the aggregates.
Therefore, what follows reveals the efficacy of the exhaustion of consciousness.

If the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, then your present sense faculties will function interchangeably. From this interchangeability, you will be able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*vimalā*).
Within this state, the perfectly luminous and refined essence of mind gives rise to transformations, like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon within.
In this way, one transcends the stages of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, the four minds of application,
and the bodhisattva’s conduct of the ten vajra grounds and equal-enlightenment; entering the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment,
one fulfills bodhi and returns to the state of non-attainment.
The Vajra Dry Wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*) is realized only after one has discerned and broken through [the delusions].
Thus, among the fifty *skandhas*, one must investigate and examine each *skandha* through *dhyāna* until they are discerned; only then does it fully manifest.
Therefore, know that this Dry Wisdom is identical to the initial revelation in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; ultimately, there is no difference. All subsequent stages are likewise...

At that time, both [the sudden and the gradual] are penetrated, yet this does not obstruct the sequential unfolding (*xingbu*). One does not speak of a "sudden transcendence" (*dunchao*) apart from this;

rather, this sudden transcendence occurs precisely when consciousness is shattered and realization is attained simultaneously. Some claim that one attains the "dry wisdom" (*ganhui*) through the three gradual stages and only thereafter shatters the aggregates (*skandha*), asserting that the demonic visions within the aggregates should not be present as they contain both the refined and the coarse.
I, however, maintain that within the fifty aggregates, one need not distinguish between them.

It has already been explained that whether one has previously realized [the truth] or not, all distinctions in the meditative states (*dhyāna*) are intended to facilitate the practitioner’s purification of the mind.
Once one reaches the point of awakening through discernment, it matters not whether realization was previously attained or not; in all cases, one may achieve sudden transcendence.

This is because such realization is attained through the culmination of practice, which differs from those of keen faculties who directly obtain the original mind and thereby become equal to the Buddhas.

In essence, while the principle is sudden, the practice is gradual; one must further traverse the stages. This differs from the *āgama* and *vaipulya* teachings only in that one stage is not yet known by another.
The "perfectly bright and refined mind" is all said to be the substance of the fruit (*phala-dharmakāya*). Its manifestation and transformation are the sublime functions upon the fruit.

What was previously described as the ten directions being as clear as pure lapis lazuli, containing a precious moon within, still pertains to the causal stage; this [present state] is actual realization.
The fruition and its virtues possess no separate essence or function; it is like gold being enhanced by color—a further transformation of the realm itself.

The "Ocean of Sublime Adornments" refers to the fulfillment of merit (*puṇya*), while "Perfecting Bodhi" refers to the fulfillment of wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding the "returning to non-attainment," the *Prajñāpāramitā* states:
"At the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I did not obtain a single dharma through which I attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Bodhi. Upon reaching this, one may know that all sentient beings have already realized perfect enlightenment; this is what is called true speech and real speech.
△ Seven: Reaffirming the cleansing of the mind and the eradication of heterodoxy, in order to follow the established model.
This is the subtle demonic activity analyzed through the luminous discernment of *vipaśyanā* within *śamatha*, as taught by the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
When such demonic realms manifest before you, if you can recognize them, the defilements of the mind will be washed away, and you will not fall into false views.
The demon of the aggregates is extinguished; the celestial demons are crushed to pieces. Greatly powerful spirits and ghosts lose heart and flee;
goblins, specters, and imps shall no longer be born. Until one reaches Bodhi, there will be no lack of anything whatsoever. Those of inferior capacity shall advance toward Great Nirvana.

Their minds will not become confused or distressed. If there are sentient beings in the final age who are dull-witted and ignorant, who do not yet recognize *dhyāna* nor know how to preach the Dharma, yet delight in practicing *samādhi*, you should fear they might fall into heterodoxy;
with a single mind, you must urge them to uphold my Buddha-Crown *dhāraṇī* mantra.
If you are unable to recite it, write it down in your meditation hall or carry it upon your person; then no demons whatsoever will be able to disturb you.
You should reverently honor this as the ultimate instruction for cultivation and progress, the final legacy bequeathed by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
This has been repeated three times with earnest exhortation: you must follow the balance of samādhi and prajñā employed by the former Buddhas during their causal stages;
by awakening to and comprehending these subtle demonic affairs, you shall cause all mental demons, celestial demons, and all ghosts and spirits to be simultaneously extinguished.
For all those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties, there are no divergent paths.
Furthermore, for those in the final age who are of dull and ignorant capacity, yet who delight in practicing samādhi, I fear they might fall into false views;

therefore, I have them recite, uphold, and transcribe the *dhāraṇī* of the heart-mantra so that it may provide mutual protection. The Tathāgata’s compassionate instruction is most profound and urgent.
The preceding eight sections conclude the examination of the *skandha-māra*. △ Ninth, explaining the sequence of the dissolution of the *skandhas* and the limits of the realms.
This is divided into two parts. First, the request for instruction.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat; having heard the Buddha’s instructions, he prostrated himself in reverent reception, memorizing them without loss. At that time, in the great...

Within the assembly, they addressed the Buddha once more: "As the Buddha has stated, within the characteristics of the five aggregates, there are five kinds of delusion that serve as the fundamental source of thought.

We have not previously received the Tathāgata’s subtle and detailed instruction on this. Furthermore, regarding these five aggregates: are they to be eliminated simultaneously, or are they exhausted sequentially?
As for these five layers, what constitutes their ultimate boundary? We only pray that the Tathāgata will graciously proclaim this."
Great Compassionate One, for the sake of this great assembly, please clarify their minds and eyes, so as to serve as a guiding eye for all sentient beings of the future age.

Within the preceding discussion of the five aggregates, it was stated that deluded thought is the root; building upon this, the specific categories are now further opened up. [The Buddha] asked again: "How is it eliminated?"
The sudden and gradual [approaches] regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), as well as the five boundaries (*pañca-dhātu*), are explained here in exhaustive detail.

Thus, the practitioner’s mind and eyes become clear and bright, and within *dhyāna*, they attain subtle and refined awakening. One may truly call Ānanda a compassionate vessel for saving the world; his *siddhānta* is all-inclusive and without obstruction.

How could it be described through words or metaphors? △ Second, the Tathāgata’s direct answer, divided into five parts. First, revealing that the True manifests and the delusive emerges. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The essence of purity and the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment are perfectly pure; they do not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements."
Even up to empty space, all are produced by deluded thoughts. This is originally the wondrously luminous true essence of fundamental enlightenment;
through delusion, it gives rise to the various vessel-worlds, just as Yajñadatta, in his confusion, mistook his own head for a reflection. Delusion has no original cause.
Within the midst of deluded conceptualization, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions; those who are confused about causes and conditions call it "spontaneity.
That nature of space is likewise truly produced from illusion; both causes and conditions and spontaneity are all the conceptual reckonings of the deluded minds of sentient beings.

Ānanda, when you know where delusion arises, you speak of the causes and conditions of delusion; if delusion were fundamentally non-existent, then the causes and conditions of delusion would fundamentally not exist at all—how much more so [the nature of space]?
Because you do not know how to infer the principle of spontaneity, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is likewise but deluded thought.

Their nature is wondrously luminous awareness, which fundamentally has no birth or death, nor does it possess form or emptiness; yet, through this, all birth and death, as well as form and emptiness, are made manifest.
Within the awakening to the nature, there is no cause, yet delusion arises; knowing that this delusion is causeless, one realizes that it exists only through confusion.

To establish the nature of causes and conditions is already a falsehood; to further confuse it with spontaneity is a further falsehood. Therefore, it is said: "causes and conditions" and "spontaneity."
All these are the conceptual constructions and calculations of sentient beings. To know that which arises from delusion is to know that the essence of awareness has no inherent nature;

it is through the movement of delusion that karma is generated, resulting in the transformation and manifestation [of the world]. Now, if the essence of awareness has no inherent nature, then the movement of delusion likewise does not exist.

Even down to the transformations and manifestations, as well as the manifest physical sense organs, bodies, and the vessel-world, they are, within the awareness of one's own mind, like illusions and like shadows;
therefore it is said that the causes and conditions of delusion are fundamentally non-existent. Since causes and conditions do not exist, what further can there be to confront?
Yet you speak of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). This further confirms that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are likewise fundamentally non-existent;

they are all but deluded thoughts, existing and yet not existing of themselves. Within the bodhicitta, they have never wavered. △ Second, showing the fundamental cause of the five aggregates, divided into five parts.
First, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Your body was originally produced from the perceptions of your parents; yet your mind is not itself a perception, so it could not have come into this state of perception to transmit life.
As I previously said: when the mind perceives the taste of vinegar, saliva is produced in the mouth; when the mind perceives climbing a high place, a tingling pain arises in the soles of the feet.
Since there is no precipice present and no sour substance has yet arrived, your body must not be of the same category as empty delusions.
How could saliva emerge from speaking of the sour? Therefore, you should know that this manifest physical body of yours is called the first false imagination of solidity.
When the parents unite, the vital essences flow forth. This occurs because the parents first have this thought within their minds.
If your mind did not possess this thought, you would certainly not come into the parents' thoughts to transmit life.

That which is called "affection formed through shared thoughts" results in the union of these three places, thereby forming this body. Since the body arises from thought, it is entirely composed of delusion. Thought is like vinegar...

Saliva from the mouth; the sensation of numbness upon stepping [on ice]; these are seen as delusive and pervasive across categories. Among all forms of attachment, that which is "solid" is the most solid within the conceptualizations of hatred and love.
As for the physical obstruction of material form (*rūpa*), it likewise possesses the sense of solidity. △ Second, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
This aforementioned mind that contemplates height can cause your physical form to truly experience astringency and bitterness; arising from these sensations, it can move the material body.
As you now experience both the favorable and the adverse before you, driven by these two manifest states, this is called the second false discrimination of "empty luminosity."

Because one truly experiences bitterness and astringency due to causes, one knows that feeling (*vedanā*) is what moves the substance. Adverse and favorable conditions are precisely the two feelings of suffering and pleasure;
even that which is currently driven about constitutes the moving substance of feeling. Because it is empty, it receives and accepts; because it is luminous, it discerns the flavor.
All these are merely the manifestations of delusion. △ Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*):

It is because of your thoughts and deliberations that you cause your physical body to exist. The body is not of the same category as thought; for what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought?
Various forms are grasped; the mind gives rise to the apprehension of shapes, corresponding with mindfulness. When awake, this is the conceptualizing mind; when asleep, it becomes various dreams.
Thus, your conceptual thoughts and the flickering of deluded sentiments are called the third false discrimination, "interfusion."

This illustrates that the physical body is constantly enslaved by mental preoccupations, thereby revealing that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) permeates and interpenetrates the entire form, extending through both waking and sleeping states, such that the whole body is the awakened mind.
Yet, as deluded emotions cause agitation, sentient beings remain lost in ignorance; though true, they are unable to awaken to themselves on their own.
△ Fourth, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

The principle of transformation does not abide; it shifts and migrates in secret moment by moment. Nails grow and hair sprouts; vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles. Day and night they alternate, yet there is never any awakening to this.
Ānanda, if these were not you, how could your physical body undergo such change? If they must indeed be you, why do you have no awareness of it?
Thus, your various formations (*saṃskāra*) ceaselessly flow from moment to moment; this is called the fourth subtle and hidden deluded thought.

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) shifts secretly; while a person is unaware of it, nails grow and hair sprouts, the vital breath wanes and the face wrinkles—all of these occur within this secret shifting that goes unnoticed.
It is not that your physical body undergoes transition; rather, this is truly the state of non-awareness, clearly manifesting that the entire whole is illusory.
Subtle and profound, it is extremely difficult to reveal unless one has exhausted all conceptual thought. △ Fifth, the aggregate of consciousness:

Furthermore, that which is your own brilliant clarity, profoundly still and unwavering, and which you name "eternal," does not depart from the body in its functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
If it were truly essential and genuine, it could not tolerate the cultivation of delusion. For what reason did you all once, in years past, behold a strange object?
Through the passing of years, there was neither memory nor forgetting of it; yet later, upon suddenly beholding that former anomaly again, the memory returned as vivid as ever.
It has never been lost or forgotten. Thus, within this state of refined clarity and profound stillness, it is perfumed moment by moment;

how could there be any calculation of this? Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not the ultimate truth. It is like a swift-flowing stream that appears tranquil at first glance; because the flow is so rapid, its movement is not seen.
It is not that they are without outflows; yet if it were not the source of perception, how could one undergo the habitual tendencies of delusion?

This delusive thought does not cease at any time through the mutual functioning, opening, or closing of your six sense faculties. Therefore, within your current seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, how many such habitual patterns have been cultivated?
Then, within the profound clarity, there is a formless void. This is the fifth inverted, subtle, and refined perception; its brilliance and purity are eternally still.
This is what is seen when birth-and-death has already ceased. Because of long-standing habituation, it is perfumed moment by moment;

it appears to be still, yet is not truly still. What was seen in the past is seen again now; this is verified by the fact that memory and retention remain perfectly intact, which is not unrelated [to the preceding states].
Therefore, it is remembered; nor can it be forgotten. This clarifies that the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is its function of memory and retention.

It is not something that joins with or separates from your six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). This deluded thought has no time when it can cease; rather, it is only when consciousness is exhausted that the six sense-faculties join or separate.
It is not that consciousness is exhausted only after the six faculties have been joined or separated. Indeed, the six faculties are fundamentally not isolated; they are divided by consciousness.
Thus, while birth and death have already ceased, subtle memories still persist in a state of stagnation. Therefore, it is only when consciousness is fully exhausted that one attains perfection.
Although these same functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are currently tranquil and clear, as long as one has not yet returned to the source, [they remain conditioned].
[This is] understood. Yet, one part remains indistinct, as if separated by a layer of fine silk; this is what is called "subtle and refined conceptualization.
The above two sections conclude the demonstration of the fundamental causes of the five aggregates. △ Third, the demonstration of the causal realms.
Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by the five kinds of false imagination.

Because of false imagination, the aggregates are obtained; the aggregates are established through feeling and perception. This binding of the five aggregates gives rise to the subsequent aggregates and realms.
If you now wish to know the depth of the causal realms: form and emptiness alone constitute the limit of form; contact and separation alone constitute the limit of sensation;
recollection and forgetfulness alone constitute the limit of perception; cessation and arising alone constitute the limit of formations.
The profound stillness merges with profound stillness, returning to the limit of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The previous question asked where these five layers reach as their boundary; this now answers the question regarding the causal boundary. For the five aggregates have no inherent boundary;
it is through mutual causality that they form a boundary, just as form depends upon space to constitute the limit of form. Thus, one knows the reality of form.
When that which is exhausted is exhausted, emptiness is likewise exhausted. Even when one reaches the point where the profound stillness is exhausted, the union with that stillness is also exhausted.

Now, consciousness revolves through arising and ceasing; yet when it enters the profound stillness, it merges with the essence of wondrous enlightenment. Thus, both "entering" and "uniting" are merely the limits of consciousness; they do not constitute the exhaustion of consciousness itself.
By this, one knows that the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous, and cannot be reached by means of conceptual discrimination. △
Fourth, regarding the demonstration of awakening and the removal [of delusions], there are the sudden and gradual methods.
These five aggregates originally arise in successive layers; their arising is caused by consciousness, while their cessation proceeds from the elimination of form. In principle, awakening is sudden.
As one rides upon awakening, all is simultaneously dissolved. Yet, phenomena are not eliminated instantaneously; they are exhausted through a gradual process.
Delusion conceals the source and becomes consciousness (*vijñāna*), whereby all perceptions and appearances arise. Therefore, it is said that the cause of arising exists because of consciousness.
If one understands that [arising] is due to consciousness, then all internal and external marks of arising are entirely without discrimination. Once discrimination ceases...
When the characteristic of non-arising ceases accordingly, it is said that cessation results from the removal of form.

When the practitioner of dhyāna illuminates their own mind and perceives the nature of original enlightenment—wherein there is only this single enlightened nature and nothing else—then the nature of all forms is itself the nature of enlightenment.
The nature of all sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is itself the nature of awakening. It is neither form nor emptiness; it is neither touched nor separated from;
it is neither recorded as neutral nor forgotten; it neither arises nor ceases. There is no profound entry, nor is there anything that merges with the profound.

It is solely the nature of awakening, which has been thus from the beginning, identical even to the state of non-awakening. This is what is meant by "sudden awakening to the principle," whereby one simultaneously eliminates [delusions] through the power of awakening.
Nevertheless, in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is said that at the very moment of the first resolve for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), one attains perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*).

While the three stages of worthiness and ten stages of sainthood involve gradual realization and cultivation, when not a single thought arises, one knows there is nothing else apart from this. If the six sense faculties can function interchangeably (*ṣaḍindriya-samprayoga*), such a state must surely occur at times.

The objects and phenomena before one’s eyes are not merely objects of conceptualization; as for the sands of dust beyond the realms, one must believe they await fulfillment within the causal stage. Regarding these matters:
This means that the objects are not removed instantaneously; they are exhausted only through successive stages. △ Fifth, the conclusion and instruction for transmission:
"I have already shown you the knots of the *kārpāsa* cloth. What is there that you do not understand that you must inquire about again?
You should take this root-source of deluded thought and cause your mind to attain penetration, so as to transmit it to all practitioners of the future age of dharma."

This causes one to realize that [the aggregates] are empty and illusory, to develop a profound weariness with their spontaneous arising, to know that there is *nirvāṇa*, and to no longer cling to the triple world.
This instruction to Ānanda concerns thoroughly understanding the root source of delusive thoughts within the aggregates (*skandha*), so that the mind may be precise and meticulous in its discernment.

Only then should it be transmitted to future generations, enabling them to penetrate the illusory nature of the five aggregates and turn back toward the true and eternal. Regarding the five aggregates—
Form and mind are subject to exhaustion; the fire-house of the triple world is difficult to dwell in. Nirvana is inherently present; do not follow along with birth and death.
[The first two sections on the primary doctrine are concluded.

Third, the section on the circulation [of the teaching], which is divided into two parts. First, the circulation of the main sutra, which is divided into three parts. First, the superiority of the accumulation of merit.

"Ānanda, suppose there were a person who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures, and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them without a single thought of negligence. What do you think?
By virtue of this cause and condition of giving to the Buddhas, would that person obtain much merit? Ānanda replied, "The empty space is inexhaustible, and the precious treasures..."
It is boundless. In the past, there was a sentient being who offered seven coins to a Buddha; even after casting off his body, he still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.

How much more so when one fills the entirety of space before them with Buddha-lands and bestows precious jewels upon them all—such that even contemplating this for an entire kalpa could not reach its limit.
How, then, could this merit have any further boundary?
In weighing the excellence of merit, nothing surpasses the wealth, the field, and the mind. Now, as for the wealth, it fills the void of space; there is nothing that excels this in terms of wealth.

As for the Buddhas, numerous as motes of dust, there is nothing that excels them in terms of the field. When one makes offerings and serves with a mind that does not let such an opportunity pass in vain, the merit is supreme.

There is no mental state superior to this. By means of these three forms of superiority, he exhausted the measure of his giving; furthermore, he offered seven coins to the Buddha to repay the King of the Cakravartins.
Comparing the inferior with the superior, one sees that the entirety of his merit is beyond full description.
△ Second, the superiority in extinguishing transgressions.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are never false.

If there should be a person who has committed the four grave offenses and the ten pārājikas, they will, in an instant, pass through this world and other worlds into the Avīci Hell, remaining there until it is utterly exhausted."

Throughout the ten directions, there is nowhere they have not traveled. If one can, with a single thought, take up this Dharma-door and reveal it to those of later learning during the final age, that person’s karmic obstacles will be extinguished at that very moment, and the causes for the suffering of the hells they were to undergo will be transformed.

They shall attain the Land of Peace and Bliss. The merit they obtain shall surpass that of the person who previously gave the gift by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten million billionfold—indeed, to such an extent that it cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.
Furthermore, when weighing and comparing such transgressions, they do not exceed the four grave offenses or the ten *pārājika* rules.
If one commits even one of these, how can one escape the hells? If one possesses all [the other offenses] in their entirety, how could the Avīci hell ever end?

Yet, if such a person can, with a single thought, reveal and teach this Dharma-gate to those of later learning, their sins will be instantly extinguished; suffering will be transformed into joy, and sin will be transformed into merit.
Compared to the person who gave alms previously, this is ten thousand million times greater, even to the point of being ineffable.
In sum, while great merit has its limit and heavy transgression has its end, this Buddha-mind exceeds the void, perfectly encompassing the three periods of time.

This scripture is shown to people to reveal their fundamental nature, exhausting all hearing through the realization of emptiness. How could such a thing be subject to the fluctuations of sin and merit? Therefore, although it is but one—
Reflecting on the returning light, one has already attained what was originally inherent; how much more so for those who take it upon themselves to save all sentient beings!
△ Third, Dispelling Demons and Achieving Victory.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra as I have extensively explained, even throughout an entire kalpa—
It is not so. By relying on my teachings and practicing the Way according to those instructions, one will directly achieve Bodhi, and no further demonic activities will arise.
This is a further exhortation regarding the benefits obtained from reciting sutras and upholding mantras;

yet it ultimately emphasizes that avoiding demonic activities depends upon practicing the Way according to the teachings. The Tathāgata’s expectations for those with the initial resolve are none other than this one great matter.
The conditions [for this] are such that the debt of gratitude is great and difficult to repay. All who possess a mind should strive with earnest diligence.
This concludes the initial edition of the circulation of the aforementioned sutra. △ Second, the circulation of various other sutras.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, all the devas, humans, asuras,
and others from other directions— including bodhisattvas, followers of the two vehicles, holy seers, youths,
and even powerful spirits who had first resolved their minds— were all greatly rejoiced. They paid homage and departed.
The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states that there are three kinds of meanings for which one joyfully practices:
first, the purity of the speaker, because they are not defiled by attachment to gain or offerings; second, the purity of what is spoken, because of knowing the essence of phenomena as they truly are;
and third, the purity of attaining the fruit, which refers to the benefit of the teaching.
